title: Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics
text:
Welcome
This is the online edition of Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics.
Bioinformatics is learned the way laboratory work is learned: by doing it, making mistakes, and developing judgement about what the results mean. This book is built on that assumption. Every method it describes is demonstrated on data you can download, with code you can run, producing output that is shown exactly as it was produced. Nothing in these pages is illustrated with results that were never computed.
The book takes you from the first command you type in a terminal to a complete, reproducible analysis written up to the standard a journal would expect. Along the way it covers the archives where biological data lives, the algorithms that compare sequences, the Unix, Python and R skills that make large files tractable, the analysis of genomes and sequencing reads, protein structure, biological networks, statistics and machine learning for omics data, the clinical and public-health applications of all of it, and the ethical obligations that come with working on human genomes.

title: Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics
text:
How to read this book
If you are new to the field, read Chapters 1 and 2, then work through Part 4 (the toolchain) before going further; the later chapters assume you can move around a filesystem and read code. If you already program, you can start at Chapter 3 and treat Part 4 as reference. The front matter chapter How to use this book explains the conventions, how to install the software and how to get the data.

title: Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics
text:
Reproducing everything in the book
git clone https://github.com/babasaraki/practical-bioinformatics
cd practical-bioinformatics
conda env create -f environment.yml && conda activate pablb
python scripts/fetch_data.py       # ~12 MB of example data from public archives
quarto render                      # rebuilds the whole book
Every dataset used in the book is listed in data/MANIFEST.tsv with its source archive, accession and SHA-256 checksum, so you can confirm that the files you have are the files the book was written against.

title: Foreword

title: Preface
text:
What this book assumes
It assumes you have seen the central dogma before and can be reminded rather than taught. It assumes no programming experience whatsoever. It assumes you have a computer with a terminal and the patience to type into it.
It does not assume you are a computer scientist, and it does not try to make you one. There is no complexity analysis here, and the algorithms are derived only to the depth that changes how you use them. There is, however, a sustained insistence on one point that is genuinely computational: that an analysis you cannot repeat is not a result. Scripts, environments, version control and recorded provenance appear from Chapter 1 and never go away.

title: Preface
text:
What this book is not
It is not a reference manual. Tools change; the documentation for any one of them will be more current than this book by the time you read it. What is durable is the reasoning — why you align before you count, why a p-value from a genome-wide test needs correcting, why an annotation inherited from a homologue is a hypothesis. That reasoning is what I have tried to write down.
Nor is it a clinical text. Chapter 13 covers variant interpretation and pharmacogenomics because they are now part of the field, but patient-facing decisions belong to accredited laboratories and qualified clinicians, and the chapter says so.

title: Preface
section: A note on where this was written
text:
A note on where this was written
Much of my own work has been done in settings where compute is shared, bandwidth is intermittent and software licences are out of reach. That shapes the book. Every tool used here is free and open source. Every dataset is small enough to download over a poor connection. Nothing requires a cluster, though Chapter 5 explains how to use one when you have access. Genomics will only be as global as its methods are accessible, and I have tried to write accordingly.

title: Preface
text:
Acknowledgement of the reader
Bioinformatics rewards stubbornness more than talent. The first time an aligner fails with an error you have never seen, it will be tempting to conclude that you are not the sort of person who does this. You will be wrong. Everyone who works in this field spends a substantial fraction of their time confused, and the difference between those who continue and those who do not is mostly a willingness to read the error message carefully and try again.
Umar Ahmad Bauchi, Nigeria

title: Structure of the book
text:
Part I — Foundations
Chapter 1 defines the field as it is actually practised, works through the arithmetic that makes computation unavoidable, traces how the methods grew with the data, and sets up your computer. By the end of it you will have run your first analysis.
Chapter 2 covers the molecular biology that shows up in files: reading frames, reverse complements, splicing, coordinate systems, and the vocabulary of variation. Every concept is tied to something that will otherwise bite you later.

title: Structure of the book
section: Part II — Biological data and databases
text:
Part II — Biological data and databases
Chapter 3 is about the archives: what distinguishes a primary archive from a curated knowledgebase, what accession numbers and versions actually mean, how to read a record, and how to retrieve data programmatically without abusing a public service.

title: Structure of the book
text:
Part III — Sequence analysis
Chapter 4 derives pairwise alignment from first principles, implements it, then shows what scoring matrices do, how BLAST makes search tractable, what an E-value means, how multiple alignment works and how a phylogeny follows from one.

title: Structure of the book
text:
Part IV — The bioinformatics toolchain
Chapter 5 teaches the command line as a working environment: streams and pipes, the text-processing tools, scripting, and job submission on a cluster.
Chapter 6 teaches Python through biological data, ending with a reusable module and a command-line tool of your own.
Chapter 7 teaches R and Bioconductor: the tidyverse, ggplot2 as a grammar, and the Bioconductor classes — GRanges, SummarizedExperiment — that the analysis chapters rely on.

title: Structure of the book
section: Part V — Genomes, reads and structures
text:
Part V — Genomes, reads and structures
Chapter 8 goes from assembled sequence to annotated genome, including a real comparison between an ab initio gene prediction and the reference annotation.
Chapter 9 is the longest chapter: sequencing data end to end, from FASTQ and quality encodings through alignment, SAM/BAM anatomy and variant calling, to a complete differential expression analysis.
Chapter 10 computes real quantities from protein coordinates, and takes predicted structures seriously enough to explain what their confidence measures do and do not mean.

title: Structure of the book
section: Part VI — Systems biology and data science
text:
Part VI — Systems biology and data science
Chapter 11 treats biological networks quantitatively and implements enrichment analysis from first principles so that you know what the tools are doing.
Chapter 12 covers the statistics and machine learning that omics data demands, with particular attention to the ways high-dimensional data produces confident nonsense.

title: Structure of the book
section: Part VII — Applications and responsible practice
text:
Part VII — Applications and responsible practice
Chapter 13 applies all of it to cancer genomics, rare disease diagnostics, pharmacogenomics and pathogen surveillance.
Chapter 14 addresses privacy, consent, governance, equity and data sovereignty — the obligations that attach to human genomic data.

title: Structure of the book
text:
Part VIII — Consolidation
Chapter 15 is a capstone project carried out in full, including the parts that usually go unrecorded: the dead ends, the environment capture, the write-up.
Chapter 16 synthesises the whole book, provides a graded question bank with worked answers, and sets out learning pathways for different starting points.

title: Structure of the book
text:
Appendices
A glossary of every technical term used in the book; the software environment and how to install it; the provenance of every bundled dataset; and a command and function reference for quick lookup.

title: How to use this book
text:
Conventions
Code you type and output you receive are shown in monospaced blocks. Where a block shows a shell session, the command is given without a prompt character so that you can copy it directly:
Blocks labelled with a language in braces — {python}, {r} — were executed when the book was built, and the output beneath them is exactly what that code produced. Blocks that are shown but not executed carry a note saying so, and their output was captured from a real run and quoted.
Terms appear in bold at first definition and are collected in the glossary. File formats are capitalised (FASTA, FASTQ, SAM, BAM, VCF, GFF3). Human gene symbols are italic and upper case (TP53); the protein is roman (p53).
Five kinds of marginal note appear:
Solutions to exercises are in a collapsed block at the end of each chapter. Open them after you have tried the exercise, not before.

title: How to use this book
text:
Setting up
You need a Unix-like command line. On macOS and Linux you already have one. On Windows, install the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2) and work inside it; a native Windows installation will cause problems that this book cannot help you with.
Install Miniforge, then:
git clone https://github.com/babasaraki/practical-bioinformatics
cd practical-bioinformatics
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate pablb
That single environment contains every Python package, R package and command-line tool used anywhere in the book. Chapter 1 walks through the installation in detail and verifies it.

title: How to use this book
text:
Getting the data
python scripts/fetch_data.py
python scripts/fetch_data.py --check
The first command downloads roughly 12 MB from NCBI, UniProt, RCSB PDB, AlphaFold DB, Bioconductor and STRING. The second verifies every file against the SHA-256 checksums in data/MANIFEST.tsv, so you know your copy matches the one the book was written against. Appendix C lists each file, where it came from and what it is used for.
Chapter code never contains a literal path. It calls a helper that locates the data directory from wherever you are working:
from pybfx import book_data
book_data("proteins", "globins.fasta")
book_data("proteins", "globins.fasta")

title: How to use this book
text:
If something does not work
Check, in this order: that the environment is activated (conda env list shows a * beside pablb); that you are in the repository root; that python scripts/fetch_data.py --check reports no problems; and that your package versions match those in environment.yml. If the problem persists, the issue tracker on the repository is the right place to raise it, and a report that includes the command, the full error and your conda list output will be answered much faster than one that does not.

title: How to use this book
text:
For instructors
Each chapter is sized for one teaching session with the exercises as homework. The worked solutions are part of the text rather than a separate instructor’s manual, on the view that students who look up an answer early learn more than students who cannot check their work at all. The question bank in Chapter 16 is graded by cognitive level and can be used for assessment. The whole book is openly licensed for non-commercial use, so chapters may be adapted for your own course provided the licence is preserved.

title: About the author
text:
Umar Ahmad, PhD, is Senior Lecturer in the Department of Anatomy and the Human Genetics Informatics Unit, Faculty of Basic Medical Sciences, Sa’adu Zungur University, Bauchi, Nigeria, and Senior Technical Officer for Pathogen Genomics at the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. He took his PhD in human genetics and genomics at Universiti Putra Malaysia and the Malaysia Genome Institute, and has worked for more than twelve years across genomics research, bioinformatics and multi-country scientific collaboration in Africa.
His research is in cancer genomics: transcriptome profiling of bladder and other urothelial cancers, using RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to identify molecular drivers, therapeutic resistance and protein interaction networks, and the mechanisms by which oncolytic Newcastle disease virus establishes persistent infection in cancer cells.
At Africa CDC he coordinates genomic surveillance, bioinformatics and workforce development across African Union Member States, and leads AGARI, the continental platform for pathogen genomic data sharing and public health intelligence. He has contributed to genomic surveillance strategies at both continental and national level, among them the Pathogen Genomic Surveillance Policy Framework, the roadmap for malaria genomic surveillance in Africa, the AC-GCAT genomics capacity assessment tool and its manual, and continental technical guidance on mpox testing and sequencing.
In 2021 he founded BioSeq, a genomics and bioinformatics company built on four pillars: genomics, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence and capacity building. He also founded the Open Science Community Nigeria, which has since grown into the Open Science Community Network. He is an Academic Editor of PLOS ONE and of Applied Research, a member of the Bioconductor Community Advisory Board, a board member of the Directory of Open Access Journals and of the International Network of Open Science and Scholarship Communities, and a founding member both of the Nigerian Bioinformatics and Genomics Network and of the Community of Practice on Human Genomics and Genomic Medicine at the Africa Bioinformatics Institute.
He teaches human genetics, bioinformatics and R programming, supervises postgraduate research, and has designed genomics and bioinformatics training for professionals across the continent. This book is a direct expression of the conviction that computational skills are learned by use.

title: Acknowledgements
text:
This book rests on software and data that other people built and gave away. The analyses in these pages run on Biopython, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib, scikit-learn, R, the tidyverse and Bioconductor, and on command-line tools — BLAST+, MAFFT, BWA, SAMtools, BCFtools, Prodigal, SeqKit — maintained in many cases by very small teams for very little reward. The data comes from NCBI, EMBL-EBI, UniProt, the RCSB Protein Data Bank, the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, STRING and ClinVar, all of which make their holdings freely available. The book itself is built with Quarto. Everyone who contributes to that ecosystem has a share in whatever is useful here.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.1 What bioinformatics is as a working discipline
A dictionary will tell you that bioinformatics is the application of computational methods to biological data. That is true and nearly useless. A more serviceable description is this: bioinformatics is the practice of turning large, noisy, machine-generated measurements of biological molecules into statements a biologist can act on. Three words in that sentence carry the weight. Large, because the volume removes the option of inspecting the data by eye. Noisy, because every instrument makes errors with its own characteristic signature, and distinguishing instrument from biology is most of the work. Act on, because the output is a claim — this gene is differentially expressed, this variant is pathogenic, these two isolates are related — and someone will make a decision on the strength of it.
The companion term, computational biology, is often used interchangeably, and in job advertisements it usually is. The distinction worth keeping is one of product. A bioinformatician’s product is an answer about a specific dataset: these are the variants in this patient’s exome, this is the phylogeny of these isolates. A computational biologist’s product is a model or a method: a simulation of how a regulatory network behaves, an algorithm that aligns sequences faster, a statistical framework for estimating dispersion in count data. The same person frequently does both in the same week, and the same tools serve both. But the distinction changes what counts as success. A method is successful if it is correct and general; an analysis is successful if it is correct, reproducible and relevant to the sample in front of you. This book teaches the second, and borrows from the first only where a decision depends on knowing how a method works.
The questions the discipline answers fall into a small number of recurring shapes, and recognising the shape is most of knowing how to proceed.
Every chapter of this book sits under one of those five headings. When you meet an unfamiliar dataset, asking which of the five you are facing will usually tell you which chapter to reread.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
What is this sequence? Identification by similarity: a contig from a metagenome, an unknown isolate, a gene of unclear function. Answered by alignment and database search (Altschul et al. 1990).

How do these sequences relate? Evolutionary and epidemiological questions: phylogenies, transmission chains, gene families. Answered by multiple alignment and tree inference.

What is different between these two groups? Differential analysis: tumour versus normal, treated versus untreated, resistant versus susceptible. Answered by counting, modelling and multiple-testing correction.

Where are the features in this genome? Annotation: genes, regulatory elements, repeats, resistance determinants. Answered by pattern models trained on known examples.

What does this variant do? Interpretation: linking a change in sequence to a change in protein, to a phenotype, to a clinical recommendation.








Bioinformatics, biostatistics and data science



Biostatistics supplies the inference — what counts as evidence, how to correct for testing thousands of genes at once. Data science supplies the engineering — how to move, store and visualise data at scale. Bioinformatics is the part that knows what the measurements mean biologically and what the file formats actually contain. A competent analyst borrows from all three; the chapters on statistics and machine learning in this book are there because you cannot do the third without some of the first two.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.2 The scale that forces computation
The reason biologists learn to program is arithmetic, not fashion. Work through the numbers for a single, unremarkable experiment: whole-genome sequencing of one human sample at 30-fold coverage with 150 bp paired-end reads.
The human genome is about 3.1 Gb. Thirty-fold coverage means the instrument must produce about 93 gigabases of sequence. At 150 bp per read that is 620 million reads. Each read in a FASTQ file is four lines: an identifier, the bases, a separator and one quality character per base. In the bundled read file used later in this book, those four lines occupy an average of 332 bytes per read, measured directly from the file. Six hundred and twenty million reads at 332 bytes each is about 206 gigabytes of uncompressed text for one sample.
Now consider holding that in a spreadsheet. The most widely used spreadsheet format stops at 1,048,576 rows. The FASTQ file has 2.48 billion lines — roughly 2,400 times the limit, and that is before you have done anything to it. Even if a spreadsheet could load it, the operations you need are not row-by-row arithmetic: they are “align each read to a 3.1 Gb reference allowing mismatches”, “at every position, model the distribution of observed bases given the error profile”, “test 20,000 genes and control the proportion of false discoveries”. None of those is a spreadsheet operation. The scale does not merely make manual work tedious; it makes a different class of method necessary.
Figure 1.1 puts the numbers on one axis so the ratios are visible. Note that it is a logarithmic axis: each gridline is a hundredfold.

import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from pybfx import book_data, style, PALETTE
style()


import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

BYTES_PER_READ = 332          # measured from data/reads/mgen_sim_R1.fastq.gz
READ_LENGTH = 150

def fastq_bytes(genome_bp, coverage):
    """Uncompressed FASTQ size for one sample at a given fold coverage."""
    return genome_bp * coverage / READ_LENGTH * BYTES_PER_READ

labels = ["One SARS-CoV-2\ngenome (FASTA)", "One bacterial\ngenome (FASTA)",
          "1,000 SARS-CoV-2\ngenomes", "Bundled read pair\n(40,000 reads)",
          "Bacterial WGS,\n50x coverage", "Human WGS,\n30x coverage"]
sizes = [30_429, 588_426, 1_000 * 30_429,
         2 * 20_000 * BYTES_PER_READ,
         fastq_bytes(580_076, 50), fastq_bytes(3.1e9, 30)]

The drawing itself is routine, but the labelling matters: a figure whose axis the reader has to decode is a figure that will be misread.

def human_readable(n_bytes):
    for unit, divisor in (("GB", 1e9), ("MB", 1e6), ("kB", 1e3)):
        if n_bytes >= divisor:
            value = n_bytes / divisor
            return f"{value:,.0f} {unit}" if value >= 10 else f"{value:,.1f} {unit}"
    return f"{n_bytes:,.0f} B"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8))
ax.barh(range(len(sizes)), sizes, color=[PALETTE[0]] * 3 + [PALETTE[3]] * 3,
        hatch=[""] * 3 + ["//"] * 3, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(sizes))); ax.set_yticklabels(labels)
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_xlim(1e4, 3e13)
#> (10000.0, 30000000000000.0)
ax.set_xlabel("Approximate file size (bytes, log scale)")
for row, value in enumerate(sizes):
    ax.text(value * 1.6, row, human_readable(value), va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Assembled sequence (solid) and raw reads (hatched)")
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 1.1: Approximate sizes of the datasets discussed in this chapter, on a logarithmic scale. Solid bars are assembled reference sequences; hatched bars are the raw sequencing reads that produced them. The read-file estimates assume 150 bp reads and the 332 bytes per read measured from the book’s bundled FASTQ file.




The figure shows the gap that defines the working day. A reference genome is a small file you can open in a text editor. The reads that produced it are four to six orders of magnitude larger. Almost every frustration in practical bioinformatics — disk quotas, jobs that run overnight, pipelines that fail at step seven — comes from that gap, and almost every skill in this book is a way of crossing it without losing track of what you did.
Compression helps, but less than people expect. The bundled read file compresses only 2.2-fold, because its simulated quality strings are close to random and random data does not compress; real instrument data, whose quality values are strongly correlated along the read, typically compresses three- to four-fold. Either way, a 30-fold human genome remains tens of gigabytes after compression, and compressed files must still be decompressed to be read.






Estimate before you download



Before starting any project, do this arithmetic on the back of an envelope: genome size times coverage, divided by read length, times about 330 bytes. If the answer is larger than the free space on your laptop, you need a server, a subsample, or a different plan — and it is far cheaper to discover that now than three hours into a download.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.3 How the field got here
The history of bioinformatics is best read as a sequence of data problems and the methods invented to meet them. Told that way it stops being a list of dates and becomes an argument about why the tools look the way they do.
The 1960s and 1970s: sequences become comparable. Margaret Dayhoff assembled the first systematic collection of protein sequences and, with it, the first substitution matrices (Dayhoff, Schwartz, and Orcutt 1978) — the insight that an alignment is a statistical statement about evolution, not a visual impression. The formal method arrived with the dynamic programming algorithm for global alignment of two sequences (Needleman and Wunsch 1970), later adapted to find the best local match rather than forcing an end-to-end one (Smith and Waterman 1981). These algorithms are exact and quadratic in time, which made them usable when databases held hundreds of sequences.
The 1980s and 1990s: databases outgrow exact methods. As collections grew, exact alignment against every entry became impossible, and heuristic search took over: first FASTA (Pearson and Lipman 1988), then BLAST (Altschul et al. 1990), which trades a guarantee of optimality for a speed-up of orders of magnitude and remains the most-used tool in biology. Scoring improved in parallel, with substitution matrices derived from alignments of conserved protein blocks. This is the period in which the field’s characteristic bargain was struck: accept an approximation that is almost always right, in exchange for being able to search at all.
2001: the human genome, and the industrialisation of sequencing. The publicly funded consortium (Lander et al. 2001) and a competing private effort (Venter et al. 2001) published draft human genome sequences within days of each other. The draft was not complete — it was a mosaic with gaps in every centromere and most repeat arrays — but it changed the unit of analysis from the gene to the genome, and it made reference-based analysis the default.
The 2000s and 2010s: short reads and the file-format era. Massively parallel sequencing dropped the cost per base by several orders of magnitude and replaced long, accurate Sanger reads with hundreds of millions of short, error-prone ones. That shift produced the formats and tools that occupy most of this book: aligners that index a reference so that millions of reads can be placed against it, the SAM/BAM family for storing alignments and the VCF format for storing variants (Danecek et al. 2021), and quality-control tools to summarise a run before anyone trusts it (Ewels et al. 2016).
2022 and after: completion and pluralisation. Long-read sequencing allowed the first truly complete human genome assembly, closing the gaps the draft had left, including the centromeric satellite arrays (Nurk et al. 2022). Almost immediately the field moved past the idea of a single reference: a draft pangenome representing many individuals replaced one person’s chromosome with a graph of alternatives (Liao et al. 2023), because a single reference systematically mis-serves populations that are not represented in it. In parallel, protein structure prediction moved from a specialist pursuit to a routine step after a neural network began producing models of accuracy comparable to experiment (Jumper et al. 2021), with the predictions themselves distributed as a public database.
Two lessons from that arc are worth carrying into your own work. The first is that methods are answers to data problems, so when the data changes the method usually must change too — short-read tools applied to long reads give poor results, and a human-reference pipeline applied to a bacterium is nonsense. The second is that the field repeatedly discovers that its reference points are provisional. A reference genome, an annotation, a variant classification: all are current best estimates with version numbers, and treating them as fixed truth is one of the commonest sources of irreproducible results.






Who the reference represents



The genomes, annotations and variant frequencies that pipelines rely on were built overwhelmingly from populations of European ancestry. Applying them unexamined to patients from under-represented populations produces more variants of uncertain significance and more misclassifications. Sustained investment in African genomics capacity exists precisely to address this gap (Matovu et al. 2014), and the ethics chapter of this book returns to it. Note the limitation in your methods whenever it applies to your samples.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.4 The shape of an analysis
Analyses differ in their tools but rarely in their shape. Figure 1.2 shows the five stages, and the point of the figure is the caption underneath each box rather than the boxes themselves: at every stage you make a decision, and the decision must end up in a script.

from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch

stages = [("Raw data", "FASTQ reads\nfrom the\nsequencer"),
          ("Quality control", "read quality,\nadapters,\ncontamination"),
          ("Processing", "trim, align\nor assemble,\ncall features"),
          ("Statistics", "test, model,\ncorrect for\nmultiplicity"),
          ("Interpretation", "biology and\npublic-health\ndecision")]
width, height, gap = 1.8, 1.55, 0.42
span = len(stages) * width + (len(stages) - 1) * gap + 0.4

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 2.9))
ax.set_xlim(0, span); ax.set_ylim(0, 4); ax.axis("off"); ax.grid(False)
#> (0.0, 11.08)
#> (0.0, 4.0)
#> (np.float64(0.0), np.float64(11.08), np.float64(0.0), np.float64(4.0))
for index, (heading, detail) in enumerate(stages):
    left = 0.2 + index * (width + gap)
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((left, 1.6), width, height, boxstyle="round,pad=0.04",
                                facecolor="#EAF0F5", edgecolor=PALETTE[0], linewidth=1.2))
    ax.text(left + width / 2, 2.88, heading, ha="center", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(left + width / 2, 2.15, detail, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.8)
    ax.text(left + width / 2, 1.2, "recorded\nin a script", ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=6.5, color=PALETTE[3], style="italic")
    if index < len(stages) - 1:
        ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((left + width + 0.04, 2.35), (left + width + gap - 0.04, 2.35),
                                     arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                                     color=PALETTE[0], linewidth=1.2))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((span - 0.6, 0.72), (0.6, 0.72), arrowstyle="-|>",
                             mutation_scale=10, color=PALETTE[3], linewidth=1.1,
                             linestyle=(0, (4, 2))))
ax.text(span / 2, 0.38, "re-run end to end whenever data, parameters or software change",
        ha="center", fontsize=7, color=PALETTE[3])
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 1.2: The five stages common to almost every sequence analysis. Each stage involves choices — thresholds, references, parameters — and the dashed arrow is the property that makes the whole thing science rather than craft: the ability to re-run it from raw data at any time.




Make it concrete with a named example: SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance, the analysis that the microbiologist in the opening paragraph needs, and the one that was performed hundreds of thousands of times between 2020 and 2023 (Hu et al. 2020).
Raw data. An amplicon protocol tiles the 30 kb genome with overlapping PCR products, which are then sequenced (Quick et al. 2017). The output is one pair of FASTQ files per sample. Decision: which protocol and primer scheme, because the primer positions must be removed later and the wrong scheme silently leaves primer sequence in your consensus.
Quality control. Read quality is summarised per sample and across the run (Ewels et al. 2016), adapters and low-quality tails are trimmed. Decision: the quality threshold, and what to do with samples whose coverage is too low — including them produces consensus sequences full of ambiguity codes that will distort a phylogeny.
Processing. Reads are aligned to the reference genome, primer sequence is removed, and a consensus genome is called at positions with sufficient depth. Decision: the minimum depth to call a base. Too low and sequencing errors become variants; too high and real genomes become mostly N.
Statistics and inference. Consensus genomes are aligned, a phylogeny is estimated, and each genome is assigned to a named lineage (Rambaut et al. 2020). Decision: how many differences separate two samples before you stop calling them the same transmission chain — a question with an epidemiological answer, not a computational one.
Interpretation. The tree, the lineage assignments and the sample metadata are read together, often in a visualisation designed for the purpose (Hadfield et al. 2017), and reported to the people who will act. Regional surveillance networks in Africa were built on exactly this chain of steps (Tegally et al. 2022). Decision: what to report, how to state the uncertainty, and what not to claim.
Notice that every stage has a decision and that none of the decisions is obviously right. This is why the output of a bioinformatics analysis is not a number but a number plus the record of how it was obtained.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
section: 1.5 Why this book insists on scripts, environments and version control
text:
1.5 Why this book insists on scripts, environments and version control
Suppose the microbiologist reports that two of the sixty samples differ by a single nucleotide and therefore represent one transmission event. Six months later a reviewer asks whether that conclusion holds if the minimum depth had been 20 rather than 10. If the analysis was done by clicking through a graphical tool, the honest answer is “I do not know, and finding out means starting again”. If it was done with a script, the answer is a one-line change and a re-run.
That is the entire argument for reproducibility, and it is a practical argument rather than a moral one. The standard statements of the practice (Sandve et al. 2013; Wilson et al. 2017) all reduce to the same three habits, which this book applies from the first chapter.
Everything in a script. A command typed into a terminal and not saved has been lost. Keep an executable file for every step, even when the step is one line. The documents that make up this book are themselves scripts: the prose and the code live in the same file and the figures are regenerated every time it is built, an approach that goes back to the idea of literate programming (Knuth 1984) and that modern tools make routine.
Everything in a pinned environment. Results depend on software versions. An aligner changes a default; a statistical package changes how it estimates dispersion; your numbers move and you cannot say why. The answer is to declare the software your analysis needs in a file, install it from that file, and keep the file with the project. The packaging system this book uses distributes bioinformatics software through a community-maintained channel (Grüning et al. 2018), and the next section uses it to build an environment named pablb containing the exact tools used in every chapter. For multi-step pipelines, workflow managers extend the same principle to the whole analysis (Köster and Rahmann 2012); the project chapter of this book builds one.
Everything under version control. Git records what changed, when and why. Its real value is not backup but the ability to answer “what did the analysis look like when I produced the figure in the paper?”. Initialising a repository on the first day of a project costs about thirty seconds; recovering an un-versioned analysis costs weeks.






Edited spreadsheets destroy evidence



The commonest way to lose a result is to open a table of data, edit a cell, and save. The original is gone, the edit is unrecorded, and nothing downstream can be trusted. Treat raw data files as read-only — on Unix, literally so, with chmod 444 — and write every change as a script that reads the original and produces a new file.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.6 Setting up your machine
Everything in this book runs on a laptop with 8 GB of memory, on Linux, macOS or Windows with the Windows Subsystem for Linux. The environment is built with the conda package manager, which installs the Python stack, R and Bioconductor, and the command-line tools together, without administrator rights and without interfering with any other software on the machine.
Installing the package manager
Miniforge is a minimal conda installer configured to use the community conda-forge channel by default. Download the installer for your platform from the Miniforge releases page, then run it and restart your shell:
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh -b -p "$HOME/miniforge3"
"$HOME/miniforge3/bin/conda" init bash
exec bash
Windows users should install the Windows Subsystem for Linux first, open an Ubuntu terminal, and then follow the Linux instructions exactly; do not install the Windows version of conda for this book, because several of the command-line tools used in later chapters have no Windows build.
Creating the book’s environment
The book’s repository contains a file called environment.yml that lists every package used anywhere in the sixteen chapters, with the channels they come from. Creating the environment from that file is a single command, and it is the only installation step you need:
git clone https://github.com/babasaraki/practical-bioinformatics.git
cd practical-bioinformatics
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate pablb
The download is substantial — the environment includes R, Bioconductor and several compiled aligners — so expect it to take between ten and thirty minutes on a reasonable connection, and do it before you need it rather than during a class. If the solver is slow, conda install -n base conda-libmamba-solver and then conda config --set solver libmamba will speed it up considerably.
Getting the data
Every example in this book runs against files in the data/ directory, and none of them is downloaded while a chapter runs. The script scripts/fetch_data.py downloads each file from its primary archive, derives the simulated read files deterministically, and writes data/MANIFEST.tsv recording the size, SHA-256 checksum and provenance of each one:
python scripts/fetch_data.py          # download everything (about 16 MB)
python scripts/fetch_data.py --check  # verify what you already have
The --check form recomputes every checksum and compares it with the manifest. Running it on the machine this book was built on prints:
all files verified
If a file is reported as modified, delete it and re-run the download; a silently corrupted input is far worse than a missing one.
Checking the installation
Four commands confirm that the environment is complete. Run them in the activated environment:
python --version
python -c "import Bio, numpy, pandas; print(Bio.__version__, numpy.__version__)"
blastn -version | head -1
seqkit version
samtools --version | head -1
On the machine used to build this book these produced:
Python 3.11.17
Biopython 1.88
NumPy 2.4.6
pandas 3.0.6
blastn: 2.17.0+
seqkit v2.14.0
samtools 1.24
Your version numbers will differ, and that is expected and harmless provided each command runs. What matters is that none of them reports command not found, which means the environment is not active — run conda activate pablb and try again.
One more command exercises the data and a command-line tool at the same time, and is the quickest single check that everything is wired together:
seqkit stats data/sequences/*.fasta
file                                                    format  type  num_seqs    sum_len  min_len  avg_len  max_len
data/sequences/TP53-NM_000546.6.fasta                   FASTA   DNA          1      2,512    2,512    2,512    2,512
data/sequences/mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta  FASTA   DNA          1    580,076  580,076  580,076  580,076
data/sequences/sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta             FASTA   DNA          1     29,903   29,903   29,903   29,903
Starting a project the right way
Finally, put the work under version control before you do any of it:
git init
printf 'data/raw/\n_book/\n*.bam\n' > .gitignore
git add . && git commit -m "Start project with pinned environment"
The .gitignore entries matter: large binary files such as BAM alignments should never go into a Git repository, because Git stores a complete copy of every version and the repository will become unusable within a week.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.7 Your first analysis
With the environment built, here is a complete analysis from file to interpretation. The subject is the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome, isolate Wuhan-Hu-1, accession NC_045512.2, as deposited at the NCBI (Sayers et al. 2021). The Python library used throughout is Biopython (Cock et al. 2009), with Matplotlib (Hunter 2007) underneath every figure.
Start by reading the file and asking the two questions you should ask of any new sequence: how long is it, and what is it made of?

from Bio import SeqIO
from Bio.SeqUtils import gc_fraction

record = SeqIO.read(book_data("sequences", "sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta"), "fasta")
genome = record.seq

print(f"accession : {record.id}")
#> accession : NC_045512.2
print(f"length    : {len(genome):,} bp")
#> length    : 29,903 bp
print(f"GC content: {100 * gc_fraction(genome):.2f}%")
#> GC content: 37.97%
for base in "ACGT":
    count = genome.count(base)
    print(f"  {base}: {count:>6,}  ({100 * count / len(genome):5.2f}%)")
#>   A:  8,954  (29.94%)
#>   C:  5,492  (18.37%)
#>   G:  5,863  (19.61%)
#>   T:  9,594  (32.08%)

Both numbers are informative. A length just under 30 kb is at the top of the range for RNA viruses and is characteristic of coronaviruses. A GC content of 38% is low, and it is low in a specific way: the genome is 32% T and 30% A, so more than three-fifths of the sequence is A or T. That composition is a fingerprint. If a contig from a clinical metagenome had come out at 41% GC you would suspect human sequence; at 60% you would suspect a different organism entirely. Composition is the cheapest sanity check in bioinformatics and it costs one line of code.
The next question is whether the genome contains protein-coding potential, and where. A stretch of sequence that begins with a start codon, continues in the same reading frame without a stop codon, and ends at one is an open reading frame (ORF). Because DNA has two strands and each strand has three possible frames, there are six frames to search.

def find_orfs(sequence, min_codons=100):
    """Return (start, end, strand, length_in_codons) for ORFs in all six frames."""
    found, length = [], len(sequence)
    for strand, working in ((1, sequence), (-1, sequence.reverse_complement())):
        for frame in range(3):
            # trim to a whole number of codons so translation has no partial codon
            usable = working[frame: frame + 3 * ((length - frame) // 3)]
            protein = str(usable.translate())
            cursor = 0
            while (stop := protein.find("*", cursor)) != -1:
                first_met = protein.find("M", cursor, stop)
                if first_met != -1 and stop - first_met >= min_codons:
                    left, right = frame + first_met * 3, frame + stop * 3 + 3
                    if strand == -1:                       # map back to forward coordinates
                        left, right = length - right, length - left
                    found.append((left, right, strand, stop - first_met))
                cursor = stop + 1
    return sorted(found)

orfs = find_orfs(genome, min_codons=100)
print(f"{len(orfs)} ORFs of at least 100 codons")
#> 9 ORFs of at least 100 codons
for left, right, strand, codons in orfs[:4]:
    print(f"  {left:>6,}-{right:<6,} strand {strand:+d}  {codons:,} codons")
#>      265-13,483 strand +1  4,405 codons
#>    6,186-6,489  strand -1  100 codons
#>   13,767-21,555 strand +1  2,595 codons
#>   21,535-25,384 strand +1  1,282 codons

Nine ORFs of at least 100 codons, and the largest is over four thousand codons long. Figure 1.3 shows where they sit.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2.6))
ax.hlines(0, 0, len(genome) / 1000, color="#5D6D7E", linewidth=2)
for left, right, strand, codons in orfs:
    row = 0.6 if strand == 1 else -0.6
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((left / 1000, row - 0.18), (right - left) / 1000, 0.36,
                               facecolor=PALETTE[0] if strand == 1 else PALETTE[3]))
    if codons > 1000:
        ax.text((left + right) / 2000, row + 0.33, f"{codons:,} aa", ha="center", fontsize=7)
ax.text(6.3, -1.25, "spurious 100-codon ORF", ha="center", fontsize=7, color=PALETTE[3])
ax.set_ylim(-1.7, 1.6); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 30.5)
#> (-1.7, 1.6)
#> (-0.5, 30.5)
ax.set_yticks([0.6, -0.6]); ax.set_yticklabels(["forward\nstrand", "reverse\nstrand"], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Genome position (kb)")
ax.set_title("Open reading frames of at least 100 codons")
ax.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 1.3: Open reading frames of at least 100 codons in the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome, drawn on the strand where they were found. The forward strand carries a nearly continuous series of long reading frames; the single short reverse-strand hit is a chance arrangement of codons rather than a gene.




Read the figure as a biologist rather than as a programmer. The forward strand is almost entirely occupied by reading frames, with the first covering roughly the first 13 kb and a second running from about 14 kb to 21 kb; the remaining third of the genome carries a series of shorter frames. That is the architecture of a coronavirus: two very large replicase polyproteins occupying the 5′ two-thirds, followed by the structural and accessory genes, of which the spike protein is the first and largest. The single reverse-strand hit is a reminder that an ORF is a statistical pattern, not a gene: in 30 kb of AT-rich sequence, a run of 100 codons without a stop will occasionally occur by chance.
So the ten-minute analysis has produced a defensible statement: this is a 29,903 bp AT-rich sequence whose coding potential is concentrated on one strand in two very long reading frames followed by several short ones, which is consistent with a coronavirus genome and inconsistent with a host contaminant. Everything in the rest of the book makes statements of that kind, about larger data and with more care, but the shape of the claim does not change.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.8 How this book is organised
The chapters are grouped into parts that follow the order in which skills become useful. This chapter and the next establish what the field is and what the biology means for the files you will handle. The part that follows covers the databases that supply your data and the sequence alignment methods that interpret it. The toolchain part teaches Unix, Python and R, and is the point at which the book stops being readable without a keyboard. The later parts work through genome annotation, next-generation sequencing and RNA-seq, structures, networks, machine learning, clinical and pathogen applications, and the ethical obligations that come with human genomic data. A capstone project chapter joins them into one analysis.
You do not have to read in order, but two rules make the rest easier. First, do the exercises; the solutions are collapsed beneath each set so you can check yourself rather than read ahead. Second, run every piece of code in the chapter as you meet it rather than afterwards — the code is short precisely so that this is practical, and the understanding that comes from watching a command fail and fixing it is not available any other way.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.9 Summary

Bioinformatics is the practice of converting large, noisy, machine-generated measurements into defensible biological statements; computational biology, by contrast, produces methods and models. Judge an analysis by correctness, reproducibility and relevance to the sample in hand.
Most biological questions take one of five shapes — identification, relatedness, differential comparison, annotation and variant interpretation — and recognising the shape tells you which methods apply.
The arithmetic of a sequencing run, not preference, is what forces computation: a 30-fold human genome is about 620 million reads and 206 GB of uncompressed FASTQ, some 2,400 times the row limit of a spreadsheet.
Each methodological era answered a specific data problem: exact alignment for small collections, heuristic search for large databases, reference-based analysis after 2001, short-read tooling in the 2010s, and complete assemblies and pangenomes now.
Analyses have a common five-stage shape, and every stage contains a decision that must be recorded in a script if the result is to be defensible later.
Scripts, pinned environments and version control are practical responses to a practical problem: being asked, months later, whether a conclusion survives a change of threshold.
Base composition is the cheapest diagnostic available: the SARS-CoV-2 reference is 38% GC, and a sequence that should be viral but reads as 41% GC is probably host contamination.
An open reading frame is a pattern, not a gene. Long frames on one strand indicate coding architecture; isolated short frames arise by chance in AT-rich sequence.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.10 Exercises

Using the arithmetic in Section 1.2, estimate the uncompressed FASTQ size of a single Mycoplasmoides genitalium sample (genome 580,076 bp) sequenced at 100-fold coverage with 150 bp reads. Would it fit on a USB stick with 4 GB free?
Explain, in two or three sentences each, the difference between the products of bioinformatics and of computational biology, and give an example of a question that belongs to each.
Compute the base composition of the bundled M. genitalium genome (data/sequences/mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta) and compare its GC content with that of SARS-CoV-2. Which of the two would be harder to amplify with a GC-sensitive PCR, and why?
Re-run find_orfs on the SARS-CoV-2 genome with min_codons=50 and with min_codons=300. Record how many ORFs each threshold returns, and explain what the two numbers tell you about using ORF length as evidence of a gene.
The nucleocapsid gene of SARS-CoV-2 occupies positions 28,274 to 29,533 in the standard 1-based numbering used by GenBank. Extract it, confirm that it starts with a start codon and ends with a stop codon, and compute its GC content.
A colleague sends you a 1.2 Mb contig assembled from a clinical sample, claiming it is a novel coronavirus. Its GC content is 52%. Without running any further analysis, state two reasons to doubt the claim.
Write a function that takes a FASTA path and returns a dictionary of sequence identifier to GC content, and run it on data/proteins/globins.fasta. The function should raise a clear error rather than return nonsense if the file contains protein rather than nucleotide sequence.
Write out, as a numbered list of five steps, what you would do to make an analysis you completed last year reproducible by a colleague who has only your result file. State which step you think is most often skipped.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.11 Solutions






Solutions





1. 580,076 × 100 ÷ 150 × 332 bytes ≈ 128 MB, so it fits on the USB stick about thirty times over. Bacterial sequencing is comfortable on a laptop; human sequencing is not.

genome_bp, coverage = 580_076, 100
reads = genome_bp * coverage / READ_LENGTH
print(f"{reads:,.0f} reads, {reads * BYTES_PER_READ / 1e6:,.0f} MB uncompressed")
#> 386,717 reads, 128 MB uncompressed

2. Bioinformatics produces an answer about a particular dataset — for example, “which of these sixty isolates share a transmission chain?” — and is judged on whether that answer is correct, reproducible and relevant to those samples. Computational biology produces a method or model — for example, “an algorithm that estimates transmission trees from genomic and epidemiological data” — and is judged on whether it is correct in general. The same person often does both, but the standard of success differs.
3. M. genitalium is markedly more AT-rich than SARS-CoV-2. A GC content near 32% means AT-rich primer binding sites and low-melting-temperature templates, so this genome is the more awkward of the two for a GC-sensitive protocol; extremes of composition in either direction cause amplification bias.

mgen = SeqIO.read(book_data("sequences", "mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta"), "fasta")
for label, sequence in (("M. genitalium", mgen.seq), ("SARS-CoV-2", genome)):
    print(f"{label:<15} {len(sequence):>8,} bp   GC {100 * gc_fraction(sequence):.2f}%")
#> M. genitalium    580,076 bp   GC 31.69%
#> SARS-CoV-2        29,903 bp   GC 37.97%

4. The low threshold returns far more frames, nearly all of them chance arrangements; the high threshold returns only the longest genes and misses every short one. ORF length alone is weak evidence: it must be combined with codon usage, similarity to known proteins, or ribosome profiling data before a frame is called a gene.

for threshold in (50, 100, 300):
    print(f"min_codons={threshold:>3}: {len(find_orfs(genome, threshold)):>3} ORFs")
#> min_codons= 50:  47 ORFs
#> min_codons=100:   9 ORFs
#> min_codons=300:   4 ORFs

5. The gene is 1,260 bp, begins ATG and ends with a stop codon. Its GC content is about nine percentage points above the genome-wide value, which is a reminder that a whole-genome average hides substantial local variation and that compositional checks should be made on windows rather than on whole sequences. Note the subtraction of one from the start coordinate: GenBank counts from 1 and includes both ends, whereas Python counts from 0 and excludes the end. The next chapter treats this conversion in detail.

n_gene = genome[28274 - 1:29533]
print(f"length {len(n_gene):,} bp, starts {n_gene[:3]}, ends {n_gene[-3:]}")
#> length 1,260 bp, starts ATG, ends TAA
print(f"translates to {n_gene.translate()[:5]}... ending {n_gene.translate()[-1]}")
#> translates to MSDNG... ending *
print(f"GC {100 * gc_fraction(n_gene):.2f}% versus {100 * gc_fraction(genome):.2f}% genome-wide")
#> GC 47.22% versus 37.97% genome-wide

6. First, the length is wrong: coronavirus genomes are about 30 kb, and 1.2 Mb is forty times too long for any known member of the family. Second, the composition is wrong: coronaviruses are AT-rich, near 38% GC, and 52% is well outside that range. Both observations point to a bacterial contig rather than a virus, and both cost nothing to check.
7. The guard matters: gc_fraction will happily return a number for a protein sequence, because G and C are also amino acid codes, and the number will be meaningless.

def gc_by_record(fasta_path):
    """Map each sequence identifier in a nucleotide FASTA file to its GC percentage."""
    results = {}
    for entry in SeqIO.parse(fasta_path, "fasta"):
        letters = set(str(entry.seq).upper())
        if not letters <= set("ACGTUN"):
            raise ValueError(f"{entry.id} is not a nucleotide sequence")
        results[entry.id] = 100 * gc_fraction(entry.seq)
    return results

try:
    gc_by_record(book_data("proteins", "globins.fasta"))
except ValueError as problem:
    print(f"rejected as expected: {problem}")
#> rejected as expected: sp|P69905|HBA_HUMAN is not a nucleotide sequence

print(gc_by_record(book_data("sequences", "sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta")))
#> {'NC_045512.2': 37.97277865097147}

8. A defensible list: (i) recover the raw data and record where it came from, with checksums; (ii) write every processing step as a script, replacing any manual editing; (iii) declare the software in an environment file and rebuild the environment from it; (iv) put the scripts, the environment file and the documentation in a version-controlled repository; (v) re-run the whole thing from raw data on a different machine and check that the result matches. Step (v) is the one most often skipped, and it is the only one that actually tests the other four.

title: 1  What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
text:
1.12 Further reading


Wilson et al. (2017) is the most useful single paper for a new computational researcher: it describes file organisation, scripting and collaboration habits that cost little and prevent most disasters.

Sandve et al. (2013) states the reproducibility problem in ten rules short enough to pin above a desk; read it before your first manuscript rather than after.

Cock et al. (2009) is the Biopython reference. Its accompanying tutorial is the fastest route to competence with SeqIO, Seq and the alignment modules used throughout this book.

Grüning et al. (2018) explains the packaging infrastructure behind the environment.yml file you built in Section 1.6, and is worth reading when a package will not install.

Lander et al. (2001) and Nurk et al. (2022) are best read together: the draft human genome and the first complete one, twenty-one years apart, show exactly what changed and what did not.

Liao et al. (2023) presents the pangenome that is replacing the single human reference, and explains why one reference was never adequate for a species.

Sayers et al. (2021) describes the NCBI resources that supply most of the data in this book, and is the reference to cite when you obtain sequences from GenBank.

Hu et al. (2020) provides the virological background to the SARS-CoV-2 examples used here and in the chapters on annotation and pathogen genomics.







Altschul, Stephen F., Warren Gish, Webb Miller, Eugene W. Myers, and David J. Lipman. 1990. “Basic Local Alignment Search Tool.” Journal of Molecular Biology 215 (3): 403–10. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-2836(05)80360-2.


Cock, Peter J. A., Tiago Antao, Jeffrey T. Chang, Brad A. Chapman, Cymon J. Cox, Andrew Dalke, Iddo Friedberg, et al. 2009. “Biopython: Freely Available Python Tools for Computational Molecular Biology and Bioinformatics.” Bioinformatics 25 (11): 1422–23. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp163.


Danecek, Petr, James K Bonfield, Jennifer Liddle, John Marshall, Valeriu Ohan, Martin O Pollard, Andrew Whitwham, et al. 2021. “Twelve Years of SAMtools and BCFtools.” GigaScience 10 (2). https://doi.org/10.1093/gigascience/giab008.


Dayhoff, Margaret O., Robert M. Schwartz, and Bruce C. Orcutt. 1978. “A model of evolutionary change in proteins.” In Atlas of Protein Sequence and Structure, 5:345–52. Suppl. 3. Washington, DC: National Biomedical Research Foundation.


Ewels, Philip, Måns Magnusson, Sverker Lundin, and Max Käller. 2016. “MultiQC: Summarize Analysis Results for Multiple Tools and Samples in a Single Report.” Bioinformatics 32 (19): 3047–48. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btw354.


Grüning, Björn, Ryan Dale, Andreas Sjödin, Brad A. Chapman, Jillian Rowe, Christopher H. title: 2  Molecular biology for people who analyse data
text:
2.1 Two strands, one file
A DNA molecule is two antiparallel chains held together by base pairing: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine. Each chain has a direction, conventionally written 5′ to 3′ after the carbon atoms of the deoxyribose sugar that carry the phosphate links. The two chains run in opposite directions, so the 5′ end of one sits opposite the 3′ end of the other.
A FASTA file contains one of those two chains, written 5′ to 3′. Which one? By convention, the one the database curators chose, and nothing in the file records why. For a viral genome it is the strand that carries the genes. For a chromosome it is an arbitrary choice made once and never revisited, which is why about half of human genes are annotated on the minus strand. The other chain is not stored, because it is completely determined by the first: reverse the sequence and complement every base.
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from pybfx import book_data, style, PALETTE
style()
from Bio.Seq import Seq

fragment = Seq("ATGGCATTAGC")
print(f"given        5'-{fragment}-3'")
#> given        5'-ATGGCATTAGC-3'
print(f"complement   3'-{fragment.complement()}-5'")
#> complement   3'-TACCGTAATCG-5'
print(f"rev. comp.   5'-{fragment.reverse_complement()}-3'")
#> rev. comp.   5'-GCTAATGCCAT-3'
Three operations, three different answers, and only one of them is usually what you want. The complement alone is almost never useful, because it is written in the wrong direction: printed left to right it reads 3′ to 5′, and every tool that consumes it will assume 5′ to 3′. The reverse complement is the other strand written the way every file format expects it.
This is the source of a whole family of bugs that produce no error message. A primer designed from the wrong strand will not amplify. A variant reported as C>T on one strand is G>A on the other, so a comparison between a VCF file and a paper that used the opposite convention will show every single variant as discordant. A gene annotated on the minus strand must be extracted, then reverse complemented, before it can be translated — and if you forget the second step the translation will still produce amino acids, just the wrong ones.
Biopython’s feature objects carry the strand for you, which is one good reason to parse annotation files rather than to slice sequences by hand. The extract method of a feature takes the orientation into account and returns the sequence in the direction the gene is read.

title: 2  Molecular biology for people who analyse data
text:
A sequence has no memory of its strand



Nothing in a FASTA record states which strand it came from. If you extract a region from a minus-strand gene and pass it on, the strand information exists only in your code. Carry the strand explicitly in every data structure, name variables so the strand is visible (cds_plus_strand, not seq2), and reverse complement at the moment of extraction rather than three functions later.

title: 2  Molecular biology for people who analyse data
section: 2.2 The genetic code and reading frames
text:
2.2 The genetic code and reading frames
Translation reads the nucleotide sequence three bases at a time. Sixty-four codons encode twenty amino acids plus a stop signal, so the code is redundant: most amino acids have more than one codon, and third positions are frequently interchangeable. That redundancy is the reason a change in DNA need not change the protein, and it underlies the distinction between synonymous and non-synonymous variants that Section 2.7 depends on.
Because the code is read in triplets, a sequence has three possible starting points on each strand, and six in total. Only one of them is usually the real one.

from Bio import SeqIO

record = SeqIO.read(book_data("sequences", "sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta"), "fasta")
genome = record.seq
start_of_orf1ab = genome[265:325]      # the first 60 bases of the replicase gene

for frame in range(3):
    usable = start_of_orf1ab[frame: frame + 3 * ((len(start_of_orf1ab) - frame) // 3)]
    print(f"frame +{frame + 1}: {usable.translate()}")
#> frame +1: MESLVPGFNEKTHVQLSLPV
#> frame +2: WRALSLVSTRKHTSNSVCL
#> frame +3: GEPCPWFQRENTRPTQFAC

Only the first frame gives a translation that begins with methionine; the other two are perfectly well-formed strings of amino acids that correspond to no protein the virus has ever made. A reader who sees amino acids appear often assumes the translation worked. It always works — translation is a lookup table, and it has no way to tell you that you started in the wrong place. The diagnostic is not whether amino acids appear but whether the product starts with M, ends at a single stop, and contains no internal stop codons.
Three codons act as stops (TAA, TAG and TGA in DNA) and one, ATG, normally serves as both the start and the codon for methionine. A run of codons that begins with ATG, proceeds in one frame with no stop codon, and ends at a stop is an open reading frame (ORF). The expected length of an ORF arising purely by chance follows from the stop codon frequency: in a random sequence with the base composition of SARS-CoV-2, about one codon in fifteen is a stop, so chance ORFs of a few dozen codons are common and ones of several hundred codons are not.






Genetic codes, plural



The standard code is not universal. Vertebrate mitochondria read TGA as tryptophan rather than stop, and several bacteria and ciliates reassign other codons. Biopython exposes these as numbered translation tables, and translate(table=2) will give a different and correct answer for a mitochondrial gene. Using the default table on mitochondrial DNA produces proteins truncated at the first TGA, which is a common and easily missed error.

title: 2  Molecular biology for people who analyse data
section: 2.3 Finding open reading frames, and checking them
text:
2.3 Finding open reading frames, and checking them
An ORF finder is a short piece of code, and writing one is the fastest way to understand what gene prediction does and does not achieve. The function below scans all six frames and returns every ORF above a length threshold.

def find_orfs(sequence, min_codons=100):
    """Return (start, end, strand, length_in_codons) for ORFs in all six frames.

    Coordinates are 0-based half-open on the forward strand, so that
    sequence[start:end] returns the ORF including its stop codon.
    """
    found, length = [], len(sequence)
    for strand, working in ((1, sequence), (-1, sequence.reverse_complement())):
        for frame in range(3):
            usable = working[frame: frame + 3 * ((length - frame) // 3)]
            protein = str(usable.translate())
            cursor = 0
            while (stop := protein.find("*", cursor)) != -1:
                first_met = protein.find("M", cursor, stop)
                if first_met != -1 and stop - first_met >= min_codons:
                    left, right = frame + first_met * 3, frame + stop * 3 + 3
                    if strand == -1:
                        left, right = length - right, length - left
                    found.append((left, right, strand, stop - first_met))
                cursor = stop + 1
    return sorted(found)

predicted = find_orfs(genome, min_codons=100)
print(f"{len(predicted)} ORFs of at least 100 codons")
#> 9 ORFs of at least 100 codons

Nine candidates. The only way to know whether they are genes is to compare them with an annotation produced by people who had evidence beyond sequence. The bundled GenBank record for the same accession carries that annotation as CDS features.

genbank = SeqIO.read(book_data("sequences", "sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.gb"), "genbank")
annotated = [feature for feature in genbank.features if feature.type == "CDS"]

print(f"{len(annotated)} annotated CDS features")
#> 12 annotated CDS features
for feature in annotated:
    gene = feature.qualifiers["gene"][0]
    codons = len(feature.location) // 3 - 1
    print(f"  {gene:<7} {int(feature.location.start):>6,}-{int(feature.location.end):<6,} {codons:>5,} codons")
#>   ORF1ab     265-21,555 7,096 codons
#>   ORF1ab     265-13,483 4,405 codons
#>   S       21,562-25,384 1,273 codons
#>   ORF3a   25,392-26,220   275 codons
#>   E       26,244-26,472    75 codons
#>   M       26,522-27,191   222 codons
#>   ORF6    27,201-27,387    61 codons
#>   ORF7a   27,393-27,759   121 codons
#>   ORF7b   27,755-27,887    43 codons
#>   ORF8    27,893-28,259   121 codons
#>   N       28,273-29,533   419 codons
#>   ORF10   29,557-29,674    38 codons

Two features of that table deserve attention before any comparison. First, ORF1ab and ORF1a overlap almost entirely: they are two products of the same stretch of sequence, because a ribosomal frameshift near position 13,468 lets the ribosome slip back one base and continue in a different frame. The GenBank location for ORF1ab is a join of two intervals whose coordinates overlap by one base, which is how the format records exactly that event. Second, four of the genes are shorter than 100 codons, so no threshold-based ORF scan set at 100 will find them.

orf1ab = annotated[0]
print(f"location : {orf1ab.location}")
#> location : join{[265:13468](+), [13467:21555](+)}
print(f"parts    : {[(int(p.start), int(p.end)) for p in orf1ab.location.parts]}")
#> parts    : [(265, 13468), (13467, 21555)]
print(f"joined   : {len(orf1ab.location):,} nt -> {len(orf1ab.location) // 3 - 1:,} codons")
#> joined   : 21,291 nt -> 7,096 codons

Now compare the two sets. Because a predicted start codon may sit upstream of the annotated one, the reliable key for matching an ORF to a CDS is the stop position, which is fixed by the frame.

annotated_ends = {int(f.location.parts[-1].end): f.qualifiers["gene"][0] for f in annotated}
predicted_ends = {end for _, end, strand, _ in predicted if strand == 1}

matched = sorted({annotated_ends[end] for end in predicted_ends & set(annotated_ends)})
missed = sorted({gene for end, gene in annotated_ends.items() if end not in predicted_ends})
spurious = [(left, right) for left, right, strand, _ in predicted if strand == -1]

print(f"matched  ({len(matched)}): {', '.join(matched)}")
#> matched  (7): M, N, ORF1ab, ORF3a, ORF7a, ORF8, S
print(f"missed   ({len(missed)}): {', '.join(missed)}")
#> missed   (4): E, ORF10, ORF6, ORF7b
print(f"reverse-strand predictions with no annotation: {spurious}")
#> reverse-strand predictions with no annotation: [(6186, 6489)]

The scan recovers most of the genome’s genes, misses every gene below the length threshold, and produces one prediction on the strand that carries nothing. Figure 2.1 draws the comparison.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))
for feature in annotated:
    left, right = int(feature.location.start), int(feature.location.end)
    gene = feature.qualifiers["gene"][0]
    not_found = int(feature.location.parts[-1].end) not in predicted_ends and gene != "ORF1ab"
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((left / 1000, 1.05), (right - left) / 1000, 0.30,
                               facecolor="white" if not_found else PALETTE[1],
                               hatch="///" if not_found else "",
                               edgecolor=PALETTE[1], linewidth=0.7))
for left, right, strand, codons in predicted:
    row = 0.55 if strand == 1 else 0.05
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((left / 1000, row), (right - left) / 1000, 0.30,
                               facecolor=PALETTE[0] if strand == 1 else PALETTE[3],
                               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5))
for gene, midpoint in (("ORF1ab", 10.9), ("S", 23.5)):
    ax.text(midpoint, 1.20, gene, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color="white")
ax.annotate("E, ORF6, ORF7b and ORF10:\nreal genes under 100 codons", xy=(27.4, 1.05),
            xytext=(20.0, 1.78), fontsize=6.8, color=PALETTE[1], ha="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PALETTE[1], linewidth=0.8))
ax.annotate("false positive", xy=(6.3, 0.2), xytext=(9.5, -0.30), fontsize=6.8,
            color=PALETTE[3], ha="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PALETTE[3], linewidth=0.8))
ax.set_yticks([1.20, 0.70, 0.20])
ax.set_yticklabels(["annotated CDS", "ORFs found,\nforward", "ORFs found,\nreverse"], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(-0.45, 2.1); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 30.5); ax.set_xlabel("Genome position (kb)")
ax.set_title("What a plain ORF scan finds, and what it misses")
ax.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 2.1: Annotated coding sequences of SARS-CoV-2 (top) compared with the output of a plain open reading frame scan at a threshold of 100 codons. Hatched boxes in the top row are genes the scan could not find because they are shorter than the threshold; the single box on the bottom row is a chance reading frame on the strand that carries no genes.




Two conclusions follow, and they generalise far beyond this genome. First, a length threshold trades false positives against false negatives and there is no setting that avoids both: lower it to catch ORF10 at 38 codons and the reverse strand fills with noise. Second, real annotation uses evidence that sequence alone does not contain — ribosome profiling, transcript data, similarity to known proteins, and models of codon usage trained on confirmed genes. Production gene finders for prokaryotes work this way (Hyatt et al. 2010), as do eukaryotic predictors that must additionally model splice sites (Stanke et al. 2006). Your ORF finder is a filter that proposes candidates, not an annotator.
One more discrepancy is instructive. The scan places the start of the spike gene nine codons upstream of the annotated start, because there is an in-frame ATG before the real one. Choosing among in-frame start codons is a genuinely hard problem, and getting it wrong shifts the N-terminus of the predicted protein without affecting anything downstream — the kind of error that survives into a database and is then propagated by everyone who downloads it.
