title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.1 Why R, and where it wins
R is an open implementation of the S language, which was designed at Bell Laboratories for interactive data analysis (R Core Team 2024). Three features of that design matter daily.
Everything is a vector. length(3.14) is 1. Arithmetic, comparison and most functions operate on whole vectors at once, so the loop you would write in another language is usually absent in R. That is not merely cosmetic: a loop you do not write is a loop whose index you cannot get wrong.
Statistics is in the language, not bolted on. t.test, lm, p.adjust, quantile and the full family of probability distributions ship with R. When an analysis reaches the point of needing a p-value, there is nothing to install.
Packages are a first-class concern. CRAN holds over twenty thousand packages, each required to pass automated checks on several platforms before release; Bioconductor adds a biological layer on top with its own, stricter, review and a twice-yearly coordinated release.
Where R loses is equally worth knowing. It is slower than Python for text processing and for explicit loops, it has no equivalent of Biopython’s parsers for the long tail of file formats, and its tooling for general software engineering is thinner. The honest division of labour is that pipelines and parsers tend to be written in Python and in shell, and the statistical analysis of what they produce tends to be written in R.
Every R chapter of this book opens with the same setup, which makes the bundled data reachable and sets the plotting style.
source(file.path("..", "R", "_common.R"))
cat(R.version.string, "\n")
#> R version 4.4.3 (2025-02-28)

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.2 Vectors, vectorisation and recycling
Read the count matrix with base R first, because the base functions are what you will meet in older scripts and in package source code.

counts_df <- read.delim(book_data("expression", "pasilla_gene_counts.tsv"))
count_matrix <- as.matrix(counts_df[, -1])
rownames(count_matrix) <- counts_df$gene_id

dim(count_matrix)
#> [1] 14599     7
count_matrix[1:3, 1:4]
#>             untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4
#> FBgn0000003          0          0          0          0
#> FBgn0000008         92        161         76         70
#> FBgn0000014          5          1          0          0

read.delim returns a data frame; dropping the first column with [, -1] and calling as.matrix gives a numeric matrix, and the gene identifiers move from a column to the row names. A matrix holds one type of value, which is what allows colSums and friends to be fast.
A row of that matrix is a named numeric vector, and most of what you want to know about it is a single function call.

pasilla_gene <- count_matrix["FBgn0000008", ]
pasilla_gene
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>         92        161         76         70        140         88 
#>   treated3 
#>         70
c(mean = mean(pasilla_gene), sd = sd(pasilla_gene), median = median(pasilla_gene))
#>   mean     sd median 
#>  99.57  36.29  88.00

Vectorisation means an operation applies to every element without a loop. Comparison returns a logical vector, and logical vectors are how you select.

pasilla_gene > 100
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>      FALSE       TRUE      FALSE      FALSE       TRUE      FALSE 
#>   treated3 
#>      FALSE
names(which(pasilla_gene > 100))
#> [1] "untreated2" "treated1"
sum(pasilla_gene > 100)
#> [1] 2

sum on a logical vector counts the TRUE values, because TRUE becomes 1 when a numeric answer is required. That is coercion, R’s rule for mixing types: a vector holds one type, so combining types silently promotes everything to the most general one, in the order logical → integer → double → character. c(1, 2, "three") is a character vector in which the 1 is now the text "1". A column of counts arriving as character because one spreadsheet cell said not done is this rule in action, and the symptom is arithmetic refusing to work on data that looks numeric.
Normalising counts to counts per million exposes the second rule, recycling: when two vectors of different lengths meet, R repeats the shorter one until it matches the longer.

c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60) / c(1, 2)
#> [1] 10 10 30 20 50 30
library_size <- colSums(count_matrix)
library_size
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>   13972512   21911438    8358426    9841335   18670279    9571826 
#>   treated3 
#>   10343856

Recycling is convenient when the short vector has length one — count_matrix / 1000 divides everything by 1,000 — and dangerous otherwise. Dividing the whole matrix by the vector of library sizes looks correct and is not.

wrong_cpm <- 1e6 * count_matrix / library_size
right_cpm <- 1e6 * t(t(count_matrix) / library_size)

round(wrong_cpm["FBgn0000008", ], 2)
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>       4.20      16.82       9.09       6.77      14.23       6.30 
#>   treated3 
#>       3.75
round(right_cpm["FBgn0000008", ], 2)
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>       6.58       7.35       9.09       7.11       7.50       9.19 
#>   treated3 
#>       6.77
round(colSums(right_cpm))
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>      1e+06      1e+06      1e+06      1e+06      1e+06      1e+06 
#>   treated3 
#>      1e+06

A matrix in R is a vector with a dimension attribute, filled column by column, so dividing it by a length-7 vector recycles that vector down the rows, not across the columns. Each count is divided by whichever library size happens to land on it. The result is numerically plausible — all seven values are small positive numbers of the right order of magnitude, and one of them, untreated3, is even correct by coincidence — which is exactly why this is a dangerous bug rather than an obvious one. Transposing twice, as right_cpm does, aligns the vector with the columns; the check that proves it is that every column of the corrected matrix now sums to exactly one million.
Missing values follow their own rule. NA is contagious: any arithmetic involving it returns NA, so that a missing measurement cannot be silently treated as zero.

measurements <- c(12, 7, NA, 31)
mean(measurements)
#> [1] NA
mean(measurements, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 16.67
sum(is.na(measurements))
#> [1] 1

The design decision is deliberate, and it is one of the places R is clearly better than a language in which a missing value becomes an empty string or a zero. If you want the mean of what you have, you must say so with na.rm = TRUE, and saying so is a decision recorded in the code.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
section: 7.3 Factors, and the trouble they cause
text:
7.3 Factors, and the trouble they cause
A factor is R’s type for a categorical variable: it stores the data as integer codes plus a table of levels, the permitted categories. Statistical functions need this — lm and t.test must know that treated and untreated are two levels of one variable rather than two arbitrary strings — and the level order sets the reference category, which decides the sign of every coefficient a model reports.

condition <- factor(c("untreated", "treated", "treated", "untreated"))
condition
#> [1] untreated treated   treated   untreated
#> Levels: treated untreated
levels(condition)
#> [1] "treated"   "untreated"
as.integer(condition)
#> [1] 2 1 1 2

The levels came out in alphabetical order, so treated is the reference and a model fitted on this variable would report changes relative to the treated samples — the opposite of what the experiment means. Set the order explicitly whenever it matters.

condition <- factor(c("untreated", "treated", "treated", "untreated"),
                    levels = c("untreated", "treated"))
levels(condition)
#> [1] "untreated" "treated"

Three failure modes follow from the integer-plus-levels design, and all three appear in real analyses.

lane_counts <- factor(c("5", "2", "2", "2", "6", "2", "2"))
as.numeric(lane_counts)
#> [1] 2 1 1 1 3 1 1
as.numeric(as.character(lane_counts))
#> [1] 5 2 2 2 6 2 2

treated_only <- condition[condition == "treated"]
table(treated_only)
#> treated_only
#> untreated   treated 
#>         0         2
table(droplevels(treated_only))
#> 
#> treated 
#>       2

The first trap is the serious one: as.numeric on a factor returns the internal codes, not the labels, so a column of lane counts converted this way becomes a different set of numbers with no error anywhere. The route through as.character is the only safe one. The second trap is that subsetting keeps levels that no longer occur, so table reports a category with zero members and ggplot2 draws an empty box for it; droplevels removes them. The third is that combining two factors with different levels works on the integer codes rather than the labels, so convert to character, combine, and re-factor.






A factor is not its labels



Before R 4.0, read.csv turned every character column into a factor by default, and a decade of analyses carry bugs from it. The default is now stringsAsFactors = FALSE, so modern code gets character columns — but data read with older code, loaded from an .RData file, or returned by a package that still converts, may be factors. When a numeric column behaves strangely, check class() before anything else, and convert with as.numeric(as.character(x)), never as.numeric(x).

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
section: 7.4 Data frames, tibbles and two ways to subset
text:
7.4 Data frames, tibbles and two ways to subset
A data frame is a list of equal-length vectors presented as a table, so each column has its own type. It is the structure almost all R analysis passes through. A tibble is the tidyverse’s data frame: the same thing with three behaviours changed, all of them to remove surprises (Wickham et al. 2019).

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

samples <- read_csv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_sample_annotation.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(lanes = `number of lanes`, exon_counts = `exon counts`) |>
  mutate(sample = sub("fb$", "", file), .before = 1) |>
  select(sample, condition, type, lanes, exon_counts)

samples
#> # A tibble: 7 x 5
#>   sample     condition type        lanes exon_counts
#>   <chr>      <chr>     <chr>       <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 treated1   treated   single-read     5    15679615
#> 2 treated2   treated   paired-end      2    15620018
#> 3 treated3   treated   paired-end      2    12733865
#> 4 untreated1 untreated single-read     2    14924838
#> 5 untreated2 untreated single-read     6    20764558
#> 6 untreated3 untreated paired-end      2    10283129
#> 7 untreated4 untreated paired-end      2    11653031

The sample names in the annotation file carry an fb suffix that the count matrix columns do not; sub strips it so the two tables can be joined. That mismatch is typical, and noticing it early is the difference between a join that works and a join that silently returns nothing.
Printing shows the first differences. A tibble reports its dimensions and the type of every column, and prints ten rows rather than every row. The deeper differences appear when you subset.

samples_df <- as.data.frame(samples)

class(samples_df[, "condition"])   # a data frame drops to a vector
#> [1] "character"
class(samples[, "condition"])      # a tibble stays a tibble
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
samples_df$cond[1:3]               # partial matching: $ finds "condition"
#> [1] "treated" "treated" "treated"

A data frame with one column selected returns a vector, which breaks any code downstream that expected a table; a tibble always returns a tibble, and samples$condition or samples[["condition"]] is how you ask for the vector. And $ on a data frame matches partially, so a typo such as samples_df$cond returns the condition column instead of NULL. On a tibble it returns NULL with a warning, which is the behaviour you want: a mistyped column name should be an error, not a silent substitution.
Base R and dplyr express the same selection differently, and you need to read both, because thirty years of published R code uses the first idiom.

# base R: rows by logical vector, columns by name, inside one [ ]
samples_df[samples_df$condition == "treated" & samples_df$lanes == 2,
           c("sample", "type", "exon_counts")]
#>     sample       type exon_counts
#> 2 treated2 paired-end    15620018
#> 3 treated3 paired-end    12733865

# dplyr: one verb per operation, chained
samples |>
  filter(condition == "treated", lanes == 2) |>
  select(sample, type, exon_counts)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   sample   type       exon_counts
#>   <chr>    <chr>            <dbl>
#> 1 treated2 paired-end    15620018
#> 2 treated3 paired-end    12733865

The results are identical; the difference is where the complexity sits. Base R’s [ does two jobs at once and requires you to repeat the name of the data frame inside the condition, which is where typos hide. dplyr splits the work into verbs, evaluates column names inside the data, and reads left to right. For interactive analysis the second is easier to get right; for package code the first has the advantage of depending on nothing.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.5 Verbs, pipes and tidy data
dplyr provides a small set of verbs that each do one thing: filter chooses rows, select chooses columns, mutate adds or changes columns, arrange sorts, summarise collapses, and group_by makes the verb after it work within groups. The native pipe |> passes the value on its left into the first argument of the call on its right, so a chain of verbs reads as a sentence.

samples |>
  mutate(counts_per_lane = exon_counts / lanes) |>
  group_by(condition, type) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_per_lane = mean(counts_per_lane), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(mean_per_lane))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>   condition type            n mean_per_lane
#>   <chr>     <chr>       <int>         <dbl>
#> 1 treated   paired-end      2      7088471.
#> 2 untreated paired-end      2      5484040 
#> 3 untreated single-read     2      5461589.
#> 4 treated   single-read     1      3135923

Four groups, one line each: the design is unbalanced, with a single treated single-read library and two of everything else. That imbalance is the chapter’s recurring theme and it matters for the analysis in the RNA-seq chapter, because library type is partly confounded with condition.






Two pipes, and which to use



R has two pipes. The magrittr pipe %>%, which the tidyverse introduced, is a function from a package and allows a . placeholder: x %>% f(y, .). The native pipe |> has been part of base R since version 4.1, needs no package, and always passes into the first argument. Use |> in new code — it works in a script with no libraries attached, and it is what current tidyverse documentation uses — and expect to meet %>% in everything written before about 2022.


Tidy data and pivoting
Data is tidy when each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each type of observational unit is a table. The count matrix is not tidy: its seven columns are not seven variables but seven values of one variable, sample. Wide form is the right shape for matrix algebra and for every Bioconductor assay class; long form is the right shape for ggplot2 and for group_by. Converting between them is the most common single operation in a tidyverse analysis.

library(tidyr)

long_counts <- read_tsv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_gene_counts.tsv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(-gene_id, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(samples, by = "sample")

dim(long_counts)
#> [1] 102193      7
head(long_counts, 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>   gene_id     sample     count condition type        lanes exon_counts
#>   <chr>       <chr>      <dbl> <chr>     <chr>       <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 FBgn0000003 untreated1     0 untreated single-read     2    14924838
#> 2 FBgn0000003 untreated2     0 untreated single-read     6    20764558
#> 3 FBgn0000003 untreated3     0 untreated paired-end      2    10283129

pivot_longer(-gene_id, ...) means “pivot every column except gene_id”, turning 14,599 rows by 7 columns into 102,193 rows of three. The left_join then attaches the annotation by matching the sample column in both tables — which only works because the fb suffix was stripped earlier.
With the data long, a per-sample summary is one grouped summarise.

library_summary <- long_counts |>
  group_by(sample, condition, type) |>
  summarise(library_size = sum(count), genes_detected = sum(count > 0),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(library_size)

library_summary
#> # A tibble: 7 x 5
#>   sample     condition type        library_size genes_detected
#>   <chr>      <chr>     <chr>              <dbl>          <int>
#> 1 untreated3 untreated paired-end       8358426          10202
#> 2 treated2   treated   paired-end       9571826          10323
#> 3 untreated4 untreated paired-end       9841335          10281
#> 4 treated3   treated   paired-end      10343856          10332
#> 5 untreated1 untreated single-read     13972512          10529
#> 6 treated1   treated   single-read     18670279          11208
#> 7 untreated2 untreated single-read     21911438          11154

The four paired-end libraries are the four smallest, between 8.4 and 10.3 million counts, and the three single-read libraries are the three largest, between 14.0 and 21.9 million. Library size and library type are not independent in this experiment, and neither is independent of condition. pivot_wider reverses the operation when a matrix is needed again, and running it on long_counts reproduces the original table exactly — a check worth making the first few times you pivot anything.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.6 The grammar of graphics
ggplot2 is not a collection of plot types. It is an implementation of a grammar: a plot is a dataset, a mapping from variables to aesthetics (position, colour, shape, size), one or more geometries that draw the mapped data, scales that control how a variable becomes an aesthetic, optional facets that split the plot into panels, and a theme that governs everything carrying no data. Each of those is added with +, and a plot can be stored in a variable and extended later. Building one figure in stages is the fastest way to see what each layer does.
Start with the data and a mapping, and add the simplest geometry.

library(ggplot2)

expressed <- long_counts |> filter(count > 0)
counts_plot <- ggplot(expressed, aes(x = sample, y = count))
counts_plot + geom_boxplot()






Figure 7.1: Distribution of non-zero gene counts in each pasilla sample, drawn on a linear scale. Each box is a sample; the points are the values ggplot2 classifies as outliers. The plot is unreadable because the counts span five orders of magnitude.




Figure 7.1 is a useful failure. The boxes are flattened onto the axis and the only visible feature is a column of outliers, because gene counts run from 1 to over 300,000 and a linear axis gives almost all of its height to the few thousand genes above 50,000. Nothing about the comparison between samples is legible. The fault is not the geometry — a boxplot is the right summary here — but the scale.
Add a logarithmic scale, and map condition to the fill aesthetic so that the two groups are distinguishable.

scaled_plot <- counts_plot +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = condition)) +
  scale_y_log10()
scaled_plot






Figure 7.2: The same distributions on a log scale, with colour mapped to experimental condition. Changing one scale makes the comparison between samples legible; the default colour palette has not yet been changed.




Figure 7.2 is the same data and the same geometry, with one scale changed, and it now shows a real pattern: the medians differ between samples by about a factor of two, and the differences do not line up with the colours. Treated and untreated samples are interleaved, which means the largest visible source of variation is not the treatment. Note also what the aesthetic mapping did — fill = condition was placed inside aes(), because the colour is determined by a variable. A fixed colour that carries no information goes outside aes(), as a plain argument.
The last stage adds facets, the book palette and labels. Faceting by library type is a hypothesis: if library preparation explains the pattern, the panels will be internally consistent.

final_plot <- scaled_plot +
  facet_grid(. ~ type, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = book_palette[c(2, 1)]) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Counts per gene (log scale)", fill = NULL,
       title = "Library type dominates the count distributions") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
final_plot






Figure 7.3: Non-zero gene counts per sample, faceted by library preparation type and coloured by condition. Within each panel the four distributions are closely matched; between panels the medians differ by roughly a factor of two, which identifies library type rather than treatment as the dominant source of variation.




Figure 7.3 answers the question. The paired-end libraries have medians near 150 to 200 counts and the single-read libraries near 260 to 340, and within each panel treated and untreated samples sit on top of one another. A difference between the panels that is larger than the difference between the colours is the visual signature of a batch effect, and it is why the differential expression model in the RNA-seq chapter includes library type as a term rather than ignoring it. Adding a second scale_y_log10() also demonstrates a detail of the grammar: when two scales for the same aesthetic are added, the later one replaces the earlier rather than combining with it.
Three habits make ggplot2 easier. Keep the data long, because every aesthetic must map to a column. Store the plot in an object and add to it, so that experiments cost one line. And remember that theme() controls only what carries no data — fonts, grid lines, legend position — so to change what a plot says you need a different aesthetic, geometry or scale, not a theme.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.7 Iteration and functions
R’s answer to “do this to every column” is a family of functions that take a function as an argument. apply works over the rows or columns of a matrix, sapply and lapply over the elements of a list or vector, and vapply does what sapply does while requiring you to state the type of the result, which turns a class of silent failures into errors.

head(round(rowMeans(count_matrix), 2), 3)
#> FBgn0000003 FBgn0000008 FBgn0000014 
#>        0.14       99.57        1.43
apply(count_matrix, 2, median)
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>         27         46         18         19         47         20 
#>   treated3 
#>         22
vapply(as.data.frame(count_matrix), function(x) sum(x == 0), integer(1))
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>       4070       3445       4397       4318       3391       4276 
#>   treated3 
#>       4267

Prefer the specialised functions where they exist: rowMeans, colSums, rowSums and colMeans are implemented in C and are much faster than apply on a large matrix. Reach for apply only when there is no specialised version, as for median.
The purrr package covers the same ground with a consistent interface and type-stable variants — map_dbl always returns a double vector, map_int an integer vector, map a list — and a compact formula notation in which .x is the current element.

library(purrr)

map_dbl(as.data.frame(count_matrix), ~ sum(.x) / 1e6) |> round(2)
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>      13.97      21.91       8.36       9.84      18.67       9.57 
#>   treated3 
#>      10.34

A real use of iteration: test every well-expressed gene for a difference between conditions. Filtering first is not optional — a gene seen a handful of times carries no information and costs multiple-testing power.

keep <- rowSums(count_matrix >= 10) >= 3
log_cpm <- log2(right_cpm[keep, ] + 1)
groups <- samples$condition[match(colnames(log_cpm), samples$sample)]

p_values <- apply(log_cpm, 1, function(gene) t.test(gene ~ groups)$p.value)
q_values <- p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH")

c(tested = length(p_values),
  raw_below_0.05 = sum(p_values < 0.05),
  bh_below_0.05 = sum(q_values < 0.05))
#>         tested raw_below_0.05  bh_below_0.05 
#>           8148           1547            195

Of 14,599 genes, 8,148 pass the expression filter. Of those, 1,547 have an uncorrected p-value below 0.05 — but roughly 407 would be expected by chance alone at that threshold, so the raw count is close to uninterpretable. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995), one call to a base R function, controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among the genes called significant and leaves 195. The analysis is deliberately naive: a t-test on log counts per million ignores the mean–variance relationship of count data, which is what DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2009) model, and the RNA-seq chapter redoes it properly. It is here because three lines took a 14,599-gene matrix from raw counts to a corrected result.
Writing functions
A function in R is a value like any other. The body’s last expression is the return value, arguments may have defaults, and defaults may refer to other arguments.

counts_per_million <- function(count_column, library_size = sum(count_column)) {
  if (!is.numeric(count_column)) {
    stop("count_column must be numeric", call. = FALSE)
  }
  1e6 * count_column / library_size
}

round(counts_per_million(count_matrix[, "untreated1"])[1:3], 3)
#> FBgn0000003 FBgn0000008 FBgn0000014 
#>       0.000       6.584       0.358
tryCatch(counts_per_million(letters), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "count_column must be numeric"

The input check is the part most often left out and the part that saves the most time. Without it, passing a character vector produces an error from deep inside the arithmetic, far from the mistake; with it, the message names the argument.
When non-standard evaluation bites
dplyr lets you write filter(samples, condition == "treated") without quoting condition, because the verbs capture the expression and evaluate it inside the data rather than in the calling environment. This is non-standard evaluation, and it is pleasant until you try to write a function around it.

summarise_by_broken <- function(data, group_column) {
  data |>
    group_by(group_column) |>
    summarise(observations = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

tryCatch(summarise_by_broken(long_counts, condition),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "Must group by variables found in `.data`.\nx Column `group_column` is not found."

The error is exact: dplyr looked for a column literally called group_column. The fix is to embrace the argument with { }, which tells dplyr to substitute what the caller passed before evaluating.

summarise_by <- function(data, group_column) {
  data |>
    group_by({{ group_column }}) |>
    summarise(observations = n(), total_counts = sum(count), .groups = "drop")
}

summarise_by(long_counts, condition)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   condition observations total_counts
#>   <chr>            <int>        <dbl>
#> 1 treated          43797     38585961
#> 2 untreated        58396     54083711
summarise_by(long_counts, type)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   type        observations total_counts
#>   <chr>              <int>        <dbl>
#> 1 paired-end         58396     38115443
#> 2 single-read        43797     54554229

One pair of braces turns a function that cannot work into one that works for any grouping column. This is the single most common point at which people who are fluent in interactive dplyr get stuck when they start writing functions, and the symptom — an error naming your own argument as a missing column — is distinctive enough to recognise immediately.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.8 Bioconductor
Bioconductor began in 2001 with a practical problem: every microarray group was writing its own code to attach probe identifiers to measurements, and none of it was interoperable (Gentleman et al. 2004). The answer was to define shared classes and require packages to use them, so that the output of one package is the input of the next. Three commitments follow, and they explain most of what looks unusual about Bioconductor code.
Packages use S4 classes, a formal object system with declared slots and validity checking, rather than the looser S3 system of base R. You access parts of an object through accessor functions — assay(), colData(), seqnames() — rather than reaching into slots with $ or @. And the whole collection is released twice a year as a tested set, with every package checked against every other, which is why a Bioconductor version number is a meaningful statement about an analysis (Huber et al. 2015).
Installing with BiocManager
Bioconductor packages are not installed with install.packages. The BiocManager package resolves the correct package versions for your release.

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("Biostrings", "GenomicRanges", "rtracklayer",
                       "SummarizedExperiment"))
BiocManager::valid()

Those commands reach CRAN and the Bioconductor repositories, so they are not run when this book is built. The output below was captured from a real run of BiocManager::version() and BiocManager::valid() in the environment this chapter was written in, abridged where the report lists individual packages.
[1] '3.20'

Bioconductor version '3.20'

  * 17 packages out-of-date
  * 0 packages too new

create a valid installation with

  BiocManager::install(c(
    "BH", "BiocParallel", "Biostrings", "GenomeInfoDb", "IRanges",
    "MatrixGenerics", "RCurl", "SparseArray", "callr", "colorspace", "curl",
    "edgeR", "lambda.r", "limma", "restfulr", "selectr", "tinytex"
  ), update = TRUE, ask = FALSE, force = TRUE)
BiocManager::valid() is the command worth remembering: it reports any installed package that is out of step with your Bioconductor release, which is the usual cause of an error message that makes no sense.






Record the Bioconductor version, not just the package version



A Bioconductor release pins a set of mutually tested package versions to one R version. Stating “Bioconductor 3.20 under R 4.4” in a methods section identifies the software far more precisely than a list of individual package versions, and BiocManager::version() returns it in one call. Annotation packages change between releases as the underlying databases are rebuilt, so a result can shift when only the annotation has moved.


Biostrings
Biostrings stores sequences in a compressed representation that holds a whole genome in a fraction of the memory a character vector would need, and provides the operations the alphabet implies (Lawrence et al. 2013). Attach the Bioconductor packages now; note that they mask a few base and dplyr names, which is why they are loaded after the tidyverse work is done.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(Biostrings)
  library(GenomicRanges)
  library(rtracklayer)
  library(SummarizedExperiment)
})

genome <- readDNAStringSet(book_data("sequences",
                                     "mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta"))
genome
#> DNAStringSet object of length 1:
#>      width seq                                          names               
#> [1] 580076 TAAGTTATTATTTAGTTAATA...CTTTAATACTAAAAAAATAC NC_000908.2 Mycop...


letterFrequency(genome, c("G", "C", "A", "T"))
#>          G     C      A      T
#> [1,] 92306 91515 200544 195711
round(100 * letterFrequency(genome, "GC", as.prob = TRUE), 2)
#>        G|C
#> [1,] 31.69

chromosome <- genome[[1]]
subseq(chromosome, 1, 48)
#> 48-letter DNAString object
#> seq: TAAGTTATTATTTAGTTAATACTTTTAACAATATTATTAAGGTATTTA
reverseComplement(subseq(chromosome, 1, 48))
#> 48-letter DNAString object
#> seq: TAAATACCTTAATAATATTGTTAAAAGTATTAACTAAATAATAACTTA

A DNAStringSet is a set of sequences; [[ takes one out as a DNAString. The GC content of 31.69% is low even for a reduced bacterial genome, and it has a direct consequence for the codon usage and oligonucleotide composition you can measure in the same two lines.

head(sort(oligonucleotideFrequency(chromosome, 3), decreasing = TRUE), 5)
#>   AAA   TTT   TTA   TAA   ATT 
#> 34109 32295 22898 22558 20365
countPattern("TTTAAA", chromosome)
#> [1] 1706
length(matchPattern("GGAGG", chromosome))
#> [1] 139

The five commonest trinucleotides are all A or T only, as a 31.7% GC genome requires. matchPattern returns the positions of every match of the Shine–Dalgarno-like GGAGG motif, not merely the count. Protein sequences use the parallel class.

orthologs <- readAAStringSet(book_data("proteins", "p53-orthologs.fasta"))
width(orthologs)
#> [1] 393 390 391 386 386 393 373 352
head(sort(alphabetFrequency(orthologs[[1]])[1:20], decreasing = TRUE), 4)
#>  P  S  L  E 
#> 45 38 32 30

The eight p53 orthologues range from 352 to 393 residues (Bateman et al. 2022), and the human protein’s commonest residues are proline, serine, glycine and alanine — consistent with the large intrinsically disordered regions at both ends of p53.
GRanges and genomic intervals
Half of genomics is interval arithmetic: which variants fall in which genes, which peaks overlap which promoters, how much of a genome is annotated. GenomicRanges provides GRanges, a vector of intervals each with a sequence name, start, end and strand, plus arbitrary metadata columns, and rtracklayer reads GFF3, GTF, BED and BigWig into it (Lawrence et al. 2013).

annotation <- import(book_data("annotation", "mycoplasma-genitalium.gff"))
class(annotation)
#> [1] "GRanges"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "GenomicRanges"
table(annotation$type)
#> 
#>      region        gene         CDS        tRNA        exon  pseudogene 
#>           1         546         524          36          42          20 
#>        rRNA     SRP_RNA RNase_P_RNA       tmRNA 
#>           3           1           1           1

The file is the RefSeq annotation produced by NCBI’s prokaryotic pipeline (Tatusova et al. 2016). Keep the gene features and the three metadata columns worth carrying, then declare the sequence length, which is what lets GRanges refuse an interval running off the end of the chromosome.

genes <- annotation[annotation$type == "gene"]
mcols(genes) <- mcols(genes)[, c("locus_tag", "gene", "gene_biotype")]
seqlengths(genes) <- 580076

genes[1:3]
#> GRanges object with 3 ranges and 3 metadata columns:
#>          seqnames    ranges strand |   locus_tag        gene   gene_biotype
#>             <Rle> <IRanges>  <Rle> | <character> <character>    <character>
#>   [1] NC_000908.2  686-1828      + |  MG_RS00005        dnaN protein_coding
#>   [2] NC_000908.2 1828-2760      + |  MG_RS00010        <NA> protein_coding
#>   [3] NC_000908.2 2845-4797      + |  MG_RS00015        gyrB protein_coding
#>   -------
#>   seqinfo: 1 sequence from an unspecified genome
summary(width(genes))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>      74     442     838    1004    1309    5418

Now a real overlap computation. In a genome this compact, adjacent genes are expected to abut and sometimes to overlap, because the intergenic regions have been eroded. findOverlaps answers the question directly, returning every pair of indices whose intervals share at least one base; keeping only pairs where the first index is smaller removes self-matches and the duplicate of each pair.

hits <- findOverlaps(genes, genes, ignore.strand = TRUE)
hits <- hits[queryHits(hits) < subjectHits(hits)]
overlap_width <- width(pintersect(genes[queryHits(hits)],
                                  genes[subjectHits(hits)],
                                  ignore.strand = TRUE))

length(hits)
#> [1] 189
length(unique(c(queryHits(hits), subjectHits(hits))))
#> [1] 300
summary(overlap_width)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>     1.0     4.0    10.0    13.1    17.0   113.0

189 pairs of annotated genes overlap, involving 300 of the 546 genes — more than half the genome’s gene complement. The median overlap is 10 bp and the largest is 113 bp. An overlap of a few bases is the signature of translational coupling, where the stop codon of one gene and the start codon of the next share sequence in an arrangement such as ATGA, and it is a well-documented feature of reduced genomes. Without an interval class this would be a nested loop; here it is one call, backed by an interval tree, so it stays fast on a human genome with two million features.
Intervals also answer density questions. tileGenome cuts the chromosome into fixed windows and countOverlaps counts the features in each, which is the computation behind every coverage track you have ever looked at.

tiles <- tileGenome(seqlengths(genes), tilewidth = 10000,
                    cut.last.tile.in.chrom = TRUE)
tiles <- tiles[width(tiles) == 10000]        # drop the short final window
tiles$n_genes <- countOverlaps(tiles, genes, ignore.strand = TRUE)
summary(tiles$n_genes)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>     5.0     8.0    10.0    10.3    12.0    21.0

Figure 7.4 plots that count along the genome. Converting a Bioconductor object for ggplot2 is a standard move: as.data.frame on a GRanges gives columns for seqnames, start, end, width, strand and every metadata column.

gene_density <- as.data.frame(tiles) |>
  dplyr::mutate(midpoint_kb = (start + end) / 2000)

ggplot(gene_density, aes(x = midpoint_kb, y = n_genes)) +
  geom_col(width = 9, fill = book_palette[1]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(gene_density$n_genes),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = book_palette[4]) +
  labs(x = "Genome position (kb)", y = "Genes per 10 kb window",
       title = "Gene density along a reduced bacterial genome")






Figure 7.4: Annotated genes per 10 kb window across the Mycoplasmoides genitalium G37 chromosome. The dashed line is the genome-wide mean of 10.3 genes per window. The sparsest window, at 430-440 kb, contains only five genes because two of them are the 4.2 kb and 3.9 kb RNA polymerase subunits rpoB and rpoC.




Density varies from five to 21 genes per window around a mean of 10.3, and the variation is almost entirely a matter of gene length rather than of gene-free sequence: the sparsest window holds the two RNA polymerase subunit genes, which between them occupy 8 kb of the 10 kb, while the densest holds 21 protein-coding genes averaging 522 bp. A density track answers the question “how many features per window”, which is not the question “how much of this region is functional”.
SummarizedExperiment
A quantitative experiment is three things that must stay aligned: a matrix of measurements, a table describing the columns, and a table describing the rows. Keeping them in three separate variables works until something reorders one of them, at which point every result is wrong and nothing errors. SummarizedExperiment is the class that makes that impossible (Huber et al. 2015).
The failure it prevents is worth seeing first. The annotation table lists the samples in a different order from the count matrix columns.

samples$sample
#> [1] "treated1"   "treated2"   "treated3"   "untreated1" "untreated2"
#> [6] "untreated3" "untreated4"
colnames(count_matrix)
#> [1] "untreated1" "untreated2" "untreated3" "untreated4" "treated1"  
#> [6] "treated2"   "treated3"


naive <- data.frame(sample = colnames(count_matrix),
                    condition = samples$condition)
naive
#>       sample condition
#> 1 untreated1   treated
#> 2 untreated2   treated
#> 3 untreated3   treated
#> 4 untreated4 untreated
#> 5   treated1 untreated
#> 6   treated2 untreated
#> 7   treated3 untreated

Six of the seven labels in that table are wrong: three untreated samples are called treated and three treated samples untreated, because a character vector was pasted beside a matrix on the assumption that both were in the same order. A differential expression analysis built on it would run to completion, produce a volcano plot, and be meaningless. It is the commonest serious bug in expression analysis, and no diagnostic plot reveals it.
Build the object properly. The sample table is reordered by name to match the matrix columns, and the row annotation is computed from the matrix itself.

sample_table <- samples |>
  tibble::column_to_rownames("sample") |>
  dplyr::mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("untreated", "treated")),
                type = factor(type))
sample_table <- sample_table[colnames(count_matrix), ]

gene_table <- DataFrame(total_count = rowSums(count_matrix),
                        detected_in = rowSums(count_matrix > 0),
                        row.names = rownames(count_matrix))

storage.mode(count_matrix) <- "integer"
pasilla_se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
                                   colData = sample_table,
                                   rowData = gene_table)
pasilla_se
#> class: SummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 14599 7 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(14599): FBgn0000003 FBgn0000008 ... FBgn0261574
#>   FBgn0261575
#> rowData names(2): total_count detected_in
#> colnames(7): untreated1 untreated2 ... treated2 treated3
#> colData names(4): condition type lanes exon_counts

The printed summary is the anatomy of the class. dim gives features by samples, 14,599 by 7. assays lists the matrices — here one, named counts, and a second could hold normalised values on the same grid. rowData holds one row per gene, colData one row per sample, and metadata is a free-form list for provenance. The accessors return each part.

assay(pasilla_se, "counts")[1:3, 1:4]
#>             untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4
#> FBgn0000003          0          0          0          0
#> FBgn0000008         92        161         76         70
#> FBgn0000014          5          1          0          0
colData(pasilla_se)
#> DataFrame with 7 rows and 4 columns
#>            condition        type     lanes exon_counts
#>             <factor>    <factor> <numeric>   <numeric>
#> untreated1 untreated single-read         2    14924838
#> untreated2 untreated single-read         6    20764558
#> untreated3 untreated paired-end          2    10283129
#> untreated4 untreated paired-end          2    11653031
#> treated1   treated   single-read         5    15679615
#> treated2   treated   paired-end          2    15620018
#> treated3   treated   paired-end          2    12733865
head(rowData(pasilla_se), 3)
#> DataFrame with 3 rows and 2 columns
#>             total_count detected_in
#>               <numeric>   <numeric>
#> FBgn0000003           1           1
#> FBgn0000008         697           7
#> FBgn0000014          10           3

The guarantee is that the object cannot be built wrong. Passing sample annotation whose row names do not match the matrix columns is refused outright, and so is a table with the wrong number of rows.

shuffled <- sample_table[c(3, 1, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6), ]
tryCatch(SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
                              colData = shuffled),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "the rownames and colnames of the supplied assay(s) must be NULL or\n  identical to those of the SummarizedExperiment object (or\n  derivative) to construct"

tryCatch(SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = count_matrix),
                              colData = sample_table[1:6, ]),
         error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "invalid class \"SummarizedExperiment\" object: \n    nb of cols in 'assay' (7) must equal nb of rows in 'colData' (6)"







Sample order is not metadata



The order of columns in a matrix is an accident of how a file was written. Never rely on it. Match sample annotation to measurements by name — sample_table[colnames(count_matrix), ] — and put both in one object so the question cannot arise again. It prevents a class of error that no plot will reveal and no reviewer will catch.


From then on the object behaves like a two-dimensional array in which everything moves together. Subsetting rows filters the gene annotation; subsetting columns filters the sample annotation; and $ reaches into colData directly.

expressed_se <- pasilla_se[rowData(pasilla_se)$detected_in >= 3, ]
paired_se <- expressed_se[, expressed_se$type == "paired-end"]

dim(expressed_se)
#> [1] 10948     7
dim(paired_se)
#> [1] 10948     4
as.character(paired_se$condition)
#> [1] "untreated" "untreated" "treated"   "treated"


assay(pasilla_se, "cpm") <- 1e6 * t(t(assay(pasilla_se, "counts")) /
                                      colSums(assay(pasilla_se, "counts")))
metadata(pasilla_se) <- list(
  source = "Brooks et al. 2011, GEO GSE18508",
  counted_with = "HTSeq, gene level",
  built_in = "Chapter 7 of Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics"
)

assayNames(pasilla_se)
#> [1] "counts" "cpm"
round(assay(pasilla_se, "cpm")["FBgn0000008", ], 2)
#> untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4   treated1   treated2 
#>       6.58       7.35       9.09       7.11       7.50       9.19 
#>   treated3 
#>       6.77

A second assay sits on the same grid as the first, so a gene selected from one is the same gene in the other. The counts themselves were produced by counting reads per gene with HTSeq (Anders, Pyl, and Huber 2014), which is the kind of fact the metadata slot exists to carry. Saving the object with saveRDS writes matrices, both annotation tables and the metadata to one file, and this is the object the RNA-seq chapter loads and hands to DESeq2 — where DESeqDataSet is simply a SummarizedExperiment with a design formula attached, which is why the hand-over needs no conversion at all. The same holds for most of Bioconductor: limma (Ritchie et al. 2015) and edgeR accept or return the same structure, and a class understood once is understood everywhere.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.9 Reproducible reporting
Everything in this chapter was produced by a document holding both the prose and the code, rendered by Quarto with the knitr engine (Xie 2016). The idea is Knuth’s literate programming, inverted for data analysis (Knuth 1984): the figures and the numbers in the text cannot disagree with the analysis, because they are generated from it every time the document is built.
A Quarto document is Markdown with executable chunks. Each chunk has options set in #| comment lines: a label for cross-referencing, a caption, whether to show the code, whether to run it.

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(gene_density, aes(midpoint_kb, n_genes)) + geom_col()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Genes per 10 kb window.](07-introduction-to-r-for-bioinformatics_files/figure-html/fig-07-density-example-1.png){#fig-07-density-example fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::
Rendering with quarto render chapter.qmd runs every chunk in a fresh R session, in document order, and fails if any of them fails. That last property is the one that matters: a document that renders is a document whose code runs from a clean start, which is a guarantee a notebook cannot make.
The remaining piece is a record of the software. sessionInfo() reports the R version, the platform and the version of every attached package, and belongs at the end of any analysis document.

session <- sessionInfo()
session$R.version$version.string
#> [1] "R version 4.4.3 (2025-02-28)"
head(vapply(session$otherPkgs, function(pkg) pkg$Version, character(1)), 6)
#> SummarizedExperiment              Biobase       MatrixGenerics 
#>             "1.36.0"             "2.66.0"             "1.18.0" 
#>          matrixStats          rtracklayer        GenomicRanges 
#>              "1.5.0"             "1.66.0"             "1.58.0"

Printing sessionInfo() on its own gives the full report — operating system, locale and loaded-but-not-attached packages — tedious to read and invaluable when an analysis stops reproducing. Pair it with a pinned environment file, as described in the Unix chapter, so the versions are not merely recorded but restorable (Sandve et al. 2013).

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.10 Summary

R has no scalars. Operations apply to whole vectors, which removes most loops and, with them, most index errors.
Recycling repeats the shorter operand silently. On a matrix it recycles down the columns, so dividing a count matrix by a vector of library sizes gives a plausible, wrong answer.
Coercion promotes mixed types to the most general one, and a factor is integer codes plus labels: a numeric column that will not do arithmetic is almost always character or factor, and only as.numeric(as.character(x)) recovers a factor’s labels.
Tibbles differ from data frames in the ways that matter for safety: no partial matching, no dropping to a vector, no silent factor conversion.
Base R subsetting and dplyr verbs express the same operations. Write the second; be able to read the first.
Tidy data has one variable per column, which is the shape ggplot2 and group_by require, and the opposite of the shape Bioconductor assays require. pivot_longer and pivot_wider move between them.
A ggplot is data, aesthetics, geometries, scales, facets and a theme. When a plot is unreadable, change the scale before the geometry.
Bioconductor’s value is its shared classes. Biostrings for sequences, GRanges for intervals and SummarizedExperiment for assay matrices cover most of what a genomics analysis needs to hold.
Keeping counts, sample annotation and feature annotation in one SummarizedExperiment makes the commonest serious bug in expression analysis — a mismatch between samples and their labels — impossible to commit.
A rendered Quarto document plus sessionInfo() is a result that can be rebuilt. A result that cannot be rebuilt is a claim.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.11 Exercises

Predict, before running it, what c(TRUE, 2L, 3.5, "four") returns and what class() reports for it. Then check.
Create the factor factor(c("10", "20", "30")) and convert it to the numbers 10, 20 and 30. Explain in one sentence what as.numeric() alone returns and why.
Using samples, write one dplyr pipeline that returns the sample name, condition and exon counts for every paired-end library, sorted from largest to smallest. Then write the same selection in base R.
Compute the median counts per million of each sample from right_cpm, and say which library type has the higher median. Why is this not evidence of a biological difference?
Add a geom_jitter() layer of 200 randomly chosen genes on top of Figure 7.2. What does the layer order tell you about how ggplot2 draws a plot?
Using matchPattern, find every occurrence of the start codon ATG on the forward strand of the M. genitalium chromosome, and compare the count with the 524 annotated coding sequences. Explain the discrepancy.
Build a GRanges of the transfer RNA genes only (gene_biotype == "tRNA"), and use distanceToNearest to find how far each one lies from the nearest protein-coding gene. Report the median distance.
Write a function filter_by_detection(se, min_samples) that returns a SummarizedExperiment containing only genes detected in at least min_samples samples, and show that the returned object’s colData is unchanged.
The pasilla_se object contains one treated single-read library and two treated paired-end libraries. Using table() on colData, show the design, and explain in two or three sentences why this makes the effect of condition and the effect of library type partly inseparable.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.12 Solutions






Solutions





1. Everything is coerced to character, because character is the most general of the four types present.

mixed <- c(TRUE, 2L, 3.5, "four")
mixed
#> [1] "TRUE" "2"    "3.5"  "four"
class(mixed)
#> [1] "character"

2. as.numeric() alone returns 1, 2, 3 — the internal integer codes of the three levels, which happen to be in the same order as the labels here and so look almost right. The safe route converts to character first.

sizes <- factor(c("10", "20", "30"))
as.numeric(sizes)
#> [1] 1 2 3
as.numeric(as.character(sizes))
#> [1] 10 20 30

3.

samples |>
  filter(type == "paired-end") |>
  select(sample, condition, exon_counts) |>
  arrange(desc(exon_counts))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   sample     condition exon_counts
#>   <chr>      <chr>           <dbl>
#> 1 treated2   treated      15620018
#> 2 treated3   treated      12733865
#> 3 untreated4 untreated    11653031
#> 4 untreated3 untreated    10283129

samples_df[order(-samples_df$exon_counts), ][
  samples_df$type[order(-samples_df$exon_counts)] == "paired-end",
  c("sample", "condition", "exon_counts")]
#>       sample condition exon_counts
#> 2   treated2   treated    15620018
#> 3   treated3   treated    12733865
#> 7 untreated4 untreated    11653031
#> 6 untreated3 untreated    10283129

The base R version needs the ordering applied twice, once to the rows and once to the vector used in the condition, which is a fair illustration of why the verb form is easier to get right.
4. The single-read libraries have the higher median. This is a property of library preparation and sequencing depth, not of biology: counts per million corrects for total depth but not for the different distribution of reads across genes that paired-end and single-read protocols produce, and the two protocols are not randomly assigned to conditions in this experiment.

median_cpm <- apply(right_cpm, 2, median)
data.frame(median_cpm = round(median_cpm, 3),
           type = samples$type[match(names(median_cpm), samples$sample)])
#>            median_cpm        type
#> untreated1      1.932 single-read
#> untreated2      2.099 single-read
#> untreated3      2.154  paired-end
#> untreated4      1.931  paired-end
#> treated1        2.517 single-read
#> treated2        2.089  paired-end
#> treated3        2.127  paired-end

5. The jittered points are drawn on top of the boxes, because layers are drawn in the order they are added. Adding geom_jitter() before geom_boxplot() would hide the points behind the boxes.

set.seed(20250101)
sampled_genes <- dplyr::slice_sample(expressed, n = 200)

scaled_plot +
  geom_jitter(data = sampled_genes, width = 0.2, size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5)







6. There are far more ATG occurrences than coding sequences, because most are internal codons, out of frame, or in the reverse-strand genes, which this search does not see at all.

atg_hits <- matchPattern("ATG", chromosome)
c(atg_occurrences = length(atg_hits), annotated_cds = 524)
#> atg_occurrences   annotated_cds 
#>            9020             524

Gene finding needs a model of reading frames, ribosome binding sites and codon statistics, which is what Prodigal and the NCBI pipeline provide; counting start codons is not even a first approximation.
7.

trnas <- genes[genes$gene_biotype == "tRNA"]
coding <- genes[genes$gene_biotype == "protein_coding"]
nearest_hits <- distanceToNearest(trnas, coding, ignore.strand = TRUE)

length(trnas)
#> [1] 36
summary(mcols(nearest_hits)$distance)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>     0.0    35.8   102.5   135.1   225.5   390.0

The median distance is small — a few tens of base pairs — which is another expression of the compactness seen in Figure 7.4.
8.

filter_by_detection <- function(se, min_samples) {
  stopifnot(is(se, "SummarizedExperiment"), min_samples >= 0)
  detected <- rowSums(assay(se, "counts") > 0)
  se[detected >= min_samples, ]
}

filtered <- filter_by_detection(pasilla_se, min_samples = 5)
dim(filtered)
#> [1] 10044     7
identical(colData(filtered), colData(pasilla_se))
#> [1] TRUE

identical returning TRUE is the point: subsetting rows cannot disturb the sample annotation, because the subsetting method is defined on the whole object rather than on the matrix.
9.

table(colData(pasilla_se)$condition, colData(pasilla_se)$type)
#>            
#>             paired-end single-read
#>   untreated          2           2
#>   treated            2           1

The design is unbalanced: one treated single-read library against two untreated, and two treated paired-end against two untreated. Because every cell of the table is occupied, library type can be included as a term in a model and its effect estimated — the design is not fully confounded. But with one sample in the smallest cell, the estimate of the single-read effect in treated samples rests on a single library, so a technical oddity in that one library is indistinguishable from a treatment effect specific to single-read preparation. A balanced design with equal numbers in all four cells would have cost nothing extra and removed the ambiguity.

title: 7  R and Bioconductor
text:
7.13 Further reading


Wickham et al. (2019) is the paper that introduced the tidyverse as a coherent set; read it for the design principles that explain why the verbs are shaped as they are.

Gentleman et al. (2004) is the original Bioconductor paper and is still the clearest statement of why shared classes, rather than shared functions, were the right thing to standardise.

Huber et al. (2015) describes the modern Bioconductor infrastructure, including SummarizedExperiment, and is the reference to cite when you use the class.

Lawrence et al. (2013) sets out the range-based classes and the algorithms behind findOverlaps; worth reading before you write any interval arithmetic of your own.

Love, Huber, and Anders (2014) is the DESeq2 paper, and its methods section explains why the naive t-test in Section 7.7 is the wrong model for count data.

Xie (2016) documents knitr, the engine that executes the chunks in this book; its chapter on chunk options answers most questions about controlling output.

Yu et al. (2012) is a well-built Bioconductor package to read as code: it takes a gene list and returns an enrichment result, using the shared classes throughout.

Cock et al. (2009) is the Biopython reference, worth comparing with Biostrings: the same operations, a different design, and an illustration of how much of a library’s shape follows from its host language.







Anders, Simon, Paul Theodor Pyl, and Wolfgang Huber. 2014. “HTSeq – a Python Framework to Work with High-Throughput Sequencing Data,” February. https://doi.org/10.1101/002824.


Bateman, Alex, Maria-Jesus Martin, Sandra Orchard, Michele Magrane, Shadab Ahmad, Emanuele Alpi, Emily H Bowler-Barnett, et al. 2022. “UniProt: The Universal Protein Knowledgebase in 2023.” Nucleic Acids Research 51 (D1): D523–31. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkac1052.


Benjamini, Yoav, and Yosef Hochberg. 1995. “Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology 57 (1): 289–300. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x.


Brooks, Angela N., Li Yang, Michael O. Duff, Kasper D. Hansen, Jung W. Park, Sandrine Dudoit, Steven E. Brenner, and Brenton R. Graveley. 2010. “Conservation of an RNA Regulatory Map Between <i>drosophila</i> and Mammals.” Genome Research 21 (2): 193–202. https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.108662.110.


Cock, Peter J. A., Tiago Antao, Jeffrey T. Chang, Brad A. Chapman, Cymon J. Cox, Andrew Dalke, Iddo Friedberg, et al. 2009. “Biopython: Freely Available Python Tools for Computational Molecular Biology and Bioinformatics.” Bioinformatics 25 (11): 1422–23. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp163.


Gentleman, Robert C, Vincent J Carey, Douglas M Bates, Ben Bolstad, Marcel Dettling, Sandrine Dudoit, Byron Ellis, et al. 2004. “Bioconductor: Open Software Development for Computational Biology and Bioinformatics.” Genome Biology 5 (10). https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2004-5-10-r80.


Huber, Wolfgang, Vincent J Carey, Robert Gentleman, Simon Anders, Marc Carlson, Benilton S Carvalho, Hector Corrada Bravo, et al. 2015. “Orchestrating High-Throughput Genomic Analysis with Bioconductor.” Nature Methods 12 (2): 115–21. https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.3252.


Knuth, D. E. 1984. “Literate Programming.” The Computer Journal 27 (2): 97–111. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97.


Lawrence, Michael, Wolfgang Huber, Hervé Pagès, Patrick Aboyoun, Marc Carlson, Robert Gentleman, Martin T. Morgan, and Vincent J. Carey. 2013. “Software for Computing and Annotating Genomic Ranges.” Edited by Andreas Prlic. PLoS Computational Biology 9 (8): e1003118. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003118.


Love, Michael I, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders. 2014. “Moderated Estimation of Fold Change and Dispersion for RNA-Seq Data with DESeq2,” February. https://doi.org/10.1101/002832.


R Core Team. 2024. R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing. Vienna, Austria: R Foundation for Statistical Computing. https://www.R-project.org/.


Ritchie, Matthew E., Belinda Phipson, Di Wu, Yifang Hu, Charity W. Law, Wei Shi, and Gordon K. Smyth. 2015. “Limma Powers Differential Expression Analyses for RNA-Sequencing and Microarray Studies.” Nucleic Acids Research 43 (7): e47–47. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv007.


Robinson, Mark D., Davis J. McCarthy, and Gordon K. Smyth. 2009. “<Tt>edgeR</Tt> : A Bioconductor Package for Differential Expression Analysis of Digital Gene Expression Data.” Bioinformatics 26 (1): 139–40. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp616.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
section: 8.2 Judging an assembly before you annotate it
text:
8.2 Judging an assembly before you annotate it
An assembler takes reads and reports contigs: contiguous stretches of sequence that the evidence supports without interruption. If paired-end or long-range linking information is available, contigs can be ordered and oriented into scaffolds, in which the gaps of unknown sequence between contigs are represented by runs of N. A scaffold is therefore a weaker claim than a contig — it asserts adjacency and approximate distance, not sequence. Only when scaffolds are placed on a genetic or physical map, or assembled telomere to telomere, do they become chromosomes (Nurk et al. 2022). Short-read assemblers such as SPAdes (Bankevich et al. 2012) fragment at repeats longer than the read pairs can span; long-read assemblers such as Canu (Koren et al. 2016) and Flye (Kolmogorov et al. 2018) resolve most of those repeats but inherit the higher per-base error of the underlying chemistry.
The statistic you will see quoted first is almost always N50: the length of the contig such that contigs of that length or longer contain at least half of the assembly’s total bases. It is a weighted median, and that is exactly its weakness.

def n50(lengths):
    """Length of the contig at which half the assembly's bases are reached."""
    ordered = sorted(lengths, reverse=True)
    half = sum(ordered) / 2
    running = 0
    for length in ordered:
        running += length
        if running >= half:
            return length
    raise ValueError("empty assembly")

careful = [900_000, 800_000, 700_000, 600_000, 500_000] + [1_000] * 500
reckless = [2_500_000] + [1_000] * 1_500
print(f"careful : {len(careful):4d} contigs, {sum(careful):,} bp, N50 = {n50(careful):,}")
#> careful :  505 contigs, 4,000,000 bp, N50 = 700,000
print(f"reckless: {len(reckless):4d} contigs, {sum(reckless):,} bp, N50 = {n50(reckless):,}")
#> reckless: 1501 contigs, 4,000,000 bp, N50 = 2,500,000

Both assemblies have the same total length. The second has a much larger N50 and is much worse: it was produced by an assembler that resolved an ambiguity aggressively and fused regions that the data did not justify joining. N50 rewards exactly that behaviour, because it measures contiguity and says nothing about correctness. It is also not comparable between assemblies of different total size, which is why NG50, computed against an expected genome size rather than the assembled total, is preferred when a reference size is known. QUAST (Gurevich et al. 2013) reports both, along with misassembly counts when a reference is available.
Two further checks matter more than contiguity. Completeness is usually estimated with BUSCO (Manni et al. 2021), which searches the assembly for a lineage-specific set of genes present in single copy in nearly all members of that lineage and reports each as complete, duplicated, fragmented or missing. A high fragmented count points at an under-assembled or error-rich draft; a high duplicated count points at uncollapsed haplotypes or genuine polyploidy. Contamination is the other check: Kraken 2 (Wood, Lu, and Langmead 2019) classifies contigs taxonomically, and contigs whose taxonomy disagrees with the rest of the assembly are candidates for removal. Annotating a contaminated assembly produces genes that are real but belong to the wrong organism, and they propagate into every database that mirrors your submission.






Three numbers before you annotate



Record total length, number of contigs and BUSCO completeness in your laboratory notebook before the annotation step, and again after. If the gene count surprises you later, these three numbers tell you immediately whether to suspect the assembly or the gene finder.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
text:
8.3 Measuring the genome in hand
The bundled M. genitalium assembly is a finished, circular, single-contig genome, so contiguity statistics are trivial: N50 equals the genome length. What is worth measuring is composition, because composition constrains everything that follows.

from collections import Counter
from Bio import SeqIO

record = SeqIO.read(book_data("sequences", "mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta"),
                    "fasta")
genome = str(record.seq).upper()
counts = Counter(genome)
gc_percent = 100 * (counts["G"] + counts["C"]) / len(genome)

print(f"{record.id}: {len(genome):,} bp")
#> NC_000908.2: 580,076 bp
print(f"A={counts['A']:,}  C={counts['C']:,}  G={counts['G']:,}  T={counts['T']:,}")
#> A=200,544  C=91,515  G=92,306  T=195,711
print(f"ambiguous bases: {len(genome) - sum(counts[b] for b in 'ACGT')}")
#> ambiguous bases: 0
print(f"GC content: {gc_percent:.2f}%")
#> GC content: 31.69%

Three things follow from that output. There are no ambiguous bases, so this is a finished sequence rather than a draft with gaps. The GC content of 31.69% is low, which matters for gene finding because codon usage and start-codon preference both shift with composition, and because a naive open-reading-frame scan in an AT-rich genome produces more spurious long ORFs by chance. And at 580,076 bp the genome is small enough that an exhaustive six-frame analysis costs nothing.
M. genitalium belongs to the Mollicutes, which use genetic code 4: the codon TGA encodes tryptophan rather than termination. Getting this wrong is not a subtlety. Under the bacterial default, code 11, every internal TGA is read as a stop, and genes are chopped into fragments.






The genetic code is a parameter, not a default



Translation tables differ between bacterial clades, between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, and between some ciliates and everything else. A gene finder run with the wrong table does not fail — it returns a plausible-looking answer with roughly twice as many, roughly half as long, genes. You will see this quantified in Section 8.4. Always look up the translation table for your organism before the first run, and record it in your methods.


Repeats and why masking comes first
A repeat is a sequence that occurs in multiple copies in a genome: tandem satellite arrays, transposable elements, segmental duplications, and the dispersed families such as Alu and LINE-1 that between them cover roughly half of the human genome (Lander et al. 2001). Repeats cause two separate problems. They break assemblies, as described above. And they wreck gene prediction, because a transposon carries its own open reading frames, its own splice-site-like motifs and its own promoters; an unmasked eukaryotic genome yields thousands of predicted “genes” that are transposase fragments.
Masking marks repetitive regions so that downstream tools can ignore or down-weight them. Hard masking replaces the bases with N, soft masking lower-cases them, and soft masking is almost always the right choice because it preserves the sequence for any tool that wants it while letting repeat-aware tools skip it. Prokaryotic genomes are repeat-poor enough — M. genitalium has no large repeat families — that masking is usually skipped, which is one of several reasons bacterial annotation is easier.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
section: 8.4 Finding genes in a compact bacterial genome
text:
8.4 Finding genes in a compact bacterial genome
Bacterial protein-coding genes are, with rare exceptions, uninterrupted: one start codon, one reading frame, one stop codon. That makes the search space finite. A gene finder enumerates every open reading frame (ORF) — every stretch from a potential start codon to the next in-frame stop — and then has to decide which ORFs are real and, for each real one, which of several possible start codons the ribosome actually uses.
Prodigal (Hyatt et al. 2010) makes both decisions with models it trains on the genome itself, which is why it needs no reference database. It first builds a coding model from the hexamer composition of long, unambiguous ORFs, so that a candidate’s coding score reflects how closely its codon statistics resemble the genome’s own genes. It then examines the region immediately upstream of each candidate start and learns the translation initiation signal: in most bacteria a Shine–Dalgarno ribosome-binding site, a purine-rich motif such as AGGAGG positioned 5–10 bp before the start codon and complementary to the 3’ end of the 16S rRNA. Where no Shine–Dalgarno signal is detectable, Prodigal switches to a generic upstream motif model. The final start call combines coding score, upstream motif score and start-codon type.
Prodigal is an external binary, but it is pinned in the book’s environment.yml and runs on this genome in well under a second, so the chapter runs it for real rather than quoting a stored result. The command-line form is the one you would type:
prodigal -i data/sequences/mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta \
         -o mgen_prodigal.gff -f gff -a mgen_prodigal.faa -g 4
-f gff asks for GFF output rather than Prodigal’s default GenBank-like format, -a writes the translated proteins, and -g 4 selects the genetic code. The same command is issued below from Python so that its output feeds the rest of the chapter.

import subprocess, tempfile, shutil, os

if shutil.which("prodigal") is None:
    raise RuntimeError("prodigal is not on PATH; install the book environment first")

workdir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="mgen_annotation_")
fasta = book_data("sequences", "mycoplasma-genitalium-NC_000908.2.fasta")

def run_prodigal(table):
    """Predict genes with the given translation table; return the GFF path."""
    out = os.path.join(workdir, f"prodigal_table{table}.gff")
    subprocess.run(["prodigal", "-i", fasta, "-o", out, "-f", "gff",
                    "-g", str(table), "-q"], check=True)
    return out

gff_code4 = run_prodigal(4)
gff_code11 = run_prodigal(11)

The two runs differ only in the translation table, and that single parameter changes the answer completely.

def count_cds(path):
    with open(path) as handle:
        return sum(1 for line in handle if not line.startswith("#") and line.strip())

print(f"genetic code 4  (Mollicutes): {count_cds(gff_code4):4d} predicted CDS")
#> genetic code 4  (Mollicutes):  527 predicted CDS
print(f"genetic code 11 (bacterial default): {count_cds(gff_code11):4d} predicted CDS")
#> genetic code 11 (bacterial default):  995 predicted CDS

Nearly twice as many genes, because every internal TGA tryptophan codon terminated a reading frame prematurely and the true gene was reported as two or three fragments. Nothing in the output flags the problem; the GFF is well-formed and the proteins are translatable. Only the biology is wrong. The rest of the chapter uses the code-4 predictions.

def parse_gff(path):
    """Yield one dictionary per GFF3 feature line, attributes already split."""
    features = []
    with open(path) as handle:
        for line in handle:
            if line.startswith("#") or not line.strip():
                continue
            fields = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
            if len(fields) != 9:
                continue
            attributes = dict(pair.split("=", 1)
                              for pair in fields[8].rstrip(";").split(";")
                              if "=" in pair)
            features.append({"seqid": fields[0], "source": fields[1],
                             "type": fields[2], "start": int(fields[3]),
                             "end": int(fields[4]), "score": fields[5],
                             "strand": fields[6], "phase": fields[7],
                             "attributes": attributes})
    return features

predicted = parse_gff(gff_code4)
print(f"{len(predicted)} predicted CDS features")
#> 527 predicted CDS features
print(Counter(feature["attributes"]["start_type"] for feature in predicted))
#> Counter({'ATG': 458, 'GTG': 50, 'TTG': 19})

The start-codon distribution is itself informative: ATG dominates, but GTG and TTG together account for a substantial minority. A gene finder that only considered ATG would truncate every one of those genes at the first internal ATG, shortening the protein and shifting the annotated promoter region.
