title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
section: 8.5 Comparing two annotations of the same genome
text:
8.5 Comparing two annotations of the same genome
The RefSeq annotation of this genome was produced by the NCBI Prokaryotic Genome Annotation Pipeline (Tatusova et al. 2016), which combines ab initio prediction with protein homology evidence and curated rules. It is a useful comparator precisely because it was built differently from the Prodigal run.

reference = parse_gff(book_data("annotation", "mycoplasma-genitalium.gff"))
print(Counter(feature["type"] for feature in reference).most_common())
#> [('gene', 546), ('CDS', 524), ('exon', 42), ('tRNA', 36), ('pseudogene', 20), ('rRNA', 3), ('region', 1), ('SRP_RNA', 1), ('RNase_P_RNA', 1), ('tmRNA', 1)]

Count the feature types before anything else. There are 546 gene features but only 524 CDS features, and 20 pseudogene features; the difference is made up of the tRNA, rRNA and other structural RNA genes, which have a gene parent but no CDS child. Conflating “number of gene lines” with “number of proteins” is the single most common arithmetic error in annotation summaries.
The right way to ask whether two annotations agree is to match genes by their stop codon, not their start. The stop is determined by the reading frame and is rarely ambiguous; the start is a prediction in its own right. On the plus strand the stop is at the feature’s end coordinate, on the minus strand at its start.

reference_cds = [f for f in reference if f["type"] == "CDS"]

def stop_key(feature):
    """Strand plus the coordinate of the 3' end: a frame-anchored gene identity."""
    return (feature["strand"],
            feature["end"] if feature["strand"] == "+" else feature["start"])

reference_by_stop = {stop_key(f): f for f in reference_cds}
predicted_by_stop = {stop_key(f): f for f in predicted}
shared = set(reference_by_stop) & set(predicted_by_stop)

print(f"RefSeq CDS        : {len(reference_cds)}")
#> RefSeq CDS        : 524
print(f"Prodigal CDS      : {len(predicted)}")
#> Prodigal CDS      : 527
print(f"shared 3' ends    : {len(shared)}")
#> shared 3' ends    : 501
print(f"RefSeq only       : {len(set(reference_by_stop) - set(predicted_by_stop))}")
#> RefSeq only       : 23
print(f"Prodigal only     : {len(set(predicted_by_stop) - set(reference_by_stop))}")
#> Prodigal only     : 26

Of 524 RefSeq coding sequences and 527 Prodigal predictions, 501 share a 3’ end. That is roughly 95% gene-level agreement between an evidence-informed curated pipeline and a database-free ab initio run, which is the usual state of affairs for a compact bacterial genome and should not be extrapolated to anything larger or more repetitive.
The 23 RefSeq-only features are the more interesting side of the disagreement.

reference_only = set(reference_by_stop) - set(predicted_by_stop)
pseudo = [key for key in reference_only
          if reference_by_stop[key]["attributes"].get("pseudo") == "true"]
print(f"{len(pseudo)} of {len(reference_only)} RefSeq-only features are pseudogenes")
#> 19 of 23 RefSeq-only features are pseudogenes
for key in sorted(pseudo)[:3]:
    attributes = reference_by_stop[key]["attributes"]
    print(" -", attributes.get("product"), "|", attributes.get("Note"))
#>  - hypothetical protein | incomplete%3B partial in the middle of a contig%3B missing N-terminus and C-terminus
#>  - adhesin P1 | incomplete%3B partial in the middle of a contig%3B missing N-terminus and C-terminus
#>  - adhesin | incomplete%3B partial in the middle of a contig%3B missing N-terminus and C-terminus

Nineteen of the 23 are annotated pseudogenes: genes that homology evidence shows were once functional but that now carry a frameshift or an internal stop. RefSeq records them because a reader needs to know the locus exists and is broken. Prodigal does not report them because they are not open reading frames. Neither behaviour is a bug; they answer different questions. Five of these RefSeq CDS features have a length that is not a multiple of three, which is a deliberate signal that the feature spans a frameshift and must not be naively translated.
Boundary disagreements are the other, larger, class.

def start_offset(reference_feature, predicted_feature):
    """Signed distance from the RefSeq start to the Prodigal start, in bp."""
    if reference_feature["strand"] == "+":
        return predicted_feature["start"] - reference_feature["start"]
    return reference_feature["end"] - predicted_feature["end"]

offsets = {key: start_offset(reference_by_stop[key], predicted_by_stop[key])
           for key in shared}
identical = sum(1 for value in offsets.values() if value == 0)
print(f"identical at both ends: {identical} of {len(shared)}")
#> identical at both ends: 464 of 501
print(f"start-codon disagreements: {len(shared) - identical}")
#> start-codon disagreements: 37
in_frame = sum(1 for value in offsets.values() if value and value % 3 == 0)
print(f"of which in-frame (a different start in the same frame): {in_frame}")
#> of which in-frame (a different start in the same frame): 36

Of the 501 genes both methods find, 464 agree on both coordinates exactly. Of the 37 that differ, 36 differ by a multiple of three: the two methods chose different start codons within the same reading frame. The single exception is a RefSeq pseudogene annotated across a frameshift, whose CDS length is deliberately not a multiple of three. This is the classic boundary disagreement and it has a biological cause. Many bacterial genes have several in-frame candidate starts within the first 60 bp, the ribosome-binding signal is weak or absent, and the choice between them rests on a probabilistic model rather than on evidence. Two models trained on different data choose differently. The consequence is a protein that is a handful of residues longer or shorter at the N-terminus — usually harmless, occasionally fatal if the difference removes a signal peptide or a start-proximal catalytic residue.
Figure 8.1 shows what these two gene sets look like side by side.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

reference_lengths = np.array([f["end"] - f["start"] + 1 for f in reference_cds])
predicted_lengths = np.array([f["end"] - f["start"] + 1 for f in predicted])
bins = np.logspace(np.log10(80), np.log10(12000), 40)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(reference_lengths, bins=bins, alpha=0.55, label="RefSeq")
ax.hist(predicted_lengths, bins=bins, alpha=0.55, label="Prodigal")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Coding sequence length (bp, log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of genes")
ax.set_title("Gene length distributions")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 8.1: Distribution of coding sequence lengths in the RefSeq annotation and in the Prodigal prediction for Mycoplasmoides genitalium G37. The two distributions are nearly superimposed, with the small excess of very short Prodigal features at the left representing predictions RefSeq does not make.




The distributions are close to identical, with a median near 855 bp in both cases, which corresponds to a protein of about 285 residues. The visible excess of short Prodigal features on the left is where 10 of the 26 Prodigal-only predictions sit: short ORFs with acceptable coding scores that the RefSeq pipeline rejected for lack of homology support. Short ab initio predictions in an AT-rich genome are the category that most often turns out to be noise, and also the category where genuine small proteins are most often missed. Neither annotation can settle the question without proteomic or ribosome-profiling evidence.
Figure 8.2 shows how densely those genes are packed along the chromosome.

coded = np.zeros(len(genome), dtype=bool)
for feature in reference_cds:
    coded[feature["start"] - 1:feature["end"]] = True

window = 5000
edges = range(0, len(genome) - window, window)
density = [100 * coded[i:i + window].mean() for i in edges]
gc_window = [100 * (genome.count("G", i, i + window) + genome.count("C", i, i + window))
             / window for i in edges]
positions = [i / 1000 for i in edges]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(positions, density, linewidth=1.2, label="coding density")
ax.plot(positions, gc_window, linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--", label="GC content")
ax.set_xlabel("Genome position (kb)")
ax.set_ylabel("Percentage of window")
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
#> (0.0, 100.0)
ax.set_title("Coding density and composition")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 8.2: Coding density and GC content of Mycoplasmoides genitalium G37 in non-overlapping 5 kb windows, computed from the RefSeq CDS features. Coding density stays above 74% in every window except the one beginning at 170 kb, which falls to 0.5% because it contains the ribosomal RNA operon and no protein-coding genes.




The single conspicuous feature is the window beginning at 170 kb, where coding density collapses to 0.5%: that window holds the 16S, 23S and 5S ribosomal RNA genes, which are transcribed but not translated and therefore contribute no CDS. Across the whole chromosome, 94.64% of bases fall inside an annotated CDS, and 96.05% fall inside some annotated feature once the structural RNAs are included. That is extreme even for a bacterium, and it is a direct consequence of genome reduction: this organism has discarded almost everything that is not a gene. Two practical lessons follow. First, intergenic distance is a usable diagnostic here — 197 adjacent CDS pairs actually overlap, most commonly by 1, 8 or 11 bp, which is the signature of translationally coupled operons in which a stop codon and the next start codon share or nearly share bases. Second, a window of low coding density in a genome like this is worth investigating rather than ignoring; in a eukaryote it would be unremarkable.
Figure 8.3 summarises the comparison in the form you would put in a methods supplement.

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))

categories = ["identical", "start\ndiffers", "RefSeq\nonly", "Prodigal\nonly"]
values = [identical, len(shared) - identical,
          len(reference_only), len(set(predicted_by_stop) - set(reference_by_stop))]
left.bar(categories, values)
for index, value in enumerate(values):
    left.text(index, value + 8, str(value), ha="center", fontsize=9)
left.set_ylabel("Number of genes")
left.set_title("Gene-level agreement")

differences = [value for value in offsets.values() if value != 0]
right.hist(differences, bins=np.arange(-180, 181, 15), color="#117864")
right.axvline(0, color="#922B21", linewidth=1)
right.set_xlabel("Prodigal start − RefSeq start (bp)")
right.set_ylabel("Number of genes")
right.set_title("Start-codon offsets")

fig.tight_layout()






Figure 8.3: Agreement between the Prodigal prediction and the RefSeq annotation. Left: gene-level classification by shared 3’ end. Right: signed distance from the RefSeq start codon to the Prodigal start codon for the 37 genes that share a stop but not a start; negative values mean Prodigal chose an upstream start.




The left panel is the summary a reviewer wants: 464 genes identical, 37 differing only in their start, 23 found only by RefSeq and 26 only by Prodigal. The right panel shows that the start disagreements are not a smooth distribution around zero but a set of discrete in-frame offsets, and that they are close to balanced in direction: Prodigal places its start upstream of RefSeq’s in 17 genes and downstream in 20. The disagreement is therefore not a systematic bias in one method but a genuine ambiguity in the data, resolved differently by a motif model and by an alignment to a homologous protein. Homology evidence is the more defensible tie-breaker, which is the single best argument for running an evidence-based pipeline such as Prokka (Seemann 2014) or PGAP rather than a bare gene finder.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
text:
8.6 Gene prediction in eukaryotes
Everything above depended on the assumption that a gene is one uninterrupted reading frame. In eukaryotes it is not, and every part of the problem becomes harder.
A eukaryotic protein-coding gene is transcribed as a pre-mRNA containing exons separated by introns that are spliced out. The spliceosome recognises short, degenerate signals: a GT at the intron’s 5’ end, an AG at its 3’ end, a branch point and a polypyrimidine tract. Those motifs are far too short to locate reliably on their own — a genome contains a GT every 16 bp by chance — so a predictor must combine them with coding-potential models on both sides and with constraints on intron length. Human introns range from under 100 bp to over a megabase, so the search space is enormous. Alternative splicing then means that the correct answer is not one gene model but several: the same locus can produce transcripts with different exon content, different reading frames and different protein products. A tool asked to report a single model per locus is being asked the wrong question.
Ab initio eukaryotic predictors such as AUGUSTUS (Stanke et al. 2006) use generalised hidden Markov models whose states correspond to the parts of a gene — intergenic, 5’ UTR, initial exon, intron, internal exon, terminal exon — and whose parameters must be trained on a set of known genes from a related species. Run on a novel genome with mis-matched training parameters, they produce gene sets whose counts can be wrong by a factor of two.
Modern practice is therefore evidence-based annotation: predictions are made in the presence of data that directly observes transcription. RNA-seq reads aligned with a spliced aligner give exon boundaries and splice junctions empirically — a junction supported by 200 reads is not a hypothesis — and full-length long-read cDNA gives complete models. Proteins from related species, aligned to the genome, confirm coding regions and reading frames. A combiner reconciles all three into a consensus gene set, so the annotation’s quality is bounded by the tissue coverage of the evidence: a gene expressed only in a developmental stage you did not sample will be annotated badly or not at all.






Annotation versions are not interchangeable



Ensembl (Cunningham et al. 2021) and RefSeq (Sayers et al. 2021) annotate the same human genome and do not produce identical gene models, and each changes between releases. Gene counts, exon boundaries and even the set of genes considered protein-coding move. Record the exact annotation release used in any analysis — Ensembl 110, RefSeq GCF_000001405.40-RS_2023_10 — because a count computed against one release cannot be compared with a count computed against another.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
section: 8.7 From a predicted protein to a biological function
text:
8.7 From a predicted protein to a biological function
Structural annotation says where the genes are. Functional annotation says what they do, and it is almost entirely an exercise in inference by similarity.
The simplest form is homology transfer: search the predicted protein against a curated database with BLAST (Altschul et al. 1990) or a more sensitive profile method, and copy the description of the best hit. This works when the hit is strong, nearly full length and to a protein whose function was experimentally determined. It fails in characteristic ways. Similarity over a shared domain does not imply shared overall function; a protein kinase domain tells you the protein phosphorylates something, not what. Enzymes in the same superfamily can differ in substrate. And best-hit transfer confuses orthologues — genes in different species that descend from a single ancestral gene via speciation, and usually do keep their function — with paralogues, which arose by duplication within a lineage and frequently diverge in function. Orthology-aware resources exist because the best BLAST hit is often a paralogue.
Domain annotation is more conservative and more durable. Pfam (Mistry et al. 2020) models protein families and domains as profile hidden Markov models built from curated seed alignments, and searching a protein against them with HMMER (Eddy 2011) reports which domains are present, in what order, and over which residues. InterPro (Paysan-Lafosse et al. 2022) integrates Pfam with a dozen other signature databases and maps the result onto Gene Ontology terms. A domain architecture is a statement about the protein’s parts and is far less likely to be wrong than a transferred description, which is why curated resources show domains and evidence rather than a single functional label.






Annotation errors propagate and compound



When a protein is annotated by copying the description of its best database hit, and that description was itself copied from an earlier best hit, the chain of inference can be many steps long and no step is recorded. A single mis-annotation in a well-populated family can be re-copied into hundreds of genomes within a few years, and the resulting consensus looks like independent corroboration. The defences are specific: prefer domain-level and orthology-based assignments to best-hit transfer; demand alignment coverage of at least 70–80% of both query and subject before transferring a description; treat a hit whose own annotation carries an electronic evidence code as a hypothesis, not a fact; and propagate the evidence alongside the label so the next person can re-evaluate it.


It is worth measuring how much of a well-studied proteome is still unexplained.

products = [f["attributes"].get("product", "") for f in reference_cds]
hypothetical = sum(1 for p in products if "hypothetical" in p)
duf = sum(1 for p in products if "DUF" in p)
print(f"hypothetical protein : {hypothetical}")
#> hypothetical protein : 27
print(f"domain of unknown function (DUF): {duf}")
#> domain of unknown function (DUF): 27
print(f"combined: {100 * (hypothetical + duf) / len(products):.1f}% of coding sequences")
#> combined: 10.3% of coding sequences

Just over 10% of the proteome of one of the most intensively studied minimal organisms is still unannotated after three decades of work on it. That is a useful calibration for how much of any new genome’s functional annotation is genuinely known.
Controlled vocabularies and evidence codes
Free-text product descriptions cannot be computed on: DNA polymerase III subunit beta, DNA pol III beta and beta clamp are the same thing to a reader and three different strings to a program. Controlled vocabularies solve this by assigning stable identifiers to concepts.
The Gene Ontology (Ashburner et al. 2000; Aleksander et al. 2023) is the most widely used. It provides three independent hierarchies — molecular function, biological process and cellular component — organised as a directed acyclic graph in which a term may have several parents and in which an annotation to a term implies annotation to all its ancestors. A gene annotated to GO:0003887 (DNA-directed DNA polymerase activity) is thereby also annotated to the broader nucleotidyltransferase and catalytic activity terms, which is what makes enrichment analysis possible. EC numbers provide a complementary four-level classification of enzymatic reactions (2.7.7.7 is DNA-directed DNA polymerase), and KEGG (Kanehisa 2000) maps gene products onto metabolic and signalling pathways.
Every GO annotation carries an evidence code stating how it was arrived at. EXP and its children mark experimental evidence; IDA is a direct assay; IMP is inference from a mutant phenotype; ISS is inference from sequence similarity, assigned by a curator; IEA is inferred from electronic annotation, assigned automatically with no curator review. The RefSeq GFF carries these in its go_function, go_process and go_component attributes.

evidence = Counter()
with_go = 0
for feature in reference_cds:
    has_go = False
    for key in ("go_function", "go_process", "go_component"):
        if key in feature["attributes"]:
            has_go = True
            for item in feature["attributes"][key].split(","):
                parts = item.split("|")
                if len(parts) >= 4:
                    evidence[parts[3]] += 1
    with_go += has_go

print(f"CDS with at least one GO term: {with_go} of {len(reference_cds)}")
#> CDS with at least one GO term: 331 of 524
print("evidence codes:", dict(evidence))
#> evidence codes: {'IEA': 985}

Every one of the 985 GO annotations in this file carries the code IEA. Not one was reviewed by a curator for this organism. This is entirely normal — the overwhelming majority of GO annotations in any genome are IEA — but it changes how you should read an enrichment result. An enrichment of a GO term among your differentially expressed genes, computed against an IEA-only background, is a statement about which sequence features your gene set shares, filtered through a transfer pipeline. It is a hypothesis-generating observation, not evidence that the process is active.






Read the evidence code before the term



When a functional enrichment result surprises you, retrieve the evidence codes for the genes driving it. A term driven entirely by IEA annotations on hypothetical proteins is a different kind of finding from one driven by IDA annotations on characterised enzymes, and only the second justifies a confident claim in a discussion section.

section: 8.8 The anatomy of GFF3 and GTF
text:
8.8 The anatomy of GFF3 and GTF
Annotation is exchanged as tab-delimited feature tables, and almost every frustrating bug in a genomics pipeline is a misunderstanding of one of nine columns. A GFF3 line has exactly these fields, in order: seqid, source, type, start, end, score, strand, phase, attributes.

first_cds = next(f for f in reference if f["type"] == "CDS")
for name in ("seqid", "source", "type", "start", "end", "score", "strand", "phase"):
    print(f"{name:8s} = {first_cds[name]}")
#> seqid    = NC_000908.2
#> source   = Protein Homology
#> type     = CDS
#> start    = 686
#> end      = 1828
#> score    = .
#> strand   = +
#> phase    = 0
for name in ("ID", "Parent", "gene", "product", "protein_id", "transl_table"):
    print(f"  attr {name:12s} = {first_cds['attributes'].get(name)}")
#>   attr ID           = cds-WP_009885562.1
#>   attr Parent       = gene-MG_RS00005
#>   attr gene         = dnaN
#>   attr product      = DNA polymerase III subunit beta
#>   attr protein_id   = WP_009885562.1
#>   attr transl_table = 4

seqid must match the FASTA identifier exactly, and the commonest cause of an empty result from a tool that takes both files is a mismatch between NC_000908.2 here and NC_000908 or chr1 there. source records the program or database that made the claim, which lets you filter a mixed annotation by provenance — here RefSeq genes carry RefSeq while their CDS children carry Protein Homology, recording that the coding region was called from protein alignment evidence. type should be a Sequence Ontology term. score and phase are . when not applicable; phase on a CDS is 0, 1 or 2 and gives the number of bases to skip at the start of that feature to reach the first complete codon, which matters only for CDS split across multiple lines.






Coordinates are not interchangeable between formats



GFF3, GTF, SAM and VCF are 1-based and inclusive: a feature from 686 to 1828 includes both endpoints and has length 1828 − 686 + 1 = 1143 bp. BED and the internal coordinates of most programming libraries are 0-based and half-open: the same interval is written 685–1828 and its length is simply 1828 − 685. Python and R slicing inherit this split — Python strings are 0-based half-open, R vectors are 1-based inclusive. Converting in the wrong direction shifts every feature by one base, which silently changes reading frames, moves variants between codons, and produces proteins that are almost but not quite right. Write the conversion once, in a named function, and test it on a feature whose sequence you know.


The attributes column is a semicolon-separated list of tag=value pairs, and it is where the structure lives. ID is unique within the file; Parent points at another feature’s ID and builds the hierarchy. In GFF3 the relationship is explicit and may be many levels deep: gene → mRNA → exon and CDS. GTF, the older format that many RNA-seq tools still require, instead encodes the same hierarchy implicitly through gene_id and transcript_id attributes on every line, and uses spaces and quotes rather than =. A GTF parser applied to a GFF3 file will often run without error and return nothing.

by_id = {f["attributes"]["ID"]: f for f in reference if "ID" in f["attributes"]}
children = Counter()
for feature in reference:
    parent = feature["attributes"].get("Parent")
    if parent in by_id:
        children[(by_id[parent]["type"], feature["type"])] += 1
for (parent_type, child_type), number in children.most_common():
    print(f"{parent_type:12s} -> {child_type:8s} : {number}")
#> gene         -> CDS      : 504
#> gene         -> tRNA     : 36
#> tRNA         -> exon     : 36
#> pseudogene   -> CDS      : 20
#> gene         -> rRNA     : 3
#> rRNA         -> exon     : 3
#> gene         -> SRP_RNA  : 1
#> SRP_RNA      -> exon     : 1
#> gene         -> RNase_P_RNA : 1
#> RNase_P_RNA  -> exon     : 1
#> gene         -> tmRNA    : 1
#> tmRNA        -> exon     : 1

Two hierarchies are visible. Protein-coding genes have a single CDS child and no exon feature, because a bacterial CDS is contiguous. The structural RNA genes have an RNA-level child which in turn has an exon child. That asymmetry is the second classic pitfall: CDS and exon are not the same feature. An exon is what is present in the mature transcript, including untranslated regions; a CDS is the translated part. A read-counting tool configured to count over exon features will report nothing for a bacterial annotation that contains CDS features only, and will count UTR reads in a eukaryotic annotation that contains both. Always check which feature type your counter is using.
The third pitfall is discontinuous features. A spliced CDS is written as several lines sharing one ID, not as one line spanning the introns. Code that treats each line as a separate gene will multiply your gene count by the mean exon number; code that takes min(start) and max(end) will include the introns in the length. Group by ID and sum the segment lengths.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
text:
8.9 Assessing and releasing an annotation
An annotation needs its own quality assessment, separate from the assembly’s.
Start with internal consistency. Every CDS length should be a multiple of three unless it is explicitly marked as a pseudogene or as partial; every complete CDS should begin with a valid start codon and end with a stop codon in the chosen translation table; no CDS should contain an internal stop.

stop_codons = {"TAA", "TAG"}          # genetic code 4: TGA encodes tryptophan
complement = str.maketrans("ACGT", "TGCA")

def cds_sequence(feature):
    """Extract a CDS in its coding orientation, 1-based inclusive coordinates."""
    segment = genome[feature["start"] - 1:feature["end"]]
    return segment if feature["strand"] == "+" else segment.translate(complement)[::-1]

bad_length = sum(1 for f in predicted if (f["end"] - f["start"] + 1) % 3)
bad_stop = sum(1 for f in predicted if cds_sequence(f)[-3:] not in stop_codons)
internal = sum(1 for f in predicted
               if any(cds_sequence(f)[i:i + 3] in stop_codons
                      for i in range(0, len(cds_sequence(f)) - 3, 3)))
print(f"length not a multiple of three : {bad_length}")
#> length not a multiple of three : 0
print(f"does not end in a stop codon   : {bad_stop}")
#> does not end in a stop codon   : 0
print(f"contains an internal stop codon: {internal}")
#> contains an internal stop codon: 0

All three counts are zero, which is the expected result for a complete ab initio gene set run with the right translation table. The same check applied to the code-11 predictions is where the earlier mistake finally becomes visible.

wrong_table = parse_gff(gff_code11)
ends_in_tga = sum(1 for f in wrong_table if cds_sequence(f)[-3:] == "TGA")
print(f"code-11 predictions ending in TGA: {ends_in_tga} of {len(wrong_table)}")
#> code-11 predictions ending in TGA: 612 of 995

Under code 4, TGA is tryptophan, so 612 of the 995 code-11 predictions terminate at a codon that is not a stop codon in this organism. A check of this kind — does the gene set obey the rules of the genetic code you believe applies? — costs three lines and catches an error that no amount of staring at a GFF file will reveal.
Then compare against expectation. Coding density of 85–90% is normal for bacteria; a prediction at 60% suggests a missed translation table or a contaminated assembly, and one at 99% suggests spurious short ORFs. Mean protein length near 300 residues is typical; a sharp drop indicates fragmentation. BUSCO can be run on the predicted proteins rather than the genome, which separates “the gene is absent from the assembly” from “the gene is present but was not predicted”. Checking the fraction of proteins with a Pfam domain gives a rough measure of how much of the gene set is plausible.
For release, the conventions are strict and worth learning early. Sequences go to GenBank, ENA or DDBJ, which exchange records nightly, so a deposit in one appears in all three. A prokaryotic submission is usually contigs plus a feature table; NCBI will run PGAP on it, and the RefSeq record you download later is NCBI’s annotation, not necessarily yours. Locus tags must be requested as a registered prefix — MG_RS00005 follows that convention — and must be unique and stable, because they become the handle by which your genes are cited. Product names follow guidelines that forbid molecular weights, database identifiers and the unqualified word “homolog”. The assembly receives a versioned accession such as GCF_000027325.1, and that accession, not the organism name, belongs in a methods section.






Annotation provenance is part of the result



When you publish an analysis that depends on an annotation, record the assembly accession, the annotation source and release, the gene finder and its version, the translation table, and the evidence used for functional assignment. Without these a reader cannot reproduce your gene counts, and an unreproducible gene count undermines every statistic computed from it. This is as true for a clinical pipeline, where an annotation release change can alter a variant’s reported consequence, as for a comparative genomics paper.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
text:
8.10 Summary

An assembly is a hypothesis; check its contiguity, completeness and contamination before annotating, because annotation inherits every assembly error and adds its own.
N50 measures contiguity, not correctness, and rewards over-aggressive assembly. Report it with total length, contig count, BUSCO completeness and, where a reference size is known, NG50.
The translation table is a parameter you must set deliberately. On M. genitalium the bacterial default produces 995 predicted genes against 527 with the correct code 4, and nothing in the output signals the error.
Prokaryotic gene finding is a solved problem to a first approximation: ab initio Prodigal and the curated RefSeq pipeline agree on the 3’ end of 501 genes out of roughly 525, and on both ends of 464.
Disagreements between annotations concentrate in start codons rather than in gene presence, because the start is a prediction and the stop is a consequence of the reading frame.
Eukaryotic prediction requires external evidence — RNA-seq, long-read cDNA, protein alignments — because introns and alternative splicing make the ab initio problem underdetermined.
Functional annotation is inference by similarity, and the inference chain is usually invisible. Prefer domain and orthology assignments to best-hit transfer, and read the evidence code before the term: all 985 GO annotations in this genome are IEA.
GFF3 bugs are coordinate bugs. Remember that GFF3 is 1-based inclusive and BED is 0-based half-open, that CDS and exon are different features, and that a spliced feature occupies several lines sharing one ID.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
text:
8.11 Exercises

The genome has a GC content of 31.69%. Compute the GC content of the Prodigal predicted coding regions only, and of the non-coding remainder. Which is higher, and why would you expect that?
Compute the number of Prodigal predictions shorter than 300 bp and their median length. How many of them share a 3’ end with a RefSeq CDS?
Using the RefSeq GFF, count features by type and reconcile the 546 gene features with the 524 CDS features. Which gene biotypes make up the difference?
Write a function that converts a GFF3 interval to BED format and apply it to the first five RefSeq CDS features. Verify that the length computed from the BED coordinates matches the length computed from the GFF3 coordinates.
For the 37 genes where Prodigal and RefSeq disagree on the start codon, determine how often Prodigal’s start is upstream of RefSeq’s. What does the direction of the bias suggest about the two methods’ assumptions?
Extract the 197 overlapping adjacent CDS pairs from the RefSeq annotation and tabulate the overlap lengths. Which overlap lengths are most frequent, and what does a 1 bp or 4 bp overlap imply about how the two genes are translated?
Run Prodigal on the SARS-CoV-2 genome bundled with the book (data/sequences/sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta) in metagenomic mode, -p meta, which is required because 30 kb is too little sequence for Prodigal to train its own coding model. Compare the predictions with the twelve coding sequences the RefSeq record annotates, and explain both the matches and the misses. This exercise introduces no new technique but will make you cautious about gene finders applied outside their design envelope.
A collaborator sends you a GFF3 file for a fungal genome and reports 48,000 genes, which is three times what you expected. Without seeing the file, list four specific checks you would run, in order, and state what result from each would explain the inflated count.

title: 8  From assembled sequence to annotated genome
text:
8.12 Solutions






Solutions





1. Coding regions are GC-richer than the remainder. In an AT-rich genome, selection on codon usage and on amino acid composition keeps coding sequence closer to a compositional equilibrium than the unconstrained intergenic DNA, which drifts towards the mutational bias.

coding_mask = np.zeros(len(genome), dtype=bool)
for feature in predicted:
    coding_mask[feature["start"] - 1:feature["end"]] = True

bases = np.frombuffer(genome.encode(), dtype="S1")
is_gc = (bases == b"G") | (bases == b"C")
print(f"coding GC    : {100 * is_gc[coding_mask].mean():.2f}%")
#> coding GC    : 31.79%
print(f"non-coding GC: {100 * is_gc[~coding_mask].mean():.2f}%")
#> non-coding GC: 29.91%

2. Most of the short predictions are confirmed by RefSeq, but a tenth of the Prodigal gene set is short and a quarter of those short genes have no independent support — which is the honest statement of how much to trust a short ab initio ORF.

short = [f for f in predicted if (f["end"] - f["start"] + 1) < 300]
confirmed = sum(1 for f in short if stop_key(f) in reference_by_stop)
print(f"{len(short)} predictions under 300 bp; median "
      f"{int(np.median([f['end'] - f['start'] + 1 for f in short]))} bp")
#> 42 predictions under 300 bp; median 228 bp
print(f"{confirmed} of them share a 3' end with a RefSeq CDS")
#> 32 of them share a 3' end with a RefSeq CDS

3. The difference is made up of the structural RNA genes and the pseudogenes, which have gene features but no protein-coding CDS child of their own.

biotypes = Counter(f["attributes"].get("gene_biotype")
                   for f in reference if f["type"] == "gene")
for biotype, number in biotypes.most_common():
    print(f"{str(biotype):18s} {number}")
#> protein_coding     504
#> tRNA               36
#> rRNA               3
#> SRP_RNA            1
#> RNase_P_RNA        1
#> tmRNA              1

4. The conversion subtracts one from the start and leaves the end unchanged; the length is then simply end - start.

def gff_to_bed(feature):
    """GFF3 1-based inclusive -> BED 0-based half-open."""
    return (feature["seqid"], feature["start"] - 1, feature["end"])

for feature in reference_cds[:5]:
    seqid, bed_start, bed_end = gff_to_bed(feature)
    gff_length = feature["end"] - feature["start"] + 1
    assert bed_end - bed_start == gff_length
    print(f"{seqid}\t{bed_start}\t{bed_end}\tlength {gff_length}")
#> NC_000908.2  685 1828    length 1143
#> NC_000908.2  1827    2760    length 933
#> NC_000908.2  2844    4797    length 1953
#> NC_000908.2  4811    7322    length 2511
#> NC_000908.2  7293    8547    length 1254

5. The two directions are close to balanced, 17 upstream against 20 downstream, so neither method is systematically more permissive than the other. The disagreement reflects a real ambiguity — several in-frame candidate starts with a weak or absent ribosome-binding signal — rather than a known bias that could be corrected for. When the distinction matters, for example when the N-terminus carries a signal peptide, the start must be settled with N-terminal proteomics rather than with a better model.

upstream = sum(1 for value in offsets.values() if value < 0)
downstream = sum(1 for value in offsets.values() if value > 0)
print(f"Prodigal start upstream of RefSeq  : {upstream}")
#> Prodigal start upstream of RefSeq  : 17
print(f"Prodigal start downstream of RefSeq: {downstream}")
#> Prodigal start downstream of RefSeq: 20

6. Overlaps of 1 bp (45 pairs) and 8 bp (32 pairs) are the commonest, with 4 bp and 11 bp close behind. A 1 bp overlap is the TAATG arrangement, in which the final A of the stop codon TAA is also the first base of the downstream ATG; a 4 bp overlap is the ATGA arrangement, in which the whole start codon sits inside the stop codon. Both are hallmarks of translational coupling, where the ribosome reinitiates on the downstream cistron without releasing the message, which in turn means the two genes are obligately co-expressed. Note that the tabulation below pairs features by position alone and so includes some pairs on opposite strands, which are not translationally coupled; a stricter analysis would first filter on a shared strand.

ordered = sorted(reference_cds, key=lambda f: f["start"])
overlaps = [first["end"] - second["start"] + 1
            for first, second in zip(ordered, ordered[1:])
            if second["start"] <= first["end"]]
print(f"{len(overlaps)} overlapping adjacent pairs")
#> 197 overlapping adjacent pairs
print("most frequent overlap lengths:", Counter(overlaps).most_common(5))
#> most frequent overlap lengths: [(1, 45), (8, 32), (11, 17), (4, 14), (14, 14)]

7. Prodigal makes nine predictions. Eight of them match an annotated RefSeq CDS at both coordinates exactly — S, ORF3a, M, ORF6, ORF7a, ORF8, N, and the 13,218 bp first segment of ORF1ab — which is better than the exercise’s framing suggests. The failures are the instructive part. ORF1ab is reported as two separate genes because it is translated as one polyprotein only through a programmed −1 ribosomal frameshift, and no ORF-based model represents that. The envelope protein E (228 bp), ORF7b (132 bp) and ORF10 (117 bp) are missed entirely because they fall below the length at which an ORF can be distinguished from chance in a 30 kb sequence. The lesson is not that the tool is bad but that its gene model — one ORF, one protein, no frameshifting, enough sequence to train on — does not describe a coronavirus.

covid_fasta = book_data("sequences", "sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta")
covid_out = os.path.join(workdir, "sars_prodigal.gff")
subprocess.run(["prodigal", "-i", covid_fasta, "-o", covid_out,
                "-f", "gff", "-p", "meta", "-q"], check=True)
#> CompletedProcess(args=['prodigal', '-i', '/Users/umarahmad/.claude-science/orgs/2dbbb0cb-2805-4dbc-947b-19d18a9d3935/workspaces/e2774b04-77b6-40dd-b856-f7c7ffd027bd/book/data/sequences/sars-cov-2-NC_045512.2.fasta', '-o', '/Users/umarahmad/.claude-science/orgs/2dbbb0cb-2805-4dbc-947b-19d18a9d3935/workspaces/e2774b04-77b6-40dd-b856-f7c7ffd027bd/.tmp/mgen_annotation_mn7tajss/sars_prodigal.gff', '-f', 'gff', '-p', 'meta', '-q'], returncode=0)
covid = parse_gff(covid_out)
print(f"{len(covid)} predictions")
#> 9 predictions
for feature in sorted(covid, key=lambda f: f["start"]):
    print(f"  {feature['start']:6d}-{feature['end']:6d}  "
          f"{feature['end'] - feature['start'] + 1:6d} bp")
#>      266- 13483   13218 bp
#>    13768- 21555    7788 bp
#>    21563- 25384    3822 bp
#>    25393- 26220     828 bp
#>    26523- 27191     669 bp
#>    27202- 27387     186 bp
#>    27394- 27759     366 bp
#>    27894- 28259     366 bp
#>    28274- 29533    1260 bp

8. In order: check the feature types present, because counting every line rather than only gene lines inflates the total by the mean exon number; check whether spliced features have been split into one gene per exon by looking for repeated ID values; check whether the assembly was repeat-masked, because an unmasked fungal genome yields thousands of transposase ORFs; and check whether the predictions include both an ab initio set and an evidence-based set that were concatenated rather than reconciled, which shows up as near-duplicate models at the same locus.

text:
8.13 Further reading


Hyatt et al. (2010) is the Prodigal paper; its description of how the start-site model is trained explains most of the boundary disagreements seen in Section 8.5.

Seemann (2014) describes Prokka, which wraps Prodigal together with tRNA, rRNA and functional annotation steps and is the practical starting point for annotating a bacterial draft.

Tatusova et al. (2016) documents the NCBI pipeline that produced the RefSeq annotation used here, and is worth reading before you submit a genome and receive an annotation you did not make.

Stanke et al. (2006) introduces AUGUSTUS and, more usefully, sets out clearly why eukaryotic gene prediction needs training data and external evidence.

Manni et al. (2021) explains what BUSCO does and does not measure; read it before quoting a completeness percentage in a manuscript.

Paysan-Lafosse et al. (2022) describes InterPro and the integration of member databases; it is the right reference for understanding what a domain-based functional assignment is actually claiming.

Ashburner et al. (2000) and Aleksander et al. (2023) together give the original rationale for the Gene Ontology and its current state, including the evidence-code system that governs how much weight an annotation deserves.

Altschul, Stephen F., Warren Gish, Webb Miller, Eugene W. Myers, and David J. Lipman. 1990. “Basic Local Alignment Search Tool.” Journal of Molecular Biology 215 (3): 403–10. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0022-2836(05)80360-2.

Bankevich, Anton, Sergey Nurk, Dmitry Antipov, Alexey A. Gurevich, Mikhail Dvorkin, Alexander S. Kulikov, Valery M. Lesin, et al. 2012. “SPAdes: A New Genome Assembly Algorithm and Its Applications to Single-Cell Sequencing.” Journal of Computational Biology 19 (5): 455–77. https://doi.org/10.1089/cmb.2012.0021.


Cunningham, Fiona, James E Allen, Jamie Allen, Jorge Alvarez-Jarreta, M Ridwan Amode, Irina M Armean, Olanrewaju Austine-Orimoloye, et al. 2021. “Ensembl 2022.” Nucleic Acids Research 50 (D1): D988–95. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkab1049.

Fraser, Claire M., Jeannine D. Gocayne, Owen White, Mark D. Adams, Rebecca A. Clayton, Robert D. Fleischmann, Carol J. Bult, et al. 1995. “The Minimal Gene Complement of <i>mycoplasma Genitalium</i>.” Science 270 (5235): 397–404. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.270.5235.397.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
section: 9.2 Sequencing chemistries and the errors they make
text:
9.2 Sequencing chemistries and the errors they make
An analyst does not need to be able to build a sequencer, but does need to know what each chemistry does when it is uncertain, because that determines which artefacts are plausible and which are not.
Illumina sequencing by synthesis (SBS) amplifies each library fragment in place on a flow cell into a cluster of perhaps a thousand copies, then sequences one base per cycle with fluorescently labelled, reversibly terminated nucleotides, imaging the cell between cycles. Two consequences follow. The signal is averaged over a whole cluster, so the method depends on every copy staying in step; molecules that fail to incorporate fall behind (phasing) and molecules that incorporate twice run ahead (pre-phasing), the fraction out of step grows every cycle, and base-call confidence decays along the read. Every Illumina per-position quality plot slopes downwards for this reason, and it is not a fault. And because the error mechanism is a mis-read signal rather than a mis-counted base, the errors are overwhelmingly substitutions — about one base in a thousand early in a read, rising towards one in a hundred at the end — with indels rare. Reads are 50–300 bp, usually taken from both ends of a fragment.
Oxford Nanopore draws a single strand through a protein pore and records the ionic current, which a neural network converts to bases. Nothing is amplified and there is no cycle, so there is no decay along the read and no length limit; tens of kilobases are routine. The errors are insertions and deletions, concentrated in homopolymer runs where six and seven identical bases give nearly the same current. The devices are portable, which is why they became central to outbreak response (Quick et al. 2017).
PacBio HiFi reads a circularised fragment round and round with one polymerase and reports the consensus of the passes. The per-pass error rate is high but random, so averaging over ten or more passes drives the consensus below one error in a thousand while retaining 15–25 kb reads.
The chemistry decides much of what follows. Short, accurate, substitution-dominated reads suit variant calling, RNA-seq counting and population surveys; long, noisy reads resolve repeats and full-length transcripts and need a caller that models indel noise; long, accurate reads are the current basis for reference-quality assembly. The question is never which chemistry is best but which error mode you can tolerate. A homopolymer-length difference, for instance, is weak evidence from Nanopore data and strong evidence from Illumina or HiFi data.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
text:
9.3 What library preparation leaves behind
Between the sample and the flow cell sits the library: DNA fragmented to a chosen size, with synthetic adapters ligated to both ends, often amplified by PCR, and tagged with an index so that many samples can share a run. Each step leaves a signature, and recognising a signature as preparation rather than biology saves wasted interpretation.
Adapters are a handle, not genome. If a fragment (the insert) is longer than the read, the read stops before reaching the far adapter; if it is shorter, the polymerase reads off the end of the insert into the adapter beyond — read-through — and the tail of the read is synthetic sequence that will not align. Adapter contamination therefore rises as insert size falls.
Duplicates come from PCR, which copies some fragments more than others, every copy carrying the same start and end coordinates. They inflate apparent depth without adding information, because a variant seen in ten reads that are copies of one molecule has been observed once; Section 9.7 marks them. Insert size reads out the size selection step, and a long tail or a second mode in a bacterial isolate usually means a structural difference or a contaminant.
Strandedness matters only for RNA: an unstranded library loses which strand a transcript came from, so reads from overlapping genes on opposite strands cannot be assigned. Getting the setting wrong when counting is a quiet failure — most genes look plausible and the ones with antisense neighbours are wrong.






Do not remove duplicates reflexively



Marking duplicates is correct for whole-genome and exome resequencing, where fragments are randomly sheared and identical start points are improbable. It is wrong for amplicon sequencing, where every read starts at the same primer by design, and usually wrong for RNA-seq, where a highly expressed transcript genuinely produces many fragments with identical ends. Unique molecular identifiers — random barcodes added before amplification — are the only way to tell a PCR copy from a coincidence with certainty.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
section: 9.4 The FASTQ format and the Phred scale
text:
9.4 The FASTQ format and the Phred scale
FASTQ is the universal container for reads. Each record is four lines: an identifier beginning with @, the base sequence, a line beginning with +, and one quality character per base. There is no header, no version field and no index, which is why everything reads FASTQ and why nothing validates it.

read_fastq <- function(path) {
  connection <- gzfile(path, "rt")
  lines <- readLines(connection)
  close(connection)
  if (length(lines) %% 4 != 0) {
    stop("truncated FASTQ: ", length(lines), " lines is not a multiple of four")
  }
  list(name = sub("^@", "", lines[seq(1, length(lines), by = 4)]),
       seq  = lines[seq(2, length(lines), by = 4)],
       qual = lines[seq(4, length(lines), by = 4)])
}

reads_r1 <- read_fastq(book_data("reads", "mgen_sim_R1.fastq.gz"))
reads_r2 <- read_fastq(book_data("reads", "mgen_sim_R2.fastq.gz"))
cat(sprintf("%d read pairs, all %d bp\n",
            length(reads_r1$seq), unique(nchar(reads_r1$seq))))
#> 20000 read pairs, all 150 bp
cat(reads_r1$name[1], "\n")
#> SIM:1:FC1:1:1:0:386803/1
cat(substr(reads_r1$seq[1], 1, 60), "...\n")
#> AGTCTTGTTAGAAGCACCATTAAATCCTGCTATTGTTGAAACTCCTTTAAATATTGTTCA ...
cat(substr(reads_r1$qual[1], 1, 60), "...\n")
#> IIGBIIGICCIFIIHDFFFIIEFHFEBIGGEHEGCDEHHEFDE?FBBDDDGIFCEICIC? ...

A real Illumina identifier encodes the instrument, run, flow cell, lane, tile and cluster coordinates, and the /1 suffix marks the first mate. These simulated names follow the same shape with one addition: the final field before the mate suffix is the 0-based coordinate the fragment came from. That is ground truth, and Section 9.6 uses it.
The quality line is the part that carries information rather than sequence. Each character encodes a Phred quality score \(Q\), defined from the estimated probability \(P\) that the base call is wrong:
\[Q = -10 \log_{10} P\]
so \(Q = 10\) means a 1 in 10 chance of error, \(Q = 20\) means 1 in 100, \(Q = 30\) means 1 in 1,000 and \(Q = 40\) means 1 in 10,000. The score is stored as a single ASCII character whose code point is \(Q + 33\), which puts \(Q = 0\) at ! and \(Q = 40\) at I.

phred_scores <- function(quality_strings) {
  codes <- utf8ToInt(paste(quality_strings, collapse = "")) - 33L
  matrix(codes, nrow = length(quality_strings), byrow = TRUE)
}

quality_r1 <- phred_scores(reads_r1$qual)
quality_r2 <- phred_scores(reads_r2$qual)

first <- quality_r1[1, 1:12]
cat("first 12 quality characters:", substr(reads_r1$qual[1], 1, 12), "\n")
#> first 12 quality characters: IIGBIIGICCIF
cat("as Phred scores           :", first, "\n")
#> as Phred scores           : 40 40 38 33 40 40 38 40 34 34 40 37
cat("as error probabilities    :", signif(10^(-first / 10), 2), "\n")
#> as error probabilities    : 1e-04 1e-04 0.00016 5e-04 1e-04 1e-04 0.00016 1e-04 4e-04 4e-04 1e-04 2e-04

Reading a quality string as a probability is the most useful habit in read-level quality control, because it makes the scale’s non-linearity obvious: every ten points multiply the error probability by ten. Summing those probabilities across a read gives its expected number of errors, a far better per-read summary than mean quality, because averaging logarithms of probabilities is not an operation with a useful meaning.

expected_errors <- rowSums(10^(-quality_r1 / 10))
cat(sprintf("expected errors per read: median %.2f, 95th percentile %.2f\n",
            median(expected_errors), quantile(expected_errors, 0.95)))
#> expected errors per read: median 0.16, 95th percentile 0.19
cat(sprintf("reads with more than one expected error: %.2f%%\n",
            100 * mean(expected_errors > 1)))
#> reads with more than one expected error: 0.00%
cat(sprintf("bases at Q30 or better                 : %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(quality_r1 >= 30)))
#> bases at Q30 or better                 : 74.2%

One historical trap survives in old files: Illumina pipelines before version 1.8 used an offset of 64 rather than 33, so the same character meant a score 31 points higher, and such a file fed to a modern tool yields quality scores that look impossibly good or impossibly bad. A quality string containing characters below : is offset 33; one with no character below @ should be checked before it is analysed.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
section: 9.5 A quality report you can build yourself
text:
9.5 A quality report you can build yourself
FastQC (Andrews 2010) is the standard first look at a read file and MultiQC (Ewels et al. 2016) aggregates it across hundreds of samples. Neither is worth trusting if you cannot say what its plots are computed from, so this section rebuilds the two most important panels. The per-position quality plot is a distribution, not a line: at every cycle there is a population of scores across reads, and its shape matters more than its mean. Figure 9.1 shows the quartiles and the 10th and 90th percentiles for both mates.

position_summary <- function(quality_matrix, mate) {
  quantiles <- apply(quality_matrix, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9))
  data.frame(position = seq_len(ncol(quality_matrix)), mate = mate,
             lower = quantiles[1, ], q1 = quantiles[2, ], median = quantiles[3, ],
             q3 = quantiles[4, ], upper = quantiles[5, ])
}

quality_profile <- rbind(position_summary(quality_r1, "R1"),
                         position_summary(quality_r2, "R2"))

ggplot(quality_profile, aes(position, median, colour = mate, fill = mate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.18, colour = NA) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q1, ymax = q3), alpha = 0.35, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(20, 30), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = book_palette[1:2]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = book_palette[1:2]) +
  labs(x = "Position in read (bp)", y = "Phred quality score",
       colour = "Mate", fill = "Mate")






Figure 9.1: Per-position Phred quality distribution for the 20,000 simulated read pairs. The line is the median, the dark band the interquartile range and the pale band the 10th to 90th percentile range. Quality is high and tight for the first 50 cycles and decays steadily thereafter, which is the characteristic signature of phasing in sequencing by synthesis.




Read it as a decision aid. The median starts near Q37 and is still above Q20 at the last cycle, so no part of the read is unusable; the lower edge of the pale band decides trimming, because cycles where a tenth of reads have fallen below about Q20 contribute more mismatches than information. The two mates behave almost identically here. In real Illumina data R2 is routinely worse than R1 — the second read is made after the cluster has sat through the first read and an index read — and that is normal rather than a reason to discard a run.
The second panel worth rebuilding is per-read GC content, the cheapest contamination detector available.

gc_fraction <- function(sequences) {
  (lengths(regmatches(sequences, gregexpr("[GCgc]", sequences)))) / nchar(sequences)
}

gc_r1 <- gc_fraction(reads_r1$seq)
genome_gc <- 0.3169                    # measured in the genome annotation chapter
expected <- data.frame(gc = 0:150 / 150,
                       density = dbinom(0:150, 150, genome_gc) * 150)

ggplot(data.frame(gc = gc_r1), aes(gc)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1 / 150,
                 fill = book_palette[1], alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = expected, aes(gc, density), colour = book_palette[4],
            linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "GC content of read", y = "Density")






Figure 9.2: Distribution of GC content across the 20,000 R1 reads (bars) against the binomial expectation for 150 independent draws at the genome’s own GC content of 31.7% (line). The observed distribution is unimodal and matches the expectation, which is what an uncontaminated library from a single organism looks like.




A single smooth peak on the expected curve means the reads come from one genome whose composition you guessed correctly. A second peak is the signature that matters: a shoulder at high GC is often adapter dimer or a contaminating organism, and a narrow spike at one value is usually an over-represented sequence such as rRNA. The shape, not the mean, carries the diagnosis.
Three more checks complete a minimal report.

duplicate_fraction <- mean(duplicated(reads_r1$seq))
first_base <- table(substr(reads_r1$seq, 1, 1))
n_bases <- sum(lengths(regmatches(reads_r1$seq, gregexpr("N", reads_r1$seq))))
cat(sprintf("exactly duplicated R1 sequences: %.2f%%\n", 100 * duplicate_fraction))
#> exactly duplicated R1 sequences: 1.29%
cat(sprintf("ambiguous (N) base calls       : %d\n", n_bases))
#> ambiguous (N) base calls       : 0
cat("first-base composition (%):\n")
#> first-base composition (%):
print(round(100 * first_base / length(reads_r1$seq), 1))
#> 
#>    A    C    G    T 
#> 34.3 15.9 16.1 33.7

The duplicate level of 1.29% is low and expected — no PCR was simulated — where 40% in a whole-genome library would point at over-amplification of a low-input sample. The first-base composition is close to the genome’s own 34% A, 16% C, 16% G, 34% T, as a randomly fragmented library should be; a strongly skewed composition over the first 10–12 bases is normal in randomly primed RNA-seq libraries, and is one of the FastQC modules that most often raises a red flag on good data.
Trimming, and when it does more harm than good
Trimming removes adapter sequence and low-quality read ends. Adapter removal is not optional: residual adapter does not align, and in RNA-seq it causes spurious junctions. Trimmomatic (Bolger, Lohse, and Usadel 2014) and fastp (Chen et al. 2018) do both jobs in one pass. Quality trimming is the contentious half; the usual rule slides a small window from the 3’ end and cuts where its mean quality falls below a threshold.

trim_point <- function(quality_row, window = 4, threshold = 20) {
  means <- stats::filter(quality_row, rep(1 / window, window), sides = 1)
  bad <- which(means < threshold)
  if (!length(bad)) length(quality_row) else min(bad) - window
}

for (threshold in c(15, 20, 25)) {
  lengths_kept <- apply(quality_r1, 1, trim_point, threshold = threshold)
  cat(sprintf("Q%d: median length %3d bp, %5.1f%% of bases retained, %4.1f%% of reads under 50 bp\n",
              threshold, median(lengths_kept),
              100 * sum(lengths_kept) / length(quality_r1),
              100 * mean(lengths_kept < 50)))
}
#> Q15: median length 150 bp, 100.0% of bases retained,  0.0% of reads under 50 bp
#> Q20: median length 150 bp, 100.0% of bases retained,  0.0% of reads under 50 bp
#> Q25: median length 134 bp,  89.1% of bases retained,  0.0% of reads under 50 bp

At Q15 and Q20 the rule removes nothing at all: the four-base window mean never falls below the threshold, even in the final cycles, because the decay in this dataset is gentle. At Q25 it removes 11% of the bases and shortens the median read to 134 bp. What do those bases buy you? Very little in an alignment-based analysis: a modern aligner soft-clips read ends that do not match and a variant caller already uses base quality in its likelihood. Aggressive trimming, meanwhile, shortens reads and so reduces mapping uniqueness, and biases what remains, because the bases removed are not a random sample. In RNA-seq it shifts reads between transcripts whose distinguishing positions sit near read ends, changing quantification.






Trim adapters always, trim quality rarely



Remove adapters in every dataset. Quality-trim only with a reason: a de novo assembly, whose k-mer graph is genuinely damaged by erroneous bases, or a plot showing a sharp collapse rather than the gentle decay seen here. Record the threshold with the results, because a count computed after trimming is not comparable with one computed before it.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
text:
9.6 Aligning reads to a reference
Alignment answers one question per read: where in the reference did this fragment most plausibly come from? Dynamic programming against the whole genome, as in the pairwise alignment chapter, would be exact and unusably slow — roughly \(4.5 \times 10^{11}\) cell evaluations for one 150 bp read against a 3 Gb genome, out of hundreds of millions of reads.
What made short-read alignment practical is an index that answers “where does this exact substring occur?” in time proportional to the substring’s length rather than the genome’s size. The FM-index, used by BWA (Li and Durbin 2009) and Bowtie 2 (Langmead and Salzberg 2012), is built from the Burrows–Wheeler transform: sort every rotation of the sequence alphabetically and keep the last character of each. The result is a compressible permutation that can be inverted and, more usefully, searched backwards — one character at a time from the right, a rank query at each step narrowing the range of rotations beginning with the suffix matched so far, until the width of the surviving range gives the number of occurrences. The index for a human genome fits in a few gigabytes, against the hundreds a naive suffix array would need.
Exact matching alone is not enough, because reads carry errors and samples carry variants. Aligners therefore seed and extend: find near-exact seeds with the index, cluster seeds consistent with one placement, and finish with banded dynamic programming in those small windows only, so that full Smith–Waterman effort is spent on a few hundred bases per read instead of three billion.
Choosing an aligner means matching the tool to the chemistry. BWA-MEM and Bowtie 2 are the standards for short DNA reads and minimap2 (Li 2018) for long ones. RNA-seq needs a splice-aware aligner, because a read crossing an exon junction has no contiguous genomic match; STAR (Dobin et al. 2012) and its peers solve that by allowing large gaps at splice-site motifs.
The run below is real. BWA and samtools (Danecek et al. 2021) are both installed, but an alignment produces files far larger than the book ships, so the commands are shown rather than executed and the output beneath each was captured from an actual run in a scratch directory holding a copy of the bundled reference.
bwa index mgen.fasta
bwa mem -t 4 -R '@RG\tID:sim1\tSM:mgen_sim\tPL:ILLUMINA\tLB:lib1' mgen.fasta \
    ../data/reads/mgen_sim_R1.fastq.gz ../data/reads/mgen_sim_R2.fastq.gz \
  | samtools sort -o mgen_sim.bam -
samtools index mgen_sim.bam
The -R option writes a read group line into the header, recording sample, platform and library. It costs nothing now, is required by most callers, and adding it later means rewriting the file. BWA reports what it infers about the library as it goes:
[M::mem_pestat] # candidate unique pairs for (FF, FR, RF, RR): (0, 19724, 0, 0)
[M::mem_pestat] analyzing insert size distribution for orientation FR...
[M::mem_pestat] (25, 50, 75) percentile: (349, 349, 349)
[M::mem_pestat] mean and std.dev: (349.00, 0.00)
[M::mem_process_seqs] Processed 40000 reads in 0.823 CPU sec, 0.207 real sec
That is the aligner estimating insert size from the data, and it is worth reading on every run. The orientation is FR, as a paired-end Illumina library should be, and the insert size is exactly 349 bp with zero standard deviation — the tell-tale sign of simulated data, where a real library would show a roughly normal spread 50–100 bp wide.
The first summary to look at is samtools flagstat, which counts flag bits over the whole file.
samtools flagstat mgen_sim.bam
40000 + 0 in total (QC-passed reads + QC-failed reads)
40000 + 0 primary
0 + 0 secondary
0 + 0 supplementary
0 + 0 duplicates
40000 + 0 mapped (100.00% : N/A)
40000 + 0 paired in sequencing
20000 + 0 read1
20000 + 0 read2
39968 + 0 properly paired (99.92% : N/A)
40000 + 0 with itself and mate mapped
0 + 0 singletons (0.00% : N/A)
0 + 0 with mate mapped to a different chr
Three numbers carry nearly all the information. The mapped percentage says whether the reads came from the organism you think: 100% here because they were simulated from this reference, 95–99% for a good bacterial isolate, below about 70% a reason to classify the unmapped reads taxonomically. The properly paired percentage adds the constraint that both mates mapped in the expected orientation at a plausible distance; the 32 reads mapped but not properly paired are the interesting ones. Singletons above a few per cent indicate a chimeric or poor library.
Because the reads are simulated, the alignment can be checked against truth rather than a second opinion. The name encodes the fragment’s 0-based start, so mate 1 should align at that coordinate plus one and mate 2, the reverse complement of the last 150 bp of a 350 bp fragment, 200 bp further along.

true_start <- as.integer(sub(".*:", "", sub("/[12]$", "", reads_r1$name)))
cat("first three fragments start at 0-based", head(true_start, 3), "\n")
#> first three fragments start at 0-based 386803 522982 284660
cat("so mate 1 should align at POS", head(true_start + 1L, 3), "\n")
#> so mate 1 should align at POS 386804 522983 284661
cat("and mate 2 at POS           ", head(true_start + 201L, 3), "\n")
#> and mate 2 at POS            387004 523183 284861

Comparing those expectations with the POS column is an awk one-liner over samtools view; the real result on the alignment above was:
alignments checked     : 40000
placed at true position: 39975 (99.938%)
placed elsewhere       : 25
  of which MAPQ 0      : 18
  of which MAPQ > 0    : 7
Twenty-five reads out of 40,000 are in the wrong place even though every read came from this genome and there is no biological variation. That is the irreducible background of short-read alignment, and it is concentrated in repeats. Most of the misplaced reads carry a mapping quality of zero, the aligner saying honestly that it could not choose.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
section: 9.7 The anatomy of SAM and BAM
text:
9.7 The anatomy of SAM and BAM
SAM is the text format for alignments; BAM is the same content compressed in blocks and indexed so a region can be retrieved without reading the whole file; CRAM compresses further by storing only differences from the reference. A SAM file begins with header lines starting @, and the real header of the alignment above is six lines:
@HD VN:1.5  SO:coordinate
@SQ SN:NC_000908.2  LN:580076
@RG ID:sim1 SM:mgen_sim PL:ILLUMINA LB:lib1
@PG ID:bwa  PN:bwa  VN:0.7.19-r1273 CL:bwa mem -t 4 ...
@PG ID:samtools PN:samtools PP:bwa  VN:1.24 CL:samtools sort -o mgen_sim.bam -
@HD records the sort order; @SQ names every reference sequence with its length, the contract that makes coordinates meaningful and the reason two BAM files with different @SQ lines cannot be merged; @RG is the read group and each @PG one program that touched the file, a provenance chain worth reading whenever a file’s history is in doubt. Every alignment line then has eleven mandatory tab-separated fields followed by optional tagged ones. The record below is the first alignment in the real BAM, verbatim except that the sequence, quality string and trailing tags are abbreviated for the page.

sam_line <- paste("SIM:1:FC1:1:6:978:10", "99", "NC_000908.2", "11", "60", "150M",
                  "=", "211", "350", "TTTAGTTAATACT...", "FFEGHIIIGIID...",
                  "NM:i:0", "MD:Z:150", "MC:Z:150M", "MQ:i:60", "AS:i:150",
                  sep = "\t")
fields <- strsplit(sam_line, "\t")[[1]]
names(fields)[1:11] <- c("QNAME", "FLAG", "RNAME", "POS", "MAPQ", "CIGAR",
                         "RNEXT", "PNEXT", "TLEN", "SEQ", "QUAL")
for (i in 1:11) cat(sprintf("%-6s %s\n", names(fields)[i], fields[i]))
#> QNAME  SIM:1:FC1:1:6:978:10
#> FLAG   99
#> RNAME  NC_000908.2
#> POS    11
#> MAPQ   60
#> CIGAR  150M
#> RNEXT  =
#> PNEXT  211
#> TLEN   350
#> SEQ    TTTAGTTAATACT...
#> QUAL   FFEGHIIIGIID...

QNAME is shared by both mates; RNAME and POS give the 1-based leftmost coordinate and RNEXT/PNEXT do the same for the mate, = meaning the same reference sequence. TLEN is the observed template length, signed so the leftmost mate is positive — here 350 bp. SEQ and QUAL are reverse-complemented when the read aligned to the minus strand, a detail that catches everyone once. The FLAG is a bit field in which each bit answers one yes/no question; decoding it by hand once makes every later confusion evaporate.

flag_meanings <- c(
  "1"    = "read is paired",
  "2"    = "read mapped in proper pair",
  "4"    = "read unmapped",
  "8"    = "mate unmapped",
  "16"   = "read reverse strand",
  "32"   = "mate reverse strand",
  "64"   = "first in pair",
  "128"  = "second in pair",
  "256"  = "secondary alignment",
  "512"  = "fails platform quality checks",
  "1024" = "PCR or optical duplicate",
  "2048" = "supplementary alignment")

decode_flag <- function(flag) {
  bits <- as.integer(names(flag_meanings))
  flag_meanings[bitwAnd(flag, bits) > 0]
}

for (flag in c(99L, 147L, 97L)) {
  cat(sprintf("FLAG %3d = %s\n", flag, paste(decode_flag(flag), collapse = "; ")))
}
#> FLAG  99 = read is paired; read mapped in proper pair; mate reverse strand; first in pair
#> FLAG 147 = read is paired; read mapped in proper pair; read reverse strand; second in pair
#> FLAG  97 = read is paired; mate reverse strand; first in pair

FLAG 99 is the forward-strand mate of a well-behaved pair and the commonest flag in any paired-end file; its partner is 147. FLAG 97 is 99 with the proper-pair bit missing, and in this dataset those are exactly the 32 reads flagstat called mapped but not properly paired. Only four flag values occur in the whole file — 97, 99, 145 and 147 — because the simulation produced no unmapped, secondary or supplementary alignments.
MAPQ is the field most often misread. It is not the quality of the match but \(-10 \log_{10}\) of the probability that the read was placed in the wrong location, on the same Phred scale as a base quality. A MAPQ of 0 means the read aligns equally well in at least two places and the aligner reported one arbitrarily; such reads are not bad reads, they are reads about which the reference cannot be interrogated. Here 38 of the 40,000 reads have MAPQ 0, clustered around 223,900 and 273,200 in copies of the MgPa adhesin repeat family. Ground truth makes the consequence explicit: a read whose name says it came from 273,193 was placed at 223,924, in the other copy of the repeat, with a nonsensical template length of 49,122 bp.






Filtering on MAPQ changes what you can see



Most variant-calling pipelines discard alignments below MAPQ 20, and they are right to: a variant supported only by ambiguously placed reads is usually an artefact of the repeat. But the filter is not free. Every read in a repeat family disappears, and a caller that sees no reads reports no variant rather than reporting uncertainty. Genes in segmental duplications and pseudogene pairs — SMN1/SMN2, PMS2, CYP21A2 — are routinely invisible to short-read pipelines for this reason. Know which regions of your reference are unmappable before reporting an absence of variants in them.


The CIGAR string says how the read lines up, as a run-length encoded list of operations: M for an aligned column (match or mismatch), I and D for insertion into and deletion from the reference, S for soft-clipping (bases in SEQ but not aligned), H for hard-clipping (bases absent from SEQ) and N for a skipped reference region, which is what a spliced aligner emits across an intron. Thirteen of the 40,000 real alignments carry a CIGAR other than 150M; the commonest is dissected below.

parse_cigar <- function(cigar) {
  parts <- regmatches(cigar, gregexpr("[0-9]+[MIDNSHP=X]", cigar))[[1]]
  data.frame(length = as.integer(sub("[A-Z=]$", "", parts)),
             operation = sub("^[0-9]+", "", parts))
}

consumes_reference <- c("M", "D", "N", "=", "X")
consumes_query <- c("M", "I", "S", "=", "X")

cigar <- "3S147M"
operations <- parse_cigar(cigar)
print(operations)
#>   length operation
#> 1      3         S
#> 2    147         M
cat(sprintf("read bases accounted for   : %d\n",
            sum(operations$length[operations$operation %in% consumes_query])))
#> read bases accounted for   : 150
cat(sprintf("reference bases spanned    : %d\n",
            sum(operations$length[operations$operation %in% consumes_reference])))
#> reference bases spanned    : 147
cat(sprintf("alignment ends at reference: %d\n",
            35397 + sum(operations$length[operations$operation %in% consumes_reference]) - 1))
#> alignment ends at reference: 35543

The read is 150 bp and POS is 35,397, but only 147 bases align: the first three were soft-clipped because they did not match, almost certainly simulated errors. Two rules follow. Operations consuming the query must sum to the read length or the record is malformed; operations consuming the reference give the alignment’s span, which is how an end coordinate is computed — POS + length(SEQ) is wrong whenever the CIGAR contains I, S, N or D.
Marking duplicates
Duplicate marking compares the outer coordinates of each pair and flags all but one copy of each set that agrees. The samtools route needs a name-sorted pass first, to fill in mate coordinates before they are compared.
samtools sort -n -o namesort.bam mgen_sim.bam
samtools fixmate -m namesort.bam fixmate.bam
samtools sort -o positionsort.bam fixmate.bam
samtools markdup -s positionsort.bam mgen_sim.markdup.bam
The -s flag asks for statistics, and the real run reported:
READ: 40000
WRITTEN: 40000
EXCLUDED: 0
EXAMINED: 40000
PAIRED: 40000
DUPLICATE PAIR: 708
DUPLICATE SINGLE: 0
DUPLICATE PAIR OPTICAL: 0
DUPLICATE TOTAL: 708
ESTIMATED_LIBRARY_SIZE: 558285
Note what marking does: 40,000 reads in, 40,000 out, duplicates flagged by bit 1024 rather than deleted. Every one of those 708 flagged reads — 354 pairs — is a coincidence rather than a PCR copy, because the simulator performed no amplification, and the birthday problem predicts how many to expect.

fragments <- 20000
start_positions <- 580076 - 350
distinct_expected <- start_positions * (1 - (1 - 1 / start_positions)^fragments)
cat(sprintf("fragments simulated          : %d\n", fragments))
#> fragments simulated          : 20000
cat(sprintf("distinct start points expected: %.0f\n", distinct_expected))
#> distinct start points expected: 19659
cat(sprintf("coincidental duplicate pairs  : %.0f\n", fragments - distinct_expected))
#> coincidental duplicate pairs  : 341

About 340 predicted against the 354 samtools marked. On a 580 kb genome collisions are common; on a 3 Gb genome with the same number of fragments they would be negligible. Duplicate rate is therefore uninterpretable without the target size and the depth, which is why “our duplicate rate was 18%” means nothing on its own.
