title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
text:
9.8 From alignments to variants
A variant caller turns alignments into a statement about genotype. At each position it assembles the pileup — every base from every overlapping read, with its base quality and its read’s mapping quality — and asks which genotype best explains the evidence. The calculation is a likelihood, not a vote: three alternative bases among thirty reads mean one thing if those three are low quality and quite another if they are not. bcftools (Danecek et al. 2021) does this directly; GATK’s HaplotypeCaller (McKenna et al. 2010) first reassembles each active region into candidate haplotypes, which is what lets it call indels and clustered substitutions that a position-by-position model mishandles (DePristo et al. 2011).
Running bcftools on the alignment from Section 9.6 is instructive precisely because there is nothing to find: the reads came from the reference, so every candidate is an artefact of sequencing error.
bcftools mpileup -f mgen.fasta -q 20 -Q 20 -a FORMAT/AD,FORMAT/DP mgen_sim.markdup.bam \
  | bcftools call -mv -Ov -o raw_calls.vcf
bcftools view -H raw_calls.vcf
The single record it produced, verbatim:
NC_000908.2 430570  .   T   C   3.07051 .   DP=7;VDB=0.92;SGB=-0.453602;
RPBZ=-0.387298;MQBZ=0;MQSBZ=0;BQBZ=-0.401918;SCBZ=0;MQ0F=0;AC=1;AN=2;
DP4=5,0,0,2;MQ=60   GT:PL:DP:AD 0/1:34,0,110:7:5,2
One false positive in 580 kb at roughly ten-fold coverage, and it announces itself. QUAL is 3.07, so the caller is barely more confident in the variant than in the reference; DP=7 is below the average depth; and DP4=5,0,0,2 — reference-forward, reference-reverse, alternative-forward, alternative-reverse — puts both alternative reads on one strand, the classic strand-bias signature of an artefact. Filtering on QUAL >= 30 && INFO/DP >= 10 leaves an empty call set, the correct answer here.
The VCF format (Danecek et al. 2011) is where most of the day-to-day difficulty lives. A VCF has a header of ## lines defining every key used below, a #CHROM line naming the columns, then one line per site with eight fixed fields — CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, QUAL, FILTER, INFO — optionally followed by FORMAT and one column per sample. The bundled ClinVar slice is sites-only: it describes variants in the abstract rather than genotypes in an individual, so it has no sample columns.

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(VariantAnnotation))

clinvar <- readVcf(book_data("variants", "tp53_clinvar.vcf"), genome = "hg38")
cat(sprintf("%d variant records, %d sample columns\n", nrow(clinvar), ncol(clinvar)))
#> 3888 variant records, 0 sample columns
cat("INFO keys:", paste(colnames(info(clinvar)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
#> INFO keys: AF_TGP, ALLELEID, CLNDN, CLNREVSTAT, CLNSIG, CLNVC, GENEINFO, MC
head(rowRanges(clinvar)[, c("REF", "ALT")], 3)
#> GRanges object with 3 ranges and 2 metadata columns:
#>           seqnames    ranges strand |            REF                ALT
#>              <Rle> <IRanges>  <Rle> | <DNAStringSet> <DNAStringSetList>
#>     35555       17   7668434      * |              T                  G
#>   3051986       17   7668440      * |              T                  C
#>    325619       17   7668449      * |              A                  C
#>   -------
#>   seqinfo: 1 sequence from hg38 genome

rowRanges returns the fixed fields as a GRanges object (Lawrence et al. 2013), so interval operations apply to a VCF without conversion. Note that ALT is a list, because a site may carry several alternative alleles; code assuming one alternative per line mis-handles multi-allelic sites, which is why splitting them with bcftools norm -m -any before comparing call sets is a standard and much-skipped step. The INFO column is a semicolon-separated set of key=value pairs defined in the header, describing the site.

clinical <- sapply(info(clinvar)$CLNSIG, paste, collapse = ",")
review <- sapply(info(clinvar)$CLNREVSTAT, paste, collapse = ",")
consequence <- sapply(info(clinvar)$MC, function(x) sub(".*\\|", "", x[1]))

head(sort(table(clinical), decreasing = TRUE), 6)
#> clinical
#>                       Uncertain_significance 
#>                                          956 
#>                                Likely_benign 
#>                                          761 
#>                                   Pathogenic 
#>                                          743 
#> Conflicting_classifications_of_pathogenicity 
#>                                          532 
#>                         Benign/Likely_benign 
#>                                          273 
#>                 Pathogenic/Likely_pathogenic 
#>                                          211

The commonest classification in TP53 is Uncertain_significance, which is the most important fact about clinical variant databases: most observed variation in even the most studied gene in cancer has no interpretation. Reporting such a variant as though it were pathogenic is a clinical error, and the ACMG/AMP framework (Richards et al. 2015) keeps the distinction auditable. The review status field records how much scrutiny each classification received.

star_level <- dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("practice_guideline", review)           ~ "4 stars: practice guideline",
  grepl("reviewed_by_expert_panel", review)     ~ "3 stars: expert panel",
  grepl("no_conflicts", review)                 ~ "2 stars: multiple, no conflict",
  grepl("^criteria_provided", review)           ~ "1 star: criteria provided",
  TRUE                                          ~ "0 stars: no assertion criteria")
print(sort(table(star_level), decreasing = TRUE))
#> star_level
#>      1 star: criteria provided 2 stars: multiple, no conflict 
#>                           2261                           1145 
#> 0 stars: no assertion criteria          3 stars: expert panel 
#>                            291                            191

A filtering strategy follows from those two fields, and it has the form every filtering strategy should take: a few criteria, each with a stated reason, applied in order.

confident <- data.frame(clinical, star_level, consequence,
                        position = start(rowRanges(clinvar))) |>
  filter(grepl("^Pathogenic|^Likely_pathogenic", clinical),
         !grepl("^0 stars", star_level))

cat(sprintf("pathogenic or likely pathogenic, with assertion criteria: %d of %d\n",
            nrow(confident), nrow(clinvar)))
#> pathogenic or likely pathogenic, with assertion criteria: 1080 of 3888
print(head(sort(table(confident$consequence), decreasing = TRUE), 5))
#> 
#>      frameshift_variant        missense_variant                nonsense 
#>                     470                     247                     113 
#>    splice_donor_variant splice_acceptor_variant 
#>                      73                      69

Truncating changes dominate — frameshifts, nonsense variants and splice-site disruptions together are the majority — with missense variants next. That is what the biology of a tumour suppressor predicts: TP53 is inactivated both by losing the protein and by substitutions in the DNA-binding domain that leave it intact but unable to bind its response elements, the structural basis for which is the next chapter’s subject. Note too that the anchor in ^criteria_provided matters: the string no_assertion_criteria_provided contains criteria_provided, and an unanchored match would promote 189 unreviewed records to one star.
INFO describes the site; FORMAT describes a sample. The FORMAT column is a colon-separated list of keys — GT:PL:DP:AD in the bcftools record above — and each sample column carries the matching values in the same order: GT the genotype (0/1 heterozygous, 1/1 homozygous alternative, ./. no call), DP the depth at that site in that sample, AD the per-allele depth, PL the Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods. When call sets are merged, INFO must be recomputed while FORMAT is carried through per sample; tools that concatenate VCFs without understanding this produce files whose INFO describes a different cohort from their genotypes.
Filtering a call set takes one of two approaches. Hard filtering applies thresholds to INFO fields — depth, quality by depth, strand bias, mapping quality — and suits small call sets and organisms with no truth set. Variant quality score recalibration trains a model on known-true variants and is more sensitive, but needs a large call set and a trustworthy truth set, so it is a human-genomics technique. Either way, look at what survives: inspecting the pileup at a few called positions in IGV (Thorvaldsdottir, Robinson, and Mesirov 2012) catches classes of error no filter expresses.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
section: 9.9 RNA-seq from experimental design to differential expression
text:
9.9 RNA-seq from experimental design to differential expression
Everything so far has been about locating reads. RNA-seq asks how much of each transcript was present, and the answer is a count, which brings its own statistics.
Design, replication and confounding
Design decisions are made before sequencing and cannot be repaired afterwards. Biological replicates are independent samples under the same condition; technical replicates are one library sequenced repeatedly. Only biological replicates estimate the variability a differential expression test compares against, and technical variability in modern RNA-seq is small enough to be rarely worth buying. Three biological replicates per group is the practical minimum; once depth is adequate, more replicates beat more reads per replicate, because the limiting quantity is the estimate of biological variance.
Confounding is the failure analysis cannot fix: if every treated sample was prepared on Monday and every control on Tuesday, batch and condition are one variable and no method can separate them (Leek et al. 2010). The defence is randomising samples across batches and days, and recording every technical covariate so it can be modelled if it matters. The bundled pasilla dataset is not perfectly designed — seven samples, three treated with RNAi against pasilla and four untreated, sequenced with two library protocols.

counts <- as.matrix(read.delim(book_data("expression", "pasilla_gene_counts.tsv"),
                               row.names = 1))
samples <- read.csv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_sample_annotation.csv"))
samples$sample <- sub("fb$", "", samples$file)
samples <- samples[match(colnames(counts), samples$sample), ]
samples$condition <- factor(samples$condition, levels = c("untreated", "treated"))
samples$type <- factor(sub("-", "_", samples$type))
print(table(samples$condition, samples$type))
#>            
#>             paired_end single_read
#>   untreated          2           2
#>   treated            2           1
cat(sprintf("%d genes x %d samples; library sizes %.1f-%.1f million reads\n",
            nrow(counts), ncol(counts),
            min(colSums(counts)) / 1e6, max(colSums(counts)) / 1e6))
#> 14599 genes x 7 samples; library sizes 8.4-21.9 million reads

Library type is partially confounded with condition — two of three treated samples are paired-end against two of four untreated — but not completely, so the protocol effect can be estimated and removed rather than merely worried about. That is what putting type in the design formula does.
Counting, and what a count is
Counting assigns each alignment to a gene. featureCounts (Liao, Smyth, and Shi 2013) does this against a GFF3 or GTF annotation, and needs three deliberate decisions: which feature type to count over (exon, summarised to gene_id), what to do with a read overlapping two genes (discard it, in the standard union model), and whether the library is stranded. Lightweight quantifiers such as salmon (Patro et al. 2017) skip genome alignment altogether, assigning reads to transcripts probabilistically against a transcriptome index, which is faster and handles reads shared between isoforms properly.
Three properties of the resulting integer matrix drive everything that follows. Counts are discrete, so a continuous model misbehaves at low values. Their variance grows strongly with their mean, so an analysis assuming constant variance is dominated by the most highly expressed genes. And they are compositional: library size is fixed, so when one transcript takes a larger share every other count falls although nothing happened.






Do not feed normalised values to a count model



TPM and FPKM divide counts by transcript length and library size to make values comparable across genes within a sample. They answer “is this gene expressed?” and are the wrong input for differential expression, because the division destroys the count nature of the data and with it the information about how precisely each value was measured. DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2009) require raw counts and handle library size internally. If a collaborator sends TPMs and asks for a differential expression analysis, ask for the counts.


Building the dataset and normalising it

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DESeq2))

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts, colData = samples,
                              design = ~ type + condition)
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3
dds <- dds[keep, ]
cat(sprintf("%d genes retained of %d after requiring 10+ reads in 3+ samples\n",
            nrow(dds), length(keep)))
#> 8148 genes retained of 14599 after requiring 10+ reads in 3+ samples

Pre-filtering is not a statistical step — DESeq2’s independent filtering would handle these genes anyway — but it speeds everything up. In the formula ~ type + condition the variable of interest goes last, the convention results() follows when no contrast is named.
Normalisation corrects for libraries sequenced to different depths and compositions. Dividing by total count is the obvious approach and the wrong one, because a few very highly expressed genes take a large share of a library and drag every other gene down. DESeq2 uses median-of-ratios instead, which is simple enough to compute by hand.

log_counts <- log(counts(dds))
reference <- rowMeans(log_counts)                     # geometric mean across samples
usable <- is.finite(reference)                        # drop genes with any zero
ratios <- log_counts[usable, ] - reference[usable]
manual_size_factors <- exp(apply(ratios, 2, median))

dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds)
comparison <- rbind(manual = manual_size_factors, DESeq2 = sizeFactors(dds))
print(round(comparison, 4))
#>        untreated1 untreated2 untreated3 untreated4 treated1 treated2
#> manual      1.144      1.791      0.646     0.7507     1.63   0.7612
#> DESeq2      1.144      1.791      0.646     0.7507     1.63   0.7612
#>        treated3
#> manual   0.8303
#> DESeq2   0.8303

The two rows agree. In words: for each gene take the ratio of its count in a sample to its geometric mean across samples, then for each sample take the median of those ratios. If a sample differed from the average only in depth, every ratio would be the same number — the depth factor. The median makes the estimate robust: genes that genuinely changed shift their own ratios, but as long as most genes are not differentially expressed the median is unaffected. That assumption fails in a global transcriptional shutdown, where spike-in controls become necessary.
Dispersion, and why it must be shrunk
Counts from replicate samples vary more than a Poisson process allows. The extra variability — between individuals, cages, cultures — is captured by a negative binomial model with a per-gene dispersion \(\alpha\), giving variance \(\mu + \alpha\mu^2\). With three or four replicates the per-gene estimate of \(\alpha\) is very noisy, and a gene whose replicates happen to agree closely gets a dispersion near zero, which would make every difference look significant. DESeq2 therefore borrows strength across genes: it fits a smooth trend of dispersion against mean expression, then pulls each gene’s noisy estimate towards that trend by an amount reflecting how uncertain the individual estimate is. Figure 9.3 shows all three quantities.

dds <- estimateDispersions(dds)
plotDispEsts(dds, main = "Dispersion before and after shrinkage")






Figure 9.3: Dispersion estimates for the pasilla dataset. Black points are the per-gene maximum-likelihood estimates, the red line is the fitted mean–dispersion trend, and blue points are the final shrunken values used in testing. Points circled in blue are dispersion outliers, which are left unshrunken so that a genuinely variable gene is not forced to look reproducible.




Two features carry the message. Dispersion falls with mean expression, which is why one variance assumption for all genes would be wrong. And the blue points sit much closer to the red line than the black ones: each gene’s variance estimate is now informed by the thousands of genes expressed at a similar level. The exception is deliberate — genes whose own estimate is far above the trend keep it, because shrinking those would manufacture false positives.
Testing, and what the adjusted p-value promises

dds <- nbinomWaldTest(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "treated", "untreated"), alpha = 0.05)
summary(res)
#> 
#> out of 8148 with nonzero total read count
#> adjusted p-value < 0.05
#> LFC > 0 (up)       : 508, 6.2%
#> LFC < 0 (down)     : 600, 7.4%
#> outliers [1]       : 0, 0%
#> low counts [2]     : 0, 0%
#> (mean count < 5)
#> [1] see 'cooksCutoff' argument of ?results
#> [2] see 'independentFiltering' argument of ?results

The Wald test divides the estimated log2 fold change by its standard error and refers the result to a normal distribution. The estimate is itself shrunk — a two-fold change supported by four reads is reported as a smaller change than the same ratio supported by four thousand — so fold changes for weakly expressed genes are conservative by design.
Testing 8,148 genes at \(p < 0.05\) would yield around 407 significant results if nothing were differentially expressed at all. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995) controls the false discovery rate by adjusting the p-values so that, among genes called significant at padj < 0.05, the expected proportion of false positives is 5%.

cat(sprintf("raw p < 0.05            : %d genes\n", sum(res$pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)))
#> raw p < 0.05            : 1928 genes
cat(sprintf("expected by chance alone: %.0f genes\n", 0.05 * nrow(res)))
#> expected by chance alone: 407 genes
cat(sprintf("BH-adjusted padj < 0.05 : %d genes\n", sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)))
#> BH-adjusted padj < 0.05 : 1108 genes
cat(sprintf("  of those, |log2FC| > 1: %d genes\n",
            sum(res$padj < 0.05 & abs(res$log2FoldChange) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)))
#>   of those, |log2FC| > 1: 224 genes







What an FDR of 5% does and does not promise



It promises that the list as a whole is expected to contain 5% false positives. It says nothing about any individual gene: one with padj = 0.049 is not “95% likely to be real”. It is not a statement about importance — a gene can be highly significant and change by 10%, because significance measures evidence against the null, not effect size. It does not survive changing the gene set, since adding or removing genes changes every adjusted p-value, which is why filtering must be decided before testing and never after seeing the results. And it assumes the p-values were valid, which they are not if the design was confounded. Choosing a list by padj and a fold-change threshold is a pragmatic compromise, but the threshold is a judgement and should be stated as one.


Reading the result
Figure 9.4 is the first plot to draw after any differential expression analysis.

ma_data <- as.data.frame(res) |>
  mutate(significant = !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05)

ggplot(ma_data, aes(baseMean, log2FoldChange, colour = significant)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey65", `TRUE` = book_palette[4]),
                      labels = c("not significant", "padj < 0.05")) +
  labs(x = "Mean normalised count", y = expression(log[2]~fold~change),
       colour = NULL)






Figure 9.4: MA plot of the pasilla analysis: log2 fold change against mean normalised count, with genes at an adjusted p-value below 0.05 in red. The funnel shape is expected — fold changes are estimated poorly at low counts — and the symmetry of significant genes above and below zero indicates that normalisation has not introduced a systematic shift.




Read it for shape, not for individual genes. The cloud should be centred on zero across the whole expression range; one that drifts upwards at low counts means normalisation has failed. The widening at the left is a reminder that the largest fold changes in any RNA-seq result are almost always the least reliable.
Figure 9.5 puts effect size against evidence, which is the plot for choosing candidates.

volcano <- as.data.frame(res) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("gene") |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(class = case_when(padj >= 0.05 ~ "not significant",
                           log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "up in treated",
                           TRUE ~ "down in treated"))

ggplot(volcano, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(data = filter(volcano, gene == "FBgn0261552"),
                           aes(label = gene), colour = "black", size = 3,
                           min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("not significant" = "grey70",
                                 "up in treated" = book_palette[3],
                                 "down in treated" = book_palette[1])) +
  labs(x = expression(log[2]~fold~change), y = expression(-log[10]~adjusted~p),
       colour = NULL)






Figure 9.5: Volcano plot of the pasilla analysis. Each point is a gene; the dashed lines mark an adjusted p-value of 0.05 and a two-fold change. The labelled gene FBgn0261552 is pasilla itself, the target of the RNAi knockdown, which the analysis recovers as strongly down-regulated without being told to look for it.




The knockdown target is the internal control that validates the whole analysis.

print(as.data.frame(res["FBgn0261552", c("baseMean", "log2FoldChange", "padj")]))
#>             baseMean log2FoldChange     padj
#> FBgn0261552     5135         -1.868 3.48e-33

The pasilla gene is down by a factor of about 3.7, with an adjusted p-value far below any threshold: an effective knockdown. Had it not been, nothing else would be worth interpreting — find the result you already know before trusting the ones you do not. Finally, Figure 9.6 shows the most strongly regulated genes across all seven samples.

vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)
top_genes <- head(order(res$padj), 25)
annotation <- data.frame(condition = samples$condition, protocol = samples$type,
                         row.names = samples$sample)

pheatmap::pheatmap(assay(vsd)[top_genes, ], scale = "row",
                   annotation_col = annotation, show_rownames = TRUE,
                   fontsize_row = 6, fontsize_col = 8,
                   color = colorRampPalette(c(book_palette[1], "white",
                                              book_palette[4]))(50),
                   main = "Top 25 differentially expressed genes")






Figure 9.6: Variance-stabilised expression of the 25 genes with the smallest adjusted p-values, scaled by row so that colour shows each gene’s deviation from its own mean. Samples cluster by condition rather than by library protocol, which is the reassurance that the effect being measured is the treatment and not the batch.




The variance-stabilising transformation does necessary work here: clustering raw or log-transformed counts puts the highly expressed genes in charge, whereas vst gives values whose variance is roughly constant across the expression range, so distances between samples reflect overall similarity. Scaling by row then shows relative change rather than expression level. Note what a heatmap cannot establish: these genes were selected because they separate the conditions, so their clean separation is guaranteed by the selection and is not independent evidence of anything.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
text:
9.10 Summary

Each chemistry fails characteristically: Illumina substitutions with quality decaying along the read, Nanopore indels in homopolymers, HiFi accuracy bought by re-reading one molecule. Downstream choices follow from which failure you have.
Duplicates, adapter read-through, insert size and strandedness are properties of the library, not the organism. Recognise them before interpreting them as biology.
A Phred score is a log-scaled error probability; convert it back and sum across a read for expected errors, a better per-read summary than mean quality.
Trim adapters always and quality-trim rarely: at Q20 this dataset loses nothing and at Q25 it loses 11% of its bases for no gain in an alignment-based analysis.
Alignment is never perfect. Twenty-five of 40,000 reads simulated from this reference were placed elsewhere, almost all in repeats and almost all flagged MAPQ 0 — which means “equally good elsewhere”, not “bad read”.
The CIGAR string, not the read length, determines where an alignment ends; duplicate marking flags rather than deletes and cannot tell a PCR copy from a coincidence.
In a VCF, INFO describes the site and FORMAT a sample. Filter on a few stated criteria, split multi-allelic records before comparing call sets, and look at the pileup of anything you report.
Differential expression needs raw counts, biological replicates and a design where the variable of interest is not confounded with a batch; median-of-ratios normalisation and dispersion shrinkage both borrow strength across genes.
An FDR of 5% is a property of the whole list, not of any gene in it, and says nothing about effect size or biological importance.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
text:
9.11 Exercises

Compute the mean Phred score at the first and last cycle of the R2 file and express both as error probabilities. By what factor does the error rate rise across the read?
Compute per-read GC content for R2 as well as R1 and compare the two distributions with a two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Should they differ, given how the reads were simulated?
Decode SAM FLAG values 83, 163 and 141 with decode_flag, and describe in one sentence each the situation that produces them.
A read has POS = 1000 and CIGAR = 10S80M2D30M8S. Compute the number of read bases, the reference span and the 1-based coordinate of the last aligned base, then check your answer with parse_cigar.
Re-run the trimming simulation at Q25 with a 10 bp window instead of 4 bp. Does the longer window remove more or fewer bases, and why?
Repeat the differential expression analysis with the design ~ condition alone. How many genes pass padj < 0.05, and what does the change say about the protocol’s contribution to the variance?
Of the 1,108 genes significant at padj < 0.05, how many have an absolute log2 fold change below 0.5? In two or three sentences, say what kind of experiment would make such genes worth following up and what kind would not.
A collaborator reports 9,000 differentially expressed genes out of 12,000 tested at an FDR of 5%, comparing two treatment groups with three replicates each. List four checks you would run, in order, and what result from each would explain the finding.

title: 9  Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
text:
9.12 Solutions






Solutions





1. The error probability rises about twenty-fold across the read, which is the quantitative content of the downward slope in Figure 9.1.

ends <- quality_r2[, c(1, 150)]
cat(sprintf("cycle %3d: mean Q %.1f, error probability %.5f\n",
            c(1, 150), colMeans(ends), 10^(-colMeans(ends) / 10)))
#> cycle   1: mean Q 37.2, error probability 0.00019
#>  cycle 150: mean Q 23.7, error probability 0.00426
cat(sprintf("ratio of error probabilities: %.1f\n",
            10^(-mean(ends[, 2]) / 10) / 10^(-mean(ends[, 1]) / 10)))
#> ratio of error probabilities: 22.1

2. They should not differ. Both mates come from the same fragments of the same genome, so their GC distributions are two samples from one distribution; a significant difference would indicate a bug in the simulation or in your code rather than biology.

gc_r2 <- gc_fraction(reads_r2$seq)
cat(sprintf("mean GC: R1 %.4f, R2 %.4f\n", mean(gc_r1), mean(gc_r2)))
#> mean GC: R1 0.3170, R2 0.3174
print(suppressWarnings(ks.test(gc_r1, gc_r2)))
#> 
#>  Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
#> 
#> data:  gc_r1 and gc_r2
#> D = 0.0068, p-value = 0.7
#> alternative hypothesis: two-sided

3. FLAG 83 is a properly paired first mate on the reverse strand; FLAG 163 is its partner, a properly paired second mate on the forward strand; FLAG 141 is an unmapped second mate whose partner is also unmapped — what both records of an unmappable pair look like.

for (flag in c(83L, 163L, 141L)) {
  cat(sprintf("FLAG %3d = %s\n", flag, paste(decode_flag(flag), collapse = "; ")))
}
#> FLAG  83 = read is paired; read mapped in proper pair; read reverse strand; first in pair
#> FLAG 163 = read is paired; read mapped in proper pair; mate reverse strand; second in pair
#> FLAG 141 = read is paired; read unmapped; mate unmapped; second in pair

4. 10 + 80 + 30 + 8 = 128 read bases; reference span 80 + 2 + 30 = 112; last aligned base at 1000 + 112 − 1 = 1111. Soft-clipped bases consume no reference and the deletion consumes no query.

operations <- parse_cigar("10S80M2D30M8S")
query_length <- sum(operations$length[operations$operation %in% consumes_query])
reference_span <- sum(operations$length[operations$operation %in% consumes_reference])
cat(sprintf("read bases %d, reference span %d, last aligned base %d\n",
            query_length, reference_span, 1000 + reference_span - 1))
#> read bases 128, reference span 112, last aligned base 1111

5. The longer window removes fewer bases: 91.7% survive against 89.1% with the four-base window, because a ten-base window must see a sustained drop before its mean falls below the threshold. Neither choice is more correct, which is the point: the trimmed dataset is a function of parameters you picked.

for (window in c(4, 10)) {
  kept <- apply(quality_r1, 1, trim_point, window = window, threshold = 25)
  cat(sprintf("window %2d bp at Q25: median length %3d bp, %.1f%% of bases retained\n",
              window, median(kept), 100 * sum(kept) / length(quality_r1)))
}
#> window  4 bp at Q25: median length 134 bp, 89.1% of bases retained
#> window 10 bp at Q25: median length 136 bp, 91.7% of bases retained

6. Dropping type leaves the protocol effect in the residual variance, inflating the dispersion estimates and costing power, so fewer genes reach significance. The size of the drop measures how much of this dataset’s variability is technical.

simple <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts[keep, ], samples, design = ~ condition)
simple <- DESeq(simple, quiet = TRUE)
simple_res <- results(simple, alpha = 0.05)
cat(sprintf("~ type + condition: %d genes at padj < 0.05\n",
            sum(res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)))
#> ~ type + condition: 1108 genes at padj < 0.05
cat(sprintf("~ condition only  : %d genes at padj < 0.05\n",
            sum(simple_res$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)))
#> ~ condition only  : 853 genes at padj < 0.05

7. A substantial minority of the significant genes change by less than 1.4-fold. Such genes are worth following up when the question is about a coordinated process, where many small changes in one pathway can matter more than one large change in an isolated gene, or where small shifts are known to have consequences, as for dosage-sensitive transcription factors. They are not worth following up as individual knockout or biomarker candidates, because a change too small to detect reliably in another assay will not reproduce.

significant <- res[!is.na(res$padj) & res$padj < 0.05, ]
cat(sprintf("%d significant genes; %d of them with |log2FC| < 0.5 (%.0f%%)\n",
            nrow(significant), sum(abs(significant$log2FoldChange) < 0.5),
            100 * mean(abs(significant$log2FoldChange) < 0.5)))
#> 1108 significant genes; 473 of them with |log2FC| < 0.5 (43%)

8. In order: whether the design was confounded with batch, because a batch effect aligned with treatment produces exactly this pattern; whether the normalisation assumption holds, because a global shift in transcription breaks median-of-ratios; whether the samples are genuine biological rather than technical replicates, because technical replicates understate variance and make everything significant; and whether raw counts were supplied rather than TPMs, because normalised values break the variance assumption in the same direction. A principal component plot of the variance-stabilised data answers the first and third in one picture.

9.13 Further reading


Danecek et al. (2021) is the current reference for samtools and bcftools, and describes the file formats more readably than their specifications do.

Li and Durbin (2009) sets out the Burrows–Wheeler approach to alignment; read it beside Langmead and Salzberg (2012), which solves the same problem with different trade-offs.

Love, Huber, and Anders (2014) is the DESeq2 paper, and the place to find the detail of dispersion shrinkage and fold-change moderation that Section 9.9 describes only in words.

Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth (2009) describes edgeR, whose different variance model makes clear which parts of the method are essential and which are choices.

Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) is the original false discovery rate paper: short, readable and worth the hour.

Leek et al. (2010) documents how badly batch effects distort high-throughput results; read it before designing an experiment rather than after.

Richards et al. (2015) is the ACMG/AMP framework any clinically reported variant must be assessed against.

Brooks et al. (2010) is the study the pasilla data come from, and a good example of asking a question with differential splicing rather than differential expression.

10.1 Setting up
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from pybfx import book_data, style, PALETTE
style()

import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from Bio.PDB import PDBParser, Superimposer, PPBuilder

warnings.simplefilter("ignore")      # PDBParser warns about 1970s formatting quirks
parser = PDBParser(QUIET=True)
crumbs: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
text:
10.2 From sequence to fold
The primary structure is the covalent sequence of amino acids, written from the free amino terminus to the free carboxyl terminus. It is the only level encoded directly in the gene, and in principle it determines all the others.
Secondary structure is local, regular backbone geometry stabilised by hydrogen bonds between backbone amide and carbonyl groups. The α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn and a hydrogen bond from the carbonyl of residue i to the amide of residue i + 4; the β-strand is extended, and strands hydrogen-bond to each other side by side to form parallel or antiparallel sheets. Turns and loops connect them. Because secondary structure is defined by hydrogen-bond patterns rather than by sequence, it is assigned from coordinates, and the standard assignment algorithm is DSSP (Kabsch and Sander 1983).
Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional arrangement of the whole chain, and the forces holding it together are weak individually and decisive in aggregate. The hydrophobic effect dominates: burying non-polar side chains away from water increases the entropy of the solvent, and this is what drives collapse into a compact globule with a non-polar core. Hydrogen bonds and salt bridges give specificity, selecting one fold among the many compact arrangements available. Disulphide bonds between cysteines are the only covalent cross-links, and are largely confined to secreted and extracellular proteins because the cytoplasm is reducing. Metal coordination can be structural in the same way, as it is in p53: Section 10.5 measures the zinc site that holds its DNA-binding surface in shape.
Quaternary structure is the assembly of several chains into a functional complex. Full-length p53 works as a tetramer, and 1TUP contains three copies of its DNA-binding domain in the crystal’s asymmetric unit — which, as Section 10.6 shows, is not the same statement as “p53 is a trimer”.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
section: 10.4 The PDB file and its mmCIF successor
text:
10.4 The PDB file and its mmCIF successor
The PDB format is a fixed-column text format designed in the 1970s for punched cards, and its limits are those of that design: a one-character chain identifier, a five-character atom serial number and a four-character residue number. Structures larger than roughly 100,000 atoms or 62 chains cannot be represented at all. mmCIF replaced it as the archive’s master format and has no such limits, being a dictionary of named data items rather than fixed columns; every entry in the Protein Data Bank (Berman 2000; Burley et al. 2022) is now distributed in both. Use mmCIF for anything large or recent, and read PDB files fluently because thirty years of software emits them.
Each coordinate line begins ATOM for a polymer atom or HETATM for anything else — ligands, metals, water, modified residues — and carries an atom name, an alternate location indicator, a residue name, a chain, a residue number, three Cartesian coordinates in ångströms, an occupancy and a B factor.

with open(book_data("structures", "1tup.pdb")) as handle:
    first_atom = next(line for line in handle if line.startswith("ATOM"))

fields = [("record", 0, 6), ("serial", 6, 11), ("atom name", 12, 16),
          ("altLoc", 16, 17), ("residue", 17, 20), ("chain", 21, 22),
          ("resSeq", 22, 26), ("x", 30, 38), ("y", 38, 46), ("z", 46, 54),
          ("occupancy", 54, 60), ("B factor", 60, 66), ("element", 76, 78)]
for name, start, end in fields:
    print(f"{name:10s} = {first_atom[start:end].strip()!r}")
#> record     = 'ATOM'
#> serial     = '1'
#> atom name  = "O5'"
#> altLoc     = ''
#> residue    = 'DT'
#> chain      = 'E'
#> resSeq     = '1001'
#> x          = '25.930'
#> y          = '6.224'
#> z          = '81.661'
#> occupancy  = '1.00'
#> B factor   = '67.33'
#> element    = 'O'

Bio.PDB (Cock et al. 2009) parses this into a hierarchy that is worth learning by name: Structure contains Models, a model contains Chains, a chain contains Residues and a residue contains Atoms. Each residue carries a three-part identifier whose first element is a hetero-flag: " " for a standard polymer residue, "W" for water, "H_XXX" for any other heteroatom group. Filtering on that flag is how you separate protein from solvent, and forgetting to do it is the commonest beginner’s error in structural scripting.

structure = parser.get_structure("1tup", book_data("structures", "1tup.pdb"))
model = structure[0]

for chain in model:
    polymer = [r for r in chain if r.id[0] == " "]
    waters = [r for r in chain if r.id[0] == "W"]
    other = sorted({r.get_resname() for r in chain if r.id[0] not in (" ", "W")})
    print(f"chain {chain.id}: {len(polymer):3d} polymer residues, "
          f"{len(waters):3d} waters, heteroatoms {other}")
#> chain E:  21 polymer residues,  22 waters, heteroatoms []
#> chain F:  21 polymer residues,  14 waters, heteroatoms []
#> chain A: 196 polymer residues, 198 waters, heteroatoms ['ZN']
#> chain B: 194 polymer residues,  70 waters, heteroatoms ['ZN']
#> chain C: 195 polymer residues,  80 waters, heteroatoms ['ZN']

The output describes the crystal’s asymmetric unit precisely: three protein chains of about 195 residues each, two 21-nucleotide DNA strands, one zinc ion per protein chain and a few hundred ordered waters. Chains A, B and C are the same protein, and chains E and F are the two strands of one double helix.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
text:
10.5 Measuring a structure
Everything beyond this point is arithmetic on coordinates. The first and most basic operation is a distance, and the right first question to ask of p53’s zinc is which atoms hold it.

zinc = next(atom for atom in model["A"].get_atoms() if atom.element == "ZN")
protein_atoms = [atom for residue in model["A"] if residue.id[0] == " "
                 for atom in residue]

distances = sorted((atom - zinc, atom) for atom in protein_atoms)
for distance, atom in distances[:4]:
    residue = atom.get_parent()
    print(f"Zn - {residue.get_resname()}{residue.id[1]:>4} {atom.get_id():<4} "
          f"{distance:.2f} A")
#> Zn - HIS 179 ND1  1.99 A
#> Zn - CYS 242 SG   2.23 A
#> Zn - CYS 238 SG   2.28 A
#> Zn - CYS 176 SG   2.33 A

The zinc is held by Cys176, His179, Cys238 and Cys242 at 1.99–2.33 Å, which is textbook tetrahedral coordination geometry. This is a structural metal, not a catalytic one: it staples together two loops that form part of the DNA-binding surface, which is why mutations at these four residues are inactivating even though none of them touches DNA.
Asking which residues do touch DNA is the same calculation applied to two sets of atoms, and it is worth doing for all three protein chains rather than one.

dna_atoms = np.array([atom.coord for chain in "EF" for residue in model[chain]
                      if residue.id[0] == " " for atom in residue])

for chain_id in "ABC":
    atoms = [atom for residue in model[chain_id] if residue.id[0] == " "
             for atom in residue]
    coords = np.array([atom.coord for atom in atoms])
    separations = np.linalg.norm(coords[:, None, :] - dna_atoms[None, :, :], axis=2)
    close = {atoms[i].get_parent() for i in np.where(separations.min(axis=1) < 4.0)[0]}
    labels = sorted(f"{r.get_resname()}{r.id[1]}" for r in close)
    print(f"chain {chain_id}: {len(labels)} residues within 4 A of DNA: {labels}")
#> chain A: 4 residues within 4 A of DNA: ['GLN165', 'GLN167', 'HIS168', 'LYS101']
#> chain B: 12 residues within 4 A of DNA: ['ALA119', 'ALA276', 'ARG248', 'ARG273', 'ARG280', 'ARG283', 'ASN239', 'CYS275', 'CYS277', 'LYS120', 'MET243', 'SER241']
#> chain C: 4 residues within 4 A of DNA: ['ARG248', 'LYS120', 'SER121', 'SER241']

Only chain B is bound in the major groove; chains A and C make a few peripheral contacts and are, in effect, crystallographic neighbours. The twelve residues of chain B are the biologically important result: Lys120, Ser241, Arg248, Arg273, Arg280 and Arg283 are among the most frequently mutated positions in human cancer (Kato et al. 2003), and the structure explains why. Arg248 reaches into the minor groove, Arg273 contacts the phosphate backbone and Arg280 reads a base directly, so a substitution at any of them abolishes specific binding without unfolding the protein — which is exactly the pattern seen when p53 variants are assayed systematically (Giacomelli et al. 2018).
A contact map generalises this to the whole chain: a matrix in which entry (i, j) is set when residues i and j are closer than some cut-off. It is the two-dimensional shadow of a three-dimensional fold, and it makes secondary structure visible. 1 shows it for chain B.

residues = [r for r in model["B"] if r.id[0] == " " and "CA" in r]
ca_coords = np.array([r["CA"].coord for r in residues])
numbers = [r.id[1] for r in residues]
contact = np.linalg.norm(ca_coords[:, None, :] - ca_coords[None, :, :], axis=2) < 8.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.imshow(contact, cmap="Greys", origin="lower",
          extent=[numbers[0], numbers[-1], numbers[0], numbers[-1]])
for position in (120, 248, 273, 280):
    ax.axvline(position, color=PALETTE[3], linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Residue number")
ax.set_ylabel("Residue number")
ax.set_title("Contact map, p53 DNA-binding domain")
ax.grid(False)
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 10.1: Cα–Cα contact map of the p53 DNA-binding domain (1TUP chain B) at an 8 Å cut-off. The thick diagonal is local chain connectivity; the short bands running perpendicular to it are pairs of antiparallel β-strands packed against each other, which is the signature of a β-sandwich fold. Vertical lines mark four of the residues that contact DNA.




The map is almost entirely off-diagonal bands running at right angles to the main diagonal. Each such band is a pair of antiparallel β-strands: residue i contacts residue j, residue i + 1 contacts j − 1, and so on. A parallel sheet would give bands running parallel to the diagonal instead, and an α-helical protein gives a thick diagonal with little else. The DNA-contacting positions marked in red are scattered across the sequence and adjacent in space, which is the general lesson of a contact map: a binding site is a property of the fold, not of a stretch of sequence.
Secondary-structure content can be estimated from the backbone dihedral angles φ and ψ, which is what Figure 10.2 plots. This is an approximation to what DSSP computes from hydrogen bonds, and it is reported here as one.

import math

def dihedrals(chain):
    """(phi, psi) in degrees for every residue with both angles defined."""
    angles = []
    for peptide in PPBuilder().build_peptides(chain):
        for phi, psi in peptide.get_phi_psi_list():
            if phi is not None and psi is not None:
                angles.append((math.degrees(phi), math.degrees(psi)))
    return np.array(angles)

myoglobin = parser.get_structure("1mbn", book_data("structures", "1mbn.pdb"))[0]
p53_angles = dihedrals(model["B"])
mb_angles = dihedrals(myoglobin["A"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.6))
ax.scatter(*p53_angles.T, s=9, alpha=0.7, color=PALETTE[0], label="p53 DBD (1TUP B)")
ax.scatter(*mb_angles.T, s=9, alpha=0.7, color=PALETTE[2], marker="^",
           label="myoglobin (1MBN A)")
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axvline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_xlim(-180, 180); ax.set_ylim(-180, 180)
#> (-180.0, 180.0)
#> (-180.0, 180.0)
ax.set_xlabel("phi (degrees)"); ax.set_ylabel("psi (degrees)")
ax.set_title("Backbone conformation")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 10.2: Ramachandran plot of backbone dihedral angles for the p53 DNA-binding domain (1TUP chain B, blue) and sperm whale myoglobin (1MBN chain A, orange). Myoglobin occupies the α-helical region at lower left almost exclusively; p53 is concentrated in the broad β region at upper left. The empty areas are sterically forbidden, and a residue plotted there in a new structure is a modelling error until proved otherwise.




The two proteins separate cleanly. Classifying each residue by which region it falls in puts numbers on that impression.

def classify(angles):
    """Crude phi/psi classification; DSSP uses hydrogen bonds and is more accurate."""
    phi, psi = angles[:, 0], angles[:, 1]
    helix = (phi > -160) & (phi < -20) & (psi > -120) & (psi < 50)
    strand = (phi > -180) & (phi < -40) & ((psi > 90) | (psi < -150)) & ~helix
    return {"helix": helix.mean(), "strand": strand.mean(),
            "other": 1 - helix.mean() - strand.mean()}

for name, angles in (("p53 DBD", p53_angles), ("myoglobin", mb_angles)):
    fractions = classify(angles)
    print(f"{name:10s} " + "  ".join(f"{k} {100 * v:4.1f}%" for k, v in fractions.items()))
#> p53 DBD    helix 27.1%  strand 62.5%  other 10.4%
#> myoglobin  helix 86.8%  strand  6.6%  other  6.6%

Myoglobin is about 86% helical by this measure and p53’s DNA-binding domain about 62% β-strand: a globin and a β-sandwich, which is what their classifications say. Treat the percentages as approximate — a dihedral-based rule has no way to tell a strand from an extended loop, and DSSP would assign several per cent differently — but the contrast between the two folds is far larger than the method’s error.
One more global quantity is worth computing, because it is the cheapest check that a structure is compact at all. The radius of gyration is the root-mean-square distance of atoms from their centre of mass.

def radius_of_gyration(atoms):
    coords = np.array([atom.coord for atom in atoms])
    return float(np.sqrt(((coords - coords.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()))

for label, chain in (("p53 DBD (1TUP B)", model["B"]), ("myoglobin (1MBN A)", myoglobin["A"])):
    atoms = [atom for residue in chain if residue.id[0] == " " for atom in residue]
    print(f"{label:20s} {len(atoms):5d} atoms, Rg = {radius_of_gyration(atoms):.1f} A")
#> p53 DBD (1TUP B)      1522 atoms, Rg = 16.2 A
#> myoglobin (1MBN A)    1216 atoms, Rg = 15.3 A

Both sit near 15–16 Å, which is what a compact single domain of 150–200 residues should give; a folded globular protein’s radius of gyration scales roughly as the cube root of its residue count. Section 10.7 uses the same function on a structure that is not compact, and the number immediately says so.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
section: 10.6 Superposing structures and reading an RMSD
text:
10.6 Superposing structures and reading an RMSD
Comparing two structures means first removing the arbitrary part of the comparison. The coordinates in a PDB file are expressed in a frame chosen by the crystallographer, so two identical molecules can have completely different coordinates. Superposition finds the rotation and translation that minimise the root-mean-square deviation between two sets of paired atoms, which is a solved problem with a closed-form answer (Kabsch and Sander 1983). Bio.PDB’s Superimposer implements it.

def alpha_carbons(chain_id):
    """Cα atoms of one chain, indexed by residue number so chains can be paired."""
    return {residue.id[1]: residue["CA"] for residue in model[chain_id]
            if residue.id[0] == " " and "CA" in residue}

chains = {c: alpha_carbons(c) for c in "ABC"}
superimposer = Superimposer()

for first, second in (("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C")):
    shared = sorted(set(chains[first]) & set(chains[second]))
    superimposer.set_atoms([chains[first][n] for n in shared],
                           [chains[second][n] for n in shared])
    print(f"chain {first} vs chain {second}: {len(shared)} Ca pairs, "
          f"RMSD = {superimposer.rms:.2f} A")
#> chain A vs chain B: 194 Ca pairs, RMSD = 0.84 A
#> chain A vs chain C: 195 Ca pairs, RMSD = 1.03 A
#> chain B vs chain C: 194 Ca pairs, RMSD = 0.78 A

The three copies of the same domain in one crystal differ by 0.78–1.03 Å over about 195 Cα atoms. That number is the chapter’s most useful calibration, because it is a lower bound on what “the same structure” means: three chemically identical molecules, in one crystal, refined against one dataset, still disagree by about one ångström. An RMSD of 2 Å between two structures of the same protein from different crystals is therefore not evidence of a conformational change, and an RMSD of 5 Å between a model and an experiment does not mean the model is wrong in any interesting way — it may mean a domain has rotated about a hinge while every domain is individually correct.
Two cautions follow. RMSD is dominated by the worst-fitting atoms, because it squares the deviations, so a single badly placed loop can double it while the core is perfect; quoting it alongside the number of atoms aligned is essential, and inspecting per-residue deviations is better than either. And superposition requires a correspondence between atoms, which is easy here — the chains are identical and share residue numbering — and hard between homologues, where the alignment itself becomes part of the answer. Structural alignment programs solve that by optimising correspondence and superposition together, and they are what you need when sequence identity falls below about 25%.






The asymmetric unit is not the biological unit



1TUP contains three protein chains, but p53 does not function as a trimer. What a crystal structure contains is the asymmetric unit: whatever happened to pack into the repeating box of that crystal. The biological assembly — the oligomer that exists in solution — is a separate annotation, derived from the crystal symmetry and from experiment, and the PDB distributes it as a separate file. Counting chains in a coordinate file and reporting the answer as a stoichiometry is a common and avoidable error.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
section: 10.7 Predicted structures and what their confidence means
text:
10.7 Predicted structures and what their confidence means
Experimental structures exist for a small fraction of known proteins, so prediction fills the gap. Homology modelling is the classical approach and still a reasonable one: find an experimental structure of a homologue, align the target sequence to the template’s, copy the backbone where they align, rebuild the loops where they do not, and repack the side chains. Its accuracy is governed almost entirely by the sequence identity to the template — above 50% a model is usually accurate to 1–2 Å in the core, below about 25% the alignment itself becomes unreliable and so does everything built on it — and it can never predict a fold that is not already in the database.
AlphaFold (Jumper et al. 2021) broke that dependence by learning the relationship between sequence and structure directly. It takes a multiple sequence alignment of the target’s homologues, reads correlated substitution patterns across that alignment as evidence that two positions are in contact, and refines a geometric representation of the whole chain until it is consistent. RoseTTAFold (Baek et al. 2021) arrived at comparable accuracy independently, and AlphaFold 3 (Abramson et al. 2024) extends the approach to complexes with nucleic acids, ligands and modifications. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (Varadi et al. 2021) distributes predictions for most of UniProt, including the model of p53 used here.
What matters in practice is that these models carry per-residue and per-pair confidence estimates, and that those estimates are informative. pLDDT is a predicted score on the 0–100 scale of the local distance difference test, reported per residue and stored in the B-factor column of the distributed PDB file. Above 90 the backbone and most side chains are reliable; 70–90 means the backbone is reliable; 50–70 is low confidence; below 50 the residue is very likely to be in a region with no fixed structure at all. The last point is the one most often missed: a low pLDDT is not only a statement about the prediction but frequently a correct prediction of disorder.

alphafold = parser.get_structure("af", book_data("structures",
                                                 "AF-P04637-F1-model.pdb"))[0]
af_residues = [r for r in alphafold["A"] if r.id[0] == " "]
plddt = np.array([r["CA"].get_bfactor() for r in af_residues])

domains = [("transactivation + proline-rich", 1, 93),
           ("DNA-binding domain", 94, 292),
           ("nuclear localisation linker", 293, 325),
           ("tetramerisation domain", 326, 356),
           ("C-terminal regulatory", 357, 393)]
print(f"{len(plddt)} residues, mean pLDDT {plddt.mean():.1f}")
#> 393 residues, mean pLDDT 75.1
for name, start, end in domains:
    segment = plddt[start - 1:end]
    print(f"  {name:30s} {start:3d}-{end:3d}  mean pLDDT {segment.mean():5.1f}")
#>   transactivation + proline-rich   1- 93  mean pLDDT  48.4
#>   DNA-binding domain              94-292  mean pLDDT  95.3
#>   nuclear localisation linker    293-325  mean pLDDT  48.3
#>   tetramerisation domain         326-356  mean pLDDT  91.3
#>   C-terminal regulatory          357-393  mean pLDDT  43.4

The model is a textbook illustration. The DNA-binding domain scores 95 and the tetramerisation domain 91 — both are folded, both have experimental structures — while the transactivation region, the linker and the C-terminal regulatory tail score 48, 48 and 43. Those low-scoring regions are not a failure of the method. They are intrinsically disordered in the protein, which is why no crystal structure of full-length p53 exists and why 1TUP’s construct stops where it does.
Predicted aligned error (PAE) answers a different question, and it is the one that decides whether a multi-domain model can be used at all. PAE at position (i, j) is the expected error in the position of residue i when the prediction and the true structure are superposed on residue j. Low PAE within a block of residues means that block is internally well predicted; low PAE between two blocks means their relative orientation is predicted too. High PAE between two confidently folded domains means each domain is reliable and the way they are arranged with respect to each other is not.

import json

with open(book_data("structures", "AF-P04637-F1-confidence.json")) as handle:
    pae = np.array(json.load(handle)[0]["predicted_aligned_error"])

fig, (top, bottom) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 6.2),
                                  gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1, 2]})
top.plot(np.arange(1, len(plddt) + 1), plddt, color=PALETTE[0], linewidth=0.9)
for _, start, end in (domains[1], domains[3]):
    top.axvspan(start, end, color=PALETTE[1], alpha=0.15)
#> <matplotlib.patches.Rectangle object at 0x17f832d50>
#> <matplotlib.patches.Rectangle object at 0x168a2aa50>
top.axhline(70, linestyle="--", color="grey", linewidth=0.7)
#> <matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x17f7ca010>
top.axhline(50, linestyle="--", color="grey", linewidth=0.7)
#> <matplotlib.lines.Line2D object at 0x17f832d90>
top.set_xlim(1, len(plddt)); top.set_ylim(0, 100)
#> (1.0, 393.0)
#> (0.0, 100.0)
top.set_xlabel("Residue"); top.set_ylabel("pLDDT")
#> Text(0.5, 0, 'Residue')
#> Text(0, 0.5, 'pLDDT')

image = bottom.imshow(pae, cmap="viridis_r", origin="upper", vmin=0, vmax=32)
bottom.set_xlabel("Aligned residue"); bottom.set_ylabel("Scored residue")
#> Text(0.5, 0, 'Aligned residue')
#> Text(0, 0.5, 'Scored residue')
bottom.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=bottom, label="Predicted aligned error (A)", shrink=0.85)
#> <matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar object at 0x17f849b10>
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 10.3: Confidence of the AlphaFold model of full-length human p53. Top: per-residue pLDDT, with the DNA-binding and tetramerisation domains shaded; the dashed lines mark the 70 and 50 thresholds. Bottom: the predicted aligned error matrix, in which yellow is low expected error and dark purple is high. The two confident domains appear as yellow blocks on the diagonal, and the dark region between them shows that their relative orientation is not predicted.




Read the two panels together. The pLDDT trace is high across residues 94–292 and 326–356 and low everywhere else; the PAE matrix shows two yellow squares on the diagonal at exactly those positions, and high error everywhere between and around them. The model therefore supports statements about the internal geometry of either domain and supports no statement at all about where the tetramerisation domain sits relative to the DNA-binding domain. Taking the coordinates of the full-length model at face value and measuring a distance between the two domains would produce a number with no meaning.
Because p53’s DNA-binding domain has been solved experimentally, the prediction can be checked rather than merely believed.

experimental = alpha_carbons("B")
predicted = {r.id[1]: r["CA"] for r in af_residues if r.id[1] in experimental}
shared = sorted(predicted)

superimposer.set_atoms([experimental[n] for n in shared],
                       [predicted[n] for n in shared])
print(f"AlphaFold vs 1TUP chain B: {len(shared)} Ca pairs, "
      f"RMSD = {superimposer.rms:.2f} A")
#> AlphaFold vs 1TUP chain B: 194 Ca pairs, RMSD = 0.73 A

whole_chain = [atom for residue in af_residues for atom in residue]
domain_only = [atom for residue in af_residues if 94 <= residue.id[1] <= 292
               for atom in residue]
print(f"Rg, full-length model : {radius_of_gyration(whole_chain):.1f} A")
#> Rg, full-length model : 33.5 A
print(f"Rg, DNA-binding domain: {radius_of_gyration(domain_only):.1f} A")
#> Rg, DNA-binding domain: 16.6 A

The prediction reproduces the experimental domain to 0.73 Å over 194 Cα atoms — tighter than the 0.78–1.03 Å spread between the three experimental copies of that same domain measured in Section 10.6. For this domain, in other words, the prediction is at least as close to the crystal structure as the crystal structure is to itself. The radius of gyration makes the complementary point: 16.6 Å for the domain alone against 33.5 Å for the full-length model, which is not a compact protein but a pair of domains on disordered tethers, drawn in one arbitrary arrangement.






What a predicted structure cannot be used for



A high pLDDT is a statement about the backbone of a single chain in an unspecified state. It does not tell you which conformation of a flexible protein you are looking at, and AlphaFold reports one model where a transporter or kinase may have several functionally distinct states. Side-chain rotamers are predicted far less reliably than backbones, which is why docking into a predicted pocket gives systematically worse enrichment than docking into a crystal structure of the same protein. Ligands, metals, waters and post-translational modifications are absent from the model unless it was explicitly predicted with them, so a pocket may be modelled closed, or collapsed, simply because its ligand was not there. Mutation effects are not predicted: feeding a point-mutant sequence to a structure predictor and comparing the output with the wild-type model measures the predictor’s sensitivity, not the mutation’s consequence. Use predicted structures for fold assignment, domain boundaries, hypothesis generation and the interpretation of variants in a structural context — and say in your methods that the structure was predicted.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
section: 10.8 Comparing structures, and what structure-based design needs
text:
10.8 Comparing structures, and what structure-based design needs
Structure is more conserved than sequence, so two proteins can share a fold with no detectable sequence similarity. That fact is the basis of structural classification. SCOP and CATH are the two long-standing hierarchies: both group domains into folds, superfamilies and families, the first by expert judgement and the second by a mix of automatic and manual assignment. The useful products for an analyst are the domain definitions — where one structural unit stops and the next begins — and the statement that two proteins share a superfamily, which is evidence of common ancestry that sequence alone may not provide. Sequence-level domain resources such as Pfam (Mistry et al. 2020) and the integrated signatures of InterPro (Paysan-Lafosse et al. 2022) answer the same question more cheaply when a structure is unavailable.
Finding those relationships requires structural alignment, which differs from superposition in that the correspondence between residues is unknown and must be found. Algorithms differ in how they score a match and in whether they allow the chain order to change, and all of them return both an alignment and a similarity score that is normalised for length, because RMSD alone rewards short alignments. A score normalised by length is what makes “these two domains have the same fold” a statement that can be thresholded.
Molecular docking predicts how a small molecule binds a target: a search over the ligand’s position, orientation and rotatable bonds inside a defined pocket, scored by an empirical function that approximates binding free energy. AutoDock Vina (Trott and Olson 2009) is the most widely used open implementation. It is not installed in this book’s environment, so no docking is run here and no scores are quoted; what a Vina run would look like is shown below purely to make the shape of the workflow concrete.
vina --receptor p53_core.pdbqt --ligand compound.pdbqt \
     --center_x 92.0 --center_y 20.5 --center_z 48.3 \
     --size_x 24 --size_y 24 --size_z 24 --exhaustiveness 16
Three things about that command matter more than the software. The receptor and ligand must be prepared — hydrogens added, protonation states chosen at the right pH, charges assigned — and those choices change the result more than most users expect. The search box must be defined, which means you must already know roughly where the site is; docking is not a site-finding method. And the output is a ranked list with scores in kcal/mol whose absolute values are not reliable binding affinities: docking scores rank poses adequately, rank compounds poorly, and predict affinity badly. A virtual screen is a filter that enriches a library for testing, not a measurement, and its hits are hypotheses for an assay.
Finally, visualisation. A structure viewer such as ChimeraX (Pettersen et al. 2020) is not an optional extra; looking at a structure catches errors that no script will, and every quantity computed in this chapter should be checked by eye at least once. Three habits make the difference between a figure that informs and one that decorates. Show only what the point requires — a cartoon of the backbone with three side chains drawn explicitly beats a full atomic model of everything. Colour by a quantity that carries information, such as B factor, pLDDT or chain, rather than by aesthetics. And state the viewpoint and what is hidden in the caption, because a structure figure is a projection and the reader cannot see what you rotated away.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
text:
10.9 Summary

Secondary structure is local hydrogen bonding, tertiary structure is the fold driven mainly by the hydrophobic effect, and quaternary structure is the assembly. Only the first level is directly encoded in the sequence file.
Judge a crystal structure by resolution, R-free, B factors and missing residues before using it. 1TUP reports no R-free and 1MBN no R factor at all, which is a fact about when they were deposited and a limit on what can be checked.
Residues missing from a model are in REMARK 465, not in the coordinates. Seventy-two residues of 1TUP are modelled nowhere, all at chain termini, and AlphaFold independently assigns those regions its lowest confidence.
Bio.PDB’s structure–model–chain–residue–atom hierarchy makes geometry a few lines of code: the zinc of p53 is held tetrahedrally by Cys176, His179, Cys238 and Cys242 at 1.99–2.33 Å, and only chain B of 1TUP is bound in the DNA major groove.
A contact map turns a fold into a picture: bands perpendicular to the diagonal mean antiparallel β-strands, and the DNA-binding residues of p53 are scattered in sequence and adjacent in space.
Three copies of one domain in one crystal differ by 0.78–1.03 Å. That is the scale against which any other RMSD should be read, and RMSD must always be quoted with the number of atoms aligned.
pLDDT measures local confidence and predicted aligned error measures confidence in relative orientation. A model with two confident domains and high PAE between them supports no statement about their arrangement.
The AlphaFold p53 DNA-binding domain matches chain B of the crystal structure to 0.73 Å, closer than the three experimental copies come to each other; its disordered regions score below 50, which is a correct prediction rather than a failure.
Docking scores rank poses adequately and affinities badly. A virtual screen produces hypotheses for an assay, not measurements.

text:
10.10 Exercises

Compute the mean B factor of each of the three protein chains in 1TUP. Which chain is the best ordered, and does that agree with which chain is bound to DNA?
Using missing_residues, list the missing residues of chain C of 1TUP and state where in the sequence they fall. What does their position imply about the construct that was crystallised?
Compute the distance between the Cα atoms of Arg248 and Arg273 in chain B of 1TUP. Both are mutational hotspots; does the distance suggest they contact the same part of the DNA?
Repeat the contact-map calculation for myoglobin and compare the result with

Describe in two sentences how an all-α contact map differs from an all-β one.


Compute the fraction of residues in the AlphaFold p53 model with pLDDT above 90, between 70 and 90, between 50 and 70, and below 50. Then state which single region of the protein you would be willing to use for docking, and why.
Superpose the AlphaFold model onto chain A and chain C of 1TUP as well as chain B. Are the three RMSDs similar, and what would it mean if one were much larger?
A colleague reports that two proteins “have the same fold because their RMSD is 2.5 Å”. Explain in three or four sentences what else you would need to know before accepting that, and what measurement you would ask for instead.
The AlphaFold model places the tetramerisation domain at a specific position relative to the DNA-binding domain. Using the PAE matrix, quantify how much that placement should be trusted: report the mean predicted aligned error between residues 94–292 and residues 326–356, and compare it with the mean within each block.

title: 10  Protein structure and what you can compute from it
text:
10.11 Solutions






Solutions





1. Chain A is the best ordered at a mean B factor of 26.0 Å², then chain B at 35.7 and chain C at 44.8 — and that order does not follow DNA binding, since chain B is the one in the major groove. The lesson is that B factors report on the crystal, not on biology: how tightly a chain is held by its lattice neighbours matters at least as much as what it binds, and a B-factor difference between chains is not evidence about function.

for chain_id in "ABC":
    values = np.array([atom.get_bfactor() for residue in model[chain_id]
                       if residue.id[0] == " " for atom in residue])
    print(f"chain {chain_id}: mean B = {values.mean():5.1f} A^2, "
          f"max = {values.max():5.1f} A^2")
#> chain A: mean B =  26.0 A^2, max =  70.0 A^2
#> chain B: mean B =  35.7 A^2, max =  70.0 A^2
#> chain C: mean B =  44.8 A^2, max =  70.0 A^2

2. The missing residues of every chain are at the termini, not in the middle. The crystallised construct was longer than the ordered domain, and the extra residues at each end are disordered; nothing internal to the fold is missing, which is reassuring.

chain_c = sorted(n for c, n in gaps if c == "C")
print(f"chain C missing {len(chain_c)} residues: {chain_c}")
#> chain C missing 24 residues: [94, 290, 291, 292, 293, 294, 295, 296, 297, 298, 299, 300, 301, 302, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 308, 309, 310, 311, 312]
ordered = [r.id[1] for r in model["C"] if r.id[0] == " "]
print(f"ordered range in the model: {min(ordered)}-{max(ordered)}")
#> ordered range in the model: 95-289

3. The two Cα atoms are 9.2 Å apart — close enough to act on the same stretch of DNA but too far to touch the same base pair. They contact it differently: Arg273 grips the phosphate backbone in the major groove while Arg248 reaches into the minor groove. Two hotspots can therefore both abolish binding by entirely separate mechanisms, which is why “hotspot mutation” is not one phenotype.

separation = model["B"][248]["CA"] - model["B"][273]["CA"]
print(f"Arg248 CA to Arg273 CA: {separation:.1f} A")
#> Arg248 CA to Arg273 CA: 9.2 A

4. Myoglobin’s map is a thick diagonal with a few isolated off-diagonal patches where helices pack against each other; p53’s is dominated by long bands perpendicular to the diagonal. An α-helical protein makes most of its contacts locally, within three or four residues, whereas a β-sheet makes its defining contacts between strands that may be fifty residues apart.

mb_residues = [r for r in myoglobin["A"] if r.id[0] == " " and "CA" in r]
mb_ca = np.array([r["CA"].coord for r in mb_residues])
mb_contact = np.linalg.norm(mb_ca[:, None, :] - mb_ca[None, :, :], axis=2) < 8.0
local = np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(len(mb_ca)), np.arange(len(mb_ca)))) <= 4
print(f"myoglobin: {100 * mb_contact[~local].mean():.1f}% of non-local pairs in contact")
#> myoglobin: 1.3% of non-local pairs in contact
distant = np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(len(ca_coords)), np.arange(len(ca_coords)))) <= 4
print(f"p53 DBD  : {100 * contact[~distant].mean():.1f}% of non-local pairs in contact")
#> p53 DBD  : 2.6% of non-local pairs in contact

5. Just over half the residues are above 90 and nearly a third below 50, with very little in between — confidence in this protein is bimodal, not graded. Only the DNA-binding domain, and arguably the tetramerisation domain, could be considered for docking; the termini have no fixed structure to dock into, and a pocket apparently formed by them in the model is an artefact of drawing a disordered chain in one arrangement.

bands = [(90, 100, "very high"), (70, 90, "confident"),
         (50, 70, "low"), (0, 50, "very low")]
for low, high, label in bands:
    fraction = ((plddt >= low) & (plddt < high)).mean()
    print(f"pLDDT {low:3d}-{high:3d} ({label:10s}): {100 * fraction:4.1f}%")
#> pLDDT  90-100 (very high ): 52.7%
#> pLDDT  70- 90 (confident ):  7.1%
#> pLDDT  50- 70 (low       ): 10.4%
#> pLDDT   0- 50 (very low  ): 29.8%

6. The three RMSDs are all close to 1 Å, which says the prediction matches every experimental copy equally well. A much larger value against one chain only would mean that chain adopts a different conformation — most likely in a loop responding to a crystal contact — rather than that the prediction is wrong.

for chain_id in "ABC":
    experimental = alpha_carbons(chain_id)
    shared = sorted(set(experimental) & {r.id[1] for r in af_residues})
    predicted = {r.id[1]: r["CA"] for r in af_residues if r.id[1] in experimental}
    superimposer.set_atoms([experimental[n] for n in shared],
                           [predicted[n] for n in shared])
    print(f"AlphaFold vs chain {chain_id}: {len(shared)} pairs, "
          f"RMSD = {superimposer.rms:.2f} A")
#> AlphaFold vs chain A: 196 pairs, RMSD = 1.05 A
#> AlphaFold vs chain B: 194 pairs, RMSD = 0.73 A
#> AlphaFold vs chain C: 195 pairs, RMSD = 0.87 A

7. You would need the number of residues aligned, because RMSD over 40 residues and over 400 are not comparable; the sequence identity, because it changes what “same fold” would imply; whether the 2.5 Å is over the whole chain or over a structurally conserved core; and whether the correspondence came from a structural alignment or from a sequence alignment that may itself be wrong. The measurement to ask for is a length-normalised structural similarity score with its alignment length, together with the classification both domains receive in CATH or SCOP.
8. The mean predicted aligned error between the two domains is 20.1 Å, against 3.6 Å within the DNA-binding domain and 2.7 Å within the tetramerisation domain — six to eight times larger, and well over half the matrix’s maximum of 32 Å. The relative placement is therefore not predicted at all, and any distance measured between the two domains in this model is meaningless.

dbd = slice(93, 292)             # residues 94-292, zero-based
tet = slice(325, 356)            # residues 326-356
print(f"mean PAE within DNA-binding domain : {pae[dbd, dbd].mean():5.2f} A")
#> mean PAE within DNA-binding domain :  3.60 A
print(f"mean PAE within tetramerisation    : {pae[tet, tet].mean():5.2f} A")
#> mean PAE within tetramerisation    :  2.65 A
print(f"mean PAE between the two domains   : {pae[dbd, tet].mean():5.2f} A")
#> mean PAE between the two domains   : 20.10 A
print(f"maximum PAE in the whole matrix    : {pae.max():5.2f} A")
#> maximum PAE in the whole matrix    : 32.00 A

10.12 Further reading


Berman (2000) and Burley et al. (2022) describe the Protein Data Bank at its founding and as it now operates; read the second for what the archive validates and what it does not.

Kabsch and Sander (1983) is the DSSP paper, and the definition of secondary structure that most software still implements.

Jumper et al. (2021) is the AlphaFold paper; its supplementary material is where pLDDT and predicted aligned error are actually defined.

Varadi et al. (2021) describes the AlphaFold database and is the right citation when you use a downloaded model, together with the UniProt accession and model version.

Baek et al. (2021) solves the same problem by a different route, and reading it alongside Jumper et al. (2021) separates what is essential to the approach from what is particular to one implementation.

Trott and Olson (2009) introduces AutoDock Vina and is candid about what its scoring function can and cannot do; read it before interpreting any docking score.

Cho et al. (1994) is the structure used throughout this chapter, and its discussion of why particular residues are cancer hotspots is a model of reading biology out of coordinates.

Pettersen et al. (2020) describes ChimeraX, which is the practical tool for looking at everything computed here.
