title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
section: 11.2 What a network adds to a gene list
text:
11.2 What a network adds to a gene list
A gene list is a set. A network is a set plus a relation, and almost every question worth asking about a group of genes is a question about the relation. Are these genes connected to each other more than chance would predict? Do they cluster into separable groups? Is there a small number of genes through which most of the connections run? Which genes, not in the list, sit between the ones that are?
That last question is the one that most often changes an experiment. If 20 genes from a 400-gene list all connect to a single transcription factor that is itself not differentially expressed, the factor becomes a candidate even though no measurement flagged it. This is the characteristic move of network biology: using known relations to reach the entities a measurement did not see, because their activity changed without their messenger RNA (mRNA) abundance changing.
The move has a cost, and it is worth stating before the first line of code. A measurement — a read count, a peak height — is an observation of the system under study. An edge in a public interaction network is an observation about a different system, usually a cell line, under different conditions, reported by somebody else, sometimes inferred rather than observed at all. When you put your measurement into a network, you are mixing two kinds of knowledge with very different error structures, and the network’s errors are mostly invisible to you. Everything else in this chapter follows from taking that seriously.
Systems biology, understood narrowly, is the attempt to explain a phenotype by the behaviour of an interacting set of components rather than by any one component. Understood broadly, it is simply the admission that genes do not act alone. The narrow version demands quantitative models — rate constants, differential equations, perturbation data — and is out of scope here. The broad version is where most practical bioinformatics lives, and its tools are graphs and annotation databases.
crumbs: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
section: 11.3 Kinds of network and the evidence behind an edge
text:
11.3 Kinds of network and the evidence behind an edge
Four classes of network cover most of what you will meet. They look identical once loaded into igraph (Csardi and Nepusz 2006), which is exactly the problem, because their edges mean entirely different things.
A protein–protein interaction (PPI) network has proteins as nodes and physical association as edges. “Physical association” conceals a range of evidence: a solved co-crystal structure, a yeast two-hybrid positive, an affinity-purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS) co-precipitation, or a sentence in an abstract saying two proteins “interact”. These have wildly different false positive rates, and high-throughput screens are known to be noisy in both directions.
A gene regulatory network has directed edges: transcription factor to target. Evidence ranges from a ChIP-seq peak near a promoter — which shows binding, not regulation — to a reporter assay with mutated binding sites, which shows regulation in one construct in one cell type. Direction is the valuable part and the part most often asserted from correlation.
A metabolic network is the best-grounded of the four. Nodes are metabolites and edges are enzyme-catalysed reactions with a stoichiometry established by biochemistry, often decades ago. Its uncertainty lies not in whether the reaction exists but in whether a given organism runs it under given conditions.
A co-expression network has an edge wherever two genes’ expression profiles correlate above a threshold across samples. Nothing physical is claimed. The edges are a property of the expression dataset, and change when you change the samples, the normalisation or the correlation cut-off.






A PPI network is not a measurement of your system



Interaction databases are aggregations of published results, and publication is not a random sample of biology. A protein studied by two hundred laboratories will have hundreds of recorded partners; an equally important protein studied by two will have three. Degree in a PPI network is therefore partly a measurement of scientific attention. You will quantify this bias later in the chapter.


The STRING subnetwork bundled with the book makes this visible, because STRING keeps its evidence channels separate instead of reporting only a combined score.

string_edges <- read_tsv(book_data("networks", "p53_string_network.tsv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)

cat("edges:", nrow(string_edges),
    " combined score range:", min(string_edges$score), "-",
    max(string_edges$score), "\n")
#> edges: 210  combined score range: 0.701 - 0.999
names(string_edges)
#>  [1] "stringId_A"      "stringId_B"      "preferredName_A" "preferredName_B"
#>  [5] "ncbiTaxonId"     "score"           "nscore"          "fscore"         
#>  [9] "pscore"          "ascore"          "escore"          "dscore"         
#> [13] "tscore"

The columns from nscore to tscore are the individual channels: genomic neighbourhood, gene fusion, phylogenetic co-occurrence, co-expression, experiments, curated databases and text mining. Each is a probability-like score between 0 and 1, and the combined score integrates them. Counting how many edges each channel supports tells you what this network is actually made of.

channels <- c(neighbourhood = "nscore", fusion = "fscore",
              cooccurrence = "pscore", coexpression = "ascore",
              experiments = "escore", database = "dscore",
              textmining = "tscore")

support <- sapply(channels, function(col) sum(string_edges[[col]] > 0))
print(support)
#> neighbourhood        fusion  cooccurrence  coexpression   experiments 
#>             0             0             4           123           176 
#>      database    textmining 
#>            85           210

# Edges with no experimental and no curated-database support at all.
cat("edges resting on inference alone:",
    sum(string_edges$escore == 0 & string_edges$dscore == 0), "\n")
#> edges resting on inference alone: 26

Every one of the 210 edges has a text-mining score above zero, 176 have experimental support and only 85 appear in a curated database. Twenty-six edges rest on no experimental or curated evidence whatsoever: they exist because two gene names co-occur in the literature and because the genes are co-expressed. Those 26 edges are not wrong, but they are a different kind of claim from a co-crystal structure, and a result that depends on them is correspondingly weaker. Filtering by individual channel rather than by combined score is often the right first move, and is one line of dplyr: filter(escore >= 0.4) keeps the experimentally supported subnetwork.






Record the confidence threshold with the result



STRING’s default web threshold is 0.400 (medium confidence); this bundle used 0.700 (high). The number of edges roughly doubles between the two, and so does every topology statistic computed from them. A network figure without a stated score threshold cannot be reproduced or compared.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
section: 11.4 Graph vocabulary and the shape of a real network
text:
11.4 Graph vocabulary and the shape of a real network
A graph is a set of nodes (also called vertices) and a set of edges joining pairs of them. An edge may be directed or undirected, and may carry a weight. The degree of a node is the number of edges touching it. A path is a sequence of edges leading from one node to another, and the shortest path between two nodes is the one with fewest edges; its length is the distance. A component is a maximal set of nodes all reachable from each other. The density of a graph is the fraction of possible edges that are present. These seven terms carry most of the chapter.

p53_net <- string_edges |>
  select(preferredName_A, preferredName_B) |>
  graph_from_data_frame(directed = FALSE) |>
  simplify()  # drop duplicate edges and any self-loops

cat("nodes:", vcount(p53_net), " edges:", ecount(p53_net), "\n")
#> nodes: 30  edges: 210
cat("density:", round(edge_density(p53_net), 3),
    " mean degree:", mean(degree(p53_net)), "\n")
#> density: 0.483  mean degree: 14
cat("components:", components(p53_net)$no,
    " largest:", max(components(p53_net)$csize), "\n")
#> components: 1  largest: 30

Thirty nodes, 210 edges, a single connected component and a density of 0.483: nearly half of all possible pairs are joined. That is extraordinarily dense for a biological network, and the reason is the sampling, not the biology. These 30 genes were chosen as a coherent functional group and then queried against a database that already knows they belong together. A query-driven subnetwork is not a random sample of the interactome and must never be described as one.
Distances in such a graph are short by construction.

cat("diameter:", diameter(p53_net), "\n")
#> diameter: 2
cat("mean shortest path:", round(mean_distance(p53_net), 3), "\n")
#> mean shortest path: 1.517
cat("global clustering coefficient:",
    round(transitivity(p53_net, type = "global"), 3), "\n")
#> global clustering coefficient: 0.646
cat("mean local clustering coefficient:",
    round(transitivity(p53_net, type = "average"), 3), "\n")
#> mean local clustering coefficient: 0.726

shortest_paths(p53_net, from = "LZTR1", to = "BAX", output = "vpath")$vpath[[1]]
#> + 3/30 vertices, named, from d94d007:
#> [1] LZTR1 TP53  BAX

The diameter is two: every gene reaches every other in at most two steps. The clustering coefficient measures how often a node’s neighbours are themselves neighbours — formally, the fraction of connected triples that close into triangles. At 0.646 globally this network is highly cliquish, which again reflects the curated selection of genes. A genome-scale PPI network typically has a mean distance near four and a clustering coefficient around 0.1.
The degree distribution is where the most common over-claim in network biology lives. Figure 11.1 shows it two ways: as a histogram, and as the complementary cumulative distribution on logarithmic axes, which is the plot people use when arguing that a network is scale-free.

node_degree <- degree(p53_net)

hist_panel <- ggplot(data.frame(k = node_degree), aes(k)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = book_palette[1], colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Degree k", y = "Number of genes", title = "Degree distribution")

ccdf <- data.frame(k = sort(unique(node_degree))) |>
  mutate(p_ge_k = sapply(k, function(x) mean(node_degree >= x)))

ccdf_panel <- ggplot(ccdf, aes(k, p_ge_k)) +
  geom_point(colour = book_palette[4], size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Degree k (log scale)", y = "P(K >= k)", title = "Cumulative tail")

patchwork::wrap_plots(hist_panel, ccdf_panel)






Figure 11.1: Degree in the 30-gene STRING subnetwork. Left: the degree distribution is broad but has no long tail, and the most connected node (TP53, degree 29) is joined to every other gene. Right: the same degrees as a complementary cumulative distribution on logarithmic axes; with 30 nodes the curve is too short to distinguish a power law from any other heavy-tailed shape.




Read the right-hand panel carefully. It contains 17 points. A straight line through 17 points on log–log axes is not evidence of a power law, and the claim that biological networks are scale-free — that the probability of degree k falls as k raised to some negative power, producing a few enormous hubs — has been tested far more loosely than its popularity suggests (Broido and Clauset 2019). Fitting a power law requires hundreds of nodes, a maximum-likelihood estimate of the exponent, a lower cut-off chosen by the data rather than by eye, and a goodness-of-fit test against alternatives such as the log-normal. None of that is possible here, and saying “the network is scale-free” on the strength of a plot like this one is a claim your reader cannot check.
What survives is weaker and more useful: degree is unevenly distributed, with a handful of genes far above the mean of 14 and several at the bottom. That unevenness is worth investigating regardless of what functional form generates it.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.5 Centrality, hubs and study bias
Centrality is any measure of how important a node is to the structure of a graph, and the choice of measure encodes what you mean by important. Degree counts connections. Betweenness counts how many shortest paths between other pairs of nodes pass through a node, identifying bridges between otherwise separate regions. Closeness measures how near a node is to all others on average.

centrality <- data.frame(
  gene        = names(node_degree),
  degree      = as.integer(node_degree),
  betweenness = round(betweenness(p53_net, normalized = TRUE), 3),
  closeness   = round(closeness(p53_net, normalized = TRUE), 3)
) |> arrange(desc(degree))

head(centrality, 8)
#>          gene degree betweenness closeness
#> TP53     TP53     29       0.170     1.000
#> BRCA1   BRCA1     22       0.037     0.806
#> MDM2     MDM2     21       0.034     0.784
#> PTEN     PTEN     21       0.034     0.784
#> MYC       MYC     21       0.034     0.784
#> CDKN2A CDKN2A     20       0.033     0.763
#> CDKN1A CDKN1A     19       0.020     0.744
#> AKT1     AKT1     19       0.025     0.744

TP53 has degree 29 in a 30-node graph: it is joined to everything. Its normalised betweenness, 0.170, is five times that of the next gene, so it also lies on most shortest paths. In a network assembled by querying a database for p53-associated genes, this is not a discovery. It is the query, returned.
The deeper problem is that hub status in any literature-derived network partly measures how much a gene has been studied. The bundled GO annotation file gives a direct proxy for study intensity — the number of GO terms a gene carries — and the relationship is strong.

go_annotations <- read_tsv(book_data("annotation", "human_go_annotations.tsv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)

gene_to_go <- go_annotations |>
  filter(!is.na(`Gene Ontology IDs`), !is.na(`Gene Names (primary)`)) |>
  transmute(gene = `Gene Names (primary)`, go = `Gene Ontology IDs`) |>
  separate_longer_delim(go, delim = "; ") |>
  distinct()

terms_per_gene <- count(gene_to_go, gene, name = "n_go")
bias <- inner_join(centrality, terms_per_gene, by = "gene")

cat("Spearman correlation of degree with GO-term count:",
    round(cor(bias$degree, bias$n_go, method = "spearman"), 3), "\n")
#> Spearman correlation of degree with GO-term count: 0.746
cat("median GO terms, all human proteins:", median(terms_per_gene$n_go),
    " in this network:", median(bias$n_go), "\n")
#> median GO terms, all human proteins: 9  in this network: 54.5

The rank correlation between degree and annotation count is 0.746. Genes in this network carry a median of 54.5 GO terms against a genome-wide median of nine. Two explanations compete: important genes attract both interactions and annotations, or well-studied genes accumulate both. Both are partly true, and no analysis of the network alone can separate them.






Report hubs as candidates, never as conclusions



“We identified TP53 as a hub and therefore a key regulator” is a sentence that cannot be falsified by the data that produced it. The defensible version names the hub, states the evidence channels behind its edges, acknowledges the literature bias, and proposes the experiment that would settle it — a knockdown, a degron, a dose–response.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.6 Finding modules
A community or module is a group of nodes with more edges inside the group than to the rest of the network. Modularity, written Q, scores a partition by comparing its within-group edge count to the count expected if edges were rewired at random; Q above roughly 0.3 is usually taken as meaningful structure. Community detection algorithms search for partitions with high Q.
Two popular algorithms take different routes. The Louvain method (Blondel et al. 2008) moves nodes between communities greedily and then collapses communities into nodes, repeating until Q stops improving. Fast greedy modularity optimisation instead merges the pair of communities that most increases Q, building a dendrogram and cutting it at the maximum. Running both on the same graph is the minimum honest practice.

set.seed(20250101)
louvain  <- cluster_louvain(p53_net)
greedy   <- cluster_fast_greedy(p53_net)
walktrap <- cluster_walktrap(p53_net)

partitions <- list(Louvain = louvain, FastGreedy = greedy, Walktrap = walktrap)
for (method in names(partitions)) {
  result <- partitions[[method]]
  cat(method, ": k =", length(result),
      " Q =", round(modularity(result), 3),
      " sizes =", paste(sizes(result), collapse = ","), "\n")
}
#> Louvain : k = 3  Q = 0.137  sizes = 11,13,6 
#> FastGreedy : k = 3  Q = 0.135  sizes = 12,7,11 
#> Walktrap : k = 4  Q = 0.109  sizes = 15,4,10,1

Louvain finds three communities with Q = 0.137; fast greedy also finds three, with Q = 0.135; walktrap finds four with Q = 0.109. All three values are far below 0.3. The correct conclusion is that this network has no strong modular structure — which is what you should expect from a dense, hand-picked set of genes that all participate in one broad process. The algorithms still return a partition, because they always do. An algorithm that cannot say “no structure here” will never say it.
How much do the two best partitions agree? The adjusted Rand index compares two clusterings, scoring 1 for identical partitions and about 0 for the agreement expected by chance.

cat("adjusted Rand index, Louvain vs fast greedy:",
    round(compare(louvain, greedy, method = "adjusted.rand"), 3), "\n")
#> adjusted Rand index, Louvain vs fast greedy: 0.7
table(Louvain = membership(louvain), FastGreedy = membership(greedy))
#>        FastGreedy
#> Louvain  1  2  3
#>       1 10  1  0
#>       2  2  0 11
#>       3  0  6  0

An adjusted Rand index of 0.700 means substantial but incomplete agreement: the cross-tabulation shows one 10-gene core assigned together by both methods, an 11-gene group likewise, and three genes that move. Those three genes are the interesting ones — they are the genes whose module membership is an artefact of the algorithm, and no biological story should be built on them.
A third algorithm illustrates how badly the choice can go. The Girvan–Newman method (Girvan and Newman 2002), available as cluster_edge_betweenness(), removes the highest-betweenness edge repeatedly and is elegant but quadratic in the number of edges. On this dense graph it returns 20 communities, 19 of them singletons, with Q = 0.009. Dense graphs defeat it, and the method suits sparse networks with genuine bottlenecks instead.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
section: 11.7 Drawing a network that can be read
text:
11.7 Drawing a network that can be read
Network figures fail in a characteristic way. Past a few hundred edges, a force-directed layout produces an undifferentiated mass — a “hairball” — in which every node is adjacent to a dark region and nothing can be traced. The failure is not aesthetic. A hairball transmits no information, so a figure that is one is a figure that should have been a table.
Figure 11.2 makes the comparison directly. The left panel places the same 30 nodes at random; the right panel uses the Fruchterman–Reingold force-directed layout, sizes nodes by degree and colours them by Louvain community.

module_colour <- book_palette[membership(louvain)]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))

set.seed(20250101)
plot(p53_net, layout = layout_randomly, vertex.label = NA,
     vertex.size = 6, vertex.color = "grey70",
     edge.color = "grey75", main = "Random layout")

set.seed(20250101)
plot(p53_net, layout = layout_with_fr,
     vertex.size = 4 + 0.6 * node_degree,
     vertex.color = module_colour, vertex.frame.color = "white",
     vertex.label.cex = 0.6, vertex.label.color = "black",
     vertex.label.family = "sans",
     edge.color = adjustcolor("grey60", alpha.f = 0.5),
     main = "Force-directed, sized and coloured")






Figure 11.2: The same 30-gene STRING subnetwork drawn two ways. Left: a random layout, in which edge density alone prevents any structure from being read. Right: a Fruchterman-Reingold layout with node area proportional to degree and colour by Louvain community; TP53 sits at the centre because it is adjacent to every other node. Even the right-hand panel is close to the density at which force-directed drawings stop being informative.




The right-hand panel is legible only because there are 30 nodes. Three habits keep larger networks readable. First, filter before drawing: raise the confidence threshold, keep the largest component, or show only the subgraph induced by the genes you will discuss. Second, encode at most two variables visually — size for one quantity, colour for another — and put everything else in a table. Third, label selectively; a label on every node is a label on none. When filtering cannot rescue the figure, present the topology as numbers and show only the subnetwork around the genes under discussion.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.8 Pathway resources and over-representation analysis
Three resources dominate functional interpretation. The Gene Ontology (GO) is a structured vocabulary of terms in three namespaces — biological process, molecular function and cellular component — arranged as a directed acyclic graph in which a term implies all its ancestors (Ashburner et al. 2000; Aleksander et al. 2023). KEGG curates metabolic and signalling pathway maps with defined reactions and topology (Kanehisa 2000). Reactome curates reactions at finer granularity, with explicit inputs, outputs, catalysts and literature evidence for each step (Milacic et al. 2023). GO annotates genes with terms; KEGG and Reactome place gene products inside a described mechanism. GO has the widest coverage, Reactome the most explicit evidence trail.
Over-representation analysis (ORA) asks a single question: given a background universe of genes, a gene set defined by an annotation term, and a query list, are more query genes annotated to that term than you would expect by chance? The exact test is the hypergeometric distribution — the distribution of the number of white balls drawn when sampling n balls without replacement from an urn holding K white and N − K black. Here N is the universe, K the term’s size, n the query list size and k the observed overlap.
The annotation table must first be reshaped from one row per protein to one row per gene–term pair — the form every enrichment tool uses internally. The separate_longer_delim() call in the previous section did exactly this, and the tidyverse idiom generalises to any semicolon-delimited annotation column (Wickham et al. 2019).

universe <- unique(gene_to_go$gene)
term_sizes <- count(gene_to_go, go, name = "K")

cat("universe:", length(universe), "genes;",
    nrow(term_sizes), "distinct GO terms;",
    nrow(gene_to_go), "gene-term pairs\n")
#> universe: 19248 genes; 17553 distinct GO terms; 247239 gene-term pairs

The query list is the 30 network genes, all of which map to the universe. The test itself is one call to phyper(). Note the k - 1 and lower.tail = FALSE: you want P(X ≥ k), and phyper(q, ...) with the upper tail returns P(X > q).

query_genes <- V(p53_net)$name
n_query <- length(query_genes)
N <- length(universe)

enrichment <- gene_to_go |>
  filter(gene %in% query_genes) |>
  count(go, name = "k") |>
  inner_join(term_sizes, by = "go") |>
  filter(K >= 5, K <= 2000) |>          # drop terms too small or too vague to test
  mutate(expected = round(n_query * K / N, 2),
         p_value  = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, n_query, lower.tail = FALSE),
         p_adj    = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_value)

cat("terms tested:", nrow(enrichment),
    " significant at BH < 0.05:", sum(enrichment$p_adj < 0.05), "\n")
#> terms tested: 830  significant at BH < 0.05: 511
head(enrichment, 6)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   go             k     K expected  p_value    p_adj
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 GO:0042802    21  1744     2.72 7.23e-16 6.00e-13
#> 2 GO:0006974    12   303     0.47 1.25e-14 5.19e-12
#> 3 GO:0008630     7    39     0.06 1.56e-13 4.32e-11
#> 4 GO:0032991    13   641     1    3.91e-12 8.11e-10
#> 5 GO:0090399     5    13     0.02 8.26e-12 1.37e- 9
#> 6 GO:0051726     9   195     0.3  1.11e-11 1.54e- 9

That is over-representation analysis in its entirety. A package such as clusterProfiler (Yu et al. 2012) adds term-name lookup, ontology-aware filtering, plotting and support for many organisms, but the statistic underneath is the call you just made. Knowing this matters when a tool and your own calculation disagree: the difference will be in the universe, the term-size filter or the ontology propagation, never in the distribution.
Two filtering decisions were made above and both are conventional rather than principled. Terms with fewer than five annotated genes produce unstable estimates and dominate the tail of small p-values for trivial reasons. Terms with more than 2,000 genes — “protein binding”, “cytoplasm” — are too vague to interpret even when significant. State both bounds in your methods; they change the answer.
Correcting for multiple testing
Testing 830 terms at a 5% threshold would be expected to yield about 42 false positives by chance alone. The Bonferroni correction divides the threshold by the number of tests, controlling the probability of even one false positive but discarding real signal. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure instead controls the false discovery rate (FDR): the expected proportion of false positives among the terms you call significant (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). For exploratory enrichment, where the output is a list of hypotheses rather than a single decision, FDR control is the right trade-off; p.adjust(method = "BH") applies it.

cat("raw p < 0.05:        ", sum(enrichment$p_value < 0.05), "\n")
#> raw p < 0.05:         617
cat("Benjamini-Hochberg:  ", sum(enrichment$p_adj < 0.05), "\n")
#> Benjamini-Hochberg:   511
cat("Bonferroni:          ",
    sum(p.adjust(enrichment$p_value, "bonferroni") < 0.05), "\n")
#> Bonferroni:           82

617 terms pass uncorrected, 511 survive FDR control and 82 survive Bonferroni. The gap between 511 and 82 is the price of the two error rates, and the fact that 511 of 830 tested terms are “significant” is itself a warning that the chapter returns to below. An alternative to BH is Storey’s q-value, which estimates the proportion of true null hypotheses rather than assuming it is one, and typically calls more terms significant (Storey and Tibshirani 2003).
The annotation file carries GO identifiers but not term names. Names come from the ontology itself; the EBI QuickGO service resolves identifiers in a single request.

# Not executed at build time: the book must render without network access.
library(jsonlite)
url <- paste0("https://www.ebi.ac.uk/QuickGO/services/ontology/go/terms/",
              paste(head(enrichment$go, 10), collapse = ","))
terms <- fromJSON(url)$results
print(terms[, c("id", "name")])

That request, run on 15 October 2026, returned the following (the service does not preserve the order of the identifiers you send):
           id                                                            name
1  GO:0002039                                                     p53 binding
2  GO:0008630 intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage
3  GO:0042802                                       identical protein binding
4  GO:0030330  DNA damage response, signal transduction by p53 class mediator
5  GO:0032991                                      protein-containing complex
6  GO:0090399                                          replicative senescence
7  GO:0006974                                             DNA damage response
8  GO:0051726                                        regulation of cell cycle
9  GO:0097193                           intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway
10 GO:0071479                         cellular response to ionizing radiation
Figure 11.3 plots them in the standard form: effect on one axis, evidence on the other.

go_labels <- c(
  "GO:0042802" = "identical protein binding",
  "GO:0006974" = "DNA damage response",
  "GO:0008630" = "intrinsic apoptosis, DNA damage",
  "GO:0032991" = "protein-containing complex",
  "GO:0090399" = "replicative senescence",
  "GO:0051726" = "regulation of cell cycle",
  "GO:0002039" = "p53 binding",
  "GO:0071479" = "response to ionising radiation",
  "GO:0097193" = "intrinsic apoptotic signalling",
  "GO:0030330" = "p53-mediated DNA damage response")

top_terms <- enrichment |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(term = go_labels[go],
         fold = k / expected)

ggplot(top_terms, aes(fold, reorder(term, fold))) +
  geom_point(aes(size = k, colour = -log10(p_adj))) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = book_palette[8], high = book_palette[4]) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 7)) +
  labs(x = "Fold enrichment", y = NULL,
       size = "Genes", colour = expression(-log[10]~italic(p)[adj]))






Figure 11.3: The ten most enriched GO terms for the 30-gene network. Fold enrichment is the observed overlap divided by the overlap expected under the hypergeometric null; point area is the number of query genes annotated to the term and colour the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value. Terms near the top of the axis are the most specific, and the two broadest terms (identical protein binding, protein-containing complex) carry the largest gene counts but the weakest fold enrichment.




The pattern in Figure 11.3 is the one every ORA produces. Specific terms — replicative senescence, p53 binding — show fold enrichments of 60 to 250 on a handful of genes. The two broadest terms, each covering hundreds of proteins, show fold enrichments under 14 across many genes. Both kinds are significant; only the specific ones say anything.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.9 Rank-based enrichment
ORA requires a cut-off. Genes are in the list or out of it, and a gene just below the threshold contributes nothing while its neighbour just above contributes fully. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) removes the cut-off by using the whole ranked list (Subramanian et al. 2005). Walk down the ranking from the top; add to a running sum when you meet a member of the gene set, subtract when you meet a non-member. If the set’s members are concentrated near the top, the running sum climbs to a large positive peak before falling back. That peak is the enrichment score (ES).
The function is short enough to write out, which is the point of writing it out.

running_enrichment <- function(ranked_stat, set_members) {
  is_hit <- names(ranked_stat) %in% set_members
  weights <- abs(ranked_stat)
  hit_sum  <- cumsum(ifelse(is_hit, weights, 0)) / sum(weights[is_hit])
  miss_sum <- cumsum(ifelse(is_hit, 0, 1)) / sum(!is_hit)
  hit_sum - miss_sum
}

A ranking is needed. In a real analysis it would be a differential expression statistic across every measured gene. Here, to keep every number in the chapter computable from bundled data, the 30 network genes are ranked by degree and tested against the p53-binding gene set. This is a demonstration of mechanics on a deliberately small list, not an analysis anyone would publish.

ranked_by_degree <- sort(node_degree, decreasing = TRUE)
p53_binders <- gene_to_go |>
  filter(go == "GO:0002039", gene %in% names(ranked_by_degree)) |>
  pull(gene)

walk <- running_enrichment(ranked_by_degree, p53_binders)
observed_es <- walk[which.max(abs(walk))]

set.seed(20250101)
null_es <- replicate(2000, {
  shuffled <- setNames(ranked_by_degree, sample(names(ranked_by_degree)))
  w <- running_enrichment(sort(shuffled, decreasing = TRUE), p53_binders)
  w[which.max(abs(w))]
})

cat("set size:", length(p53_binders),
    " ES:", round(observed_es, 3),
    " permutation p:", round((1 + sum(null_es >= observed_es)) / 2001, 4), "\n")
#> set size: 7  ES: 0.661  permutation p: 0.0195

The enrichment score is 0.661, reached after six steps, with a permutation p-value of 0.0195 against 2,000 gene-label shuffles. Figure 11.4 shows the walk.

walk_frame <- data.frame(position = seq_along(walk), score = walk,
                         hit = names(ranked_by_degree) %in% p53_binders)

ggplot(walk_frame, aes(position, score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(colour = book_palette[1], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = observed_es, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = book_palette[4]) +
  geom_rug(data = subset(walk_frame, hit), sides = "b",
           colour = book_palette[4], length = grid::unit(0.05, "npc")) +
  labs(x = "Rank position (genes ordered by decreasing degree)",
       y = "Running enrichment score")






Figure 11.4: Running enrichment score for the p53-binding GO term across the 30 network genes ranked by degree. The curve rises while hits are encountered near the top of the ranking and declines thereafter; the enrichment score is the maximum deviation from zero, marked by the dashed line. Ticks on the baseline mark the positions of the seven set members.




Two differences from ORA matter. GSEA uses every gene, so a set whose members are all modestly shifted in the same direction can be significant even though no single member passes a differential expression threshold — a pattern ORA cannot see. And the null distribution is built by permutation rather than from a closed form, which means the result depends on what you permute. Shuffling gene labels, as above, asks whether this set is more concentrated at the top than a random set of the same size — a competitive null. Shuffling sample labels and recomputing the statistic asks whether the set responds to the treatment — a self-contained null, and the one GSEA uses when sample numbers allow. The two answer different questions and frequently disagree.






Ranking statistic is part of the method



GSEA results change with the ranking statistic. Ranking by p-value discards direction; by raw fold change over-weights low-expression genes with unstable ratios; by the signed test statistic or shrunken log fold change is usually the defensible choice. Report which you used.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.10 Reading an enrichment table honestly
The enrichment table computed above declares 511 of 830 terms significant. No set of 30 genes participates in 511 distinct biological processes. Four problems explain the number, and all four are present in published analyses.
The background universe. The hypergeometric test compares your query to a specific population, and changing that population changes every p-value. If your experiment measured 12,000 expressed genes, the universe is those 12,000, not the 20,431 proteins in the proteome — testing against the proteome credits you for an enrichment that is merely the enrichment of expressed genes. Study bias makes this sharper. Replacing the universe with a background matched for study intensity — genes carrying at least 20 GO terms, a proxy for how heavily investigated a gene is — changes the answer substantially.

well_studied <- terms_per_gene$gene[terms_per_gene$n_go >= 20]
N_matched <- length(well_studied)

matched <- gene_to_go |>
  filter(gene %in% well_studied) |>
  count(go, name = "K_matched") |>
  inner_join(count(filter(gene_to_go, gene %in% query_genes), go, name = "k"),
             by = "go") |>
  filter(K_matched >= 5, K_matched <= 2000) |>
  mutate(p_value = phyper(k - 1, K_matched, N_matched - K_matched,
                          n_query, lower.tail = FALSE),
         p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"))

cat("matched background size:", N_matched, "genes\n")
#> matched background size: 3433 genes
cat("significant terms, proteome background:", sum(enrichment$p_adj < 0.05), "\n")
#> significant terms, proteome background: 511
cat("significant terms, study-matched background:",
    sum(matched$p_adj < 0.05), "\n")
#> significant terms, study-matched background: 121

The significant-term count falls from 511 to 121 — under a quarter of the original — with no change to the query list and no change to the test. The top terms survive and the long tail does not, which is exactly the diagnostic value of the comparison.
Annotation bias. Enrichment can only find processes that have been annotated. The median human gene carries nine GO terms and the genes in this network carry 54.5, so terms describing well-studied biology have more opportunity to be hit. A gene set enriched for cancer genes will appear enriched for apoptosis partly because apoptosis is what cancer genes get annotated for.
Redundancy. GO is a hierarchy, and a gene annotated to a term is annotated to all of that term’s ancestors. Significant terms therefore arrive in correlated families, and a list of twenty is rarely twenty independent findings.

top_ten <- head(enrichment$go, 10)
members <- lapply(top_ten, function(term)
  intersect(gene_to_go$gene[gene_to_go$go == term], query_genes))

jaccard <- outer(seq_along(top_ten), seq_along(top_ten),
  Vectorize(function(i, j)
    length(intersect(members[[i]], members[[j]])) /
    length(union(members[[i]], members[[j]]))))

cat("mean Jaccard overlap among the top ten terms:",
    round(mean(jaccard[upper.tri(jaccard)]), 3),
    " maximum:", round(max(jaccard[upper.tri(jaccard)]), 3), "\n")
#> mean Jaccard overlap among the top ten terms: 0.268  maximum: 0.571

The ten leading terms share a mean Jaccard overlap of 0.268 and a maximum of 0.571: the same handful of genes is driving many of them. Reporting them as ten results would be counting the same evidence ten times. Semantic-similarity clustering of terms, or reporting only the most specific significant term in each branch, is the usual remedy.
Circularity. The 30 genes in this network were selected because they are cell-cycle and DNA-damage genes. Finding that they are enriched for cell-cycle and DNA-damage terms confirms the selection, not a biological hypothesis. The same circularity appears whenever a query list is assembled using prior knowledge — genes from a pathway database, from a review, from a curated portal such as cBioPortal (Cerami et al. 2012) — and then tested against that knowledge. The protection is to fix the query list from the measurement alone, before any annotation is consulted.






A significant term is a hypothesis



An enrichment result says that an annotation category is over-represented in a list, given a background, under a test with stated filters. It does not say the process is active, that it is causal, or that it is the most important thing happening. The claim that a pathway is involved requires perturbation: inhibit it, knock it down, and measure whether the phenotype moves.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.11 Summary

A network adds a relation to a gene list, and most useful network questions — connectivity, modules, bridging nodes — are questions about that relation.
Edges in different network classes carry different evidence. STRING’s channel scores make this explicit: every edge in the bundled subnetwork has text-mining support, 176 of 210 have experimental support and only 85 are in a curated database.
Topology statistics describe the network you were given, not the interactome. A query-driven subnetwork is dense, short-pathed and cliquish by construction.
Degree distributions from small networks cannot establish scale-free architecture; claiming it requires hundreds of nodes and a fitted, tested model.
Hub status in literature-derived networks partly measures study intensity: degree correlates with GO annotation count at Spearman 0.746 in this network.
Community detection always returns communities. Low modularity across several algorithms, and disagreement between them, is the signal that the partition is not real.
Over-representation analysis is one hypergeometric test per term, and knowing that is what lets you diagnose a tool that disagrees with you.
Multiple testing correction is mandatory; Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is the right choice for exploratory enrichment.
GSEA uses the whole ranked list and so detects coordinated small shifts that ORA misses, at the cost of depending on the ranking statistic and the permutation scheme.
The background universe is a scientific choice, not a default. Matching it for study intensity cut the significant-term count in this chapter from 511 to 121.

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.12 Exercises

Load the STRING edge table and report how many edges have a combined score of at least 0.900. What fraction of the original 210 does that leave?
Build the subnetwork containing only edges with experimental support (escore > 0) and compare its node count, edge count and density with the full network.
Compute the local clustering coefficient of every node and identify the gene with the lowest value. Explain, from its degree and its neighbours, why it is low.
The chapter ranked genes by degree. Rank them instead by betweenness and rerun the running-enrichment calculation for GO:0002039. Does the enrichment score change, and should it?
Run the over-representation analysis using only the genes of the largest Louvain community as the query. How many terms are significant, and how do the leading terms differ from those found for all 30 genes?
Repeat the analysis of exercise 5 with the term-size filter removed entirely. Report how many terms become significant and inspect the five smallest terms among them.
A colleague’s manuscript states: “Network analysis identified MDM2 as a hub with high betweenness centrality, establishing it as a master regulator of the DNA damage response.” Rewrite the sentence so that it is supported by the analysis in this chapter, and list the additional evidence that would be needed for the original claim.
Using the GO annotation table alone, compare the distribution of GO-term counts for the 30 network genes with 30 genes drawn at random from the universe. What does the comparison imply for any enrichment analysis that uses the whole proteome as background?

title: 11  Biological networks and pathway analysis
text:
11.13 Solutions






Solutions





1. Just over half the edges in this already-filtered table reach the top confidence band, which follows from how the slice was built rather than from any property of STRING as a whole.

very_high <- sum(string_edges$score >= 0.900)
cat(very_high, "edges at score >= 0.900 (",
    round(100 * very_high / nrow(string_edges), 1), "% of 210 )\n")
#> 121 edges at score >= 0.900 ( 57.6 % of 210 )

2. Dropping text-mining-only edges removes a fifth of the network and lowers its density, but leaves it connected.

experimental <- string_edges |>
  filter(escore > 0) |>
  select(preferredName_A, preferredName_B) |>
  graph_from_data_frame(directed = FALSE) |>
  simplify()

cat("experimental subnetwork: nodes", vcount(experimental),
    " edges", ecount(experimental),
    " density", round(edge_density(experimental), 3), "\n")
#> experimental subnetwork: nodes 30  edges 176  density 0.405

3. The lowest local clustering coefficient belongs to TP53, the highest-degree node. Local clustering asks what fraction of a node’s neighbour pairs are themselves joined; because TP53 is adjacent to all 29 other genes its neighbourhood is the whole network, including every sparsely connected gene in it. High degree therefore pushes local clustering down, which is why degree and clustering must never be read as interchangeable measures of importance.

local_cc <- transitivity(p53_net, type = "local", isolates = "zero")
names(local_cc) <- V(p53_net)$name
lowest <- names(which.min(local_cc))
cat(lowest, ": clustering", round(min(local_cc), 3),
    " degree", node_degree[[lowest]], "\n")
#> TP53 : clustering 0.446  degree 29

4. The enrichment score rises from 0.661 to 0.874. Degree and betweenness are correlated but not identical, and reordering even a few genes near the top of a 30-element list moves the running sum substantially. The score should change, because it is a statistic of a particular ranking. What must not change between rankings is the conclusion drawn from it, and a conclusion that flips when you swap centrality measures was never supported in the first place.

ranked_by_btw <- sort(betweenness(p53_net, normalized = TRUE), decreasing = TRUE)
walk_btw <- running_enrichment(ranked_by_btw, p53_binders)
cat("ES by betweenness:", round(walk_btw[which.max(abs(walk_btw))], 3),
    " (by degree:", round(observed_es, 3), ")\n")
#> ES by betweenness: 0.874  (by degree: 0.661 )

5. The largest Louvain community holds 13 genes, and the smaller query yields 369 significant terms rather than 511. The leading terms shift: a small, specific complex term now outranks the broad binding terms that led the 30-gene analysis.

module_genes <- names(membership(louvain))[membership(louvain) ==
                  which.max(sizes(louvain))]

module_enrichment <- gene_to_go |>
  filter(gene %in% module_genes) |>
  count(go, name = "k") |>
  inner_join(term_sizes, by = "go") |>
  filter(K >= 5, K <= 2000) |>
  mutate(p_value = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, length(module_genes),
                          lower.tail = FALSE),
         p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_value)

cat("module size:", length(module_genes),
    " significant terms:", sum(module_enrichment$p_adj < 0.05), "\n")
#> module size: 13  significant terms: 369
head(module_enrichment, 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   go             k     K       p_value      p_adj
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>         <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 GO:0000152     3     6 0.00000000481 0.00000131
#> 2 GO:0071479     4    36 0.00000000728 0.00000131
#> 3 GO:0042802    10  1744 0.00000000806 0.00000131

6. Removing the size filter admits many tiny terms whose significance rests on one or two genes, inflating the count and the correction burden together.

unfiltered <- gene_to_go |>
  filter(gene %in% module_genes) |>
  count(go, name = "k") |>
  inner_join(term_sizes, by = "go") |>
  mutate(p_value = phyper(k - 1, K, N - K, length(module_genes),
                          lower.tail = FALSE),
         p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")) |>
  arrange(p_value)

cat("terms tested:", nrow(unfiltered),
    " significant:", sum(unfiltered$p_adj < 0.05), "\n")
#> terms tested: 566  significant: 447
unfiltered |> filter(p_adj < 0.05) |> arrange(K) |> head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 5
#>   go             k     K  p_value   p_adj
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 GO:0014870     1     1 0.000675 0.00496
#> 2 GO:0030575     1     1 0.000675 0.00496
#> 3 GO:0033593     1     1 0.000675 0.00496
#> 4 GO:0048640     1     1 0.000675 0.00496
#> 5 GO:0051097     1     1 0.000675 0.00496

7. A defensible version: “MDM2 has the third-highest degree (21 of a possible 29) in a high-confidence STRING subnetwork of 30 cell-cycle and DNA-damage genes. Because the subnetwork was assembled by querying a literature-derived database around p53, this reflects both interaction evidence and study intensity, and is a candidate for functional testing rather than evidence of regulatory control.” Establishing master-regulator status would require perturbation data — knockdown or degradation of MDM2 followed by transcriptome-wide measurement — in the relevant cell type, direct binding evidence for the proposed targets, and a demonstration that the effect is not reproduced by perturbing its neighbours.
8. Random genes carry far fewer annotations, so a proteome-wide background compares a heavily annotated query against a sparsely annotated population and over-states enrichment for every well-studied term.

set.seed(20250101)
random_genes <- sample(universe, 30)
cat("median GO terms - network genes:",
    median(terms_per_gene$n_go[terms_per_gene$gene %in% query_genes]),
    " random genes:",
    median(terms_per_gene$n_go[terms_per_gene$gene %in% random_genes]), "\n")
#> median GO terms - network genes: 54.5  random genes: 8

11.14 Further reading


Szklarczyk et al. (2022) documents STRING’s evidence channels and scoring scheme; read it before using a combined score as though it were a single kind of evidence.

Aleksander et al. (2023) is the current description of the Gene Ontology knowledgebase, including how annotations are assigned, evidence-coded and propagated.

Milacic et al. (2023) describes Reactome’s curation model, which is the clearest published account of what a curated pathway database does and does not contain.

Subramanian et al. (2005) introduced gene set enrichment analysis; the methods section explains the weighting and permutation choices that the simplified implementation above leaves out.

Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) is the original false discovery rate paper and remains the shortest route to understanding what an adjusted p-value means.

Yu et al. (2012) describes clusterProfiler, the package you will use in practice once you understand the hypergeometric test underneath it.

Kanehisa (2000) introduces KEGG and its pathway map abstraction, which differs from both GO’s vocabulary and Reactome’s reaction-level curation.

Huber et al. (2015) surveys the Bioconductor ecosystem in which most R-based enrichment and network workflows are assembled.

Robertson et al. (2017) is a large tumour characterisation study whose pathway-level figures are worth reading critically against the cautions in this chapter.

title: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data
section: 12.2 Designing an experiment that can answer the question
text:
12.2 Designing an experiment that can answer the question
No amount of analysis repairs a design that cannot answer the question, and the most common failure is not a shortage of data but the wrong kind of replication.
A technical replicate repeats the measurement on the same biological material: the same RNA extract sequenced twice, the same library loaded on two lanes. It estimates the variability of the measurement process. A biological replicate repeats the whole experiment on independent material: a different fly culture, a different patient, a different mouse. It estimates the variability of the biological population, which is what almost every scientific claim is about.
Technical replicates cannot substitute for biological ones. Sequencing one RNA sample across twenty lanes gives twenty highly concordant measurements of that one sample, a reassuringly small standard error, and no information whatsoever about whether another fly would have behaved the same way. The resulting p-value answers a question nobody asked. The bundled metadata records that some samples were run across five or six lanes; those lanes were summed into one count column, which is the correct treatment, because they were never independent observations of biology.

sample_info = pd.read_csv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_sample_annotation.csv"))
sample_info["sample"] = sample_info["file"].str.replace("fb", "", regex=False)
sample_info = sample_info.set_index("sample")

print(sample_info[["condition", "type", "number of lanes"]])
#>             condition         type  number of lanes
#> sample                                             
#> treated1      treated  single-read                5
#> treated2      treated   paired-end                2
#> treated3      treated   paired-end                2
#> untreated1  untreated  single-read                2
#> untreated2  untreated  single-read                6
#> untreated3  untreated   paired-end                2
#> untreated4  untreated   paired-end                2

Three further design points decide whether the analysis below is worth running.
Replicate number. Three per group is the practical floor for RNA-seq and detects only large effects; the pasilla design has three treated and four untreated. With fewer than three, variance cannot be estimated per gene at all, which is why methods such as DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2009) share information across genes to stabilise the estimate.
Randomisation. Assign samples to processing batches, lanes and extraction days at random. Processing all controls on Monday and all treated samples on Tuesday guarantees that a day effect is indistinguishable from a treatment effect.
Blocking. When a nuisance factor cannot be avoided — two sequencing runs, two operators — ensure every level of the factor contains both conditions, and record it. A recorded nuisance factor can be modelled; an unrecorded one cannot.
How many replicates are enough is a question of effect size, variability and the smallest difference worth detecting, and it has no universal answer. The useful discipline is to decide, before the experiment, what difference would change what you do next — a twofold change in a handful of genes, or a subtle shift across a pathway — and to ask whether the planned design could detect it. For RNA-seq the rough guidance from published power studies is that three replicates per group detect twofold changes in well-expressed genes, six begin to reach 1.5-fold, and detecting small coordinated shifts needs tens. A study powered for the wrong effect size produces a null result that cannot be distinguished from an absent effect, which is the most expensive outcome in the catalogue.






Confounding is a property of the design, not the data



If every treated sample was prepared with one protocol and every control with another, no statistical method can separate protocol from treatment. Batch correction, covariate adjustment and sophisticated models all fail identically, because the information is absent. The only fix is a different experiment.

title: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data
section: 12.3 The shape of an omics matrix
text:
12.3 The shape of an omics matrix
Tidy data has one row per observation and one column per variable (Wickham et al. 2019). An omics count matrix deliberately breaks that rule: it is stored with one row per gene and one column per sample, because the matrix form is what linear algebra and most statistical software expect. The tidy form is useful for plotting and joining, the matrix form for computation, and a working analysis moves between them; pandas supplies both representations and the operations that convert one into the other (McKinney 2010).

counts = pd.read_csv(book_data("expression", "pasilla_gene_counts.tsv"),
                     sep="\t", index_col=0)
counts = counts[sample_info.index]          # fix column order to match metadata

print(f"{counts.shape[0]:,} genes x {counts.shape[1]} samples")
#> 14,599 genes x 7 samples
print(counts.iloc[:3, :4])
#>              treated1  treated2  treated3  untreated1
#> gene_id                                              
#> FBgn0000003         0         0         1           0
#> FBgn0000008       140        88        70          92
#> FBgn0000014         4         0         0           5

The shape is the problem. There are 14,599 features and seven samples, so p ≫ n: vastly more variables than observations. Three consequences follow, and every statistical trap later in the chapter is one of them in disguise.
First, any two groups of samples can be separated perfectly by some subset of features, even when the labels are random. With 14,599 genes and seven samples there is always a gene that happens to split them. Second, distances become uninformative: in high dimensions the distance from a point to its nearest neighbour approaches the distance to its farthest, so “these samples cluster together” needs evidence beyond a plot. Third, the number of possible models vastly exceeds the data available to choose between them, so model selection needs external validation rather than internal fit.
Low-count genes contribute noise without information, and removing them before anything else reduces the testing burden.

expressed = counts[(counts > 5).sum(axis=1) >= 3]

print(f"genes with no counts at all: {(counts.sum(axis=1) == 0).sum():,}")
#> genes with no counts at all: 2,240
print(f"genes retained (>5 counts in >=3 samples): {expressed.shape[0]:,}")
#> genes retained (>5 counts in >=3 samples): 8,621

The filter is a judgement, not a rule. Requiring counts above five in at least three samples — the size of the smallest group — keeps genes that could show a group-specific signal and discards those that cannot. State the rule in your methods, because it changes how many tests you perform and therefore every corrected p-value.

title: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data
text:
12.4 Exploring and normalising count data
RNA-seq counts are not normally distributed. They are non-negative integers, strongly right-skewed, and their variance grows with their mean — a gene averaging 10,000 reads varies far more in absolute terms than one averaging 10. Figure 12.1 shows both facts alongside the library sizes that make raw counts incomparable.

library_sizes = expressed.sum() / 1e6
cpm = expressed / expressed.sum() * 1e6
log_cpm = np.log2(cpm + 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.2))

axes[0].bar(range(len(library_sizes)), library_sizes, color=PALETTE[0])
axes[0].set_xticks(range(len(library_sizes)))
axes[0].set_xticklabels(library_sizes.index, rotation=90, fontsize=7)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Millions of counts")
axes[0].set_title("Library size")

axes[1].hist(log_cpm.values.ravel(), bins=60, color=PALETTE[1])
axes[1].set_xlabel("log2(CPM + 1)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Genes x samples")
axes[1].set_title("Transformed distribution")

axes[2].scatter(expressed.mean(axis=1), expressed.var(axis=1), s=3,
                alpha=0.3, color=PALETTE[3])
axes[2].set_xscale("log"); axes[2].set_yscale("log")
axes[2].set_xlabel("Mean count"); axes[2].set_ylabel("Variance")
axes[2].set_title("Mean-variance relation")

fig.tight_layout()






Figure 12.1: Three views of the pasilla count matrix. Left: total mapped counts per sample differ by a factor of 2.6, so a raw count means something different in each column. Centre: the distribution of log2 counts per million is approximately symmetric once the log transform is applied, unlike the raw counts. Right: per-gene variance rises with the mean on logarithmic axes, the overdispersion that count-based models exist to handle.




Three features of the left and centre panels deserve attention before any modelling. Counts span roughly five orders of magnitude within a single sample, so an untransformed matrix is dominated by a few hundred genes; the log transform in the centre panel is what makes the rest visible. Zeros are abundant — 2,240 of the 14,599 genes have no counts in any sample — and a zero is ambiguous, meaning either that a transcript is absent or that sequencing was too shallow to see it, which is why a pseudocount is added before taking logarithms rather than discarding the zeros. And the right-hand panel shows variance rising faster than the mean, the overdispersion that makes the Poisson distribution inadequate and the negative binomial the standard choice for count models.
Library sizes range from 8.4 to 21.9 million counts. A gene with 100 reads in the smallest library is twice as abundant, proportionally, as a gene with 100 reads in the largest. Normalisation removes that difference. The simplest method, counts per million (CPM), divides each count by its library total; it is what the code above computes. The demonstration below shows what it fixes.

pair = ["untreated2", "untreated3"]
gene = "FBgn0000008"

print("raw counts:", counts.loc[gene, pair].tolist(),
      "ratio", round(counts.loc[gene, pair[0]] / counts.loc[gene, pair[1]], 2))
#> raw counts: [161, 76] ratio 2.12
print("CPM:", cpm.loc[gene, pair].round(2).tolist(),
      "ratio", round(cpm.loc[gene, pair[0]] / cpm.loc[gene, pair[1]], 2))
#> CPM: [7.35, 9.1] ratio 0.81

raw_ratio = np.log2(expressed[pair[0]] + 1) - np.log2(expressed[pair[1]] + 1)
cpm_ratio = log_cpm[pair[0]] - log_cpm[pair[1]]
print(f"median log2 ratio across all genes - raw: {raw_ratio.median():.3f}, "
      f"CPM: {cpm_ratio.median():.3f}")
#> median log2 ratio across all genes - raw: 1.443, CPM: 0.056

The gene looks 2.12-fold up in untreated2 on raw counts and 0.81-fold — that is, slightly down — after normalisation. The direction of the effect reverses. The summary line explains why: before normalisation the median log ratio across all 8,621 genes is 1.443, almost exactly the log ratio of the two library sizes, because most genes do not change and the apparent shift is entirely a depth artefact. After CPM the median is 0.056, close to the zero that a comparison of two control samples should produce.






CPM is the simplest method, not the best one



CPM assumes total counts are comparable, which fails when a few very highly expressed genes dominate one sample — common in tissue with a dominant transcript. The median-of-ratios method in DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and trimmed mean of M-values in edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2009) estimate a size factor from the bulk of genes instead, and are the defaults for differential expression. Transcript-length normalisation (TPM, FPKM) additionally divides by gene length, which is necessary when comparing different genes but not when comparing one gene across samples.

title: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data
text:
12.5 Batch effects and confounding
A batch effect is systematic variation introduced by how samples were processed rather than by what they are: reagent lot, sequencing run, extraction day, library protocol (Leek et al. 2010). Batch effects are not noise. They are reproducible, often large, and they bias in a consistent direction — which is exactly what makes them look like biology.
The pasilla design contains a real one. Four samples were sequenced paired-end and three single-read, and that split cuts across both conditions. Because it cuts across, the effect can be measured directly: compare untreated samples with one library type against untreated samples with the other, where no treatment difference exists by construction.

def two_group_p(group_a, group_b):
    """Per-gene two-sample t-test on log-CPM; returns a Series of p-values."""
    stat, p = stats.ttest_ind(log_cpm[group_a], log_cpm[group_b], axis=1)
    return pd.Series(p, index=log_cpm.index)

batch_only = two_group_p(["untreated1", "untreated2"],    # single-read
                         ["untreated3", "untreated4"])    # paired-end

n_genes = log_cpm.shape[0]
print(f"genes tested: {n_genes:,}; expected at p < 0.05 by chance: {0.05 * n_genes:.0f}")
#> genes tested: 8,621; expected at p < 0.05 by chance: 431
print(f"library-type contrast, untreated only: {(batch_only < 0.05).sum():,} genes at p < 0.05")
#> library-type contrast, untreated only: 676 genes at p < 0.05

Within a single biological condition, 676 genes reach p < 0.05 against an expectation of 431. The library protocol changes measured expression for hundreds of genes.
Now construct the failure. Take two paired-end treated samples and two single-read untreated samples. In that four-sample subset, condition and library type are perfectly confounded — exactly the design produced by processing cases and controls separately.

confounded = two_group_p(["treated2", "treated3"],        # both paired-end
                         ["untreated1", "untreated2"])    # both single-read
proper = two_group_p(["treated1", "treated2", "treated3"],
                     ["untreated1", "untreated2", "untreated3", "untreated4"])

batch_hits = set(batch_only[batch_only < 0.05].index)
conf_hits = set(confounded[confounded < 0.05].index)
proper_hits = set(proper[proper < 0.05].index)

print(f"confounded contrast: {len(conf_hits):,} genes at p < 0.05")
#> confounded contrast: 1,533 genes at p < 0.05
print(f"  of these, also significant in the pure library-type contrast: "
      f"{len(conf_hits & batch_hits):,} "
      f"({100 * len(conf_hits & batch_hits) / len(conf_hits):.1f}%)")
#>   of these, also significant in the pure library-type contrast: 342 (22.3%)
print(f"  expected by chance: {100 * len(batch_hits) / n_genes:.1f}%")
#>   expected by chance: 7.8%
print(f"  also found by the properly balanced contrast: "
      f"{100 * len(conf_hits & proper_hits) / len(conf_hits):.1f}%")
#>   also found by the properly balanced contrast: 45.5%

The confounded comparison returns 1,533 genes. Of those, 22.3% also appear in the pure library-type contrast, against 7.8% expected by chance — a nearly threefold enrichment for genes known to respond to protocol rather than treatment. Fewer than half of the 1,533 are recovered by the balanced comparison using all seven samples. Written up without the metadata, this list would read as a treatment signature; it is in substantial part a protocol signature, and nothing in the numbers themselves distinguishes the two.
The remedies, in order of effectiveness: design the experiment so batch is balanced across conditions; record batch so it can be included as a covariate in the model; or, if neither was done, apply an empirical Bayes correction such as ComBat (Johnson, Li, and Rabinovic 2006) and report it as a limitation. Correction after the fact removes variation that may contain signal, and it can only ever approximate what balanced design gives for free.
crumbs: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data

title: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data
section: 12.6 Multiple testing and the false discovery problem
text:
12.6 Multiple testing and the false discovery problem
Testing 8,621 genes at a 5% threshold produces about 431 significant results when nothing is happening. The simulation below makes that concrete, then shows what the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure does about it (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).

rng = np.random.default_rng(20250101)

def benjamini_hochberg(p_values):
    """Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values, written out rather than imported."""
    p = np.asarray(p_values)
    m = len(p)
    order = np.argsort(p)
    ranked = p[order] * m / np.arange(1, m + 1)
    adjusted = np.minimum.accumulate(ranked[::-1])[::-1]
    out = np.empty(m)
    out[order] = np.minimum(adjusted, 1)
    return out

null_data = rng.normal(size=(10_000, 20))      # no difference between groups
_, p_null = stats.ttest_ind(null_data[:, :10], null_data[:, 10:], axis=1)

print(f"pure noise: {(p_null < 0.05).sum()} of 10,000 'genes' at p < 0.05")
#> pure noise: 501 of 10,000 'genes' at p < 0.05
print(f"pure noise: {(benjamini_hochberg(p_null) < 0.05).sum()} survive BH correction")
#> pure noise: 0 survive BH correction

501 false positives before correction, none after. Now add real signal: 200 of the 10,000 genes are given a genuine difference between groups.

mixed = rng.normal(size=(10_000, 20))
mixed[:200, 10:] += 2.0                        # the first 200 genes truly differ
_, p_mixed = stats.ttest_ind(mixed[:, :10], mixed[:, 10:], axis=1)

significant = benjamini_hochberg(p_mixed) < 0.05
true_positives = significant[:200].sum()
false_positives = significant[200:].sum()

print(f"raw p < 0.05: {(p_mixed < 0.05).sum()}")
#> raw p < 0.05: 720
print(f"BH significant: {significant.sum()}  "
      f"(true {true_positives}, false {false_positives})")
#> BH significant: 133  (true 126, false 7)
print(f"observed false discovery proportion: "
      f"{false_positives / significant.sum():.3f}")
#> observed false discovery proportion: 0.053
print(f"power to detect the 200 real effects: {true_positives / 200:.2f}")
#> power to detect the 200 real effects: 0.63

The procedure delivers what it promises: 133 discoveries of which seven are false, a false discovery proportion of 0.053 against the nominal 0.05. It also shows the cost — only 126 of the 200 real effects are found, because controlling false positives always sacrifices power. The false discovery rate is the expected proportion of false positives among the results you call significant, which is the quantity that matters when the output is a list of candidates for follow-up. The family-wise error rate controlled by Bonferroni is the probability of even one false positive, which is the right target only when a single wrong call invalidates the study. Storey’s q-value refines the FDR estimate by estimating the proportion of true nulls rather than assuming it is one (Storey and Tibshirani 2003).
One legitimate way to recover power is independent filtering: removing tests that have little chance of being significant, using a criterion independent of the test statistic under the null. Mean expression is such a criterion, which is why the low-count filter applied earlier is not merely tidying — it reduces the number of tests, and therefore the correction burden, without biasing the remaining p-values. Filtering on something correlated with the test statistic, such as fold change, does bias them, and is not independent filtering at all.






Correct for every test you performed



The correction must cover all tests actually conducted, including the ones not reported. Running the analysis with three filtering thresholds and reporting the one with most hits is multiple testing with an unrecorded denominator, and no correction applied afterwards can repair it.
crumbs: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data

title: 12  Statistics and machine learning on omics data
text:
12.7 Finding structure without labels
Principal component analysis (PCA) re-expresses samples in new coordinates — principal components — that are uncorrelated linear combinations of the original features, ordered so that the first captures the most variance. It is the first diagnostic to run on any omics matrix, because the leading components usually reveal whichever factor dominates the experiment, and that factor is often not the one you intended to study.
Three choices control what PCA shows. Transform count data first, or the result will be dominated by a handful of highly expressed genes. Centre the features, always. Whether to scale them to unit variance depends: on log-CPM data, scaling gives low-expression noisy genes the same weight as informative ones, so centring without scaling is the usual choice for RNA-seq.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

expression_matrix = log_cpm.T.values            # samples as rows, genes as columns
centred = expression_matrix - expression_matrix.mean(axis=0)

pca = PCA(n_components=4).fit(centred)
scores = pca.transform(centred)

variance_explained = 100 * pca.explained_variance_ratio_
for i, pct in enumerate(variance_explained, start=1):
    print(f"PC{i}: {pct:.1f}% of variance")
#> PC1: 39.7% of variance
#> PC2: 31.8% of variance
#> PC3: 14.3% of variance
#> PC4: 6.2% of variance

PC1 accounts for 39.7% of the variance and PC2 for 31.8%. Two components of nearly equal size is a warning in itself: it means two comparably strong factors are at work. Figure 12.2 identifies them.

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.5, 3.4))

for ax, factor, title in [(axes[0], "condition", "Coloured by treatment"),
                          (axes[1], "type", "Coloured by library type")]:
    for level, colour, marker in zip(sample_info[factor].unique(),
                                     [PALETTE[0], PALETTE[3]], ["o", "^"]):
        rows = sample_info[factor] == level
        ax.scatter(scores[rows.values, 0], scores[rows.values, 1],
                   label=level, color=colour, marker=marker, s=55)
    ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({variance_explained[0]:.0f}%)")
    ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({variance_explained[1]:.0f}%)")
    ax.set_title(title); ax.legend(fontsize=7)

                         method="average")
dendrogram(linkage_matrix, labels=list(log_cpm.columns), ax=axes[2],
           leaf_rotation=90, leaf_font_size=7, color_threshold=0)

Figure 12.2: Structure in the pasilla samples. Left: the first two principal components coloured by treatment; PC1 separates treated from untreated. Centre: the same coordinates coloured by library protocol, showing that PC2 is the single-read versus paired-end split. Right: average-linkage hierarchical clustering on correlation distance, whose first split reproduces the treatment grouping and whose second isolates the one single-read treated sample.




The left panel shows a clean separation of treated from untreated along PC1. The centre panel shows the problem: PC2, carrying almost as much variance, separates single-read from paired-end libraries. Had the design been confounded, these two axes would have collapsed into one and the figure would have looked like an unambiguous treatment effect.
Loadings say which genes drive a component. Each loading is the weight of one gene in the linear combination, and the extreme ones are the genes that define the axis.

pc1_loadings = pd.Series(pca.components_[0], index=log_cpm.index)
print("strongest positive PC1 loadings:")
#> strongest positive PC1 loadings:
print(pc1_loadings.nlargest(3).round(4).to_string())
#> gene_id
#> FBgn0039155    0.1331
#> FBgn0039827    0.1120
#> FBgn0003360    0.0969
print("strongest negative PC1 loadings:")
#> strongest negative PC1 loadings:
print(pc1_loadings.nsmallest(3).round(4).to_string())
#> gene_id
#> FBgn0025111   -0.0911
#> FBgn0035189   -0.0874
#> FBgn0000071   -0.0817

Non-linear embeddings
t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) (Maaten and Hinton 2008) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (McInnes, John, and James 2018; Becht et al. 2018) place points in two dimensions so that near neighbours in the original space stay near. They are the standard display for single-cell data, where thousands of cells make a PCA scatter plot unreadable, and they genuinely reveal structure that PCA’s linearity hides. They are also systematically misread.
Both methods preserve local neighbourhoods and deliberately discard global geometry. The consequences are specific. The distance between two clusters on a t-SNE plot carries no information — clusters that appear adjacent may be no more similar than clusters at opposite corners. Cluster sizes and densities are artefacts of the algorithm’s normalisation, not measurements of spread. The embedding depends strongly on the perplexity or neighbour-count parameter, and running the same data at two settings produces two different pictures, both correct in their own terms. Finally, t-SNE and UMAP will produce apparently clean groups from pure noise if the parameters invite it.
The defensible use is as a display of a clustering computed elsewhere: cluster in the PCA space, then colour the embedding by cluster label. Treating the embedding itself as the analysis is where the trouble starts. A seven-sample dataset like this one is far too small for either method, which is why neither is run here.
Clustering, and choosing k
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree by repeatedly joining the closest pair, and requires two choices: a distance (correlation distance is usual for expression profiles, because it ignores overall magnitude) and a linkage rule (average or Ward are the safe defaults). Cutting the tree at a height gives a partition. k-means instead places k centroids and iterates, and requires k in advance.

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import fcluster
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

for k in (2, 3, 4):
    hierarchical = fcluster(linkage_matrix, k, criterion="maxclust")
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=20, random_state=0).fit_predict(expression_matrix)
    print(f"k={k}  silhouette={silhouette_score(expression_matrix, kmeans):.3f}  "
          f"hierarchical={hierarchical}  k-means={kmeans}")
#> k=2  silhouette=0.241  hierarchical=[2 2 2 1 1 1 1]  k-means=[1 1 1 0 0 0 0]
#> k=3  silhouette=0.239  hierarchical=[3 2 2 1 1 1 1]  k-means=[1 2 2 0 0 0 0]
#> k=4  silhouette=0.238  hierarchical=[4 3 3 2 1 1 1]  k-means=[2 1 1 3 3 0 0]

The silhouette score compares each point’s distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other cluster, averaged over points; higher is better. Here it is 0.241 at k = 2 and 0.239 at k = 3 — indistinguishable. The score cannot choose between them, and reporting the k with the highest silhouette would be reporting a difference of 0.002 as a finding.
A better question than “which k is best” is “which groupings are stable”. Resampling the genes and re-clustering shows which sample pairings survive.

rng_boot = np.random.default_rng(20250101)
n_resamples, n_features = 200, expression_matrix.shape[1]
co_cluster = np.zeros((7, 7))

for _ in range(n_resamples):
    picked = rng_boot.integers(0, n_features, n_features)   # bootstrap the genes
    labels = fcluster(linkage(pdist(expression_matrix[:, picked], metric="correlation"),
                              method="average"), 3, criterion="maxclust")
    co_cluster += labels[:, None] == labels[None, :]

co_cluster /= n_resamples
print(pd.DataFrame(np.round(co_cluster, 2),
                   index=log_cpm.columns, columns=log_cpm.columns).to_string())
#>             treated1  treated2  treated3  untreated1  untreated2  untreated3  untreated4
#> treated1        1.00      0.01      0.01        0.00        0.00        0.00        0.00
#> treated2        0.01      1.00      1.00        0.00        0.00        0.00        0.00
#> treated3        0.01      1.00      1.00        0.00        0.00        0.00        0.00
#> untreated1      0.00      0.00      0.00        1.00        0.99        0.99        0.99
#> untreated2      0.00      0.00      0.00        0.99        1.00        1.00        1.00
#> untreated3      0.00      0.00      0.00        0.99        1.00        1.00        1.00
#> untreated4      0.00      0.00      0.00        0.99        1.00        1.00        1.00

At k = 3 the four untreated samples co-cluster in at least 99% of resamples, treated2 and treated3 always cluster together, and treated1 joins them in only 1% of resamples. The three-group structure is stable. But treated1 is the single-read treated sample, so the third cluster is a library-protocol cluster, not a biological one. Stability establishes that a partition is reproducible from the data; it says nothing about what the partition means.
