section: 15.7 Measuring agreement under the right genetic code
text:
15.7 Measuring agreement under the right genetic code
With the diagnosis made, the fix is one flag. Because the Makefile parameterises the genetic code as a pattern, obtaining the corrected result in the real project needed no code edits at all — only make results/comparison_code4.tsv.


Table 15.1: Agreement between Prodigal predictions and the RefSeq annotation of M. genitalium G37, under the default bacterial genetic code and under the code the organism actually uses. Sensitivity is the percentage of the 524 reference coding sequences whose stop coordinate and strand were predicted; precision is the percentage of predictions matching a reference stop.

code4 = cds_table(run_prodigal(genome_path, work / "code4.gff", 4))
summary = pd.DataFrame({"genetic code 11": compare(reference_cds, code11),
                        "genetic code 4": compare(reference_cds, code4)})
summary
#>                     genetic code 11  genetic code 4
#> predicted                     995.0           527.0
#> shared stops                  341.0           501.0
#> sensitivity (%)                65.1            95.6
#> precision (%)                  34.3            95.1
#> median length (bp)            336.0           855.0
#> coding density (%)             77.1            94.8



Table 15.1 is the project’s central result. Under the correct genetic code, Prodigal recovers 95.6% of reference coding sequences and 95.1% of its predictions correspond to a reference gene end; median length and coding density both match the reference almost exactly. Sensitivity rose by 30 percentage points and precision by 61 from a single parameter.
Stop coordinates are the easy part. Start codons are chosen by a ribosome binding site model and are the known weak point of ab initio prediction, so they deserve their own measurement. Among the genes where both methods agree on the stop, we can ask how often they also agree on where translation begins.

def start_positions(cds):
    return {key: (start if strand == "+" else end)
            for key, start, end, strand in zip(cds["stop_key"], cds["start"],
                                               cds["end"], cds["strand"])}

reference_starts, predicted_starts = start_positions(reference_cds), start_positions(code4)
shared_keys = sorted(set(reference_starts) & set(predicted_starts))
offsets = np.array([predicted_starts[key] - reference_starts[key] for key in shared_keys])
identical = int((offsets == 0).sum())
print(f"{identical} of {len(shared_keys)} shared genes ({100 * identical / len(shared_keys):.1f}%) "
      f"have identical start coordinates")
#> 464 of 501 shared genes (92.6%) have identical start coordinates
print(f"of the {len(shared_keys) - identical} that differ, median absolute offset "
      f"{int(np.median(np.abs(offsets[offsets != 0])))} bp")
#> of the 37 that differ, median absolute offset 39 bp

Agreement on the start is 92.6%, and Figure 15.3 shows that the disagreements are not random noise but a systematic bias in one direction.

differing = offsets[offsets != 0]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(np.clip(differing, -400, 400), bins=np.arange(-400, 420, 40), color="#B9770E")
ax.axvline(0, color="#5D6D7E", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("predicted start − reference start (bp)")
ax.set_ylabel("coding sequences")
ax.set_title(f"{identical} of {len(shared_keys)} starts agree exactly")
ax.text(0.03, 0.9, f"{(differing < 0).sum()} predictions begin upstream\n"
                   f"{(differing > 0).sum()} begin downstream",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=8, va="top")
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 15.3: Start-codon disagreement for the 501 genes on which Prodigal under genetic code 4 and RefSeq agree about the stop coordinate. Offsets are the predicted start minus the reference start in base pairs; the 464 genes with identical starts are excluded from the histogram and noted in the annotation. Negative values are predictions that begin upstream of the curated start, which is the dominant error.




Most disagreements place the predicted start upstream of the curated one, which is what the method’s incentives predict: an ab initio scan rewards the longest open reading frame consistent with its ribosome binding site model, whereas curators prefer the start supported by homologous proteins. The practical consequence is that ab initio protein sequences carry occasional spurious N-terminal extensions, which matters for peptide-level work and barely at all for counting genes or assigning functions.

title: 15  A complete project, start to finish
text:
15.8 Where the two methods disagree
Aggregate agreement of 95% is where a careless project would stop. The remaining 5% is where the biology is, and characterising it is what distinguishes an analysis from a benchmark. There are 23 reference genes with no matching prediction and 26 predictions with no matching reference gene; the first question is whether these are the same loci seen twice.

missed = reference_cds[~reference_cds["stop_key"].isin(set(code4["stop_key"]))].copy()
extra = code4[~code4["stop_key"].isin(set(reference_cds["stop_key"]))].copy()

def overlapping_rows(row, other):
    """Rows of `other` on the same strand whose span overlaps this row."""
    return other[(other["strand"] == row.strand) & (other["start"] <= row.end)
                 & (row.start <= other["end"])]

missed["has_overlap"] = [len(overlapping_rows(row, code4)) > 0 for row in missed.itertuples()]
print(f"{len(missed)} reference genes unmatched, of which "
      f"{int(missed['has_overlap'].sum())} overlap a prediction with a different stop")
#> 23 reference genes unmatched, of which 20 overlap a prediction with a different stop
print(f"{len(extra)} unmatched predictions, median length "
      f"{int(extra['length'].median())} bp")
#> 26 unmatched predictions, median length 408 bp

Twenty of the 23 unmatched reference genes overlap a prediction that disagrees only about the boundary, so they are not missed genes at all: both methods see a gene there and differ about where it ends. Only three reference genes are absent from the prediction entirely. Pulling out their annotated products tells us what they are.

import re

for row in missed[~missed["has_overlap"]].itertuples():
    product = re.search(r"product=([^;]+)", row.attributes)
    print(f"  {row.start:>6}–{row.end:<6} {row.strand}  {row.length:>4} bp  "
          f"{product.group(1) if product else 'unannotated'}")
#>    64367–64513  -   147 bp  50S ribosomal protein L33
#>   215654–215830 +   177 bp  MgpC family cytadherence protein
#>   231431–231673 +   243 bp  MgpC family cytadherence protein

One of the three is 50S ribosomal protein L33, a genuine, essential, very short gene of 147 bp. Short coding sequences are the known blind spot of ab initio prediction: the statistical signal that distinguishes coding from non-coding sequence is weak in a window of 49 codons, and predictors set length thresholds to avoid drowning in false positives. The other two are fragments of the MgpC cytadherence protein family. Figure 15.4 shows that this is not a coincidence.

pseudogenes = annotation[annotation["type"] == "pseudogene"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 2.6))
for start, end in zip(pseudogenes["start"], pseudogenes["end"]):
    ax.axvspan(start / 1000, end / 1000, color="#D5D8DC", zorder=0)
ax.scatter(missed["start"] / 1000, np.full(len(missed), 1), marker="v",
           color="#922B21", label=f"reference gene not predicted (n={len(missed)})")
ax.scatter(extra["start"] / 1000, np.zeros(len(extra)), marker="^",
           color="#1A5276", label=f"prediction with no reference gene (n={len(extra)})")
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["extra", "missed"])
ax.set_xlabel("genome position (kb)"); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 1.8)
#> Text(0.5, 0, 'genome position (kb)')
#> (-0.6, 1.8)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", fontsize=8, ncol=1)
fig.tight_layout()






Figure 15.4: Positions of the disagreements along the 580 kb genome. Each mark is a reference coding sequence with no matching prediction (upper row) or a prediction with no matching reference gene (lower row); grey bands are the 20 loci RefSeq annotates as pseudogenes. The disagreements are not spread evenly but concentrate in the MgPa adhesin repeat region between roughly 85 kb and 465 kb.




The disagreements cluster, and they cluster on the grey bands. Of the 26 unmatched predictions, 19 overlap one of the 20 loci that RefSeq annotates as pseudogenes, and the unmatched reference genes carry products named adhesin P1, adhesin P110 and MgpC cytadherence protein. These are the MgPa adhesin gene family (Fraser et al. 1995): a set of repeated, recombining sequences that M. genitalium uses for antigenic variation, present in the genome as a functional operon plus multiple partial copies. In a repeat family of this kind the question “where does the gene end?” has no single answer, because the locus is a mosaic of complete and degenerate copies. RefSeq resolves it with homology evidence and curator judgement; Prodigal resolves it with a composition model; and they resolve it differently.
That is the project’s second result, and it is more interesting than the first. The 95% figure is not a uniform error rate of 5% spread across the genome. It is near-perfect agreement over the single-copy core and systematic disagreement in one repetitive, biologically unusual region, where the disagreement reflects genuine ambiguity rather than a mistake by either method.

title: 15  A complete project, start to finish
text:
15.9 Interpretation and limits
What the analysis shows: on a small, GC-poor, gene-dense bacterial genome analysed under the correct translation table, ab initio prediction reproduces the stop coordinates of 95.6% of curated coding sequences with 95.1% precision and identical start codons for 92.6% of the genes it recovers; its failures are concentrated in very short genes and in a repeat-expanded surface antigen family; and the single most consequential parameter is the genetic code, which moved sensitivity by 30 percentage points.
What it does not show is longer, and stating it is not modesty but method. A reader cannot use a result whose scope is undeclared.


It is one genome. Every number here is a property of M. genitalium G37. A GC-rich actinobacterium, an organism with introns, or a draft assembly in 300 contigs will behave differently, and nothing above licenses a general claim about ab initio prediction. Benchmarking would need a panel of genomes spanning GC content, assembly contiguity and taxonomic breadth.

The reference is not truth. RefSeq annotation is itself partly computational — the NCBI pipeline uses a gene finder and then applies homology and curation (Tatusova et al. 2016) — so this is agreement between two methods that share assumptions, not accuracy against a gold standard. Only experimentally determined gene boundaries, from ribosome profiling or proteomics, would support the word “accuracy”, and the disagreements in the MgPa region are exactly where the reference is least certain.

Agreement was defined on stop coordinates. That choice was deliberate and it shapes the headline figure. Scoring exact coordinate identity would have reported about 88% rather than 95.6%; scoring any overlap would have reported higher still. The metric is part of the result, which is why it must be in the abstract and not buried in the methods.

Nothing here is about function. Recovering a gene’s coordinates says nothing about whether its product is correctly identified. Functional annotation is a separate pipeline — protein similarity search (Altschul et al. 1990), profile hidden Markov models against domain libraries (Eddy 2011; Mistry et al. 2020) — with its own and considerably higher error rate.

No statistical uncertainty is attached. With one genome there is no replication, so no confidence interval is available for any of these percentages. Resampling genes would measure sampling variation within this genome, not variation between genomes, and would be a misleading thing to report.

The honest one-sentence conclusion is therefore narrower than the one a press release would write: for compact bacterial genomes, ab initio prediction is an adequate substitute for curated annotation when the translation table is correct and the question concerns the gene complement rather than exact protein termini, and it should not be trusted in repeat families or for genes under about 150 bp.






Negative and boring results are results



“The default parameters give the wrong answer for this clade, and here is the diagnostic that reveals it” is a more useful finding than a confirmation that a tool works. It is also the kind of result most often left out of write-ups, because the dead end feels like evidence of incompetence. It is evidence of having checked.

section: 15.10 Writing it up, and a reviewer’s self-check
text:
15.10 Writing it up, and a reviewer’s self-check
A project that is not written up has not happened. Three parts of the write-up are specific to computational work.
Figures carry the argument. Each figure in this chapter answers one question: what went wrong (Figure 15.1), why (Figure 15.2), how well the corrected analysis performs (Figure 15.3 and Table 15.1), and where the residual disagreement lives (Figure 15.4). Before adding a figure, state in one sentence the claim it supports; if you cannot, the figure is decoration. Generate every figure from a script that reads the results files, never by hand from a spreadsheet, so that a corrected input regenerates a corrected figure — which is precisely what the figures/ rule in the Makefile guarantees.
A reproducible methods section names versions, parameters and data. The version of this analysis’s methods section would read: “Protein-coding genes were predicted with Prodigal 2.6.3 (Hyatt et al. 2010) in single-genome mode (-p single) under NCBI translation table 4 (-g 4) from the NC_000908.2 assembly, and compared with the RefSeq annotation of the same assembly (GCF_000027325.1) by 3’ coordinate and strand. Analysis code is in the accompanying repository; the environment is pinned in environment.yml.” Every element of that sentence is checkable: a version, a mode, a flag, two accessions and a pointer to code. A methods section that says “genes were predicted using standard parameters” is not reproducible, and reviewers increasingly say so.
Data and code availability statements are commitments. A usable statement names the archive, the accession and the licence for data, and the repository, the archived version identifier and the licence for code. Deposit code in a repository and archive it at a digital object identifier so that the version you describe cannot be silently rewritten. Note that FAIR does not require open: controlled-access human data is correctly described by naming the archive and the access procedure (Wilkinson et al. 2016), as discussed in the ethics chapter.
The self-check to apply before anyone else does
Run through this list before you submit. It is the list a competent reviewer works through, and every item has been violated by published papers.


Can a stranger regenerate every number? Clone the repository into a new directory, create the environment from the specification, run make clean && make, and compare the output with the results in the manuscript. If it fails, the project is not finished.

Is every parameter in the paper? Including the defaults you did not change, since a default is a version-dependent choice. The genetic code in this project was a default, and it was wrong.

Does the metric match the claim? If the claim is about accuracy, the metric must compare against something that can be called truth. This project’s metric supports a claim about agreement, and the abstract must say so.

Is the comparison fair? Both annotations here derive from the same assembly, so no coordinate lift-over or assembly difference confounds the comparison. If your two datasets differ in reference build, read length, depth or batch, that difference is a rival explanation for your result.

Have you looked at the disagreements individually? Aggregate statistics hide structure. Twenty minutes inspecting the 23 unmatched genes changed the interpretation of this project entirely.

What is the sample size, and of what? One genome is n = 1 for claims about genomes, however many genes it contains. Pseudoreplication — treating 524 genes as 524 independent observations about annotation methods — is the most common statistical error in comparative genomics.

Could the result be an artefact of the pipeline? Name the most plausible artefact explicitly and say what rules it out. Here, the most plausible was over-prediction in a GC-poor genome; the TGA analysis ruled it out.

Is the raw data still bit-identical? Verify checksums against the manifest you recorded at the start. A silently corrupted or re-downloaded input invalidates everything downstream.

Does the limitations paragraph exist, and is it specific? “Further work is needed” is not a limitation. Section 15.9 is the length a real one takes.

Who is credited, and for what? Agree the contribution statement before submission, and cite the tools by their methods papers so that the people who wrote the software you depended on get the credit the citation system can measure.

title: 15  A complete project, start to finish
text:
15.11 Summary

A project becomes tractable when the interest is narrowed to a comparison, a measurable quantity, a dataset that can settle it, and a written statement of what an answer would look like.
The choice of metric is a scientific decision. Scoring annotation agreement on stop coordinates rather than exact coordinates measures gene detection rather than start-site prediction, and the choice belongs in the abstract.
A project directory with read-only raw data, disposable derived directories and numbered scripts prevents a class of errors that no amount of care prevents otherwise.
Commit code, configuration and provenance; never commit derived results, large inputs or anything under controlled access. Commit messages explain why, because the diff already shows what.
Pin software to patch versions and channels. A version range documents that you did not know what you ran.
A Makefile records dependencies rather than order, so that only stale results are rebuilt and editing a script invalidates its output. make clean && make is a test of whether a project is reproducible.
Silent analytical failure is the expensive kind: Prodigal exited zero, produced valid GFF3, and was wrong because the default translation table does not apply to Mycoplasma. Build an independent check into every pipeline.
Aggregate agreement conceals structure. In this genome the residual 5% is not spread evenly but concentrated in very short genes and in the MgPa adhesin repeat family, where both methods face genuine ambiguity.
Stating what a result does not show — one genome, a reference that is not truth, a metric that defines the headline number — is part of the result, not a concession.

text:
15.12 Exercises

Run Prodigal on the bundled genome under translation table 25 and compare the number of predicted coding sequences with the results for tables 4 and 11. Explain the direction of the difference from the stop codons each table defines.
The comparison in this chapter scored agreement on the 3’ stop coordinate. Recompute sensitivity and precision for genetic code 4 using exact agreement on both coordinates and strand, and state how the headline figure changes.
Compute the GC content of the 26 unmatched predictions and compare it with the genome-wide value. Does composition distinguish them from genes both methods agree on?
The three reference genes that Prodigal missed entirely are short. Determine the length of the shortest coding sequence Prodigal did predict under code 4, and use it to estimate the effective length threshold of the method on this genome.
Write a make rule that produces results/comparison_code25.tsv without editing any existing rule, and explain which feature of the Makefile makes this possible.
The reference annotation contains 20 pseudogenes. Write code to test whether reference coding sequences that overlap a pseudogene are recovered less often than those that do not, and report the two recovery rates.
A colleague reports that an ab initio predictor “achieves 95% accuracy on bacterial genomes” and proposes to replace curated annotation with it in a 400-genome survey. Write the three questions you would ask before agreeing, drawn from Section 15.9.
Take any analysis of your own and apply the ten-point self-check in Section 15.10. Report which items you cannot currently satisfy and what each would take to fix.

title: 15  A complete project, start to finish
text:
15.13 Solutions






Solutions





1. Table 25 reassigns TGA to glycine, so like table 4 it removes the stop codon that fragments Mycoplasma genes; the prediction count is therefore close to the table 4 result rather than the table 11 one. The remaining difference comes from the start-codon set and the retraining of the composition model.

code25 = cds_table(run_prodigal(genome_path, work / "code25.gff", 25))
for name, table in (("code 11", code11), ("code 4", code4), ("code 25", code25)):
    print(f"{name}: {len(table)} CDS, median {int(table['length'].median())} bp")
#> code 11: 995 CDS, median 336 bp
#> code 4: 527 CDS, median 855 bp
#> code 25: 527 CDS, median 855 bp

2. Exact agreement on both coordinates is stricter by the 37 genes whose starts differ, lowering sensitivity by about seven percentage points. The headline figure drops from 95.6% to roughly 88%, which is why the metric must be stated wherever the number is.

exact_reference = set(zip(reference_cds["start"], reference_cds["end"], reference_cds["strand"]))
exact_predicted = set(zip(code4["start"], code4["end"], code4["strand"]))
shared_exact = exact_reference & exact_predicted
print(f"exact-coordinate sensitivity {100 * len(shared_exact) / len(reference_cds):.1f}%, "
      f"precision {100 * len(shared_exact) / len(code4):.1f}%")
#> exact-coordinate sensitivity 88.5%, precision 88.0%

3. The unmatched predictions are close to the genome-wide composition, so GC content does not separate them; their distinguishing feature is position, not composition, as Figure 15.4 showed.

def gc_percent(row):
    span = genome.seq[row.start - 1:row.end]
    return 100 * (span.count("G") + span.count("C")) / len(span)

matched = code4[code4["stop_key"].isin(set(reference_cds["stop_key"]))]
print(f"unmatched predictions: {np.mean([gc_percent(r) for r in extra.itertuples()]):.1f}% GC")
#> unmatched predictions: 38.1% GC
print(f"matched predictions:   {np.mean([gc_percent(r) for r in matched.itertuples()]):.1f}% GC")
#> matched predictions:   31.7% GC
print(f"whole genome:          {100 * (genome.seq.count('G') + genome.seq.count('C')) / len(genome.seq):.1f}% GC")
#> whole genome:          31.7% GC

4. The shortest prediction sets an empirical floor on what the method will report, and the missed 147 bp ribosomal protein gene sits below or near it.

print(f"shortest predicted CDS under code 4: {int(code4['length'].min())} bp")
#> shortest predicted CDS under code 4: 90 bp
print(f"reference CDS shorter than that: {int((reference_cds['length'] < code4['length'].min()).sum())}")
#> reference CDS shorter than that: 0

5. No new rule is needed for the prediction itself: the pattern rules results/prodigal_code%.gff and results/comparison_code%.tsv match any value of %, so make results/comparison_code25.tsv builds the whole chain. A pattern rule is a rule schema, which is why parameterising the pipeline rather than editing it is the habit worth forming; in Snakemake the same idea appears as wildcards.
6. Recovery is much lower for coding sequences overlapping a pseudogene locus, which is the MgPa repeat effect quantified.

pseudo_spans = list(zip(pseudogenes["start"], pseudogenes["end"]))
near_pseudogene = np.array([any(a <= row.end and row.start <= b for a, b in pseudo_spans)
                            for row in reference_cds.itertuples()])
found = reference_cds["stop_key"].isin(set(code4["stop_key"])).to_numpy()
print(f"overlapping a pseudogene: {100 * found[near_pseudogene].mean():.1f}% recovered "
      f"(n={near_pseudogene.sum()})")
#> overlapping a pseudogene: 25.9% recovered (n=27)
print(f"elsewhere:                {100 * found[~near_pseudogene].mean():.1f}% recovered "
      f"(n={(~near_pseudogene).sum()})")
#> elsewhere:                99.4% recovered (n=497)

7. Accuracy against what reference, measured by which metric, and on which genomes? Specifically: is the 95% agreement with a curated annotation that is itself partly computational, rather than accuracy against experimentally determined boundaries; was it scored on stop coordinates, exact coordinates or overlap; and was it measured on genomes resembling the 400 in the survey in GC content, assembly contiguity and translation table? A fourth question is worth adding: what does the survey need annotation for, since gene counting tolerates a 5% boundary error and protein terminus analysis does not.
8. No model answer; the value is in the items you cannot satisfy. The two that most often fail are the first — a clean clone does not reproduce the numbers, usually because a result was generated by a command run interactively and never written into a script — and the eighth, because checksums were never recorded at the start.

text:
15.14 Further reading


Hyatt et al. (2010) describes Prodigal’s algorithm, including the translation table handling that this chapter’s first run got wrong; the paper’s own benchmarking is a model of how to scope such a claim.

Tatusova et al. (2016) documents the NCBI prokaryotic annotation pipeline that produced the reference used here, and is the right place to understand what “RefSeq annotation” actually involves.

Seemann (2014) presents Prokka, which wraps Prodigal with functional annotation and is the usual next step after this chapter’s analysis.

Köster and Rahmann (2012) introduces Snakemake, the natural successor to the Makefile once a project has samples rather than a single genome.

Wilson et al. (2017) is the most practical available statement of project organisation, and its advice on read-only raw data and disposable derived directories is the backbone of Section 15.3.

Sandve et al. (2013) gives ten rules for reproducible computational research; read it as a checklist alongside Section 15.10.

Manni et al. (2021) describes BUSCO, the standard completeness check for a new assembly or annotation, and the obvious external validation to add to a project like this one.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text: 16.1 What each chapter established

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
Chapter 1: What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it
The opening chapter defined the discipline by what it produces: defensible biological statements extracted from large, noisy, machine-generated measurements, as distinct from computational biology, which produces methods and models. It argued that the scale is what forces computation, and did the arithmetic rather than asserting it — a single human genome at 30-fold coverage with 150 bp reads is about 620 million reads and 206 GB of uncompressed FASTQ, some 2,400 times the row limit of a spreadsheet. It then placed the field’s methodological eras against the data problem each one solved, and reduced almost every analysis to a five-stage shape in which each stage contains a decision that must be recorded in a script if the conclusion is to survive questioning months later. The chapter ended by building the environment the rest of the book uses and running a first real analysis: the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome at 29,903 bp and 38% GC, with long open reading frames concentrated on one strand. Everything that follows is a specialisation of that pattern — a question, a decision, a record.
Chapter 2: Molecular biology for people who analyse data
This chapter supplied the biology the algorithms encode, and taught it through the errors it prevents. Strandedness comes first, because a FASTA record stores one strand and says nothing about which, so the reverse complement — not the complement — is what every format expects. Translation never fails, which is why a plausible-looking protein is no evidence of a correct reading frame; the diagnostics are an initial methionine, a single terminal stop and no internal stops. Testing a naive open reading frame scan against the SARS-CoV-2 annotation made the point quantitatively: a 100-codon threshold recovers the long genes, misses four real ones and produces a chance hit on the empty strand, while lowering it to 38 codons finds all eleven genes at the cost of growing the output from 9 predictions to 76. The TP53 worked example — roughly 19 kb of genomic span, a 2,512 nt mRNA, an 1,182 nt coding sequence and a 393-residue protein identical to UniProt P04637 — establishes both the central dogma and the cheapest available test of a nucleotide-to-protein pipeline. Coordinates close the chapter, because 1-based inclusive and 0-based half-open systems never announce themselves.
Chapter 3: Biological databases and how to get data out of them
Here the book moved from biology to the records that represent it, and to the question of how much a record can be trusted. Resources divide into primary archives, which store what was submitted; curated knowledgebases, which store conclusions with evidence; and derived resources, which compute — and the kind of resource determines the sentence you are entitled to write about it. Accession discipline follows: INSDC mirroring makes GenBank, ENA and DDBJ one archive under one set of accessions; prefixes encode provenance, with NM_/NP_ curated and XM_/XP_ machine-predicted, and GCA_ an author’s assembly against GCF_ the RefSeq copy; and the digits after the full stop are a version, without which an accession does not identify data. Dissecting the UniProt entry for p53 showed what curation buys — 238 papers read, 1,120 cross-references and more than 1,500 features on a protein of 393 residues — and established the chapter’s most portable habit: read the evidence code before the annotation, because IDA and IMP are experiments while IEA and ISS are hypotheses. Programmatic access and recorded provenance — accession, version, date, checksum — make the rest of the book repeatable.
Chapter 4: Sequence alignment and what it tells you
Alignment is the field’s central algorithmic idea, and the chapter built it from the recursion up. Similarity is measured and homology is inferred, so no sequence is ever “40% homologous” to another; orthologues arise by speciation and usually keep their function, paralogues by duplication and need not. Dynamic programming gives an exact optimum under a stated scoring scheme, and the worked score matrix and traceback show what that optimum is made of. The chapter then demonstrated, rather than asserted, that the scoring scheme matters: the same distant globin pair aligns over 142 columns at 27.5% identity under BLOSUM62 or PAM250, but collapses to 101 columns at an apparently better 48.5% identity under PAM30, so a matrix chosen for the wrong evolutionary distance silently shortens an alignment instead of failing. BLAST trades optimality for speed, and its statistics carry the same lesson — the bit score of an alignment is 44.3 whatever database it was found in, while the E-value scales with database size. Multiple alignment of eight p53 orthologues localised conservation to the DNA-binding domain, and a bootstrapped tree showed which clades the data actually resolve and which, at 18% and 34% support, they do not.
Chapter 5: The command line as a working environment
The toolchain chapters begin with the observation that bioinformatics data are mostly line-oriented text files too large to open. The shell is presented as a programming environment organised around one idea — programs read a stream, write a stream, and pipes compose them — so that memory use stays constant however large the file. The text-processing core of grep, cut, sort, uniq, sed, awk and join is taught against the formats the book uses, and each idiom arrives with the specific silent error it prevents: sorting before uniq -c, anchoring a regular expression, checking row counts across a join, which is how the chapter discovers that 30 genes produce 31 joined rows because CDKN2A has two reviewed UniProt entries. An awk example that computes a perfectly plausible and entirely wrong GC content of 46.42%, through nothing worse than putting two statements in the wrong order, makes the chapter’s point about silent failure. Compression is treated as streaming rather than storage, with BGZF and tabix turning a compressed VCF into a randomly accessible one, and the chapter closes on exit status, set -euo pipefail, defensive scripts and SLURM job arrays.
Chapter 6: Python for bioinformatics
This chapter turns the reader from a user of tools into an author of them. It covers the language core — types, collections, control flow, functions, files — with every example drawn from sequence data, and insists on two habits: choose the collection from the question (a list for order, a dictionary for lookup, a set for membership) and convert coordinates in one tested place rather than in your head, because Python is 0-based and half-open while GFF3, VCF and GenBank are 1-based and closed. Biopython’s SeqRecord and feature.extract then remove the hand-arithmetic entirely, which the chapter verifies by translating the SARS-CoV-2 spike feature and recovering a 1,273-residue protein beginning MFVFLVLLPLVS. NumPy earns its place on a 20,000 × 150 quality matrix, where the mean Phred score falls from Q37.2 at the first cycle to Q23.7 at the last and crosses Q30 at cycle 111 — the kind of summary that decides a trimming parameter. pandas turns a GFF3 or a VCF into a table, and the chapter ends where professional code begins: two assertions are a test suite, and a module with a __main__ guard is a tool.
Chapter 7: R and Bioconductor
R enters where statistics and figures become the task. The chapter’s organising claim is that R’s design removes loops and index errors by applying operations to whole vectors — and that the same design produces the book’s most dangerous silent error, because recycling repeats a short operand down the columns of a matrix, so dividing a count matrix by a vector of library sizes returns plausible nonsense rather than an error. Factors, coercion and the tibble–data frame distinction are treated in the same spirit: each is a category of wrong answer rather than a language feature. The grammar of graphics is taught by debugging a figure, taking an unreadable linear-scale boxplot of counts spanning five orders of magnitude to a log scale and then to facets that reveal library protocol, not treatment, as the dominant source of variation in the pasilla data. Bioconductor’s value is located in its shared classes: Biostrings, GRanges with rtracklayer, and above all SummarizedExperiment, which makes the commonest serious bug in expression analysis — sample annotation detached from its counts — impossible to commit. A three-line differential test closes it: 1,547 genes pass an uncorrected threshold against roughly 407 expected by chance, and 195 survive Benjamini–Hochberg correction.
Chapter 8: From assembled sequence to annotated genome
With sequence, tools and languages in hand, the book turns to interpretation. An assembly is a hypothesis, and the chapter checks contiguity, completeness and contamination before annotating anything, noting that N50 measures contiguity rather than correctness and rewards over-aggressive assembly. Structural annotation of Mycoplasmoides genitalium then delivers the chapter’s central lesson about parameters: under the bacterial default, genetic code 11, Prodigal predicts 995 genes where the correct code 4 predicts 527, and nothing in the output signals the error. Comparing the prediction with the RefSeq annotation of the same assembly shows what ab initio prediction is and is not good at — 464 genes agree on both coordinates, 37 share a stop but not a start, 23 are found only by RefSeq and 26 only by Prodigal — and explains the asymmetry: a stop codon is a consequence of the reading frame while a start is a prediction. Eukaryotic prediction needs external evidence because introns make the problem underdetermined. Functional annotation is inference by similarity with an invisible inference chain, which is why the chapter ends by reading evidence codes: all 985 Gene Ontology annotations in this genome are IEA, and about a tenth of the proteome remains unannotated after thirty years.
Chapter 9: Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results
This chapter connects an instrument to a result and insists that each stage is a hypothesis rather than a view of the same thing: a read is an observation, an alignment an inference about origin, a variant call an inference about genotype. It relates each chemistry to the errors it makes, separates library artefacts from biology, and builds a quality report from the bundled reads rather than trusting a tool’s traffic lights. Trimming is quantified rather than recommended: at Q25 the data loses 11% of its bases for no gain in an alignment-based analysis. Alignment introduces SAM in detail — FLAG, CIGAR and MAPQ — and the sharpest demonstration uses simulated reads whose true origin is known: 25 of 40,000 reads are placed in the wrong location, 38 carry MAPQ 0 in the MgPa adhesin repeats, and MAPQ 0 means “equally good elsewhere” rather than “bad read”. The RNA-seq half runs a full DESeq2 analysis of the pasilla experiment, recovering 1,108 genes at an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and pasilla itself down about 3.7-fold, and ends on what a 5% false discovery rate is a property of: the list, not the gene.
Chapter 10: Protein structure and what you can compute from it
Structure is where sequence becomes mechanism, and the chapter treats a structure as a measurement with error bars. Judging one means reading resolution, R factors, B factors and missing residues — 1TUP at 2.20 Å reports no R-free because it was deposited in 1995, and 72 of its residues are modelled nowhere, recorded in REMARK 465 where code that reads only ATOM lines will never see them. Bio.PDB’s structure–model–chain–residue–atom hierarchy makes geometry a few lines of code, and the geometry is biology: the p53 zinc is held tetrahedrally by Cys176, His179, Cys238 and Cys242 at 1.99–2.33 Å without touching DNA, while only chain B is bound in the major groove, through twelve residues within 4 Å of it. Superposition supplies the chapter’s most transferable number — three copies of the same domain in one crystal differ by 0.78–1.03 Å, which is the scale against which any other RMSD must be read. The AlphaFold model reproduces that domain to 0.73 Å over 194 Cα atoms and scores p53’s disordered regions below 50, which is a correct prediction rather than a failure; high predicted aligned error between two confident domains means their relative arrangement is not predicted at all.
Chapter 11: Biological networks and pathway analysis
Having treated genes one at a time, the book turns to their relations, and spends most of its effort on what an edge actually asserts. In the bundled 30-gene STRING slice every edge has text-mining support, 176 of 210 have experimental support and only 85 appear in a curated database, so a functional association is not a physical interaction and filtering by evidence channel is usually the right first move. The chapter then measures the network — 30 nodes, 210 edges, density 0.483, clustering coefficient 0.646 — and immediately disowns the measurements as properties of a query-driven selection rather than of the interactome. The same scepticism applies to hubs: TP53 has degree 29 and five times the betweenness of any other gene, which in a network built by querying for p53-associated genes is no discovery, and degree correlates with annotation count at Spearman 0.746, so hub status partly measures study intensity. Community detection always returns communities, so low modularity and disagreement between algorithms are the signal. Over-representation analysis is then built from one hypergeometric test per term, corrected with Benjamini–Hochberg, and the closing demonstration is that matching the background universe for study intensity cuts the significant-term count from 511 to 121.
Chapter 12: Statistics and machine learning on omics data
This chapter supplies the statistical reasoning the rest of the book consumes, and does it by breaking things deliberately. It distinguishes biological from technical replication, establishes that an omics matrix has far more features than samples — 14,599 genes against seven pasilla samples — and shows what that guarantees: some feature always separates any two groups. Normalisation is demonstrated rather than described, with the median log ratio between two control samples falling from 1.443, the log ratio of their library sizes, to 0.056 after conversion to counts per million. Batch effects are shown imitating biology: principal components place treatment on PC1 at 39.7% of variance and library protocol on PC2 at 31.8%, and in a deliberately confounded contrast 22.3% of the significant genes are also significant in a pure protocol comparison against 7.8% expected. Multiple testing is calibrated against simulation — 10,000 null tests give 501 results at p < 0.05 and none after correction — and the most important experiment permutes the labels: selecting features before cross-validation reports perfect accuracy in 100 of 100 permutations of meaningless labels, while selecting inside each fold reports 0.384, below the majority-class baseline, which is the truthful answer.
Chapter 13: Bioinformatics in disease and healthcare
Here the book’s methods meet the clinic, and the chapter’s discipline is to separate claims by the evidence behind them. Germline and somatic variants differ in calling strategy, expected allele fraction and consent obligations; drivers are separated from passengers by comparison against a background mutation rate that varies by orders of magnitude; mutational signatures describe the chemistry that produced a mutation and not its consequence. The bundled ClinVar slice of 3,888 TP53 records supplies the clinical reality: about a quarter are variants of uncertain significance, only 191 carry expert-panel review and 192 carry no assertion criteria at all, so review status matters more than the label. Two computed results carry the chapter. Truncating variants are classified pathogenic 81.4% of the time against 16.9% for missense variants, which is the empirical content of the ACMG/AMP criterion PVS1. And 94.1% of pathogenic missense variants fall in the DNA-binding domain at residues 102–292, against 26.1% of benign ones and the 48.6% expected from its length. The chapter closes on the distinction between pathogenic and actionable, on pharmacogenomic guidelines, and on pathogen surveillance, which is limited by sampling and reporting far more often than by sequencing.
Chapter 14: Working responsibly with genomic data
This chapter argues that the obligations attached to human genomic data follow from four properties of the data itself: it identifies, it cannot be revoked, it implicates relatives who never consented, and it predicts weakly but is read strongly. Two simulations make the first property quantitative. Twenty-five independent common markers make every one of 10,000 simulated individuals unique, and the random match probability falls below one in eight billion at 30 markers, which is why a variant file is identifiable data whatever has been stripped from its header. A reimplementation of the allele-frequency membership statistic then detects 90% of 200 pool contributors from 5,000 markers with no false positives, showing that published summary statistics are not automatically safe and that the attack strengthens as panels densify. From that mechanical basis the chapter works through consent models and the problem of enforcing them in code, controlled access and the five safes, the structure of GDPR, HIPAA, Nigeria’s data protection regime and the Nagoya Protocol, the clinical cost of the European-ancestry bias in reference data, and the design decisions — benefit sharing, authorship, governance — that separate collaboration from extraction. Its practical residue is a checklist applied before a project starts.
Chapter 15: A complete project, start to finish
The capstone assembles everything into one analysis: how much of a curated bacterial annotation does ab initio prediction recover? It builds the infrastructure first — read-only raw data, disposable derived directories, a pinned environment, a Git history whose messages record decisions, and a Makefile that rebuilds only what is stale — and then runs an analysis that fails. Prodigal’s default translation table treats TGA as a stop codon, which 71.6% of M. genitalium genes contain internally, so the first run returns 995 predictions with a median length of 336 bp against 856 bp in the reference, recovering 96.6% of TGA-free genes but only 52.5% of the rest. Diagnosing that against an independent annotation, rather than from an error message, is the chapter’s central lesson. Under the correct code the comparison recovers 95.6% of reference coding sequences at 95.1% precision with 92.6% of starts identical, and inspecting the residual disagreements shows them concentrated in very short genes and in the MgPa adhesin repeat family, where neither method is simply right. It closes on write-up: the metric belongs in the abstract, the limitations are part of the result, and a reviewer’s checklist is cheaper applied to yourself.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.2 Question bank: foundations and data
Each question is labelled by the kind of thinking it requires. Recall questions test whether a definition or fact is available to you. Application questions require you to use a method on a specific case. Interpretation questions give you a result and ask what it means or whether it is trustworthy; these are the ones that matter most in practice and the ones most often skipped. Attempt each before opening the answers.
Chapter 1: What bioinformatics is, and how to set up to do it


(recall) State the distinction Chapter 1 draws between bioinformatics and computational biology, in terms of what each produces.

(recall) Name the five stages common to almost every sequence analysis, and state what all five have in common.

(application) A 30-fold human genome sequenced with 150 bp reads produces about 620 million reads and 206 GB of uncompressed FASTQ. Show the arithmetic, and explain why the comparison with a spreadsheet’s row limit is a statement about operations as much as about size.

(interpretation) A published analysis reports a result but gives neither software versions nor parameters. State what specifically cannot be checked, and why “the method is standard” is not an adequate defence.

Chapter 2: Molecular biology for people who analyse data


(recall) Define reading frame, and state how many exist for a double-stranded DNA sequence.

(recall) Why is a plausible-looking translated protein not evidence that the reading frame was correct, and what three features should you check instead?

(application) A single-base deletion occurs early in the TP53 coding sequence. Predict the consequence for the protein product and justify it from the triplet nature of translation.

(interpretation) Scanning the SARS-CoV-2 genome for open reading frames of at least 100 codons recovers the long genes but misses four annotated ones and reports a hit on the strand that carries no genes. Lowering the threshold to 38 codons finds all eleven genes but raises the output from 9 predictions to 76. State what this trade-off is called and how you would choose a threshold.

Chapter 3: Biological databases and how to get data out of them


(recall) Distinguish a primary archive, a curated knowledgebase and a derived resource, naming one of each.

(recall) What do the digits after the full stop in NM_000546.6 specify, and what is versioned differently in an Ensembl identifier such as ENST00000269305.9?

(application) You need the canonical human p53 sequence and the boundaries of its DNA-binding domain. State which resource you would query, where in the record the boundaries sit, and what you would record as provenance.

(interpretation) Two functional annotations on the same protein carry the evidence codes IDA and IEA. State what each means, which you would build a conclusion on, and what you would check before relying on the weaker one.

Chapter 4: Sequence alignment and what it tells you


(recall) State the difference between global and local alignment, name an algorithm for each, and give the biological question that selects each one.

(recall) Explain what an affine gap penalty models that a linear penalty does not.

(application) The same distant globin pair aligns over 142 columns at 27.5% identity under BLOSUM62 and over 101 columns at 48.5% identity under PAM30. Explain why the higher identity is the worse result, and state which matrix you would report.

(interpretation) A BLAST search of myoglobin against a small protein database returns human haemoglobin alpha at 25.7% identity over 148 residues with an E-value of 9.18 × 10⁻¹⁰, and several p53 entries matching over 8 to 27 residues with E-values between 0.47 and 9.7. State which hits are evidence of homology, and why percentage identity is the weaker guide.







Answers: Chapters 1 to 4





1. Bioinformatics converts large, noisy, machine-generated measurements into defensible biological statements about a particular sample; computational biology produces the methods and models that make such conversions possible. The distinction is in the product, not in the tools, and it determines how the work is judged — correctness, reproducibility and relevance to the sample in hand for the first, generality and correctness of the method for the second.
2. Acquiring or retrieving the data; assessing its quality; reducing or transforming it; comparing it with a reference or between groups; and interpreting the comparison. What they have in common is that every stage contains a decision — a threshold, a reference, a parameter — which must be recorded in a script, because the question asked months later is whether the conclusion survives changing it.
3. A 3.1 Gb genome at 30-fold coverage is about 93 Gb of sequence; divided by 150 bp that is roughly 620 million reads, and at about 332 bytes per FASTQ record that is some 206 GB. The spreadsheet comparison matters less for the row count than for the operations: aligning each read to a 3.1 Gb reference, modelling base distributions under an error profile, and testing 20,000 genes with false discovery control are not row-by-row arithmetic, so no amount of spreadsheet capacity would help.
4. Without versions you cannot know whether the tool’s defaults, algorithms or bug fixes differ from yours, and without parameters you cannot reproduce the numbers at all; the result is unverifiable rather than merely inconvenient. “Standard” is no defence because defaults change between versions and because the parameter that mattered most in this book — the translation table in Chapters 8 and 15 — was itself a default.
5. A reading frame is one of the ways a nucleotide sequence can be partitioned into consecutive triplets, fixed by the position of the first base read. There are six for double-stranded DNA: three on each strand.
6. Because translation never fails — any sequence of bases yields a sequence of amino acids, so the output always looks like a protein. Check for an initial methionine, a single stop at the end, and no internal stops; a frame-shifted translation typically fails the last two.
7. The deletion shifts the frame for every downstream codon, so the sequence after it is wrong and a premature stop appears quickly. In the chapter’s worked example ten correct residues are followed by a short stretch belonging to no p53 and then a stop — 13 amino acids in place of 393, from one base in a 1,182 nt coding sequence. The transcript may also be destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay.
8. It is the sensitivity–precision trade-off: lowering the threshold recovers the short genes (sensitivity) and admits many chance frames and alternative starts (precision), since roughly six of every seven predictions at 38 codons are not new genes. Choose the threshold from what the prediction is for — a high threshold when you will inspect every hit by hand, a low one when the predictions feed a downstream filter such as homology search — and state the threshold with the result.
9. A primary archive such as GenBank stores records as submitted, with the submitter responsible for their content; a curated knowledgebase such as UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot or RefSeq records conclusions with evidence attached; a derived resource computes something from the others, such as a genome browser’s alignment tracks or a structure prediction database.
10. In an INSDC or RefSeq nucleotide accession the version increments when the sequence changes, so NM_000546.5 and NM_000546.6 may be different strings of bases. Ensembl versions genes and transcripts separately from the assembly and increments the suffix when the model changes, so the same genomic sequence can carry a new transcript version.
11. Query UniProtKB for P04637. The domain boundaries are in the feature table of the flat file, as the DNA_BIND 102..292 line, with its own evidence attribution. Record the accession, the entry version or release date, the date of retrieval and a checksum of the downloaded file, because UniProt annotations change.
12. IDA is inferred from direct assay — an experiment on this protein — while IEA is inferred from electronic annotation, transferred automatically from another record without curator review. Build on the IDA annotation. Before relying on the IEA one, find what it was transferred from, check that the similarity covers the functionally relevant region, and look for direct experimental evidence; an electronic annotation is a hypothesis about function, not an observation of it.
13. Global alignment aligns two sequences along their entire length (Needleman–Wunsch) and suits sequences expected to correspond throughout, such as two orthologues of the same protein. Local alignment finds the best-scoring segment pair (Smith–Waterman) and suits the search for a shared domain in otherwise unrelated sequences.
14. That an insertion or deletion is a single evolutionary event of some length, rather than a series of independent single-residue events. A linear penalty charges the same for each gap position and therefore scatters many short gaps where one long gap belongs; an affine penalty charges a large opening cost and a small extension cost, which recovers the single event.
15. PAM30 is built for sequences that have barely diverged, so it penalises the substitutions that actually occur between distant homologues and the aligner responds by truncating the alignment to a short, well-matching core. The identity rises because the denominator shrank, not because the sequences are more similar. Report the BLOSUM62 or PAM250 result — 142 columns at 27.5% — and report identity with the aligned length attached, since identity alone is uninterpretable.
16. Only the haemoglobin alpha hit. The E-value accounts for alignment length and database size, so 9.18 × 10⁻¹⁰ over 148 residues is strong evidence of homology even at 25.7% identity, which sits in the twilight zone where real homologues and convincing accidents coexist. The p53 matches over 8 to 27 residues have E-values close to or above 1, meaning roughly one such hit is expected per search by chance. Percentage identity ignores both the length of the alignment and the size of the search space.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.3 Question bank: the toolchain
Chapter 5: The command line as a working environment


(recall) Explain what a pipe does, and why it allows processing of files much larger than available memory.

(recall) State the difference between > and >>, and the specific data loss that confusing them causes.

(application) Write a one-line pipeline that counts the sequences in a FASTA file, and explain why counting lines beginning with > is correct whereas counting all lines is not.

(interpretation) An awk program reports the GC content of a read file as 46.42%, a plausible figure, when the true value is near 31.7%. The program removes the newline before accumulating base counts but after accumulating the total length. Explain the error, and state the general lesson about this class of bug.

Chapter 6: Python for bioinformatics


(recall) State what SeqIO.parse returns and how it differs from SeqIO.read.

(recall) Python slices are 0-based and half-open; GFF3, VCF and GenBank coordinates are 1-based and inclusive. Give the Python slice for the GFF3 feature 686..1828, and state the rule.

(application) Write a function returning the GC content of a sequence that handles an empty sequence without raising. State what it should return and justify the choice.

(interpretation) The mean per-cycle quality of the bundled reads falls from Q37.2 to Q23.7 and crosses Q30 at cycle 111, while the tenth percentile crosses it at cycle 83. State which of these two numbers should inform a trimming decision and why.

Chapter 7: R and Bioconductor


(recall) State what recycling is in R, and the direction in which it operates on a matrix.

(recall) What three behaviours does a tibble change relative to a data frame, and what class of error does each prevent?

(application) You have a counts matrix and a separate sample table. Describe the checks to perform before any analysis, and the single assertion that must hold between them.

(application) Explain how pivot_longer changes the shape of a 14,599-gene by 7-sample count matrix, why ggplot2 needs that shape, and why Bioconductor assays need the opposite one.

(interpretation) A boxplot of per-sample gene counts on a linear axis shows flattened boxes and a column of outliers. State the diagnosis and the single change that fixes it, and say why changing the geometry would not.

(interpretation) Faceting the pasilla count distributions by library protocol shows medians differing by roughly a factor of two between panels, while the four distributions within each panel are closely matched. State what this identifies, and what it implies for any differential expression model fitted to these samples.







Answers: Chapters 5 to 7





17. A pipe connects one program’s standard output to the next program’s standard input, so records stream through the chain one at a time. Because no stage holds the whole file, memory use stays roughly constant regardless of file size.
18. > truncates the target file before writing; >> appends. Confusing them destroys the previous contents irrecoverably, which is why raw data directories are made read-only with chmod.
19. grep -c "^>" sequences.fasta. Only header lines start with >, and each record has exactly one header, whereas sequence lines are wrapped at an arbitrary width, so a line count measures formatting rather than content. The ^ anchor matters: without it the count would include any line containing >.
20. The length accumulator sees the line with its trailing newline and the base counts do not, so every line contributes one phantom base to the denominator; with 150 bp lines the inflation is about 0.7% of the total and the GC percentage shifts by a plausible amount. The lesson is that this class of error produces a number in the right range rather than a crash, so a pipeline needs an external check — here, the genome’s own known GC content of 31.7% — rather than a plausibility judgement.
21. SeqIO.parse returns an iterator over all records in a file and suits a file with any number of sequences; SeqIO.read returns the single record in a file and raises an error if there is not exactly one. Use read when “exactly one record” is a requirement you want enforced.
22. genome[685:1828]. Subtract one from the start and leave the end unchanged; the half-open upper bound and the inclusive end coincide numerically, which is why only the start appears to move.
23. It should return a documented sentinel such as None or float("nan"), not zero and not an exception, because an empty sequence has no GC content and 0% would enter a downstream average as though it were a measurement.
def gc_fraction_safe(sequence):
    """GC content as a fraction, or None for an empty sequence."""
    if len(sequence) == 0:
        return None
    gc = sum(1 for base in sequence.upper() if base in "GC")
    return gc / len(sequence)
24. The tenth percentile, at cycle 83. The mean describes the typical read, but mismatches are contributed by the worst reads, and a cycle at which a tenth of reads have already fallen below the accuracy threshold is adding more error than information. Trimming decisions are made from the lower edge of the distribution, not from its centre.
25. Recycling repeats the shorter operand until it matches the length of the longer one, silently and without warning when the lengths divide evenly. A matrix in R is a vector with a dimension attribute filled column by column, so a short vector recycles down the columns — which is why dividing a gene-by-sample count matrix by a vector of per-sample library sizes scales genes rather than samples and returns a plausible, wrong answer.
26. No partial matching of column names, which prevents a typo silently selecting the wrong column; no dropping to a vector when a single column is selected, which prevents code that expects a table receiving something else; and no silent conversion of character columns to factors, which prevents the whole class of factor-related errors.
27. Check that the number of samples equals the number of matrix columns, that the two identifier sets are identical, and that they are in the same order; then reorder the sample table by the matrix column names rather than assuming correspondence. The assertion that must hold is that sample-table row names equal matrix column names element by element — or, better, build a SummarizedExperiment, which enforces it permanently.
28. pivot_longer turns the 14,599 × 7 wide matrix into roughly 102,000 rows of three columns — gene, sample, count — one row per observation. ggplot2 needs this because every aesthetic maps to a column, so “sample” must be a variable rather than a set of column names. Bioconductor assays need the wide form because the matrix is the computational object: linear algebra, normalisation and model fitting all operate on genes × samples.
29. The counts span five orders of magnitude, so a linear axis gives almost all its height to a few thousand very large values and compresses everything else onto the axis. Change the scale to logarithmic; the geometry is not the problem, and replacing the boxplot with a violin or a histogram would produce an equally unreadable figure on the same axis.
30. It identifies library protocol, not treatment, as the dominant source of variation — a batch effect of larger magnitude than the biological effect. Since protocol is recorded and is not perfectly confounded with condition in this dataset, it must appear in the design formula as a covariate, so that the condition term is estimated after accounting for it; fitting condition alone would attribute protocol variation to treatment and inflate the dispersion estimates.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
section: 16.4 Question bank: genomes, reads and structures
text:
16.4 Question bank: genomes, reads and structures
Chapter 8: From assembled sequence to annotated genome


(recall) Distinguish structural from functional annotation, and name one tool used for each.

(recall) State what the nine columns of a GFF3 record contain, and which attributes make a feature’s relationship to another explicit.

(application) You have a new bacterial assembly and no annotation. Give the order of steps to a first-pass annotation, and say at which step the translation table must be settled and why.

(interpretation) Comparing Prodigal with the RefSeq annotation of the same genome gives 464 genes identical at both ends, 37 sharing a stop but not a start, 23 found only by RefSeq and 26 only by Prodigal. Explain why the disagreements concentrate in start codons rather than in gene presence, and what the 23 and the 26 mostly turn out to be.

Chapter 9: Next-generation sequencing data from reads to results


(recall) State what a Phred score of 30 means, and how the score is encoded in a FASTQ quality line.

(recall) Name the eleven mandatory SAM fields’ three most frequently misread members — FLAG, CIGAR and MAPQ — and state what each encodes.

(application) Given paired FASTQ files, give the commands that produce a sorted, indexed BAM, and state why coordinate sorting must precede indexing.

(interpretation) samtools flagstat on the bundled simulated alignment reports 40,000 reads, 100% mapped and 39,968 properly paired. Say what each figure would mean for a real bacterial isolate, and which of the three you would be most suspicious of here.

(interpretation) Thirty-eight of 40,000 reads carry MAPQ 0, clustered around two positions, and 25 reads are placed somewhere other than where they were simulated from. Explain what MAPQ 0 means, why the two observations are related, and what filtering on MAPQ 20 would do to a variant call in that region.

(interpretation) The DESeq2 analysis of the pasilla data returns 1,108 genes at an adjusted p-value below 0.05, and recovers pasilla itself as down about 3.7-fold. State precisely what the 5% false discovery rate promises about this list, and what it promises about any one gene in it.

Chapter 10: Protein structure and what you can compute from it


(recall) State what the B-factor column reports in a crystal structure, and what occupies the same column in an AlphaFold model.

(recall) Where in a PDB file are residues that were not modelled recorded, and why will code that reads only ATOM records miss them?

(application) Describe how you would determine which residues of a protein chain contact a bound DNA molecule, including the atom selection and the cut-off, and what you would exclude from both sets.

(interpretation) Three copies of the p53 DNA-binding domain in one crystal differ by 0.78–1.03 Å over about 195 Cα atoms, and the AlphaFold model matches one of them to 0.73 Å over 194 Cα. State what the first range is for, and what the second number does and does not establish.

(interpretation) An AlphaFold model has two regions with pLDDT above 90 and a high predicted aligned error between them. State what each measure reports and which statements the model does and does not support.

(interpretation) The radius of gyration of the p53 DNA-binding domain alone is 16.6 Å, while that of the full-length AlphaFold model is 33.5 Å. Explain what the difference reflects, and why the full-length figure should not be quoted as a property of the protein.







Answers: Chapters 8 to 10





31. Structural annotation locates features — genes, exons, RNA genes, repeats — in an assembly; Prodigal performs it for bacteria and AUGUSTUS for eukaryotes. Functional annotation assigns biological meaning to those features; domain search against Pfam with HMMER, or InterProScan, performs it.
32. Sequence identifier, source, feature type, start, end, score, strand, phase and attributes. The ID and Parent attributes in the ninth column express the hierarchy, making a CDS a child of a transcript and a transcript a child of a gene; a spliced feature occupies several lines sharing one ID.
33. Assess the assembly — contiguity, completeness against a conserved single-copy gene set, contamination — then mask repeats, then predict coding sequences, then predict RNA genes with specialised tools, then transfer functional annotation by domain and orthology search, and finally assess the annotation before release. The translation table must be settled before gene prediction, because it determines which codons terminate an open reading frame: on M. genitalium the bacterial default produces 995 predicted genes against 527 under the correct code 4, and nothing in the output signals the error.
34. Because a stop codon is a consequence of the reading frame — once the frame and the 3’ end are right, both methods must agree — whereas a start codon is a prediction made from a ribosome binding site model among several in-frame candidates within the first 60 bp. Both unmatched groups turn out to be the same handful of loci seen from two sides. Nineteen of the 23 RefSeq-only genes coincide with annotated pseudogenes, which homology evidence supports but which carry a frameshift or internal stop that an ab initio model will not call; and 20 of those same 23 do overlap a Prodigal prediction, so they are boundary disagreements rather than genes the predictor failed to see at all. Correspondingly, 19 of the 26 Prodigal-only predictions overlap one of the 20 annotated pseudogene loci. Only three reference genes are absent from the prediction entirely, and the shortest of them, a 147 bp ribosomal protein gene, shows where the length sensitivity of ab initio prediction runs out.
35. A Phred score of 30 means an estimated one-in-1,000 probability that the base call is wrong, since \(Q = -10\log_{10}P\). It is stored as a single ASCII character whose code point is \(Q + 33\), so \(Q = 0\) is ! and \(Q = 40\) is I; files from Illumina pipelines before version 1.8 used an offset of 64 instead, which makes the same character mean a score 31 points higher.
36. FLAG is a bit field recording pairing, strand, mate strand, mate mapping, duplicate status and whether the alignment is secondary or supplementary. CIGAR describes how the read aligns — matches, insertions, deletions, soft clipping — and therefore determines where the alignment ends, which the read length alone does not. MAPQ is the Phred-scaled confidence that the read was placed in the right location.
37. Align with bwa mem piped into samtools view to produce BAM, sort with samtools sort, then index with samtools index. The index maps genomic coordinates to file offsets so a region query can seek directly to the right block; that mapping only exists if the records are stored in coordinate order.
38. For a real bacterial isolate, 95–99% mapped is expected and anything below about 70% calls for taxonomic classification of the unmapped reads; the properly paired figure adds the constraint that mates are in the expected orientation and separation, and a low value points at adapter or insert-size problems. All three figures here are suspicious because they are too good: 100% mapped and 99.92% properly paired are the signature of reads simulated from the same reference, as is the insert size of exactly 349 bp with zero standard deviation.
39. MAPQ 0 means the read aligns equally well in at least two places and the aligner reported one of them arbitrarily — it is a statement about the reference, not about read quality. The two observations are the same phenomenon: the ambiguous reads sit in copies of the MgPa adhesin repeat family, and a read whose true origin was one copy can be placed in the other. Filtering at MAPQ 20 discards those alignments, which is usually correct because a variant supported only by ambiguously placed reads is an artefact; the cost is that genuine variants in the repeat become invisible rather than wrong, and that difference must be stated in the methods.
40. It promises that, among the 1,108 genes on the list, about 5% are expected to be false discoveries. It promises nothing about any individual gene — a gene with an adjusted p-value just under the threshold is not “95% likely to be real” — and nothing at all about effect size or biological importance, which is why the fold change and the mean expression must be read alongside it. Recovering the knocked-down gene itself, without having been told to look for it, is a positive control on the whole pipeline rather than part of the statistical claim.
41. In a crystal structure the B-factor reports positional uncertainty or thermal motion for each atom. In an AlphaFold model the same column holds pLDDT, the per-residue confidence on a 0–100 scale, which is not a temperature factor and must not be interpreted as one.
42. In REMARK 465, not in the coordinate records. Code that parses only ATOM lines sees a continuous chain where there is a gap — 72 residues of 1TUP are modelled nowhere, all at chain termini — so distances computed across such a gap are meaningless and a sequence read from the coordinates is incomplete.
43. Take all atoms of standard residues in the protein chain and all atoms of standard residues in the DNA chains, compute the minimum inter-atomic distance from each protein residue to the DNA, and keep residues below a cut-off of about 4 Å, which is the range of hydrogen bonds and close van der Waals contacts. Exclude waters, ions and other heteroatoms from both sets: leaving ordered water molecules in the DNA set inflates the contact list with residues that touch solvent rather than nucleic acid.
44. The 0.78–1.03 Å range is a calibration: it is how much the same domain differs from itself within one crystal, so it is the noise floor against which any other RMSD must be read. The AlphaFold figure of 0.73 Å over 194 Cα establishes that the prediction of that domain is as close to the experiment as the experimental copies are to each other, which is as good as the comparison can resolve. It does not establish that the rest of the model is accurate, nor anything about the domain’s orientation relative to the other parts of the protein.
45. pLDDT measures local confidence — whether the backbone around each residue is placed correctly — and predicted aligned error measures confidence in the relative position of one part of the model with respect to another. Two confident domains with high error between them support statements about each domain’s internal geometry, such as the shape of a binding pocket, and support no statement about their arrangement, so inter-domain distances, overall shape and any docking that spans the two are unsupported.
46. The difference reflects the disordered regions tethering the two confident domains: 16.6 Å is what a compact 150–200 residue domain should give, while 33.5 Å describes a pair of domains drawn in one arbitrary arrangement on flexible linkers. Quoting it as a property of the protein implies a compactness the model does not assert — the arrangement is exactly what the predicted aligned error says is not predicted — and in solution the molecule samples an ensemble rather than this one conformation.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
section: 16.5 Question bank: systems, data science and application
text:
16.5 Question bank: systems, data science and application
Chapter 11: Biological networks and pathway analysis


(recall) State what an edge in a STRING network asserts, and how that differs from an edge in a curated physical interaction database.

(recall) Define degree centrality and betweenness centrality, and state what each identifies.

(application) Given 80 genes from a differential expression analysis, describe how you would test for enrichment of a biological process, and state what the background universe must be.

(interpretation) In the bundled network TP53 has degree 29 of a possible 29 and five times the betweenness of the next gene, and degree correlates with Gene Ontology annotation count at Spearman 0.746. State the two separate reasons this hub status is not a discovery.

Chapter 12: Statistics and machine learning on omics data


(recall) State what the false discovery rate controls, and how it differs from the family-wise error rate.

(application) You will train a classifier on seven samples and 14,599 features. Describe a validation scheme that does not leak information, name the step most often performed incorrectly, and give the check that detects the leak.

(interpretation) Before normalisation the median log ratio between two untreated pasilla samples is 1.443; after conversion to counts per million it is 0.056. Explain what the first number is, and what would have happened to a differential expression analysis run on the raw counts.

(interpretation) A classifier on a test set with 2.4% positives has an ROC area of 0.858 but an average precision of 0.407 against a no-skill baseline of 0.024, with precision 0.706 and recall 0.308. State which summary is honest for this problem and what the model is actually doing.

Chapter 13: Bioinformatics in disease and healthcare


(recall) State what a variant of uncertain significance is, and why its existence is a statement about evidence rather than about the variant.

(application) A patient’s exome contains a rare missense variant in a gene plausibly related to their phenotype. Give the steps you would take to assess it, in order, before any clinical statement is made.

(interpretation) In the bundled ClinVar slice, truncating TP53 variants are classified pathogenic 81.4% of the time against 16.9% of missense variants. Name the ACMG/AMP criterion this quantifies, and explain why the missense figure is not evidence that missense variants are usually benign.

(interpretation) 94.1% of pathogenic missense variants in TP53 fall in the DNA-binding domain, against 26.1% of benign ones and 48.6% expected from its length. State what this supports, which ACMG/AMP criterion it licenses, and what it does not tell you about any single variant.

Chapter 14: Working responsibly with genomic data


(recall) State why a genotype cannot be anonymised in the way a name can be removed, and give the quantitative basis for the claim.

(recall) Name the five dimensions of the five safes framework.

(application) You are asked to publish per-variant allele counts for cases and controls in a study of a stigmatised condition. State the attack this enables, the three inputs the attacker needs, and two modifications that preserve most of the scientific value.

(interpretation) A polygenic score validated in a European-ancestry cohort is proposed for clinical use in West Africa. State the mechanism by which its accuracy degrades, and what evidence would be required before deployment.

Chapter 15: A complete project, start to finish


(recall) State what belongs in a version-controlled repository for an analysis project and what must never be committed.

(recall) Explain what a Makefile records that a numbered list of scripts does not, and what make clean && make tests.

(application) Describe the test that establishes whether a project is reproducible, in the order the commands would be run.

(interpretation) Under genetic code 11 the capstone’s first run recovered 96.6% of the 149 reference genes with no internal TGA but only 52.5% of the 375 that contain one. Explain why this single comparison identifies the fault, and name the two external checks that made the failure visible when the tool itself reported none.







Answers: Chapters 11 to 15





47. A STRING edge asserts a functional association supported by some combination of evidence channels — co-expression, co-occurrence, text mining, databases, experiments — combined into a confidence score.
