A curated physical interaction edge asserts that two proteins were observed to bind. In the bundled subnetwork every edge has text-mining support, 176 of 210 have experimental support and only 85 appear in a curated database, so treating the network as a map of physical contacts would overstate two-thirds of it.
48. Degree centrality is the number of edges at a node and identifies hubs. Betweenness centrality is the fraction of shortest paths passing through a node and identifies bottlenecks connecting otherwise separate parts of the network. A node can have high betweenness and modest degree, which is often the more interesting case.
49. Map the genes to the identifier space of the annotation source, test each term for over-representation with a hypergeometric test, and correct across terms with Benjamini–Hochberg. The background universe must be the set of genes the experiment could have detected — the genes with non-zero counts in the assay, not the whole proteome — because testing against an inflated universe credits you for the enrichment of expressed genes. The chapter’s demonstration of this is blunt: matching the universe for study intensity cut the significant-term count from 511 to 121.
50. First, the network was built by querying a database for genes associated with p53 and the cell cycle, so TP53 is adjacent to every other node by construction; the topology reproduces the selection criterion. Second, degree in a literature-derived network partly measures how much a protein has been studied, which the Spearman correlation of 0.746 with annotation count makes explicit — these genes carry a median of 54.5 Gene Ontology terms against a genome-wide median of nine.
51. The false discovery rate is the expected proportion of false positives among the tests declared significant; the family-wise error rate is the probability of making even one false positive anywhere. FDR is the appropriate choice when thousands of hypotheses are tested and a known, small proportion of false discoveries is tolerable, which is why it leaves 511 enriched terms where Bonferroni leaves 82.
52. Hold out a test set before anything else, or use nested cross-validation, with normalisation, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning performed inside each training fold only. The step most often performed incorrectly is feature selection on the whole dataset before splitting. The check is label permutation: with labels randomly shuffled there is nothing to learn, so a leaky pipeline that reports a mean accuracy of 1.000 in 100 of 100 permutations has been caught, while an honest one reports a value scattered around or below the majority-class baseline — 0.384 against a baseline of 0.571 in the chapter’s demonstration.
53. It is the log ratio of the two libraries’ sizes showing up as an apparent expression difference: most genes do not change between two control samples, so the median log ratio measures sequencing depth rather than biology. Run on raw counts, a differential expression analysis would have called a large, systematic and entirely artefactual set of changes in the direction of the deeper library, and the effect would have been reproducible, which is what makes it dangerous.
54. The precision–recall summary is the honest one. With 2.4% positives the ROC area is flattered because the false positive rate is diluted by a large number of true negatives, so 0.858 sounds respectable while the model misses nearly 70% of the positives. What it is actually doing is being right when it commits — precision 0.706 — at the cost of committing rarely; whether that is useful depends entirely on the relative cost of a missed positive and a false alarm.
55. It is a variant for which the available evidence is insufficient to classify as pathogenic or benign. The classification describes the state of knowledge rather than a property of the variant, which is why reclassification is routine, why laboratories re-evaluate stored results, and why about a quarter of the TP53 records in ClinVar carry this label despite TP53 being among the most intensively studied genes in medicine.
56. Confirm the call itself — depth, allele balance, mapping quality, and whether it lies in a region short reads resolve badly. Fix the transcript and the genome build, and express the variant in standard nomenclature against them. Check population frequency in a reference matched as closely as possible to the patient’s ancestry, since a severe early-onset condition cannot be caused by a variant carried by 1% of people. Assemble consequence predictions, domain context and any functional data; consult ClinVar with attention to review status rather than label, and the literature. Then apply the ACMG/AMP criteria and consider segregation in the family. No clinical statement is made before confirmation in an accredited laboratory.
57. It quantifies PVS1, the criterion that assigns very strong evidence of pathogenicity to a null variant in a gene where loss of function is a known disease mechanism. The missense figure is not evidence that missense variants are usually benign: it is an average over a class that mixes the hotspot substitutions in the DNA-binding domain, which are almost all pathogenic, with substitutions elsewhere in the protein, which mostly are not. An average over a heterogeneous class tells you about the class, not about a variant in it.
58. It supports the claim that pathogenic missense variants in this gene concentrate in a specific structural region far beyond what its length would predict, which is the population-level evidence behind PM1 — a variant in a mutational hotspot or a critical functional domain. It does not tell you that a particular variant inside the domain is pathogenic; location is one moderate piece of evidence among several, and 26.1% of benign variants also fall inside the same domain.
59. Because the genotype is itself the identifier, so there is no field to remove. The chapter’s simulation makes the claim quantitative: every one of 10,000 simulated individuals is unique at 25 independent common markers, and the random match probability falls below one in eight billion at 30 markers. The governing concept is therefore controlled access rather than anonymisation.
60. Safe projects, safe people, safe settings, safe data and safe outputs.
61. It enables an allele-frequency membership attack. The attacker needs the published case-group frequencies, allele frequencies for a matched reference population, and the genotypes of the individual being tested; because the case group is defined by the condition, confirming membership discloses the diagnosis. Defensible modifications: publish only the variants that reach the paper’s significance threshold rather than the genome-wide table, which removes most of the accumulating evidence; or place the full summary table behind the same controlled access as the individual data and cite the accession in the paper.
62. The score’s weights were estimated for markers that tag unobserved causal variants through the linkage disequilibrium structure of the discovery population. Where that structure differs, the tags no longer track the causal variants and accuracy declines with genetic distance, so the score misclassifies risk differentially by ancestry. Deployment requires validation in a sufficiently powered cohort from the target population, reporting both discrimination and calibration, with weights re-estimated or at least re-calibrated locally.
63. Commit code, configuration, the environment specification, the workflow definition and documentation — everything a stranger needs to regenerate the results. Never commit derived results and figures, large raw inputs that are already archived under an accession, credentials, or any data under controlled access; a Git history preserves deleted files in earlier commits, so git rm does not undo the disclosure.
64. It records dependencies rather than order: which inputs and which scripts each output depends on, from which the tool computes what is stale. Listing the script itself as a prerequisite means editing the analysis invalidates its outputs, which is the dependency most often forgotten. make clean && make tests whether every result in the project can in fact be regenerated from the raw data by the code in the repository.
65. Clone the repository into an empty directory; create the environment from the pinned specification; verify the raw data against the checksums recorded in the manifest; run make clean && make; then compare the regenerated numbers and figures against those in the manuscript. A failure at any step means the project is not finished.
66. Because the comparison splits the reference genes by the one property the wrong parameter affects. Genetic code 11 reads TGA as a stop, so genes containing an internal TGA are fragmented and their true 3’ ends lost, while genes without one are unaffected — and the recovery rates, 96.6% against 52.5%, follow that split almost perfectly, which no general deficiency of the predictor would produce. The two external checks were the independent RefSeq annotation, which showed 995 predictions against 524 genes, and the coding sequence length distribution with the coding density, which showed fragmentation rather than over-prediction: a median of 336 bp against 856 bp and a density falling from 94.6% to 77.1%.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.6 Self-assessment rubric
Scores on a question bank measure recall. What an employer, supervisor or collaborator needs to know is different: what you can be left alone with. The four levels below describe competence in terms of what you can do unsupervised, and they are cumulative — each level assumes the one before it. Assess yourself honestly against the highest level at which you could complete every item without help, and treat the first item you fail as your next piece of work.
Level 1: Supervised
You can run an analysis that someone else has specified. Concretely: you can navigate a filesystem from the command line and inspect large text files without opening them in an editor; you can recognise FASTA, FASTQ, SAM/BAM, VCF and GFF3 records and say what each field means; you can run a provided script or notebook to completion and tell whether it finished successfully; you can describe what a BLAST result or an alignment shows; and you can locate a record in GenBank, UniProt or the PDB and record its accession and version. What you cannot yet do is decide which analysis to run, or detect that a result is wrong.
Level 2: Competent
You can carry out a standard analysis on new data and notice when it has gone wrong. You can write a script of fifty to two hundred lines in Python or R that reads a biological file, computes something and writes a result; you can parameterise it rather than editing constants; you can run a short-read pipeline end to end and interpret its quality-control output; you can perform a differential expression or enrichment analysis with an established package and explain why its normalisation step exists; you can use Git to record your work and reconstruct a previous state; and you can read a tool’s documentation to find the option you need rather than copying a command from a forum. Crucially, you check results against an external expectation — a count you can predict, a positive control, a known answer — rather than trusting a clean exit code.
Level 3: Proficient
You can design an analysis for a question that nobody has specified for you, and defend the design. You can choose between methods on the basis of their assumptions rather than their popularity, and state the assumption that would invalidate each; you can diagnose a silent failure by constructing a comparison that would reveal it; you can structure a project so that make clean && make regenerates every result, with a pinned environment and a workflow definition; you can quantify uncertainty appropriately, including recognising when no legitimate confidence interval is available; you can write a methods section another group could follow and a limitations paragraph that names the specific scope of the claim; and you can judge whether a dataset’s consent and governance permit the analysis you intend. You are the person a laboratory asks when a result looks surprising.
Level 4: Independent
You can take responsibility for the computational component of a programme of work. You can decide what data to generate in the first place, trading cost against the power of the analysis it will support; you can build a pipeline that others run on data you will never see, with the validation and documentation that implies; you can review someone else’s computational work and identify the artefact they have not considered; you can supervise and teach the levels below, which requires being able to explain why a method works and not only how to run it; and you can be accountable for the ethical and legal framing of a project, including data governance, benefit sharing and the decision about what may be published. Most readers of this book will reach level 3 with practice; level 4 is a matter of years and of other people’s data depending on your judgement.






Assess by artefact, not by feeling



Levels are easier to judge from products than from confidence. Level 2 is demonstrated by a script someone else ran successfully; level 3 by a repository a stranger reproduced; level 4 by a pipeline other groups use and a review you wrote that changed someone’s analysis. If you cannot point at the artefact, you are probably one level lower than you think — which is normal, and is information rather than a verdict.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.7 Learning pathways
Readers arrive at this book from three directions and should leave it in three different ones. The routes below name what to read again, what to build, and what to learn next; each assumes the book’s software environment and bundled data still work, which the check below confirms.

import hashlib
import pandas as pd
from pybfx import book_root

manifest = pd.read_csv(book_root() / "data" / "MANIFEST.tsv", sep="\t")
mismatched = []
for row in manifest.itertuples():
    path = book_root() / "data" / row.path
    digest = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest() if path.exists() else "missing"
    if digest != row.sha256:
        mismatched.append(row.path)

print(f"{len(manifest)} bundled files listed; "
      f"{len(manifest) - len(mismatched)} verified against their recorded checksum")
#> 21 bundled files listed; 21 verified against their recorded checksum
print("mismatched or missing:", mismatched if mismatched else "none")
#> mismatched or missing: none

A clean result means every example in the book will reproduce on this machine. A mismatch means a file has been edited or re-downloaded, and any result derived from it is suspect — which is the same check that appears as item eight of the capstone’s self-review.
The wet-lab biologist moving to data
Your advantage is that you know what the measurements mean and where they came from; your gap is engineering. Reread the command-line chapter until the shell is uncomfortable rather than frightening, then the Python chapter, and accept that two or three weeks of deliberate practice on small scripting problems is the price of everything that follows. Build this, in order: a script that computes summary statistics over a directory of your own laboratory’s FASTA or FASTQ files; a reanalysis of a published dataset in your own field from the raw data in a public archive, where you already know what the answer should be; and a version-controlled repository for one of your own projects, with a pinned environment and a Makefile, following the capstone.
Learn next, in this order: a workflow manager, since your analyses will be rerun more often than you expect (Köster and Rahmann 2012); the statistics of your own assay in depth, which for most wet-lab readers means count-based models and multiple testing rather than general machine learning (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014); and the Bioconductor object model, because it encodes the data-integrity discipline your experiments need (Huber et al. 2015). Read Wilson et al. (2017) twice a year. The habit that will distinguish you is the one you already have from the bench — recording exactly what was done — applied now to code rather than to a notebook.
The programmer moving to biology
Your advantage is that the tooling holds no mystery; your gaps are domain semantics and an unfamiliar standard of evidence. Reread Chapters 2, 3 and 4 slowly, and resist the instinct to treat biological file formats as merely badly designed: the awkwardness usually encodes a biological fact, as one-based inclusive coordinates and six reading frames do. Your characteristic failure mode is a technically excellent analysis of the wrong quantity — normalising counts in a way that destroys the comparison, or building a classifier that predicts library protocol. Build this: a reimplementation of pairwise alignment from the recurrence, which teaches what the scoring parameters mean; an annotation comparison like the capstone’s, which teaches what an annotation is; and a reproduction of a published figure from the authors’ deposited data, which teaches the field’s standard of evidence.
Learn next: the statistics of high-dimensional biology, particularly false discovery rate control and the validation design the data science chapter insists on (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995); enough molecular biology to interrogate a result, for which an undergraduate genetics text is a better investment than another library; and the ecosystem conventions — Bioconductor, Biopython, Bioconda — so that you build on the field’s infrastructure rather than beside it (Cock et al. 2009). The most valuable thing you can offer is software engineering discipline applied to analyses that biologists trust; the fastest way to waste it is to solve a problem the field does not have.
The clinician
Your advantage is that you know what the result has to support and what an uncertain answer costs a patient; your gaps are the pipeline that produced the variant and the statistics that qualify it. Reread the clinical chapter first, then the sequencing chapter, so that you can see which pipeline decisions a clinical call rests on — depth, mapping quality, and the repeat regions where short reads cannot resolve the sequence at all. Then reread the chapter on responsible practice, because those obligations will be yours in a way they are not for a laboratory scientist. Build this: a reanalysis of the bundled TP53 ClinVar records, grouping by review status rather than by label, until the difference between an expert-panel assertion and a single-submitter one is intuitive; and an application of the ACMG/AMP criteria to a handful of variants with the evidence written out criterion by criterion (Richards et al. 2015).
Learn next: population allele frequency resources and their ancestry composition, since frequency is the evidence that most often decides a classification and its power is unequal across populations (Karczewski et al. 2020); pharmacogenomic guidelines in the areas you prescribe in, where the evidence is already actionable (Relling and Evans 2015); and enough command-line and scripting competence to interrogate a VCF yourself rather than relying on a report. You do not need to become a bioinformatician. You do need to be able to ask the laboratory a question it cannot deflect, and to recognise a result that has outrun its evidence.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.8 Summary

The book’s through-line is representation: every method is a decision about how to turn a biological object into data, and every interpretation is a judgement about what that representation lost.
The chapters are sequentially dependent. Alignment needs molecular biology, pipelines need the shell, statistics needs the data structures, and the capstone needs all of them; a gap in an early chapter surfaces as confusion in a later one.
The expensive errors are silent ones. A wrong translation table, a recycled vector, a leaky cross-validation and an unnormalised count matrix all produce plausible output and no warning, and all are caught the same way — by an independent check.
Recall, application and interpretation are separable competences. Most readers are strongest at recall and weakest at interpretation, which is the one that practice actually rewards.
Interpretation questions almost always resolve to the same move: ask what else could produce this result, and what evidence would distinguish the alternatives.
Competence is best assessed by artefacts — a script someone else ran, a repository a stranger reproduced, a pipeline others depend on — rather than by self-report.
The three reader types need different next steps: engineering practice for the wet-lab biologist, domain semantics and evidential standards for the programmer, and pipeline literacy with statistical qualification for the clinician.
Whatever route you take, the habits of the last two chapters — pinned environments, recorded provenance, declared limitations and governance settled before the analysis — are what make the technical skills usable by anyone other than yourself.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.9 Exercises
The first three problems are integrative: each requires methods from several chapters and cannot be solved from one. The remainder are shorter.


From transcript to protein, across three resources. Using the bundled TP53 GenBank record and the bundled UniProt FASTA, extract the annotated coding sequence, translate it, and test whether the product is identical to the UniProt canonical sequence. Then state what a mismatch would have implied, listing the three most likely causes in order of probability. (Chapters 2, 3 and 6.)

What ClinVar actually contains. Using the bundled TP53 ClinVar records, tabulate clinical significance and review status, compute the proportion of records that are uncertain or conflicting, and determine how that proportion changes when restricted to records reviewed by an expert panel. Interpret the result as advice to a clinician who has been handed a variant report. (Chapters 9, 12 and 13.)

From structure to clinical significance. Using the bundled p53 core domain–DNA complex, identify the protein residues within 4 Å of the DNA in each protein chain, and compare that set with the commonly cited mutational hotspot codons 175, 245, 248, 249, 273 and 282. Explain what the overlap and the non-overlap each imply about how a missense substitution can destroy a transcription factor’s function. (Chapters 10, 11 and 13.)
For each of Chapters 4, 9 and 12, name the single assumption whose violation would most damage the chapter’s central method, and the diagnostic that detects the violation.
A collaborator sends you a results table and a figure but no code. List, in order, the four things you would request, and say what each one makes checkable.
Place yourself on the rubric in Section 16.6 and name the first item at the next level that you cannot currently do. Write the two-week plan that would let you do it, specifying the artefact you would produce.
Choose any question in the bank that you answered incorrectly. Write a short explanation of why your answer was wrong that would prevent you making the same error again — specifically, name the step in your reasoning that failed rather than the fact you did not know.
A reviewer writes: “the authors’ pipeline is standard and the result is plausible, but I cannot determine whether it is correct.” Using the capstone’s self-check, write the response that would answer the reviewer, naming what you would add to the manuscript and the repository.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.10 Solutions






Solutions





1. The translated coding sequence matches the UniProt canonical sequence exactly at 393 residues, which is the check that confirms the transcript, the annotation of its CDS feature and the protein record all refer to the same isoform.

from Bio import SeqIO

transcript = SeqIO.read(book_data("sequences", "TP53-NM_000546.6.gb"), "genbank")
coding_feature = next(f for f in transcript.features if f.type == "CDS")
translated = coding_feature.extract(transcript.seq).translate(to_stop=True)
canonical = SeqIO.read(book_data("proteins", "P04637.fasta"), "fasta").seq

print(f"translated {len(translated)} aa, UniProt canonical {len(canonical)} aa, "
      f"identical: {translated == canonical}")
#> translated 393 aa, UniProt canonical 393 aa, identical: True

Had they differed, the likeliest causes in order are: the transcript is a different isoform from the canonical protein, which is the usual explanation for a length difference; the coding sequence was extracted without respecting the feature’s strand or its joined location, which is the error the GenBank chapter warns about; or the records come from different releases. A difference at a single residue would instead suggest a reference allele difference, such as the common codon 72 polymorphism.
2. Uncertain and conflicting records together make up a large share of all TP53 records, and the share falls sharply among the 191 expert-panel-reviewed ones. The advice to a clinician is that the review status field, not the significance label, determines how much weight an assertion carries.

import re
import pandas as pd

records = []
with open(book_data("variants", "tp53_clinvar.vcf")) as handle:
    for line in handle:
        if line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        info = line.split("\t")[7]
        significance = re.search(r"CLNSIG=([^;]+)", info)
        review = re.search(r"CLNREVSTAT=([^;]+)", info)
        records.append({"significance": significance.group(1) if significance else "not_provided",
                        "review": review.group(1) if review else "not_provided"})

clinvar = pd.DataFrame(records)
unclear = clinvar["significance"].str.contains("Uncertain|Conflicting")
print(f"{len(clinvar):,} records; {100 * unclear.mean():.1f}% uncertain or conflicting")
#> 3,888 records; 38.3% uncertain or conflicting
expert = clinvar["review"] == "reviewed_by_expert_panel"
print(f"expert-panel reviewed: {expert.sum()} records, "
      f"{100 * unclear[expert].mean():.1f}% uncertain or conflicting")
#> expert-panel reviewed: 191 records, 18.3% uncertain or conflicting

3. Only chain B is bound in the major groove, with twelve residues within 4 Å of the DNA; chains A and C make four peripheral contacts each and are crystallographic neighbours. Of the six hotspot codons, only 248 and 273 are in the contact set. That split is the answer to the question: a hotspot substitution can abolish function either by removing a direct DNA contact, as at Arg248 and Arg273, or by destabilising the fold or the zinc site that holds the DNA-binding surface in shape, as at 175, 245, 249 and 282 — which is why the zinc-coordinating residues are inactivating despite touching no DNA at all.

import numpy as np
from Bio.PDB import PDBParser

structure = PDBParser(QUIET=True).get_structure("1tup", book_data("structures", "1tup.pdb"))
model = structure[0]
# Standard residues only: ordered waters in the DNA chains would inflate every contact set.
dna_atoms = np.array([atom.coord for chain in "EF" for residue in model[chain]
                      if residue.id[0] == " " for atom in residue])

contacts = {}
for chain_id in "ABC":
    atoms = [atom for residue in model[chain_id] if residue.id[0] == " "
             for atom in residue]
    coords = np.array([atom.coord for atom in atoms])
    separations = np.linalg.norm(coords[:, None, :] - dna_atoms[None, :, :], axis=2)
    contacts[chain_id] = sorted({atoms[i].get_parent().id[1]
                                 for i in np.where(separations.min(axis=1) < 4.0)[0]})
    print(f"chain {chain_id}: {len(contacts[chain_id])} residues within 4 A of DNA")
#> chain A: 4 residues within 4 A of DNA
#> chain B: 12 residues within 4 A of DNA
#> chain C: 4 residues within 4 A of DNA

hotspots = [175, 245, 248, 249, 273, 282]
contacting = sorted(set().union(*contacts.values()))
print("hotspot codons contacting DNA:    ", [h for h in hotspots if h in contacting])
#> hotspot codons contacting DNA:     [248, 273]
print("hotspot codons not contacting DNA:", [h for h in hotspots if h not in contacting])
#> hotspot codons not contacting DNA: [175, 245, 249, 282]

4. Chapter 4: that similarity implies homology, violated when an alignment is short or compositionally biased; the diagnostic is the E-value read together with the aligned length, since the chapter’s shuffled decoys reached 87.5% identity over short stretches. Chapter 9: that a read originates from the locus it aligns to, violated by repeats and paralogues; the diagnostics are MAPQ, coverage uniformity and, where ground truth exists, the read’s own simulated origin. Chapter 12: that the validation data had no influence on model fitting, violated by feature selection or normalisation performed before splitting; the diagnostic is label permutation, which must drive performance to chance.
5. The analysis code, which makes the computation checkable; the environment specification with versions, which makes the numbers reproducible; the raw inputs or their accessions and checksums, which makes the provenance checkable; and the parameters used at every step including defaults, which makes the decisions checkable. A fifth, worth adding if the table is a summary, is the intermediate file it was generated from.
6. No model answer. A good plan names one artefact — a repository, a script someone else runs, a reproduced published figure — with a date, rather than a quantity of reading.
7. No model answer. The instruction to name the failed reasoning step rather than the missing fact is the point: “I compared percentage identity instead of the E-value” is actionable, whereas “I did not know about E-values” is not.
8. Add to the manuscript: software versions and all parameters including defaults; an explicit statement of the metric and what it does and does not measure; a limitations paragraph naming the scope of the claim; and a data and code availability statement giving the archive accession and an archived repository version. Add to the repository: the workflow definition, the pinned environment, the input checksums, and a demonstration that a clean clone regenerates the manuscript numbers. The reviewer’s complaint is not about the method but about the absence of anything to check, and every item above converts an assertion into something checkable.

title: 16  Consolidation and review
text:
16.11 Further reading


Huber et al. (2015) describes the Bioconductor project’s design and the object model behind SummarizedExperiment; it is the best single explanation of why the ecosystem is organised as it is.

Wickham et al. (2019) sets out the tidyverse’s design principles, which explains why its data manipulation and plotting verbs compose the way they do.

Cock et al. (2009) is the Biopython reference and the natural companion to further Python work on sequence and structure data.

Pedregosa et al. (2011) documents scikit-learn, whose cross-validation and pipeline objects are the practical answer to the information-leakage problem in the data science chapter.

Wilson et al. (2017) is the practical statement of project organisation that the capstone follows; it is short enough to reread whenever a project begins.

Sandve et al. (2013) gives ten rules for reproducible computational research and works well as a final checklist before submission.

Richards et al. (2015) is the ACMG/AMP variant classification standard, and is the document a clinical reader will return to most often.

Szklarczyk et al. (2022) documents STRING, including the evidence channels whose separation the network chapter depends on.







Benjamini, Yoav, and Yosef Hochberg. 1995. “Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology 57 (1): 289–300. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x.


Cock, Peter J. A., Tiago Antao, Jeffrey T. Chang, Brad A. Chapman, Cymon J. Cox, Andrew Dalke, Iddo Friedberg, et al. 2009. “Biopython: Freely Available Python Tools for Computational Molecular Biology and Bioinformatics.” Bioinformatics 25 (11): 1422–23. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp163.


Huber, Wolfgang, Vincent J Carey, Robert Gentleman, Simon Anders, Marc Carlson, Benilton S Carvalho, Hector Corrada Bravo, et al. 2015. “Orchestrating High-Throughput Genomic Analysis with Bioconductor.” Nature Methods 12 (2): 115–21. https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.3252.


Karczewski, Konrad J., Laurent C. Francioli, Grace Tiao, Beryl B. Cummings, Jessica Alföldi, Qingbo Wang, Ryan L. Collins, et al. 2020. “The Mutational Constraint Spectrum Quantified from Variation in 141,456 Humans.” Nature 581 (7809): 434–43. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7.


Köster, Johannes, and Sven Rahmann. 2012. “Snakemake—a Scalable Bioinformatics Workflow Engine.” Bioinformatics 28 (19): 2520–22. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bts480.


Love, Michael I, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders. 2014. “Moderated Estimation of Fold Change and Dispersion for RNA-Seq Data with DESeq2,” February. https://doi.org/10.1101/002832.


Pedregosa, Fabian, Gaël Varoquaux, Alexandre Gramfort, Vincent Michel, Bertrand Thirion, Olivier Grisel, Mathieu Blondel, et al. 2011. “Scikit-learn: Machine Learning in Python.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 12: 2825–30.


Relling, Mary V., and William E. Evans. 2015. “Pharmacogenomics in the Clinic.” Nature 526 (7573): 343–50. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature15817.


Richards, Sue, Nazneen Aziz, Sherri Bale, David Bick, Soma Das, Julie Gastier-Foster, Wayne W. Grody, et al. 2015. “Standards and Guidelines for the Interpretation of Sequence Variants: A Joint Consensus Recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology.” Genetics in Medicine 17 (5): 405–24. https://doi.org/10.1038/gim.2015.30.


Sandve, Geir Kjetil, Anton Nekrutenko, James Taylor, and Eivind Hovig. 2013. “Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research.” Edited by Philip E. Bourne. PLoS Computational Biology 9 (10): e1003285. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285.


Szklarczyk, Damian, Rebecca Kirsch, Mikaela Koutrouli, Katerina Nastou, Farrokh Mehryary, Radja Hachilif, Annika L Gable, et al. 2022. “The STRING Database in 2023: Protein–Protein Association Networks and Functional Enrichment Analyses for Any Sequenced Genome of Interest.” Nucleic Acids Research 51 (D1): D638–46. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkac1000.
